lectures.title: Lecture 16 - Chemistry of Amino Acids, Carbohydrates and Lipids
Microbial Cultures, Culture Media and Growth
Lecture 44 - Introduction to Antimicrobial Drugs I
Lecture 45 - Introduction to Antimicrobial Drugs II
Lecture 47 - Principles of Antimicrobial Drug Therapy

questions.q: What is the essential difference between a drug and a medicine?
options: A medicine has a marketing authorisation whereas a drug does not
A medicine is the drug combined with excipients in a dosage form suitable for administration
A medicine is administered orally whereas a drug is injected
A medicine is derived from a natural source whereas a drug is synthetic
A medicine contains a higher dose of active ingredient than a drug
questions.explanation: The lecture defines the relationship as drug (API) + excipients = medicine, i.e. the medicinal or dosage form. The drug is the active substance; the medicine is the formulated product given to the patient.
questions.title: What Are Medicines?

questions.q: Why is it necessary to formulate a drug into a dosage form at all, rather than giving the pure drug?
options: Pure drug substances are always chemically unstable
Regulations forbid the supply of an unformulated active substance
Doses are typically milligram or microgram quantities of powder that must be bulked up with excipients
Excipients are needed to increase the potency of the drug
Pure drugs cannot be absorbed across biological membranes
questions.explanation: The drug is often a powder given in mg or mcg quantities, which is impractical to handle or measure. Excipients such as water or lactose bulk the dose up into a usable form.
questions.title: What Are Medicines?

questions.q: Starch is included in a tablet formulation. What is its usual role?
options: Diluent
Binder
Glidant
Disintegrant
Coating
questions.explanation: Starch is given as the example of a disintegrant (disintegrating agent), which promotes break-up of the tablet after administration.
questions.title: What Are Medicines?

questions.q: Lactose is a common tablet excipient. Which category does it belong to?
options: Diluent or filler
Disintegrant
Anti-adherent
Flocculating agent
Tonicity adjuster
questions.explanation: Lactose is listed as an example of a diluent or filler, used to bulk out the small quantity of active drug in a tablet.
questions.title: What Are Medicines?

questions.q: Which excipient forms the base of a paracetamol suppository?
options: Sucrose solution
Dispersible cellulose
Hard fat such as Witepsol H12
Water for Injections
Gelatin shell
questions.explanation: Suppositories are formulated as drug plus a base, with hard fat (Witepsol H12) given as the example.
questions.title: What Are Medicines?

questions.q: Mannitol is added to a paracetamol solution for infusion. What is it there to do?
options: Adjust the pH of the solution
Adjust the tonicity of the solution
Act as a preservative
Increase the viscosity of the solution
Improve the taste of the product
questions.explanation: In the infusion formulation, mannitol is the tonicity adjuster; hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide are the pH adjusters and Water for Injections is the diluent.
questions.title: What Are Medicines?

questions.q: Glycerol is included in an oral suspension. Which excipient function does it serve?
options: Flocculating agent
Viscosity enhancer
Dispersion medium
Wetting agent
Sweetener
questions.explanation: In the suspension formulation glycerol is the wetting agent; water is the dispersion medium, dispersible cellulose the viscosity enhancer and electrolytes or surfactants the flocculating agents.
questions.title: What Are Medicines?

questions.q: What is the typical particle size range of the drug in a pharmaceutical suspension?
options: 1 - 5 microns
10 - 50 microns
1 - 5 mm
questions.explanation: The lecture quotes a drug particle size of 10-50 microns for suspensions; these particles are insoluble in the vehicle, which is why the product is opaque.
questions.title: What Are Medicines?

questions.q: Why must an oral suspension be shaken before use?
options: To dissolve the drug fully before it is measured
To redistribute the particles so the dose measured is uniform and correct
To remove dissolved air that would otherwise cause foaming
To activate the flocculating agent
To reduce the particle size of the drug
questions.explanation: Shaking ensures uniformity of the product so that the proper dose is administered; the drug remains suspended rather than dissolved.
questions.title: What Are Medicines?

questions.q: A drug is presented as a clear, transparent oral solution rather than a suspension. What is the main consequence for absorption?
options: Absorption is delayed because the drug must first precipitate
The drug is available for immediate absorption as no disintegration or dissolution is needed
Absorption is unaffected because both forms behave identically in the gut
The drug is protected from gastric acid and absorbed only in the colon
A larger dose is required because solutions are less bioavailable
questions.explanation: In a solution the drug is already present as molecules, so it needs no disintegration or dissolution step and is available for immediate absorption.
questions.title: What Are Medicines?

questions.q: How does an elixir differ from a syrup?
options: An elixir is a suspension whereas a syrup is a solution
An elixir is sugar-free whereas a syrup contains sucrose
An elixir contains both water and alcohol in a sweetened vehicle, a syrup is a sucrose solution
An elixir is for external use only
An elixir contains no drug, only flavouring
questions.explanation: Elixirs are drug dissolved in a sweetened vehicle containing both water and alcohol; syrups are drug dissolved in a sucrose solution. Both are oral solutions.
questions.title: What Are Medicines?

questions.q: In smoking cessation therapy, by which route is nicotine absorbed from nicotine chewing gum?
options: Oral
Rectal
Pulmonary
Parenteral
Oromucosal
questions.explanation: Nicotine gum delivers drug across the oral mucosa (oromucosal). The oral route proper means the medicine is swallowed, which is not what happens with gum.
questions.title: What Are Medicines?

questions.q: Glyceryl trinitrate is given as a tablet or aerosol spray placed beneath the tongue. What is this route called?
options: Buccal
Sublingual
Oral
Transdermal
Nasal
questions.explanation: Sublingual means beneath the tongue, and glyceryl trinitrate sublingual tablets and sprays are the example given. Buccal delivery is between the gum and cheek.
questions.title: What Are Medicines?

questions.q: A mucoadhesive testosterone tablet is placed between the gum and the cheek. Which route is being used?
options: Sublingual
Oromucosal chewing gum route
Buccal
Oral
Topical
questions.explanation: Placement between the gum and cheek defines the buccal route; mucoadhesive testosterone tablets are the example used in the lecture.
questions.title: What Are Medicines?

questions.q: The word parenteral derives from para and enteron. What do these mean?
options: Beside the intestine
Through the skin
Against the stomach
Within the vein
Under the tongue
questions.explanation: Para means beside and enteron means intestine, i.e. delivery that bypasses the gut. Parenteral routes include intravenous, intramuscular, subcutaneous and intradermal.
questions.title: What Are Medicines?

questions.q: Which of these is a recognised parenteral route of administration?
options: Rectal
Intradermal
Buccal
Pulmonary
Aural
questions.explanation: The parenteral routes listed are intravenous, intramuscular, subcutaneous and intradermal. The others deliver drug across a mucosal or epithelial surface rather than by injection.
questions.title: What Are Medicines?

questions.q: Which of the following is given as a disadvantage of the oral route?
options: It requires trained staff to administer
It is invasive and carries an infection risk
Drug response is slow and absorption may be irregular
It cannot be used for systemic effects
It requires the product to be sterile
questions.explanation: The oral route is convenient, safe and uncomplicated, but the drug response is slow, absorption can be irregular (for example with food) and the drug may be destroyed by acid or gastrointestinal enzymes.
questions.title: What Are Medicines?

questions.q: Tablets are described as solid dosage forms prepared by which process?
options: Compression
Lyophilisation
Encapsulation in a gelatin shell
Fusion moulding
Spray drying
questions.explanation: Tablets are solid dosage forms prepared by compression. Enclosing drug plus excipients in a hard or soft gelatin shell describes a capsule instead.
questions.title: What Are Medicines?

questions.q: Creams, ointments and gels are grouped together as which physical type of dosage form?
options: Liquid
Solid
Semi-solid
Aerosol
Patch
questions.explanation: Dosage forms are grouped as liquid (solutions, suspensions, emulsions), semi-solid (creams, ointments, gels), solid (tablets, capsules, granules, suppositories, pessaries) and other (patches).
questions.title: What Are Medicines?

questions.q: Which devices are used to deliver drugs by the pulmonary route?
options: Enemas and cleansing solutions
Pressurised metered dose inhalers, dry powder inhalers and nebulisers
Pessaries, foams and vaginal rings
Ophthalmic solutions and ointments
Sterile implants and depot injections
questions.explanation: Pulmonary delivery uses pressurised metered dose inhalers (PMDI), dry powder inhalers (DPI), soft mist inhalers and nebulisers.
questions.title: What Are Medicines?

questions.q: A sterile implant is given subcutaneously or intramuscularly. Over what period is it designed to release drug?
options: Minutes to hours
A few hours
One to two days
Weeks to months
Several years
questions.explanation: Sterile implants given subcutaneously or intramuscularly are described as releasing drug over weeks to months, in contrast to sterile solutions, suspensions and emulsions.
questions.title: What Are Medicines?

questions.q: Vaginal and uterine preparations such as pessaries, rings and intrauterine systems are used mainly for what purpose?
options: A local effect
Rapid systemic absorption
Avoiding first-pass metabolism of oral drugs
Delivering sterile parenteral products
Producing a pulmonary effect
questions.explanation: The lecture states that vaginal and uterine delivery, including tablets, foams, gels, pessaries, rings, the IUD and IUS, is mainly for a local effect.
questions.title: What Are Medicines?

questions.q: According to lecture etiquette, students may:
options: Record the lecture on their phone
Never ask questions after the lecture
Distribute recordings publicly without permission
Skip all independent study
Ignore dosage form differences
questions.explanation: The etiquette slide states the lecturer will record the lecture and students may also record it on their phone, with questions welcomed by raising a hand or emailing after the lecture.
questions.title: What Are Medicines?

questions.q: Which drug is listed among Year 1 case examples?
options: Paracetamol
Insulin glargine only
Warfarin only
Digoxin only
Amphotericin B only
questions.explanation: Examples of drugs from Year 1 cases include aspirin, lansoprazole, morphine, chlorphenamine, codeine, ranitidine, senna, paracetamol, hydrocortisone, naproxen, ibuprofen and others.
questions.title: What Are Medicines?

questions.q: Which is listed as a route of administration?
options: Buccal
Intravenous only as a dosage form
Tablet swallowing as a separate category from oral
Manufacturing route
Distribution centre route
questions.explanation: Routes of administration listed include parenteral, oral, buccal, sublingual, oromucosal, rectal, topical, transdermal, pulmonary, nasal, vaginal, ocular and aural.
questions.title: What Are Medicines?

questions.q: For the oral route, which dosage forms are listed?
options: Solutions, suspensions, emulsions, tablets, capsules and granules
Only injections
Only patches
Only ophthalmic ointments
Only pessaries
questions.explanation: For any one route, oral administration includes solutions, suspensions, emulsions, tablets, capsules and granules, while parenteral includes injections and topical routes use gels, ointments and creams.
questions.title: What Are Medicines?

questions.q: Which paracetamol formulations are listed in the lecture?
options: Oral tablets, suspensions, suppositories and solution for infusion
Only inhalers
Only transdermal patches
Only vaginal rings
Only ear drops
questions.explanation: Paracetamol is available in many forms including oral tablets, effervescent and orodispersible tablets, capsules, paediatric suspensions, suppositories of various strengths, and solution for infusion.
questions.title: What Are Medicines?

questions.q: Nicotine replacement products for oral mucosa include:
options: Chewing gum, inhalators, lozenges and mouth spray
Only IV injections
Only rectal suppositories
Only ocular drops
Only sterile implants
questions.explanation: Nicotine replacement via oral mucosa includes chewing gum, inhalators, tablets, oral strips, lozenges and mouth spray, with nicotine having MW 162.2 g/mol and log P 1.2.
questions.title: What Are Medicines?

questions.q: Rectal suppositories may be used for:
options: Local effects (e.g. constipation) or systemic effects (e.g. paracetamol in children)
Only pulmonary delivery
Only ophthalmic sterilisation
Only IV replacement
Only diagnostic imaging
questions.explanation: The rectal route is non-invasive. Suppositories may give local effects such as treating constipation or soothing inflammation, or systemic effects such as paracetamol in children.
questions.title: What Are Medicines?

questions.q: Ointments, creams and lotions are described as:
options: Semisolid preparations with drug in a suitable base
Sterile injections
Dry powder inhalers
Oral solutions only
Intravenous emulsions only
questions.explanation: Skin preparations include semisolid ointments, creams and lotions with drug in a suitable base; choice of base depends on staying qualities, texture and desired drug release.
questions.title: What Are Medicines?

questions.q: Ophthalmic preparations must be:
options: Sterile aqueous solutions, suspensions or hydrophobic ointments free of grit
Non-sterile powders for inhalation
Rectal cleansing enemas only
Oral effervescent tablets
IV lipid emulsions only
questions.explanation: Ocular, aural and nasal routes use ophthalmic solutions and suspensions (sterile, aqueous), ophthalmic ointments (sterile, hydrophobic, grit-free), and nasal drops or sprays.
questions.title: What Are Medicines?

questions.q: A key learning outcome of this lecture is to understand:
options: The difference between a drug and a medicine (medicinal form)
Only organic reaction mechanisms
Only hospital finance
Only bacterial endospore staining
Only MAPK phosphorylation cascades
questions.explanation: Key points restate learning outcomes: understand the difference between a drug and a medicine (medicinal form) and gain awareness of different dosage forms and routes of administration.
questions.title: What Are Medicines?

questions.q: Why must a drug be formulated as a medicine?
options: To deliver tiny doses safely with appropriate release and stability
Because APIs are always liquids at room temperature
To eliminate the need for excipients
Because drugs cannot exist as powders
To prevent any route of administration choice
questions.explanation: The example SAQ asks why formulation is necessary: drugs are often powders given in tiny doses and need dosage forms to protect, stabilise, taste-mask and deliver the API appropriately.
questions.title: What Are Medicines?

questions.q: In prehistoric medicine, what was believed to be the cause of sickness?
options: An imbalance of the four humours
Failure to comply with the wishes of spirits and supernatural forces
Invisible microbes carried in air and water
Punishment sent directly by a single god
Poor diet and lack of exercise
questions.explanation: Prehistoric people believed in good and bad spirits and supernatural forces, and that sickness occurred through failure to comply with their wishes. Witch doctors or shamans acted as mediators between people and spirits.
questions.title: Origins of Drugs

questions.q: Trepanation, the intentional perforation of the cranium, is significant because it is:
options: The first procedure to be performed under anaesthesia
The earliest recorded use of an antiseptic
Perhaps the oldest surgical procedure for which there is archaeological evidence
The first operation described in the Ebers Papyrus
The earliest known method of vaccination
questions.explanation: Trepanation dates back 7,000 to 10,000 years and is perhaps the oldest surgical procedure with archaeological evidence. It exposed the dura mater to treat intracranial disease or release pressurised blood after injury.
questions.title: Origins of Drugs

questions.q: Which concepts underpin the ancient Chinese explanation of illness?
options: Balance of Yin and Yang and the flow of Chi
Balance between body, mind and soul
Appeasement of demons and angry gods
Removal of evil spirits by prayer
The four humours of blood, phlegm and bile
questions.explanation: Ancient Chinese medicine held that a person became sick if the balance between natural elements (Yin and Yang) was not maintained and the Chi, or life energy, was not flowing well.
questions.title: Origins of Drugs

questions.q: Which five elements form the basis of traditional Chinese medicine theory?
options: Earth, Air, Fire, Water and Aether
Wood, Fire, Earth, Metal and Water
Blood, Phlegm, Bile, Water and Air
Wood, Stone, Fire, Metal and Air
Fire, Water, Salt, Sulphur and Mercury
questions.explanation: The Five Elements are Wood, Fire, Earth, Metal and Water, representing qualities and functions of the body as well as natural phenomena such as climate, season, taste and emotion.
questions.title: Origins of Drugs

questions.q: The Huangdi Neijing is significant as which of the following?
options: The first pharmacopoeia produced in Europe
A 20 metre scroll of magical formulas and remedies
The first encyclopaedia of medicine written in Arabic
The oldest medical textbook in the world and the first written document of traditional Chinese medicine
The earliest surviving surgical manual from India
questions.explanation: The Huangdi Neijing, dated to 800 BC, is the first written document on traditional Chinese medicine and the oldest medical textbook in the world, covering physiology, pathology, diagnosis, prevention, treatment and acupuncture.
questions.title: Origins of Drugs

questions.q: Ayurveda, from ancient Indian medicine, translates as which of the following?
options: The healing arts
Knowledge of life
Balance of the elements
The book of remedies
Way of the physician
questions.explanation: Ayurveda means knowledge of life. It treats physical health as part of spiritual health, creating balance between body, mind and soul through lifestyle and diet.
questions.title: Origins of Drugs

questions.q: Which surgical technique was taught in ancient Ayurvedic texts?
options: Trepanation of the skull
Amputation of infected limbs
Cataract surgery
Caesarean section
Repair of the aqueduct system
questions.explanation: Ancient Ayurvedic texts taught surgical techniques including cataract surgery, alongside therapies such as herbal medicines, special diets, meditation, yoga, massage, laxatives, enemas and medical oils.
questions.title: Origins of Drugs

questions.q: The Ebers Papyrus of 1550 BC is best described as which of the following?
options: A five-volume encyclopaedia of medicine
A 110 page, 20 metre scroll containing 700 magical formulas and remedies
The first written record of the Hippocratic Oath
An illustrated set of anatomical drawings
A collection of Chinese acupuncture charts
questions.explanation: The Ebers Papyrus is a 110 page scroll, 20 metres long, containing 700 magical formulas and remedies, from ancient Egyptian medicine.
questions.title: Origins of Drugs

questions.q: Ancient Egyptian doctors used the microbes in mouldy bread for which purpose?
options: As a contraceptive
To treat eye problems
As a treatment for infections
To embalm the dead
To induce vomiting
questions.explanation: Mouldy bread was used to treat infections, foreshadowing antibiotics. Mashed pig eyes with honey and ochre were used for eye problems, and crocodile dung with honey and mud as a contraceptive.
questions.title: Origins of Drugs

questions.q: Which lasting contribution to clinical practice came from ancient Babylonian medicine?
options: The concepts of diagnosis, prognosis, physical examination and prescriptions
The first anatomical drawings from human dissection
The oath sworn by new physicians
The link between dirt and disease
The systematic use of vaccination
questions.explanation: Although Babylonian medicine attributed disease to demons or angry gods and relied heavily on magic, the Babylonians introduced the concepts of diagnosis and prognosis, physical examination and prescriptions.
questions.title: Origins of Drugs

questions.q: What does the Hippocratic Oath require of new physicians?
options: To record every treatment they give in writing
To treat patients without charging a fee
To swear to the healing gods before beginning practice, using their power to help the sick and abstaining from harm
To study the works of Galen before practising
To perform dissections only on animals
questions.explanation: The oath requires new physicians to swear to the healing gods before starting practice, promising to use their power to help the sick to the best of their ability and judgement and to abstain from harming or wronging any man.
questions.title: Origins of Drugs

questions.q: Which insight distinguished Roman medicine, and what practical consequence followed?
options: That disease came from the gods, so temples were built
That there was a link between dirt and disease, so water supply and hygiene projects were prioritised
That herbs could cure most illness, so botanical gardens were founded
That the body contained four humours, so bloodletting became routine
That illness was punishment for sin, so hospitals were built in monasteries
questions.explanation: Roman medicine, heavily influenced by the Greeks, recognised a link between dirt and disease and the importance of personal hygiene, leading to practical projects such as aqueducts and water supply.
questions.title: Origins of Drugs

questions.q: What happened to herbal remedies and potions during the Middle Ages in Europe?
options: They were catalogued systematically by monastic scholars
They were replaced by imported Arabic formulations
They were seen as witchcraft and outlawed by the church
They became the basis of the first pharmacopoeia
They were reserved for use by the aristocracy
questions.explanation: In the Middle Ages the church taught that God sent illness and that repentance would cure all evils; herbal remedies and potions were seen as witchcraft and outlawed. Public hygiene declined after the fall of Rome.
questions.title: Origins of Drugs

questions.q: Which organism caused the Black Death, and how was it mainly spread to humans?
options: Yersinia pestis, spread by infected fleas travelling on rodents
Vibrio cholerae, spread through contaminated drinking water
Mycobacterium tuberculosis, spread by airborne droplets
Variola virus, spread by direct contact
Salmonella typhi, spread by contaminated food
questions.explanation: The Black Death was bubonic plague caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis, spread mostly to humans by infected fleas travelling on rodents.
questions.title: Origins of Drugs

questions.q: What proportion of the European population is the Black Death of 1346-1353 estimated to have killed?
options: About 5 to 10 per cent
About 15 to 20 per cent
About 30 to 60 per cent
About 70 to 80 per cent
More than 90 per cent
questions.explanation: The pandemic is estimated to have killed 30 to 60 per cent of the European population, as well as approximately 33 per cent of the population of the Middle East.
questions.title: Origins of Drugs

questions.q: What role did the Arabic world play in medicine after the fall of the Roman Empire?
options: It rejected Greek and Roman texts in favour of new theory
It became the centre of scientific and medical knowledge, translating key Greek and Roman literature into Arabic
It confined medical practice to religious establishments
It abandoned herbal medicine in favour of mineral remedies
It concentrated exclusively on surgical technique
questions.explanation: After the fall of the Roman Empire the Arabic world became the centre of scientific and medical knowledge. Greek and Roman literature was translated into Arabic and treatments focused on diet, exercise and medicinal herbs.
questions.title: Origins of Drugs

questions.q: Ibn Sina (Avicenna) wrote the Laws of Medicine in 1030 AD. How is this work described?
options: A single volume on surgical practice
A scroll of magical formulas and remedies
An encyclopaedia of medicine in five books covering formulation, diagnosis, general medicine and detailed therapies
A textbook of acupuncture and moxibustion
A collection of anatomical drawings from dissection
questions.explanation: The Laws of Medicine, translated into Latin in the 12th century, was an encyclopaedia of medicine containing five books covering formulation of medicines, diagnosis of disorders, general medicine and detailed therapies.
questions.title: Origins of Drugs

questions.q: How did the voyages of discovery from 1492 affect Renaissance medicine?
options: They spread the plague to the Americas
They brought new plants for herbal remedies, as well as tobacco
They introduced acupuncture to Europe
They led directly to the discovery of vaccination
They ended the use of herbal medicine in Europe
questions.explanation: The voyages of discovery of Christopher Columbus from 1492 brought new plants to Europe for use as herbal remedies, as well as tobacco.
questions.title: Origins of Drugs

questions.q: What was Leonardo Da Vinci's contribution to medicine during the Renaissance?
options: He established the first public hospital
He identified the link between dirt and disease
He dissected human bodies and made the first anatomical drawings
He translated Arabic medical texts into Latin
He introduced the concept of prognosis
questions.explanation: Leonardo Da Vinci dissected human bodies and made the first anatomical drawings, part of the Renaissance revival of the study of science and medicine.
questions.title: Origins of Drugs

questions.q: Which developments accompanied the Industrial Revolution of the 18th and 19th centuries?
options: The birth of the pharmaceutical industry and of microbiology
The completion of the Human Genome Project
The introduction of nanomedicine and stem cell therapy
The outlawing of herbal remedies by the church
The founding of the first monastic hospitals
questions.explanation: As people moved into overcrowded towns with poor sanitation, many died of cholera, tuberculosis, measles and pneumonia. This period saw the birth of the pharmaceutical industry and of microbiology.
questions.title: Origins of Drugs

questions.q: Against which disease did Edward Jenner develop vaccination in 1796?
options: Chickenpox
Measles
Meningitis
Smallpox
Polio
questions.explanation: Jenner is credited with developing vaccination against smallpox, a major killer of the 18th century. He infected an eight-year-old boy with cowpox; the boy recovered and never caught smallpox.
questions.title: Origins of Drugs

questions.q: Who first introduced inoculation against smallpox into England, in 1721, before Jenner's work?
options: Joseph Lister
Lady Mary Wortley Montagu
Alexander Fleming
Frederick Sanger
Francis Collins
questions.explanation: Although Edward Jenner is credited with the development of vaccination, the practice was first introduced into England by Lady Mary Wortley Montagu in 1721.
questions.title: Origins of Drugs

questions.q: Which substance did Joseph Lister use in 1865 as the first antiseptic, and with what result?
options: Iodine, cutting deaths from infection by half
Alcohol, eliminating septicaemia entirely
Carbolic acid (phenol), reducing deaths from infection from 60 per cent to 4 per cent
Chlorine, reducing deaths from infection from 40 per cent to 10 per cent
Penicillin, reducing deaths from infection from 60 per cent to 4 per cent
questions.explanation: Lister used carbolic acid (phenol) to clean wounds and surgical instruments, and sprayed it over the patient to kill airborne microbes. Deaths from infection fell from 60 per cent to 4 per cent.
questions.title: Origins of Drugs

questions.q: How did average life expectancy in the UK change over the 20th century?
options: From 47 in 1901 to 77 by 2000
From 35 in 1901 to 65 by 2000
From 55 in 1901 to 70 by 2000
From 47 in 1901 to 60 by 2000
From 60 in 1901 to 85 by 2000
questions.explanation: Average UK life expectancy rose from 47 in 1901 to 77 by 2000, driven by new medicines, childhood immunisation, improved air quality and better public hygiene.
questions.title: Origins of Drugs

questions.q: Who discovered insulin in 1922 and first used it successfully in a human patient?
options: Frederick Sanger and Francis Collins
Alexander Fleming and Joseph Lister
Fred Banting and Charles Best
Edward Jenner and Mary Wortley Montagu
Ibn Sina and Imhotep
questions.explanation: Fred Banting and Charles Best discovered insulin and used it successfully to treat diabetes in a human patient, having first removed the pancreas from dogs to induce diabetes.
questions.title: Origins of Drugs

questions.q: What did Frederick Sanger's 1955 work on insulin make possible?
options: Extraction of insulin from cow and pig pancreas
Genetic engineering of bacteria to provide highly pure human insulin
The first use of insulin in a human patient
The discovery that the pancreas causes diabetes
The formulation of insulin as an oral tablet
questions.explanation: In 1955 Sanger determined the sequence of human insulin. This allowed bacteria to be genetically engineered to produce highly pure human insulin, replacing early commercial preparations from slaughtered cows and pigs.
questions.title: Origins of Drugs

questions.q: How did Alexander Fleming discover penicillin in 1928?
options: By systematically screening thousands of soil samples
By observing that mouldy bread healed infected wounds
By noticing inhibited bacterial growth in a petri dish accidentally contaminated with Penicillium notatum
By extracting the compound from a tropical plant brought back from the Americas
By culturing bacteria in the presence of carbolic acid
questions.explanation: Fleming was seeking ways to kill the bacteria that made wounds turn septic when he noticed that bacterial growth was inhibited in a petri dish accidentally contaminated with the mould Penicillium notatum.
questions.title: Origins of Drugs

questions.q: Roughly how many compounds are screened for every new medicine that reaches the market?
options: Around 100
Around 1,000
Over 10,000
Around 9,000
questions.explanation: For every new medicine that passes, over 10,000 compounds are screened. Separately, in 2023 over 9,000 medicines were reported to be in development.
questions.title: Origins of Drugs

questions.q: What did the Human Genome Project, led by Francis Collins, achieve?
options: It sequenced the genome of Penicillium notatum
It produced the first genetically engineered insulin
It completely mapped and sequenced human DNA and identified genes associated with several diseases
It catalogued every medicine in development worldwide
It demonstrated the first use of nanorobots in cells
questions.explanation: Francis Collins discovered genes associated with several diseases and led the Human Genome Project, which completely mapped and sequenced human DNA; many consider it the most important scientific undertaking of our time.
questions.title: Origins of Drugs

questions.q: Nanomedicine is identified as a future trend. What does it involve?
options: Tailoring products to the individual through predictive responses
Using nanoparticles for targeted drug delivery and nanorobots to repair cells
Growing replacement tissues from undifferentiated cells
Sequencing the genome of individual patients
Screening very large compound libraries at high speed
questions.explanation: Nanomedicine involves nanoparticles for targeted drug delivery and nanorobots to make repairs to cells. Stem cells and personalised medicine are the other future trends listed.
questions.title: Origins of Drugs

questions.q: According to the key points, what is the focus of future medicine?
options: Personalised medicine
Herbal pharmacognosy
Mass vaccination programmes
Improved public sanitation
Broad-spectrum antibiotics
questions.explanation: The closing key points state that each historical era made a seminal contribution to medicine, and that future medicine is focused on personalised medicine, with products tailored to the individual through predictive responses.
questions.title: Origins of Drugs

questions.q: Which historical periods appear on the timeline of medicine history in the lecture?
options: Prehistoric, Ancient Chinese, Babylonian, Indian, Egyptian, Greek/Roman, Islamic, Renaissance, Middle Ages and Modern/Future Medicine
Only Modern and Future Medicine
Only Greek and Roman periods
Prehistoric and Renaissance only
Islamic medicine followed immediately by the 21st century with no other eras
questions.explanation: The timeline spans from Prehistoric (8000 BC) through Ancient Chinese, Babylonian, Indian and Egyptian civilisations, Greeks and Romans (400 BC–300 AD), Islamic medicine (700–1500 AD), the Renaissance, Middle Ages (Dark Ages), and Modern & Future Medicine (18th–21st century).
questions.title: Origins of Drugs

questions.q: According to Ancient Egyptian medicine, illness was believed to be caused by:
options: Evil spirits or poisons, cured by prayers to the gods
Bacterial endotoxin alone
Vitamin deficiency only
Genetic mutations identified by microscopy
Surgical removal of the appendix
questions.explanation: Ancient Egyptian medicine attributed illness to evil spirits or poisons, and believed that removing these through prayers to the gods would cure disease. Imhotep is a key figure in this tradition.
questions.title: Origins of Drugs

questions.q: How did Greek medicine explain disease and its treatment?
options: Diseases were punishment from the gods; treatments aimed to please the gods, with extensive herbal records
Disease was caused solely by miasma with no religious element
All illness was treated only by surgery without herbs
Greeks rejected written records of herbal medicines
Treatment focused exclusively on vaccination
questions.explanation: Greek medicine (400 BC–300 AD) believed diseases were sent as punishment from the gods. Treatments aimed at pleasing the gods, and there are extensive written records on the use of herbs as medicines.
questions.title: Origins of Drugs

questions.q: Which statement best defines a functional group?
options: A grouping of atoms whose characteristic properties depend on the rest of the molecule
Any carbon-containing portion of a drug molecule
A specific grouping of atoms with its own characteristic properties, regardless of the other atoms present
The part of a molecule that binds the receptor
A group of atoms that cannot take part in chemical reactions
questions.explanation: Functional groups are specific groupings of atoms that carry their own characteristic properties regardless of the rest of the molecule, and they undergo the same types of reaction wherever they appear.
questions.title: Structure of Drugs

questions.q: Functional groups undergo the same type of reactions wherever they occur. What can limit this reactivity?
options: The molecular weight of the compound
The presence of other functional groups in close proximity
The route by which the drug is administered
The dose of the drug given
The physical state of the compound
questions.explanation: Although a functional group reacts in the same characteristic way regardless of the compound, the presence of certain functional groups within proximity can limit its reactivity.
questions.title: Structure of Drugs

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT listed as a property of a drug molecule that its functional groups influence?
options: Overall water and lipid solubility
Route of metabolism and elimination
Ability to interact with specific biological targets
The batch number assigned during manufacture
Tendency to cause adverse effects or drug interactions
questions.explanation: Functional groups determine solubility, route of administration, target interaction, mechanism of action, metabolism and elimination, duration of action and adverse effect potential. Manufacturing identifiers have nothing to do with chemistry.
questions.title: Structure of Drugs

questions.q: Which three chemical properties must be considered for every functional group in a drug molecule?
options: Electronic, solubility and steric effects
Melting point, boiling point and density
Potency, efficacy and affinity
Absorption, distribution and excretion
Acidity, alkalinity and neutrality
questions.explanation: Each functional group has an electronic effect, a solubility effect and a steric effect, and these three properties are considered for every group in a structure.
questions.title: Structure of Drugs

questions.q: How is the electronic effect of a functional group defined?
options: By its ability to form covalent bonds with a receptor
By its contribution to the molecular weight of the drug
By its ability to donate electrons to, or withdraw electrons from, adjacent atoms or groups
By the number of hydrogen bonds it can form with water
By the three-dimensional space that it occupies
questions.explanation: The electronic effect is measured by whether the group donates its electrons to adjacent atoms or groups, or pulls electrons away from them.
questions.title: Structure of Drugs

questions.q: Which two components influence the electronic effect of a functional group?
options: Hydrogen bonding and van der Waals forces
Resonance and intrinsic inductive effects
Chain length and degree of branching
Ionisation and complexation
Steric bulk and conformation
questions.explanation: The two main components given are resonance and intrinsic inductive effects.
questions.title: Structure of Drugs

questions.q: What is meant by resonance in the context of drug structure?
options: Electrons are shared among a group of atoms with adjacent double bonds and lone pairs
The molecule vibrates at a characteristic frequency
Two molecules exchange protons in solution
A functional group rotates freely around a single bond
Electrons are permanently transferred from one atom to another
questions.explanation: Resonance describes electrons being shared among a group of atoms that have adjacent double bonds and lone pairs of electrons.
questions.title: Structure of Drugs

questions.q: The intrinsic inductive character of an atom or functional group depends on which chemical property?
options: Its polarisability
Its molecular volume
Its acid dissociation constant
Its overall electronegativity
Its degree of unsaturation
questions.explanation: Intrinsic inductive character depends on overall electronegativity, the ability of an atom or group to attract electrons towards itself and away from other atoms or groups.
questions.title: Structure of Drugs

questions.q: Electronegativity is best described as the ability of an atom or functional group to do what?
options: Donate a proton to a base
Attract electrons towards itself and away from other atoms or groups
Accept a lone pair of electrons from a nucleophile
Increase the water solubility of a molecule
Stabilise a positive charge by resonance
questions.explanation: Electronegativity is defined in the lecture as the ability of an atom or functional group to attract electrons towards itself and away from other atoms or functional groups.
questions.title: Structure of Drugs

questions.q: An electron withdrawing functional group is also described as which of the following?
options: Nucleophilic
Hydrophilic
Electrophilic
Amphiphilic
Lipophilic
questions.explanation: Electron withdrawing groups are described as electrophilic, while electron donating groups are described as nucleophilic.
questions.title: Structure of Drugs

questions.q: How is the overall solubility of a drug molecule determined by its structure?
options: By the single most polar functional group present
By the number of carbon atoms in the longest chain
By the composite sum of the contributions of each functional group present
By whether the molecule contains a ring system
By the molecular weight alone
questions.explanation: Overall solubility is a composite sum of the contributions of each functional group in the structure, and a given group's contribution can vary depending on adjacent groups.
questions.title: Structure of Drugs

questions.q: Why can the same functional group contribute differently to solubility in two different drug molecules?
options: Because its contribution depends on the adjacent groups in the structure
Because solubility is measured at different temperatures for each drug
Because functional groups change identity in solution
Because larger molecules dissolve more readily than small ones
Because the effect depends on the dose administered
questions.explanation: The lecture notes that the overall solubility contribution of a specific functional group can vary depending upon adjacent groups.
questions.title: Structure of Drugs

questions.q: A medicinal chemist adds a bulky functional group to a lead compound purely for its steric effect. Which benefit is this most likely intended to achieve?
options: An increase in the melting point of the compound
Increased selectivity for the biological target
A reduction in the molecular weight of the drug
Conversion of the drug into a prodrug
An increase in the ionisation of the molecule
questions.explanation: Adding groups for their steric effects can increase selectivity for the biological target, enhance binding interactions with that target, and favourably alter the rate of metabolism.
questions.title: Structure of Drugs

questions.q: What does the steric dimension of a functional group contribute to a drug molecule?
options: Its overall charge at physiological pH
Its capacity to form hydrogen bonds
Its overall conformation or three-dimensional shape
Its rate of dissolution in gastric fluid
Its resonance stabilisation energy
questions.explanation: Each functional group has a finite size or steric dimension that contributes to the overall conformation, or three-dimensional shape, of the drug molecule.
questions.title: Structure of Drugs

questions.q: Besides increased selectivity and enhanced binding, which further therapeutic benefit can be gained by exploiting steric effects?
options: Elimination of the need for excipients
Favourable alteration of the rate of metabolism
Removal of all adverse effects
Guaranteed oral bioavailability
Conversion of a base into an acid
questions.explanation: The three benefits listed are increased selectivity for the biological target, enhanced binding interactions with it, and favourable alteration of the rate of metabolism.
questions.title: Structure of Drugs

questions.q: On what principle is the design of new drugs based, according to the key points of this lecture?
options: Increasing the dose until an effect is seen
Selecting the cheapest available starting materials
Manipulating the functional chemistry within a structure to enhance pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic behaviour
Copying the structure of an existing marketed drug
Maximising the molecular weight of the candidate
questions.explanation: The closing key point is that new drug design is based on manipulating the functional chemistry within a structure to enhance pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic behaviour.
questions.title: Structure of Drugs

questions.q: Which functional group is present when an oxygen atom links two carbon atoms and carries no hydrogen of its own?
options: Alcohol
Aldehyde
Ether
Ketone
Carboxylic acid
questions.explanation: An oxygen bridging two carbons with no attached hydrogen is an ether. An alcohol carries an -OH, while aldehydes and ketones contain a carbonyl (C=O).
questions.title: Structure of Drugs

questions.q: Which group of functional groups would you expect to support water solubility in a drug molecule?
options: Alkyl chains and aromatic rings
Alkyl halides and alkenes
Ionisable acidic and basic groups capable of hydrogen bonding
Long saturated hydrocarbon tails
Cyclic hydrocarbons with no heteroatoms
questions.explanation: Water soluble functional groups are the acidic and basic groups that can ionise and hydrogen bond, whereas hydrocarbon features such as alkyl chains and aromatic rings support lipid solubility.
questions.title: Structure of Drugs

questions.q: Why are functional groups useful when telling similar compounds apart?
options: They give each compound a unique molecular weight
They carry characteristic properties and reactions that distinguish one compound from another
They determine the colour of the compound in solution
They are the only part of the molecule that can be drawn
They fix the melting point of the compound
questions.explanation: Because functional groups have their own characteristic properties and undergo the same type of reactions wherever they occur, they can be used to distinguish similar compounds from each other.
questions.title: Structure of Drugs

questions.q: A drug candidate is modified by replacing an aromatic hydrogen with a fluorine atom. Which immediate electronic consequence would you predict?
options: The site becomes strongly electron donating
The molecule loses its capacity for resonance
The highly electronegative fluorine withdraws electron density inductively from the ring
The molecule becomes permanently positively charged
The steric bulk of the molecule roughly doubles
questions.explanation: Fluorine is highly electronegative, so it exerts a strong inductive electron withdrawing effect, pulling electron density away from adjacent atoms. Fluoxetine is used in the lecture as the worked example of this.
questions.title: Structure of Drugs

questions.q: Which functional groups should students be able to draw in a molecule according to the lecture exercise?
options: Alcohol, alkyl halide, ether, amine and thiol
Aldehyde, ketone, ester, amide and nitrile only
Carboxylic acid, anhydride, acyl chloride, imine and azide
Alkane, alkene, alkyne, arene and cycloalkane only
Phosphate, sulphate, carbonate, bicarbonate and peroxide
questions.explanation: The slide asks students to draw a molecule containing alcohol, alkyl halide, ether, amine and thiol functional groups, building on earlier identification exercises with structures such as fluoxetine and indomethacin.
questions.title: Structure of Drugs

questions.q: For the Tamoxifen SAQ, which analysis is expected?
options: Identify sites of electronegativity, electron donating/withdrawing groups and predict solubility
Calculate its oral bioavailability from clinical trial data
Determine its BCS class from partition coefficient alone
Draw its complete biosynthetic pathway in yeast
Assign its IUPAC name without reference to structure
questions.explanation: Tamoxifen is a selective oestrogen receptor modulator used to prevent breast cancer. The SAQ asks students to identify electronegative sites, electron donating or withdrawing groups, and predict the compound's solubility from its functional group chemistry.
questions.title: Structure of Drugs

questions.q: Stereochemistry is best defined as the branch of chemistry dealing with which of the following?
options: The rates at which chemical reactions proceed
The spatial arrangements of atoms in molecules and the effects of these arrangements on properties
The synthesis of carbon-containing compounds from simple precursors
The measurement of bond energies within a molecule
The behaviour of molecules at surfaces and interfaces
questions.explanation: The definition given is the branch of chemistry that deals with spatial arrangements of atoms in molecules and the effects of these arrangements on the chemical and physical properties of substances.
questions.title: Lectures 5 & 6 - Stereochemistry

questions.q: Which pattern of activity between two enantiomers of the same drug has NOT been observed?
options: Identical efficacy and toxicity
The same effects but of different magnitude
One enantiomer active while the other is biologically inactive
Different therapeutic and toxic effects for each enantiomer
Neither enantiomer showing any biological activity while the racemate is active
questions.explanation: Four patterns are listed: identical efficacy and toxicity; same effects of different magnitude; one active and one inactive; and different therapeutic and toxic effects. Activity appearing only when both enantiomers are mixed is not among them.
questions.title: Lectures 5 & 6 - Stereochemistry

questions.q: Significant antibacterial activity in chloramphenicol is found only in which absolute configuration?
options: S,S
R,S
R,R
S,R
The racemate only
questions.explanation: Maxwell and Nickel (1954) showed that significant activity is only found for the R,R-absolute configuration of chloramphenicol.
questions.title: Lectures 5 & 6 - Stereochemistry

questions.q: What was the fundamental manufacturing problem behind the thalidomide tragedy?
options: The drug was contaminated with a toxic impurity
A mixture of the isomers was produced, not just the effective and safe enantiomer
The tablets contained ten times the intended dose
The compound degraded to a toxic metabolite on storage
The wrong salt form was used in the formulation
questions.explanation: Thalidomide is chiral and exists as two enantiomers. Only one was effective and safe, but during manufacture a mixture of the isomers was produced.
questions.title: Lectures 5 & 6 - Stereochemistry

questions.q: Geometrical and optical isomerism are both subtypes of which broader category?
options: Structural isomerism
Chain isomerism
Stereoisomerism
Functional group isomerism
Position isomerism
questions.explanation: Isomerism divides into structural isomerism (chain, position, functional group) and stereoisomerism, which contains geometrical and optical isomerism.
questions.title: Lectures 5 & 6 - Stereochemistry

questions.q: What is the structural cause of geometrical isomerism in alkenes?
options: Free rotation about carbon-carbon single bonds
The presence of a chiral centre in the molecule
Hydrogen bonding between adjacent substituents
Restricted rotation of the C=C double bond
Resonance delocalisation across the molecule
questions.explanation: C=C bonds have restricted rotation, so groups at either end of the bond are frozen in position and cannot easily interchange, giving two distinct arrangements in space.
questions.title: Lectures 5 & 6 - Stereochemistry

questions.q: In the cis and trans system, what does the trans designation indicate?
options: Groups are on opposite sides across the double bond
Groups are on the same side of the double bond
The molecule rotates plane polarised light to the left
The molecule contains two chiral centres
The higher priority groups are ranked by atomic number
questions.explanation: Cis means the groups or atoms are on the same side of the double bond; trans means they lie on opposite sides across it.
questions.title: Lectures 5 & 6 - Stereochemistry

questions.q: How do geometrical isomers generally compare in their properties?
options: Identical physical properties but very different chemical properties
Different physical properties such as boiling point and density, but similar chemical properties in most cases
Identical in every respect except their rotation of polarised light
Different only in their melting points
Completely identical, which is why they cannot be separated
questions.explanation: Geometrical isomers have different physical properties, for example boiling points and density, but in most cases similar chemical properties.
questions.title: Lectures 5 & 6 - Stereochemistry

questions.q: When can an alkene NOT show geometrical isomerism?
options: When the molecule contains more than four carbon atoms
When the double bond is at the end of the chain only
When two similar atoms or groups are attached to one end of the C=C
When the molecule contains a halogen atom
When the two ends of the double bond carry different groups
questions.explanation: Once two similar atoms or groups are attached to one end of a C=C, geometrical isomerism is impossible, because swapping them produces the same molecule.
questions.title: Lectures 5 & 6 - Stereochemistry

questions.q: Of the three alkene structural isomers of C4H8, how many show geometrical isomerism?
options: None of them
Only one
Two of them
All three
It depends on the temperature
questions.explanation: There are three alkene structural isomers of C4H8 (but-1-ene, 2-methylpropene and but-2-ene), and only but-2-ene exhibits geometrical isomerism, giving cis and trans forms.
questions.title: Lectures 5 & 6 - Stereochemistry

questions.q: In the IUPAC E/Z system, what does the Z descriptor mean?
options: Zusammen - the higher priority groups are on the same side
Entgegen - the higher priority groups are on opposite sides
The molecule is a racemic mixture
The chiral centre is arranged clockwise
The molecule is laevorotatory
questions.explanation: Z stands for zusammen, meaning together, with the higher priority groups on the same side. E stands for entgegen, meaning opposite.
questions.title: Lectures 5 & 6 - Stereochemistry

questions.q: Under sequence rule 1, how are the atoms attached to each vinyl carbon ranked?
options: In order of increasing atomic mass
By the number of hydrogen atoms they carry
By their electronegativity on the Pauling scale
In order of decreasing atomic number
Alphabetically by element name
questions.explanation: Rule 1 ranks the directly attached atoms in order of decreasing atomic number, giving the sequence Br > Cl > O > N > C > H for common substituents.
questions.title: Lectures 5 & 6 - Stereochemistry

questions.q: An ethyl group and a methyl group are attached to the same carbon. How is priority decided between them?
options: They have equal priority because both begin with carbon
Methyl takes priority because it is smaller
By working outward to the first point of difference, giving ethyl the higher priority
By comparing their total molecular masses
Priority is assigned arbitrarily in such cases
questions.explanation: Rule 1 cannot separate them since both start with carbon. Rule 2 requires working outward to the first point of difference; ethyl has carbon at the next atom while methyl has hydrogen, so ethyl ranks higher.
questions.title: Lectures 5 & 6 - Stereochemistry

questions.q: How are multiply bonded atoms treated when assigning priorities?
options: They are ignored entirely
They are considered equivalent to the same number of singly bonded atoms
They automatically receive the highest priority
They are counted as half an atom each
They are ranked below all singly bonded atoms
questions.explanation: Sequence rule 3 states that multiply bonded atoms are considered equivalent to the same number of singly bonded atoms, so a double bond is broken and made up with duplicate imaginary atoms.
questions.title: Lectures 5 & 6 - Stereochemistry

questions.q: What defines a chiral centre in a molecule?
options: A carbon involved in a double bond with restricted rotation
A carbon carrying at least one halogen atom
Any carbon atom bearing a hydroxyl group
A carbon with two identical groups arranged tetrahedrally
An asymmetric carbon with four different atoms or groups arranged tetrahedrally around it
questions.explanation: A chiral centre contains an asymmetric carbon, which has four different atoms or groups arranged tetrahedrally around it. If a carbon has more than one of any group attached it cannot be chiral.
questions.title: Lectures 5 & 6 - Stereochemistry

questions.q: Why does 2-chlorobutane exhibit optical isomerism while 1-chlorobutane does not?
options: 2-chlorobutane has a double bond with restricted rotation
In 2-chlorobutane the second carbon carries four different groups, whereas every carbon in 1-chlorobutane carries repeated groups
2-chlorobutane has a higher molecular weight
1-chlorobutane is a structural isomer rather than a stereoisomer
Chlorine can only create chirality when bonded to a terminal carbon
questions.explanation: In 2-chlorobutane the second carbon has H, CH3, Cl and C2H5 attached, all different, so it is chiral. Every carbon in 1-chlorobutane carries two or three hydrogens, so none can be a chiral centre.
questions.title: Lectures 5 & 6 - Stereochemistry

questions.q: Both conditions must apply for optical isomerism. What are they?
options: The forms must be mirror images and be non-superimposable
The forms must be superimposable and have different boiling points
The molecule must be an alkene and contain a halogen
The forms must have identical melting points and densities
The molecule must contain at least two chiral centres
questions.explanation: The two forms must be mirror images AND be non-superimposable. Hands are the everyday example; spoons are mirror images but superimposable, and books are superimposable but not mirror images.
questions.title: Lectures 5 & 6 - Stereochemistry

questions.q: An optical isomer rotates plane polarised light to the left. What is it called?
options: Dextrorotatory, the d or + form
Laevorotatory, the l or - form
A meso compound
A racemate
A diastereoisomer
questions.explanation: Rotation to the left is laevorotatory, the l or - form; rotation to the right is dextrorotatory, the d or + form. Rotation is measured with a polarimeter, viewed coming towards the observer.
questions.title: Lectures 5 & 6 - Stereochemistry

questions.q: Why does a racemic mixture show no net optical rotation?
options: Neither enantiomer is optically active on its own
The mixture contains only the meso form
It is a 50-50 mixture whose opposite optical effects cancel each other out
Racemates cannot pass plane polarised light
The two enantiomers react together to form an achiral product
questions.explanation: A racemate is a 50-50 mixture of the two enantiomers, written (dl) or (plus/minus). The opposite optical effects of each isomer cancel out, so no net rotation is observed.
questions.title: Lectures 5 & 6 - Stereochemistry

questions.q: Which is a stated advantage of formulating a drug as a single optical isomer rather than as the racemate?
options: It removes the need for stability testing
It guarantees the drug will be orally bioavailable
Smaller doses can be used, with reduced side effects and improved pharmacological activity
It prevents the drug from being metabolised
It allows the drug to be given by any route of administration
questions.explanation: Many drugs must be made of one optical isomer to be effective. The stated benefits are smaller doses (safer and cost effective), reduced side effects and improved pharmacological activity.
questions.title: Lectures 5 & 6 - Stereochemistry

questions.q: In the Cahn-Ingold-Prelog system, how is a centre assigned as R?
options: The lowest priority group points towards the viewer and the rest run clockwise
With the lowest priority group pointing away from the viewer, the remaining three run clockwise in order of priority
The highest priority group points directly upwards
The molecule rotates plane polarised light to the right
The hydroxyl group lies on the right in a Fischer projection
questions.explanation: After assigning priorities 1 to 4, the centre is viewed with the lowest priority group furthest away. A clockwise order of the remaining three is R, anticlockwise is S. Note this is independent of the direction of optical rotation.
questions.title: Lectures 5 & 6 - Stereochemistry

questions.q: What is racemisation?
options: The separation of a racemate into its individual enantiomers
The conversion of a geometrical isomer from cis to trans
The process in which a racemic mixture is formed from an enantiomerically pure compound
The loss of a chiral centre by elimination
The interconversion of two diastereoisomers
questions.explanation: Racemisation is the process in which a racemic mixture is formed from an enantiomerically pure compound. Most reactions forming a new chiral compound in the absence of any chirality give racemic products.
questions.title: Lectures 5 & 6 - Stereochemistry

questions.q: A molecule contains 3 chiral centres. What is the maximum number of stereoisomers possible?
questions.explanation: The maximum number of stereoisomers is 2 to the power n, where n is the number of chiral centres. For 3 centres this gives 2 cubed, which is 8.
questions.title: Lectures 5 & 6 - Stereochemistry

questions.q: How are diastereoisomers best described?
options: Non-superimposable mirror images with identical physicochemical properties
Stereoisomers that are not enantiomers, being non-superimposable and non-mirror images
Isomers with the same molecular formula but different structural formulae
Two forms that interconvert freely at room temperature
Compounds differing only in the position of a double bond
questions.explanation: Diastereoisomers are all stereoisomers that are not enantiomers. They are non-superimposable, non-mirror images with different physicochemical properties including polarity, solubility, melting point and optical rotation, and may differ biologically.
questions.title: Lectures 5 & 6 - Stereochemistry

questions.q: Meso tartaric acid melts at 146-148 degrees C with a specific rotation of 0, while the (+) and (-) forms both melt at 168-170 degrees C. What does this illustrate?
options: That enantiomers always have different melting points from each other
That optical rotation cannot be measured for solids
That diastereoisomers such as the meso form differ in physicochemical properties from the enantiomers
That the meso form is a racemic mixture
That melting point is unrelated to stereochemistry
questions.explanation: The (+) and (-) enantiomers share the same melting point, density and solubility and differ only in the sign of rotation. The meso form is a diastereoisomer, so its melting point, density and solubility all differ, and it is optically inactive.
questions.title: Lectures 5 & 6 - Stereochemistry

questions.q: In a Fischer projection, where is the most highly oxidised functional group placed?
options: At the top of the main chain
At the bottom of the main chain
On the left-hand horizontal bond
On the right-hand horizontal bond
In the centre of the projection
questions.explanation: In a Fischer projection the main chain is drawn from top to bottom with the most highly oxidised functional group at the top; substituents on either side of the main chain come out of the plane.
questions.title: Lectures 5 & 6 - Stereochemistry

questions.q: Using the Fischer convention, a sugar is designated D when which condition is met?
options: It rotates plane polarised light to the right
The hydroxyl on the chiral carbon furthest from carbon 1 is on the right
The aldehyde group is on the left of the projection
All hydroxyl groups point to the right
It is derived from L-glyceraldehyde
questions.explanation: If the hydroxyl group on the chiral carbon furthest from carbon 1 lies to the right, the molecule is designated D. Uppercase D and L are distinct from lowercase d and l, which describe optical rotation.
questions.title: Lectures 5 & 6 - Stereochemistry

questions.q: Why was a system such as Cahn-Ingold-Prelog needed alongside the Fischer D/L convention?
options: Fischer projections cannot show more than one chiral centre
The Fischer system predicts the direction of optical rotation incorrectly
Fischer works well for sugars and amino acids but less well for other organic molecules, so a convention applicable across the board was needed
The Fischer system was found to be mathematically inconsistent
Fischer projections can only be applied to geometrical isomers
questions.explanation: The Fischer system works well for sugars and amino acids, which can be related to a reference molecule, but works less well for other organic molecules, so a generally applicable convention was required.
questions.title: Lectures 5 & 6 - Stereochemistry

questions.q: D-glucose and D-mannose differ only in the configuration at a single carbon. What term describes this relationship?
options: Enantiomers
Anomers
Geometrical isomers
Epimers
Racemates
questions.explanation: Epimers are molecules that differ from each other only in the configuration at one atom, with D-glucose and D-mannose given as the example.
questions.title: Lectures 5 & 6 - Stereochemistry

questions.q: In wedge and dash notation, what do the wedge and dashed bonds represent?
options: Bonds coming out of the paper and going into the paper respectively
Double bonds and single bonds respectively
Polar bonds and non-polar bonds respectively
Bonds to the highest and lowest priority groups
Bonds that can and cannot rotate freely
questions.explanation: Tetrahedral carbons are drawn with wedge and dash notation, the wedge denoting a bond coming out of the paper and the dash a bond going into it. Both must be on the same side of the two in-plane bonds.
questions.title: Lectures 5 & 6 - Stereochemistry

questions.q: Which answer option appears in the example MCQ about a dichloro-substituted structure?
options: Could be classified as a racemic mixture
Must be achiral due to a plane of symmetry only
Cannot show geometrical isomerism
Is always a meso compound
Has no stereogenic centres possible
questions.explanation: The example MCQ options include optical activity, E isomer, Z isomer, racemic mixture, and none of the above for the illustrated dichloro structure.
questions.title: Lectures 5 & 6 - Stereochemistry

questions.q: What does the SAQ ask students to draw for 2-bromobutane?
options: The two stereoisomers labelled R or S on the provided scaffold
Only the Fischer projection of glucose
The E and Z alkene isomers of butene
A Newman projection of ethane only
The meso form of tartaric acid
questions.explanation: The SAQ asks students to draw and label (R or S) the two stereoisomers of 2-bromobutane (CH3CH2CHBrCH3) on the scaffold provided.
questions.title: Lectures 5 & 6 - Stereochemistry

questions.q: Why are all the drawn alkane conformations considered the same structure?
options: Single covalent C-C bonds can rotate freely
C=C bonds rotate freely like single bonds
Alkanes cannot exist as conformers
Only cyclic alkanes can rotate
Hydrogen atoms are indistinguishable in all cases
questions.explanation: Single covalent bonds can easily rotate, so different written arrangements of an alkane represent the same structure, unlike restricted C=C bonds.
questions.title: Lectures 5 & 6 - Stereochemistry

questions.q: What is the energetically preferred conformation of ethane as a single bond rotates?
options: Staggered bonds with hydrogens offset
Eclipsed bonds with hydrogens aligned
Fully planar with all atoms collinear
Only the boat conformation of cyclohexane
A conformation with maximum repulsion
questions.explanation: It is more energetically stable for ethane to have staggered bonds. Lined-up eclipsed conformations increase repulsion between adjacent electron clouds.
questions.title: Lectures 5 & 6 - Stereochemistry

questions.q: Which drugs are named on the slide where cis and trans nomenclature can be misleading?
options: Z-tamoxifen and Z-clomiphene
Ibuprofen and warfarin only
Chloramphenicol and thalidomide
D-glucose and D-mannose
Glyceraldehyde and tartaric acid
questions.explanation: The slide shows Z-tamoxifen for oestrogen-dependent breast cancer and Z-clomiphene for ovulatory failure, noting that cis and trans can fall down.
questions.title: Lectures 5 & 6 - Stereochemistry

questions.q: In (E)-2-chloro-2-butene versus (Z)-2-chloro-2-butene, why does chlorine receive higher priority than methyl?
options: Chlorine has a higher atomic number than carbon in the methyl group
Methyl always outranks halogens in all cases
Hydrogen has higher priority than chlorine
Double bonds are ignored in E/Z assignment
Alphabetical order alone determines priority
questions.explanation: Chlorine has higher atomic number than carbon so it outranks methyl (CH3), which outranks hydrogen. High-priority groups on opposite sides give E; same side gives Z.
questions.title: Lectures 5 & 6 - Stereochemistry

questions.q: The 'Now try this' MCQ offers which classification for the dichloro structure?
options: Could be classified as a racemic mixture
Must be an achiral meso compound only
Cannot be an E isomer
Must be a Z isomer only
Is defined as a constitutional isomer only
questions.explanation: The repeat MCQ lists the same options: optically active, E isomer, Z isomer, racemic mixture, or none of the above.
questions.title: Lectures 5 & 6 - Stereochemistry

questions.q: The 'E or Z?' practice slide presents how many numbered structures to classify?
options: Four structures numbered 1 to 4
Two structures only
Eight structures
One structure only
Ten alkane conformers
questions.explanation: The E or Z practice slide shows four numbered structures (1, 2, 3, 4) with hydroxyl and halogen substituents around double bonds.
questions.title: Lectures 5 & 6 - Stereochemistry

questions.q: Which task is set for ibuprofen, labetalol, warfarin and benzylpenicillin on the chiral centre slide?
options: Identify chiral centres and draw a 3-D enantiomer of each drug
Calculate log P for each drug
Determine pKa by titration only
Assign only E/Z geometry at double bonds
Draw only Fischer projections of aldoses
questions.explanation: Students are asked to identify the chiral centres in the drug molecules shown and draw a 3-D representation of an enantiomer of each drug.
questions.title: Lectures 5 & 6 - Stereochemistry

questions.q: In Cahn-Ingold-Prelog notation, how are substituent priorities assigned at a chiral centre?
options: By atomic number of atoms n bonds away, starting one bond out until a distinction is found
By alphabetical order of element symbols only
By molecular weight of the whole substituent only
By boiling point of each group
By random assignment then inversion
questions.explanation: The CIP system assigns priorities 1-4 by atomic number of atoms n bonds from the chiral centre, comparing 1-bond atoms first, then 2-bond, and so on.
questions.title: Lectures 5 & 6 - Stereochemistry

questions.q: When comparing substituents at a chiral centre, which rule is stated for atoms at equal bond distance?
options: Always compare all atoms n bonds away before considering any atoms n+1 bonds away
Skip directly to the farthest atom in the chain
Only the first atom ever matters regardless of ties
Double bonds are always lowest priority
Hydrogen always receives priority 1
questions.explanation: Rule (ii) states to always compare atoms n bonds away before considering any atoms n+1 bonds away when assigning CIP priorities.
questions.title: Lectures 5 & 6 - Stereochemistry

questions.q: What is the purpose of the 'Lets try a few!' slide with structures (a) through (d)?
options: Practice assigning R or S configuration to multiple stereogenic centres
Calculate optical rotation in degrees
Determine melting points of enantiomers
Assign E/Z only to alkenes
Draw polymer repeat units
questions.explanation: The slide presents four structures labelled (a) to (d) with halogen and alkyl substituents for students to practise CIP R/S assignment.
questions.title: Lectures 5 & 6 - Stereochemistry

questions.q: Structures (e) through (h) on the practice slide are provided for what skill?
options: Further R/S designation practice at varied stereogenic centres
Calculation of pH from Ka
Micelle CMC determination
Viscosity profile interpretation
Titration end-point colour change
questions.explanation: The second practice set shows structures (e) to (h) with chloro, hydroxymethyl, iodo and bromo substituents for continued R/S practice.
questions.title: Lectures 5 & 6 - Stereochemistry

questions.q: How are the chiral centres designated in 2,3,4-trihydroxybutanal on the sequence slide?
options: Each chiral centre designated in order of sequence
Only the carbonyl carbon is chiral
All centres are automatically R
No stereogenic centres exist in the molecule
Only D configuration is possible with no R/S
questions.explanation: The slide shows 2,3,4-trihydroxybutanal with each chiral centre designated in order of sequence along the carbon chain.
questions.title: Lectures 5 & 6 - Stereochemistry

questions.q: What is the given R/S assignment for 2,3,4-trihydroxybutanal?
options: 2S, 3S, 4S only
All centres are meso
questions.explanation: The designate chirality slide gives the answer 2S, 3R, 4S for the three stereogenic centres of 2,3,4-trihydroxybutanal.
questions.title: Lectures 5 & 6 - Stereochemistry

questions.q: What question is posed about molecules with more than two stereocentres?
options: What do you do with more than 2 stereo centres?
How do you eliminate all optical activity?
Why are sugars always achiral?
How to ignore epimers in nomenclature?
When is Fischer notation forbidden?
questions.explanation: The slide asks what to do with more than 2 stereo centres and notes more application in Lectures 16 and 17.
questions.title: Lectures 5 & 6 - Stereochemistry

questions.q: Which sugars are shown in the D-aldose series slide?
options: D-allose through D-galactose in the aldose series
Only D-glucose
Only L-amino acids
Only ribose and deoxyribose
Only sucrose and lactose disaccharides
questions.explanation: The D-aldose series slide illustrates D-allose, D-altrose, D-glucose, D-mannose, D-gulose, D-idose, D-talose and D-galactose.
questions.title: Lectures 5 & 6 - Stereochemistry

questions.q: Why is glyceraldehyde important in Fischer's carbohydrate work?
options: It is the smallest carbohydrate Cn(H2O)2n recognised by Fischer with two optical forms
It has no chiral centres
It cannot rotate plane-polarised light
It is identical to tartaric acid
It defines only E/Z isomerism
questions.explanation: Fischer recognised glyceraldehyde as the smallest carbohydrate Cn(H2O)2n, existing in two forms with the same properties except optical rotation.
questions.title: Lectures 5 & 6 - Stereochemistry

questions.q: What task is set on the D- or L-configuration identification slide?
options: Identify whether shown molecules have D- or L-configurations
Calculate specific rotation in degrees only
Assign E/Z to each structure
Determine pKa of each sugar
Draw only racemic mixtures
questions.explanation: The slide asks students to identify whether the illustrated carbohydrate-related molecules have D- or L-configurations.
questions.title: Lectures 5 & 6 - Stereochemistry

questions.q: What did Louis Pasteur demonstrate about tartaric acid in 1860?
options: Moulds and yeasts can differentiate between (+)- and (-)-tartaric acid
All tartaric acid forms are identical to microbes
Tartaric acid cannot exist as enantiomers
Only meso-tartaric acid is biologically active
Optical isomers always have different melting points only
questions.explanation: Louis Pasteur showed in 1860 that moulds and yeasts can differentiate between (+)- and (-)-tartaric acid.
questions.title: Lectures 5 & 6 - Stereochemistry

questions.q: Which nomenclature items are listed as key to know?
options: cis/trans, E/Z, d and l, enantiomers/diastereomers, R/S, and D/L
Only molecular weight and density
Only pH and pKa
Only Hamaker and London forces
Only Newtonian viscosity
questions.explanation: Key nomenclature listed: cis and trans; E and Z; d and l; enantiomers and diastereomers; R and S; D and L (distinct from d and l).
questions.title: Lectures 5 & 6 - Stereochemistry

questions.q: Why must the physicochemical properties of an API be known before formulation?
options: They determine the price at which the medicine can be sold
They dictate the colour and flavour of the final product
They determine whether a particular dosage form or route of administration is viable
They are required only for regulatory paperwork
They set the shelf life independently of storage conditions
questions.explanation: Physicochemical data are needed so the drug can be formulated and to understand dissolution, absorption across membranes and therefore clinical effect. The properties of the API determine whether a given dosage form or route is viable.
questions.title: Physicochemical Properties of Drugs

questions.q: In a crystalline solid, how are the component molecules, ions or atoms arranged?
options: Randomly, with no long-range order
In a defined order that is repeated throughout the crystal
In layers that are free to slide over one another
In an exact molar ratio with water
In a continuously changing arrangement dependent on temperature
questions.explanation: Crystalline solids have their components arranged in a defined order repeated throughout the crystal, which gives them sharp, well-defined melting points.
questions.title: Physicochemical Properties of Drugs

questions.q: How many basic crystal lattice systems are there, and which do most drugs form?
options: Four systems; most drugs form cubic unit cells
Five systems; most drugs form hexagonal unit cells
Seven systems; most drugs form triclinic, monoclinic or orthorhombic unit cells
Seven systems; most drugs form cubic or tetragonal unit cells
Eleven systems; most drugs form monoclinic unit cells
questions.explanation: There are seven basic crystal unit cell systems, and most drugs form triclinic, monoclinic or orthorhombic unit cells.
questions.title: Physicochemical Properties of Drugs

questions.q: How does an amorphous solid differ from a crystalline one, and what is the practical consequence?
options: It has long-range order and is usually less soluble
Its molecules are in a random arrangement and it is usually more soluble than the crystalline form
It contains water in the lattice and dissolves more slowly
It has a sharper melting point and better stability
It cannot be compressed into tablets
questions.explanation: Amorphous solids lack the long-range order of a crystal and their molecules are randomly arranged. The amorphous form is usually more soluble than the crystalline form.
questions.title: Physicochemical Properties of Drugs

questions.q: What is polymorphism?
options: The existence of a drug in both solid and liquid states
The incorporation of water into a crystal lattice in a fixed molar ratio
The presence of several chemically distinct impurities in one batch
Crystalline forms of the same drug that are chemically identical but have different molecular packing patterns
The conversion of a drug into a salt to improve solubility
questions.explanation: Polymorphs are crystalline forms of the same drug, chemically the same but with different structures at the molecular level and different packing patterns. Phenobarbital has 11 polymorphs; carbon has diamond and graphite.
questions.title: Physicochemical Properties of Drugs

questions.q: Which type of polymorph can convert from one form to another under changing conditions such as temperature and pressure?
options: Enantiotropic
Monotropic
Amorphous
Anhydrous
Pseudopolymorphic
questions.explanation: Enantiotropic polymorphs can convert from one form to another under changing conditions. Monotropic means one form is stable at all conditions, and a metastable form will eventually convert to the preferred form.
