questions.title: Physicochemical Properties of Drugs

questions.q: Why does polymorphism matter in pharmacy?
options: Different polymorphs have different chemical structures and so different pharmacology
Polymorphs cannot be detected by any analytical method
Different polymorphs can differ in melting point, solubility, density and crystal habit, affecting processing and bioavailability
Polymorphism only affects the appearance of the powder
Polymorphs always dissolve at the same rate but taste different
questions.explanation: Different polymorphs can have different physical properties including melting point, solubility, density, crystal habit, dielectric constant and vapour pressure, so they behave differently in manufacture and in the body, affecting bioavailability.
questions.title: Physicochemical Properties of Drugs

questions.q: Why might a formulator deliberately choose a metastable polymorph, and what risk does this create?
options: It is cheaper to produce, but it may discolour
It is more soluble, dissolves faster and improves bioavailability, but may convert to the stable form during manufacture and storage
It has a higher melting point, but is harder to compress
It is chemically more stable, but less potent
It contains water of crystallisation, but is hygroscopic
questions.explanation: The less stable, metastable polymorph is often preferred because it is more soluble, dissolves faster and gives improved bioavailability. The risk of conversion to the stable form during manufacture and storage must be minimised.
questions.title: Physicochemical Properties of Drugs

questions.q: Chloramphenicol palmitate oral suspension contains which polymorph, and why is polymorph A controlled?
options: Polymorph A, because B is toxic
Polymorph C, because it is the most soluble
Polymorph B, with specified limits on the amount of A because conversion on storage reduces blood levels
A 50:50 mixture of A and B, to balance stability and solubility
Polymorph B, with limits on A because A is chemically unstable
questions.explanation: A is the stable polymorph, B is metastable and C is too unstable to formulate. The oral suspension contains B; conversion on storage is checked and specified limits are set for the amount of A, since A gives much lower blood concentrations.
questions.title: Physicochemical Properties of Drugs

questions.q: A crystal contains one mole of water for every mole of drug in the lattice. What is this called?
options: An anhydrate
A monohydrate
A dihydrate
A eutectic mixture
An amorphous solid
questions.explanation: Crystal hydrates contain water in the lattice in an exact molar ratio: 1 mole drug to 1 mole water is a monohydrate, 1 to 2 a dihydrate. The form without water is anhydrous.
questions.title: Physicochemical Properties of Drugs

questions.q: Why are crystal hydrates described as pseudopolymorphs?
options: Because they are chemically different from the parent drug
Because they revert to the amorphous state on storage
Because they have different properties from the anhydrous form despite being the same drug
Because they contain more than one drug substance
Because they have no defined melting point
questions.explanation: Crystal hydrates are described as pseudopolymorphs because, like true polymorphs, they have different properties from the anhydrous form.
questions.title: Physicochemical Properties of Drugs

questions.q: Compared with the equivalent anhydrous form, a crystal hydrate typically shows which set of properties?
options: Higher melting point, lower solubility and slower dissolution rate
Lower melting point, higher solubility and faster dissolution rate
Identical melting point but higher solubility
Lower melting point, lower solubility and faster dissolution
Higher melting point but greater solubility
questions.explanation: The lattice is held more tightly in the hydrate so more energy is required to dissolve it. The hydrate often has a higher melting point, lower solubility and slower dissolution rate, as shown for theophylline.
questions.title: Physicochemical Properties of Drugs

questions.q: How is crystal lattice energy defined?
options: The energy required to melt one mole of the crystalline solid
The energy released when the constituent atoms are placed in their positions on the crystal lattice
The energy needed to convert a crystalline solid to its amorphous form
The heat absorbed when a solid dissolves in water
The energy stored in hydrogen bonds between solvent molecules
questions.explanation: Crystal lattice energy is the energy released when the constituent atoms take up their positions on the lattice, equivalently the energy spent separating an ionic crystal into its ions. It relates to melting point and dissolution.
questions.title: Physicochemical Properties of Drugs

questions.q: What two relationships does the van't Hoff equation predict for ideal solutions?
options: Solubility increases with temperature and increases with melting point
Solubility decreases with temperature and decreases with melting point
Solubility increases with temperature and decreases as melting point increases
Solubility is independent of temperature but decreases with melting point
Solubility increases with molecular weight and with melting point
questions.explanation: The van't Hoff equation, which assumes ideal solution behaviour, predicts that solubility increases with temperature and decreases as the melting point of the solute increases.
questions.title: Physicochemical Properties of Drugs

questions.q: A series of paraben esters shows solubility falling as melting point falls, contrary to the van't Hoff prediction. What explains this?
options: The measurements were made at the wrong temperature
The parabens are ionised at the pH used
Increasing chain length raises lipophilicity, which dominates the melting point effect
The parabens form hydrates in solution
Paraben esters are amorphous rather than crystalline
questions.explanation: The sulfonamide series follows the prediction because the compounds are structurally similar. The parabens do not, because increasing chain length raises log P and the impact of chain length on lipophilicity outweighs the melting point effect.
questions.title: Physicochemical Properties of Drugs

questions.q: Which definition correctly describes dissolution?
options: The maximum amount of solute that a solvent can hold at equilibrium
The transfer of molecules or ions from the solid state into solution
A mixture of two or more components forming a single homogeneous phase
The component that determines the phase of a solution
The spontaneous movement of solute down a concentration gradient
questions.explanation: Dissolution is the transfer of molecules or ions from the solid state into a solution. Solubility is the extent to which dissolution proceeds, the amount of dissolved solute in equilibrium with undissolved solid.
questions.title: Physicochemical Properties of Drugs

questions.q: What is a saturated solution?
options: A solution in which the solute has completely dissolved with none remaining
A solution containing solute at the limit of its solubility, the concentration of which is the solubility
A solution in which the solvent has evaporated to dryness
Any solution with a concentration above 1 mol/dm3
A solution containing more than one solute
questions.explanation: When a solution contains the solute at the limit of its solubility it is saturated, and that concentration is the solubility of the solute. Solubility is therefore a concentration and can be expressed as g/L, mg/mL, % w/v or molarity.
questions.title: Physicochemical Properties of Drugs

questions.q: Which of these is listed as a factor affecting the solubility of a drug molecule?
options: The thickness of the diffusion layer
The degree of agitation of the medium
The volume of the dissolution medium
The crystal lattice energy of the molecule
The porosity of the solid particles
questions.explanation: Solubility is affected by lipophilicity (log P), molecular size and shape, pKa and crystal lattice energy. Agitation, medium volume, diffusion layer thickness and porosity affect dissolution rate rather than solubility itself.
questions.title: Physicochemical Properties of Drugs

questions.q: In pharmacopoeial terminology, a substance requiring 30 to 100 mL of water per gram at 20 degrees C is classified as which of the following?
options: Freely soluble
Soluble
Sparingly soluble
Slightly soluble
Very slightly soluble
questions.explanation: The scale runs: very soluble (<1 mL/g), freely soluble (1-10), soluble (10-30), sparingly soluble (30-100), slightly soluble (100-1000), very slightly soluble (1000-10,000) and practically insoluble (>10,000).
questions.title: Physicochemical Properties of Drugs

questions.q: A poorly soluble drug needs improved bioavailability. Which approach is suggested in the lecture?
options: Convert it to a salt form to improve solubility
Increase the melting point of the crystal
Formulate it as a hydrate rather than the anhydrous form
Increase the molecular weight of the compound
Add a hydrophobic lubricant to the formulation
questions.explanation: Soluble drugs are desirable because they have higher bioavailability, but drugs are often poorly soluble; converting to a salt form is given as a way to improve solubility.
questions.title: Physicochemical Properties of Drugs

questions.q: Magnesium stearate has a contact angle with water of 120 degrees. What does this tell you?
options: It is hydrophilic and readily wetted
It is hydrophobic and not readily wetted
It is highly wetted, with a contact angle close to zero
It is hygroscopic and will deliquesce
It has a high crystal lattice energy
questions.explanation: Hydrophobic materials have a contact angle greater than 90 degrees with water and are not readily wetted; magnesium stearate at 120 degrees is the example. Hydrophilic materials such as lactose (30 degrees) are readily wetted.
questions.title: Physicochemical Properties of Drugs

questions.q: An amorphous solid takes up water into its bulk from the atmosphere. What is this behaviour called, and what happens if the water dissolves the solid?
options: Adsorption, leading to efflorescence
Hygroscopy, leading to deliquescence if the solid dissolves
Solvation, leading to polymorphic conversion
Wetting, leading to a reduced contact angle
Sublimation, leading to loss of drug
questions.explanation: In a crystalline solid water tends to stay near the surface (adsorption), while an amorphous solid can absorb water into its bulk and is hygroscopic. If this water dissolves the solid it is called deliquescence, and such materials need protective packaging.
questions.title: Physicochemical Properties of Drugs

questions.q: In the Noyes-Whitney equation dC/dt = DA(Cs - C)/h, what does Cs represent?
options: The concentration of drug in the bulk dissolution medium
The thickness of the diffusion layer
The concentration in the diffusion layer surrounding the particle, equal to the saturation solubility
The effective surface area of the drug particles
The diffusion coefficient of the drug in the fluid
questions.explanation: Cs is the concentration of drug in the diffusion layer surrounding the solid particle, which equals the saturation solubility of the drug. C is the bulk concentration, A the effective surface area, h the diffusion layer thickness and D the diffusion coefficient.
questions.title: Physicochemical Properties of Drugs

questions.q: Why does milling a poorly soluble drug such as griseofulvin to a smaller particle size improve bioavailability?
options: It increases the saturation solubility of the drug
It lowers the crystal lattice energy of the drug
Surface area is inversely proportional to particle size, so dissolution rate increases
It converts the drug to its amorphous form
It reduces the thickness of the diffusion layer
questions.explanation: Dissolution occurs at the particle surface and its rate is proportional to surface area, which is inversely related to particle size. Making particles smaller raises the dissolution rate and can improve the bioavailability of poorly soluble drugs.
questions.title: Physicochemical Properties of Drugs

questions.q: The eutectic mixture of 55% griseofulvin with 45% succinic acid improves bioavailability. How does it work?
options: The succinic acid lowers gastric pH so the drug ionises
It is a crystalline solid dispersion whose water-soluble solid solvent dissolves, leaving a fine solution of the drug
The succinic acid acts as a disintegrant in the tablet
It converts griseofulvin into a more soluble salt
It forms a hydrate with a lower melting point
questions.explanation: The eutectic is a crystalline solid dispersion in which the solid solute is molecularly dispersed in a solid solvent. The water-soluble solid solvent dissolves and leaves a fine solution of the drug.
questions.title: Physicochemical Properties of Drugs

questions.q: Hydroxypropyl methylcellulose is very water soluble but takes many hours to hydrate and dissolve. What does this illustrate?
options: That solubility measurements are unreliable for polymers
That dissolution rate is not the same as solubility
That HPMC is practically insoluble by pharmacopoeial definition
That HPMC exists as a metastable polymorph
That sink conditions have not been achieved
questions.explanation: Dissolution is a process with a time factor, while solubility is the amount dissolved at equilibrium, a single fixed value. HPMC shows that a very soluble material can still dissolve slowly.
questions.title: Physicochemical Properties of Drugs

questions.q: Which unit is most appropriate for expressing a dissolution rate?
options: g/L
mg/mL
% w/v
mol/dm3
mg/s
questions.explanation: Dissolution rate has a time factor, so it must be expressed as an amount per unit time such as mg/s. The other units are all concentrations and therefore express solubility.
questions.title: Physicochemical Properties of Drugs

questions.q: The dissolution process has two stages. What are they?
options: Disintegration of the tablet followed by deaggregation of granules
Adsorption of solvent followed by deliquescence
An interfacial reaction at the solid surface, then migration of solute through the boundary layer to the bulk
Wetting of the powder followed by precipitation of the stable polymorph
Diffusion through the membrane followed by receptor binding
questions.explanation: Dissolution comprises an interfacial reaction at the solid surface, releasing solute molecules from the solid to the liquid phase, followed by migration or diffusion of those molecules through the boundary layers to the bulk of the solution.
questions.title: Physicochemical Properties of Drugs

questions.q: Why does a larger drug molecule tend to be less soluble?
options: Larger molecules always carry more non-polar groups
A larger cavity is required in the solvent and more solvent-solute interactions are needed
Larger molecules cannot form hydrogen bonds
Larger molecules have higher crystal lattice energies by definition
Larger molecules diffuse faster and so leave solution
questions.explanation: The surface area of the drug molecule affects solubility: the larger the molecule, the larger the cavity required in the solvent and the greater the number of solvent-solute interactions needed.
questions.title: Physicochemical Properties of Drugs

questions.q: How does ionisation of a substituent such as -COOH affect aqueous solubility?
options: It has no effect because the molecular weight is unchanged
It decreases solubility because charge repels water
-COOH is slightly hydrophilic, but -COO- is very hydrophilic, so ionisation increases solubility
It increases solubility only for basic drugs
It converts the group to a hydrophobic one
questions.explanation: Polar groups such as -OH increase solubility by hydrogen bonding with water; non-polar groups such as -CH3 and -Cl impart low solubility. Ionisation increases solubility because -COOH and -NH2 are only slightly hydrophilic whereas -COO- and -NH3+ are very hydrophilic.
questions.title: Physicochemical Properties of Drugs

questions.q: Which factor affects Cs, the solubility term in the Noyes-Whitney equation, rather than the surface area term?
options: Milling the drug to a smaller particle size
Adding a wetting agent to the formulation
The porosity of the solid particles
The crystalline form of the solid, such as polymorph, hydrate or amorphous form
The degree of agitation of the medium
questions.explanation: Cs is affected by temperature, the nature of the dissolution medium (co-solvents, pH), molecular structure of the solute, the crystalline form (polymorphs, hydrates, solvates, amorphous) and the presence of other compounds. Milling, wetting and porosity act on surface area A.
questions.title: Physicochemical Properties of Drugs

questions.q: What are sink conditions in a dissolution test?
options: The medium volume is at least three times that needed to form a saturated solution, so dissolved drug does not affect the rate
The medium is exactly saturated with drug before the test begins
The medium is stirred at a fixed rate throughout the run
The temperature is held at body temperature for the whole run
The dissolution vessel is sealed to prevent evaporation
questions.explanation: Sink conditions require the dissolution medium volume to be at least three times that required to form a saturated solution, ensuring the amount already dissolved does not affect the dissolution rate as the run progresses.
questions.title: Physicochemical Properties of Drugs

questions.q: Which factors determine h, the thickness of the diffusion layer?
options: Particle size, porosity and wettability
Degree of agitation, volume of medium and viscosity of the medium
Temperature, pH and choice of co-solvent
Crystal form, hydrate state and lattice energy
Molecular weight and shape of the solute only
questions.explanation: The diffusion layer thickness depends on the degree of agitation, the volume of the dissolution medium and its viscosity. The diffusion coefficient D depends on medium viscosity and the molecular characteristics and size of the diffusing molecules.
questions.title: Physicochemical Properties of Drugs

questions.q: In Fick's first law, J = -D(dc/dx), what does the negative sign indicate?
options: That the diffusion coefficient is always negative
That flux occurs in the direction of decreasing concentration
That the concentration gradient is measured in the opposite direction to flow
That diffusion is an energy-consuming process
That the flux is reduced by the viscosity of the medium
questions.explanation: The negative sign indicates that flux is in the direction of decreasing concentration, that is, movement from high to low concentration. J is the flux across a plane of unit area in unit time and D the diffusion coefficient.
questions.title: Physicochemical Properties of Drugs

questions.q: According to the Stokes-Einstein equation, how does the diffusion coefficient D vary?
options: Directly with solute molecular radius and directly with solvent viscosity
Inversely with solute molecular radius and inversely with solvent viscosity
Directly with molecular radius but inversely with viscosity
Inversely with temperature and directly with viscosity
Independently of both molecular size and viscosity
questions.explanation: The Stokes-Einstein equation shows the diffusion coefficient is inversely related to the solute molecular radius and to the viscosity of the solvent, and is also affected by the shape of the solute molecule.
questions.title: Physicochemical Properties of Drugs

questions.q: According to the key points, what must be true for a drug to work in the body?
options: It must be crystalline
It must be administered orally
It must be in solution
It must be formulated as a salt
It must have a low melting point
questions.explanation: For a drug to work in the body it must be in solution. This is governed by its physicochemical properties, including the properties of the solid particles and the solubility of the drug and everything that affects it.
questions.title: Physicochemical Properties of Drugs

questions.q: LO1 in this lecture requires students to recall and describe which fundamental sciences?
options: Cell biology, basic pharmacology, microbiology and pharmaceutical sciences
Organic synthesis only
Clinical diagnosis only
Hospital pharmacy law only
Patient counselling skills only
questions.explanation: Assessment slide LO1 requires recall and description of the fundamental science underpinning pharmacy, including cell biology, basic pharmacology, microbiology and pharmaceutical sciences.
questions.title: Physicochemical Properties of Drugs

questions.q: Which of the following is listed as a physicochemical property of drugs?
options: Partition coefficient
Patient compliance
Brand name
Prescribing frequency
Tablet colour only
questions.explanation: Physicochemical properties listed include molecular formula, molecular weight, physical state, appearance, solubility, pKa, melting and boiling points, vapour pressure and partition coefficient.
questions.title: Physicochemical Properties of Drugs

questions.q: Clinical response results from interaction between drug in solution and:
options: Receptors or enzymes, altering biological processes
Tablet excipients only
Packaging materials
The colour of the formulation
Prescription writing style
questions.explanation: The lecture states that clinical response results from an interaction between drug in solution and a receptor or enzyme, leading to alteration of biological processes present before administration.
questions.title: Physicochemical Properties of Drugs

questions.q: Pharmaceutically relevant solids are held in fixed positions by:
options: Intermolecular forces such as hydrogen bonds and van der Waals forces
Covalent bonds only between separate molecules
Ionic bonds only in gases
Gravity alone
No forces at all
questions.explanation: All pharmaceutically relevant solids consist of molecules with definite volume and shape, held in fixed positions by intermolecular forces including hydrogen bonds and van der Waals forces.
questions.title: Physicochemical Properties of Drugs

questions.q: The sucrose example contrasts a single molecule (~5.62×10⁻²² g) with a crystal particle because:
options: Solid drug particles are vastly heavier than individual molecules
Molecules weigh more than crystals
Sucrose has no molar mass
Crystals contain no molecules
Particle size is irrelevant to formulation
questions.explanation: For sucrose (molar mass 342.3 g/mol), each molecule weighs about 5.62×10⁻²² g, whereas a ~400 micron crystal particle weighs about 6.25×10⁻⁴ g, illustrating solid particle versus molecule scale.
questions.title: Physicochemical Properties of Drugs

questions.q: Wettability of a drug powder is estimated using:
options: Contact angle with water
Melting point alone
Optical rotation
Vapour pressure
Brand name
questions.explanation: Factors influencing dissolution include wetting, and wettability is estimated from the contact angle between the liquid/vapour interface and the substrate surface.
questions.title: Physicochemical Properties of Drugs

questions.q: An ideal solid drug formulation should be:
options: Hydrophilic enough to wet but not so hygroscopic that stability suffers
Completely hydrophobic with contact angle >120°
Highly hygroscopic regardless of stability
Unable to dissolve once added to solvent
Free of all intermolecular forces
questions.explanation: An ideal formulation is hydrophilic enough to allow wetting but not so hygroscopic that stability problems arise; once added to solvent, dissolution can begin.
questions.title: Physicochemical Properties of Drugs

questions.q: The first step in the dissolution interfacial reaction sequence involves:
options: Removal of a solute molecule from the solid
Diffusion through the bulk liquid only
Tablet coating
Protein binding in plasma
Hepatic metabolism
questions.explanation: The interfacial reaction diagram shows removal of a solute molecule from the solid, creation of a solvent cavity, and insertion of the solute into solution as sequential steps.
questions.title: Physicochemical Properties of Drugs

questions.q: During dissolution, solute molecules migrate through:
options: A boundary layer between the solid particle and bulk liquid
The tablet label
Blood vessels directly
The GI epithelium without diffusion
Air above the dissolution vessel only
questions.explanation: Step 2 of dissolution is migration/diffusion of solute molecules through the boundary layer, where concentration falls from Cs at the particle surface to C in the bulk liquid.
questions.title: Physicochemical Properties of Drugs

questions.q: Increasing effective surface area of drug exposed to dissolution medium is achieved by:
options: Disintegration and deaggregation of tablets into primary particles
Compressing tablets more tightly
Removing all excipients
Freezing the dosage form
Adding only hydrophobic lubricants
questions.explanation: The lecture shows that intact tablets dissolve slowly, granules moderately, and primary drug particles rapidly, because disintegration and deaggregation increase effective surface area.
questions.title: Physicochemical Properties of Drugs

questions.q: In the Noyes-Whitney equation, a large volume of dissolution medium promotes dissolution by:
options: Maintaining sink conditions with low C relative to Cs
Increasing Cs to zero
Eliminating the boundary layer entirely
Preventing any diffusion
Stopping interfacial reaction
questions.explanation: Concentration C in solution at time t is affected by dissolution medium volume, which influences the difference between C and Cs and helps maintain sink conditions when dissolved solute is removed or diluted.
questions.title: Physicochemical Properties of Drugs

questions.q: Molecular diffusion is defined as:
options: Spontaneous movement from high to low concentration
Active transport against a gradient
Evaporation of solvents only
Crystallisation of amorphous solids
Binding to plasma albumin
questions.explanation: Diffusion is the spontaneous movement of a substance from an area of high concentration to an area of lower concentration, occurring in liquids and gases through random particle collisions.
questions.title: Physicochemical Properties of Drugs

questions.q: In the boundary-layer diffusion diagram, Cs represents:
options: Concentration of API at the solid particle surface
Concentration in the bulk liquid only
Saturation solubility in a distant reservoir
Tablet disintegration time
Partition coefficient
questions.explanation: The diffusion of solute molecules diagram shows concentration of API Cs at the particle surface decreasing through the boundary layer to C in the bulk liquid.
questions.title: Physicochemical Properties of Drugs

questions.q: Dissolution rate is clinically significant for:
options: Formulation performance, absorption and onset of action
Only cosmetic appearance of tablets
Only storage temperature of packaging
Only the colour of the API
Only independent study reading lists
questions.explanation: The summary states diffusion is significant for dissolution and absorption, while dissolution rate is significant for formulation, rate and extent of absorption, and onset of action.
questions.title: Physicochemical Properties of Drugs

questions.q: For a drug to produce a clinical response it must first:
options: Be in solution and interact with receptors or enzymes
Be formulated as a solid only
Remain permanently bound to plasma proteins
Never cross biological membranes
Exist only as a gas
questions.explanation: The slide reiterates that clinical response results from interaction between drug in solution and receptor/enzyme, altering biological processes.
questions.title: Physicochemical Properties of Drugs

questions.q: Why is good water solubility important for an API?
options: It supports dissolution and therefore absorption and clinical effect
It prevents all metabolism
It guarantees zero protein binding
It removes the need for any formulation
It makes the drug insoluble in GI fluids
questions.explanation: The example SAQ asks why good water solubility matters: solubility affects dissolution, which in turn affects absorption and the concentration reaching the site of action.
questions.title: Physicochemical Properties of Drugs

questions.q: In an equilibrium constant expression K = [products]/[reactants], which species is always ignored?
options: Any solid present
Any gas present
A pure liquid such as water when it is acting as the solvent
The species present in lowest concentration
Any ionic species
questions.explanation: Pure liquids, for example water when acting as solvent, are always ignored in the equilibrium constant expression. The constant is based on stoichiometry and gives no indication of rate.
questions.title: Acids & Bases

questions.q: A catalyst or enzyme is added to a reaction at equilibrium. What is the effect?
options: It speeds up attainment of equilibrium but has no effect on the overall amount
It increases the yield of product at equilibrium
It changes the value of the equilibrium constant
It shifts the equilibrium towards the reactants
It has no effect on either rate or position
questions.explanation: The equilibrium constant gives no indication of rate. A catalyst or enzyme speeds up attainment of equilibrium but has no effect on the overall amount of product formed.
questions.title: Acids & Bases

questions.q: Acetic acid has a Ka of 1.8 x 10^-5 M. What is its pKa?
questions.explanation: pKa is the negative logarithm to base 10 of Ka. For Ka = 1.8 x 10^-5 M, pKa = -log(1.8 x 10^-5) = 4.75.
questions.title: Acids & Bases

questions.q: Which relationships between the p values are correct at 25 degrees C?
options: Kw = Ka + Kb and pKw = pH x pOH = 14
Kw = Ka.Kb and pKw = pH + pOH = 14
Kw = Ka/Kb and pKw = pH - pOH = 14
Kw = [H3O+] - [OH-] and pKw = 7
Kw = Ka.Kb and pKw = pH + pOH = 7
questions.explanation: Kw = [H3O+][OH-], Kw = Ka.Kb, and pKw = pH + pOH = 14 at 25 degrees C.
questions.title: Acids & Bases

questions.q: What is the approximate pKa of most compounds containing a carboxylic acid functional group?
options: Around 3, in the range 1 to 5
Around 7, in the range 6 to 8
Around 9, in the range 7 to 10.5
Around 12, in the range 10 to 14
Around 16, in the range 16 to 19
questions.explanation: Carboxylic acid containing compounds have pKa values around 3, with a range of about 1 to 5. Amine containing compounds are around 9, range 7 to 10.5, and alcohols 16 to 19.
questions.title: Acids & Bases

questions.q: Tetracycline has pKa values of 3.3, 7.7 and 9.7. What is its overall pKa?
questions.explanation: For a substance with multiple Ka values the overall pKa is the sum divided by the number of values: (3.3 + 7.7 + 9.7)/3 = 20.7/3 = 6.9, corresponding to an overall Ka of 1.3 x 10^-7.
questions.title: Acids & Bases

questions.q: Two drug molecules are compared. Which statement about pKa and strength is correct?
options: A low pKa means a strong acid; for a base, a high pKa means a stronger base
A low pKa means a weak acid; for a base, a low pKa means a strong base
A high pKa means a strong acid and also a strong base
pKa indicates concentration rather than strength
A low pKa means a strong acid and also a strong base
questions.explanation: For an acid drug, a low pKa is a strong acid and a high pKa a weaker acid. For a base drug, a low pKa is a weak base and a high pKa a stronger base. Strength is not the same as concentration.
questions.title: Acids & Bases

questions.q: Which pair of definitions is the Bronsted-Lowry theory of 1923?
options: Acid is an electron pair acceptor; base is an electron pair donor
Acid is a proton donor; base is a proton acceptor
Acid produces H+ in water; base produces OH- in water only
Acid has a pH below 7; base has a pH above 7
Acid is fully dissociated; base is partially dissociated
questions.explanation: Bronsted and Lowry defined an acid as a proton (H+) donor and a base as a proton acceptor. For an acid to exist a base must be present, and vice versa.
questions.title: Acids & Bases

questions.q: What is a conjugate base?
options: The part of a molecule remaining after proton donation
Any hydroxide-containing compound
A base that has accepted two protons
The salt formed when an acid reacts with a metal
A base whose pKb equals its pKa
questions.explanation: The conjugate base is the part of a molecule remaining after proton donation, following the HA model where ACID is in equilibrium with BASE plus PROTON.
questions.title: Acids & Bases

questions.q: How does a strong acid differ from a weak acid?
options: A strong acid is more concentrated than a weak acid
A strong acid has a higher pKa than a weak acid
A strong acid undergoes full dissociation whereas a weak acid dissociates only about 1 per cent
A strong acid contains more than one ionisable proton
A strong acid is always inorganic and a weak acid always organic
questions.explanation: A strong acid undergoes full dissociation, while a weak acid dissociates only about 1 per cent. Strength must not be confused with concentration.
questions.title: Acids & Bases

questions.q: Over what range does physiological pH rarely stray, even though the pH scale runs from 0 to 14?
options: pH 1.0 to 3.0
pH 4.0 to 8.5
pH 6.8 to 7.8
pH 10 to 14
questions.explanation: In reality physiological pH rarely exceeds the range 4.0 to 8.5. Blood itself is far tighter at 7.35 to 7.45, with 6.8 and 7.8 being fatal.
questions.title: Acids & Bases

questions.q: The ionic product of water, Kw, has what value at 25 degrees C?
questions.explanation: Kw is the equilibrium constant for the self-ionisation of water into hydronium and hydroxide ions. It is constant at 25 degrees C and equal to 1.0 x 10^-14 M, giving pKw = 14.
questions.title: Acids & Bases

questions.q: What is the levelling effect?
options: All buffers reach the same capacity at their pKa
All acids become indistinguishable in strength when placed in a strong base
The pH electrode reading drifts to a constant value over time
The activity coefficient approaches 1 in dilute solution
All titration curves have the same shape at the equivalence point
questions.explanation: The levelling effect means all acids become indistinguishable in terms of their strength when placed in a strong base, and vice versa. An acid stronger than H3O+ dissolved in water simply protonates water to make more H3O+.
questions.title: Acids & Bases

questions.q: According to the Nernst equation, a half cell potential changes by how much per tenfold change in measured ion concentration when n = 1?
options: 5.9 mV
59 mV
298 mV
questions.explanation: The Nernst equation gives E = Eo - 0.059 log10 Q at 298 K for n = 1, so a tenfold change in ion concentration, which is one pH unit, corresponds to 59 mV.
questions.title: Acids & Bases

questions.q: In the Nernst equation E0 = (RT/zF) ln Q, what does z represent?
options: Faraday's constant
The gas constant
Logarithm with base e
Temperature
Valence of the ion
questions.explanation: z is the valence of the ion, that is the number of electrons transferred. F is the Faraday constant (96,485 C/mol), R the gas constant (8.314 J/K/mol) and T the temperature in kelvin.
questions.title: Acids & Bases

questions.q: What does a glass pH electrode actually respond to?
options: The total concentration of all ions present
The activity of the ion, its effective concentration
The redox potential of the test solution
The molarity of hydroxide ions only
The absorbance of the solution at 434 nm
questions.explanation: Electrodes only use activity, A = gamma[X]. Thermodynamic activity is a measure of the effective concentration of a species in a mixture and is related to chemical potential.
questions.title: Acids & Bases

questions.q: Over which pH range do glass electrodes work best, and what happens above it?
options: pH 3 to 10; above pH 10 sodium or potassium interference makes the reading lower than the actual value
pH 1 to 14; there is no upper limitation
pH 0 to 7; above pH 7 the membrane dissolves
pH 5 to 9; above pH 9 the electrode reads higher than the actual value
pH 3 to 10; above pH 10 the electrode reads higher than the actual value
questions.explanation: Glass electrodes work best between pH 3 and 10. In alkaline solution above pH 10 the measured pH is lower than the actual value, due to sodium or potassium ion interference; an acid error occurs below pH -1.
questions.title: Acids & Bases

questions.q: At what pH does a buffer show its best buffering action, and what is the state of the acid there?
options: At pH 7, where the acid is fully ionised
At pH equal to the pKa, where the acid species is 50 per cent ionised
At pH two units below the pKa, where the acid is unionised
At pH 14 minus the pKa, where the acid is fully dissociated
At the isoelectric point, where the acid carries no charge
questions.explanation: Best buffering action occurs at pH approximately equal to the pKa. When pH = pKa the acid species is 50 per cent ionised. Commercial buffers are usually weak acids or their salts.
questions.title: Acids & Bases

questions.q: Adding 10 mL of 0.1 M HCl to 1 litre of water at pH 7 drops the pH to 3, but the same addition to 1 litre of water containing 1 gram of sodium acetate gives pH 6.9. What does this demonstrate?
options: That HCl is neutralised chemically by sodium acetate to form water
That buffering action resists a change in pH
That sodium acetate raises the ionic strength and salts out the acid
That the glass electrode is in error at low pH
That sodium acetate is a strong base
questions.explanation: This is the experimental illustration of buffering action, the resistance to pH change. Buffer examples given include amino acids, phosphates, citrates and lactates.
questions.title: Acids & Bases

questions.q: Which is the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation?
options: pH = pKa + log([salt]/[acid])
pH = pKa - log([salt]/[acid])
pH = pKw - pOH
pH = -log[H+] + log[OH-]
pH = pKa x log([acid]/[salt])
questions.explanation: The Henderson-Hasselbalch equation is pH = pKa + log[salt]/[acid], or in general pH = pKa + log[base]/[acid]. It assumes complete dissociation, mean activity coefficient tending to 1, and salt and acid concentrations far exceeding [H+] at the start.
questions.title: Acids & Bases

questions.q: Drug X is a weak acid HA with pKa 7.0, in a buffer at pH 6.5. What percentage is unionised?
options: 24 per cent
32 per cent
50 per cent
68 per cent
76 per cent
questions.explanation: log(base/acid) = 6.5 - 7.0 = -0.5, so base/acid = 0.3162. The total is 0.3162 + 1 = 1.3162 and the unionised fraction is 1/1.3162 = 0.76, that is 76 per cent.
questions.title: Acids & Bases

questions.q: What is the pH of a 0.011 mol/dm3 solution of the strong base NaOH?
questions.explanation: NaOH is a strong electrolyte and fully ionises. pOH = -log(0.011) = 1.96, and pH = pKw - pOH = 14 - 1.96 = 12.04.
questions.title: Acids & Bases

questions.q: A drug has a Ka of 1.65 x 10^-6. What is its pKa?
questions.title: Acids & Bases

questions.q: Polar surface area is used to predict solubility and penetration. Which threshold applies to good CNS penetration?
options: PSA less than 90 square angstroms
PSA less than or equal to 140 square angstroms
PSA greater than 140 square angstroms
PSA greater than 200 square angstroms
PSA equal to zero
questions.explanation: PSA models the surface area of polar atoms. Compounds with PSA at or below 140 square angstroms have high aqueous solubility, while hydrophobic drugs with PSA below 90 square angstroms have good penetration into tissues such as the CNS.
questions.title: Acids & Bases

questions.q: Calculate the ionic strength of a 0.01 M solution of MgSO4.
questions.explanation: Ionic strength I = half the sum of cz squared for all species. For 0.01 M MgSO4 both ions have valency 2, giving I = 0.5 x [(0.01 x 4) + (0.01 x 4)] = 0.04, four times that of 0.01 M NaCl.
questions.title: Acids & Bases

questions.q: What is salting-out?
options: Precipitation of a drug when the pH is raised above its pKa
Reduced solubility of certain molecules, often macromolecules, in a solution of very high ionic strength
Crystallisation of sodium chloride from a saturated solution
Conversion of a drug base into its salt to improve solubility
Loss of buffering capacity when a salt is added
questions.explanation: Salting-out is the reduced solubility of certain molecules, often large molecules or macromolecules, in solutions of very high ionic strength, caused by charge screening. Macrolide antibiotics and polyelectrolytes may precipitate.
questions.title: Acids & Bases

questions.q: How is log P defined, and what does a large positive value indicate?
options: The ratio of ionised to unionised drug; a large value means highly ionised
log of [unionised drug in octanol]/[drug in water]; a large positive value means the drug is more lipid soluble
log of [drug in water]/[drug in octanol]; a large positive value means the drug is water soluble
The ratio of drug in blood to drug in tissue; a large value means good distribution
log of the partition of drug between two aqueous buffers
questions.explanation: log P is log10 of unionised drug in octanol divided by drug in water. A large positive log P means the drug is more lipid soluble, log P of 0 means equally soluble in both phases and a negative log P means water soluble.
questions.title: Acids & Bases

questions.q: How does log D differ from log P?
options: log D is measured at 37 degrees C whereas log P is measured at 25 degrees C
log D uses chloroform as the organic phase instead of octanol
log D takes the ionised species into account, correcting log P for the species prevalent at a particular pH
log D applies only to bases and log P only to acids
log D is the reciprocal of log P
questions.explanation: log D is the distribution ratio, correcting log P for the predominant ionised species and compensating for the species prevalent at a given pH given the compound's acid or base nature and its pKa.
questions.title: Acids & Bases

questions.q: Terbinafine HCl has a log P of 6.5. What practical problem does this create?
options: It is so water soluble that it cannot cross membranes
It is extremely lipophilic and requires special solubilisation in oils, microemulsions or micelles
It is fully ionised at all physiological pH values
It cannot be given by any route other than intravenous
It has a polar surface area above 140 square angstroms
questions.explanation: Extremely lipophilic drugs such as testosterone (log P 3.3) or terbinafine HCl (log P 6.5) require special solubilisation in oils, microemulsions or micelles.
questions.title: Acids & Bases

questions.q: Which substituents favour aqueous solubility rather than lipophilicity?
options: Aliphatic -CH3 groups and benzene rings
Alkene groups and long alkane chains
Polar groups such as -NH2, -COOH, -CHO, -C=O and -OH
Aromatic rings capable of pi-stacking
Halogenated alkyl chains
questions.explanation: Aqueous solubility is favoured by electronegativity and partial charges, with polar groups such as -NH2 (-NH3+), -COOH (-COO-), -CHO, -C=O and -OH. Alkanes, aliphatic -CH3, alkenes and benzene rings disfavour it and confer lipophilicity.
questions.title: Acids & Bases

questions.q: Which interaction is the strongest, according to the bond strength table?
options: Hydrogen bonding at 10-20 kJ/mol
Ionic at 20-45 kJ/mol
Hydrophobic at 4-20 kJ/mol
Pi-stacking at 5-70 kJ/mol
Covalent at 200-630 kJ/mol
questions.explanation: Covalent bonds are by far the strongest at 200-630 kJ/mol. Pi-stacking spans 5-70, ionic 20-45, hydrogen 10-20 and hydrophobic 4-20 kJ/mol.
questions.title: Acids & Bases

questions.q: Which are the three main types of titration described?
options: Conventional acid-base, back titration and potentiometric titration
Gravimetric, volumetric and colorimetric titration
Direct, indirect and reverse titration
Redox, complexometric and precipitation titration
Manual, automated and spectrophotometric titration
questions.explanation: The three main types involving acids and bases are conventional acid-base titration, back titration (mopping up added excess reactant) and potentiometric titration using electrodes.
questions.title: Acids & Bases

questions.q: In titration work, how do accuracy and precision differ?
options: Accuracy is variability in repeats; precision is closeness to the true value
Accuracy, or trueness, is closeness of the average to the true value; precision describes variability in the individual repeats
Accuracy applies to volumes and precision to concentrations
They are two names for the same property
Accuracy is reported as %RSD; precision is reported as the mean
questions.explanation: Accuracy, also known as trueness, is the mathematical closeness of the average to the true or theoretical value. Precision describes variability in the individual repeats, expressed as variance, standard deviation, %RSD or range. Repeats should agree within 0.1 cm3.
questions.title: Acids & Bases

questions.q: What is the isoelectric point of a zwitterionic species such as an amino acid?
options: The pH at which the species has no net overall charge
The pH at which the species is fully protonated
The pH equal to the first pKa of the molecule
The pH at which the species is most soluble in water
The pH at which half of the carboxyl groups are ionised
questions.explanation: A zwitterion carries both positive and negative charges. The isoelectric point (pI or IEP) is the pH at which the species has no net overall charge. Glycine and glutamic acid are given as natural buffers.
questions.title: Acids & Bases

questions.q: Why does dissolved carbon dioxide interfere with acid-base titrations?
options: It reacts with the indicator and bleaches it
It forms carbonic acid and hydrogen carbonate, making the solution acidic so more base is needed to neutralise
It raises the pH of distilled water to about 8.4
It causes the glass electrode to become dehydrated
It precipitates the analyte as an insoluble carbonate
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide in solution forms carbonic acid and hydrogen carbonate (pKa 6.5 and 10.5), making acid. Distilled water sits at about pH 5.6, and a normal strong acid-base titration may require more base to neutralise. Boiling the solution is a compensatory strategy.
questions.title: Acids & Bases

questions.q: What is peptisation?
options: The breakdown of a peptide drug by gastric acid
Aided suspension of colloidal solids by adding an electrolyte that adsorbs on the surface
The precipitation of a protein at its isoelectric point
The conversion of an acid drug to its conjugate base
The removal of carbon dioxide from a solution by boiling
questions.explanation: Peptisation is the aided suspension of colloidal solids achieved by adding an electrolyte, which adsorbs onto the particle surface. It links pH and pKa to ionisation, charge and hence solubility or affinity.
questions.title: Acids & Bases

questions.q: Ibuprofen has a pKa of 4.43. What is its ionisation state at pH 7.0?
options: Fully unionised, because the pH is above the pKa
Exactly 50 per cent ionised
Essentially fully ionised, because the pH is well above the pKa of this acid
Unionised, because ibuprofen is a base
Ionisation cannot be predicted without the log P
questions.explanation: Ibuprofen is a weak acid with pKa 4.43. At pH 7.0, more than two pH units above the pKa, the acid drug is essentially fully ionised.
questions.title: Acids & Bases

questions.q: Which buffering agent has a pKa closest to physiological blood pH?
options: Phosphoric acid, pKa1 2.15
Citric acid, pKa1 3.13
Acetic acid, pKa 4.76
The phosphate anion H2PO4-, pKa2 7.21
Boric acid, pKa1 9.24
questions.explanation: Since best buffering occurs at pH close to the pKa, the H2PO4- anion with pKa2 of 7.21 is the closest match to blood pH of 7.35 to 7.45.
questions.title: Acids & Bases

questions.q: Lowering the pH of the aqueous phase forces a weak acid drug to partition into the organic phase. Which principle explains this?
options: The levelling effect
Le Chatelier's principle and the common ion effect
The Nernst equation
Salting-out by increased ionic strength
The Stokes-Einstein relationship
questions.explanation: Acidification protonates the conjugate base, driving the equilibrium [A-] + [H+] to [HA aq] to [HA org] towards the right and forcing the unionised species into the apolar phase. This is the basis of the common ion effect and Le Chatelier's principle.
questions.title: Acids & Bases

questions.q: In spectrophotometric titration with bromothymol blue, what is the isosbestic point?
options: The pH at which the indicator changes colour completely
The wavelength of maximum absorbance of the yellow form
The wavelength at which absorbance is the same regardless of the ratio of the two coloured forms
The point at which all analyte has been consumed
The pKa of the indicator, 8.3
questions.explanation: Bromothymol blue has absorbance maxima at 434 nm (yellow) and 600 nm (blue) with a pKa of 8.3. The isosbestic point is where the spectra of the two forms cross, so absorbance there is independent of their ratio.
questions.title: Acids & Bases

questions.q: What topics does lecture part 1 on partition coefficient, pK values, acids, bases and buffering cover?
options: Only organic synthesis routes
Partition coefficient, pK values, acids, bases and buffering
Microbial enumeration methods
Cell membrane transport only
Antimicrobial resistance mechanisms
questions.explanation: The part 1 title slide lists partition coefficient, pK values, acids, bases and buffering as the lecture focus.
questions.title: Acids & Bases

questions.q: Which pair is listed as an acid and its matching base in the common acids and bases table?
options: Hydrochloric acid and ammonium hydroxide
Sodium hydroxide and nitric acid
Acetic acid and sulfuric acid
Boric acid and potassium hydroxide
Phosphoric acid and trimethylamine only
questions.explanation: The table pairs hydrochloric acid with ammonium hydroxide, nitric acid with sodium hydroxide, sulfuric acid with potassium hydroxide, and acetic acid with trimethylamine.
questions.title: Acids & Bases

questions.q: According to the ionisable drug groups slide, which statement is correct?
options: Aspirin is shown as a base drug and codeine as an acid drug
Both aspirin and codeine lack ionisable groups
Codeine is shown as a base drug and aspirin as an acid drug
Neither drug ionises in aqueous solution
Both are classified only as zwitterions
questions.explanation: The slide illustrates ionisable groups of acid and base drugs, showing codeine as a base and aspirin as an acid.
questions.title: Acids & Bases

questions.q: Which approximate pKa range is given for carboxylate-type drug molecules?
options: Around 16 to 19
Around 3 to 5
Around 7 to 8 only
Around 12 to 14
Around 1 to 2
questions.explanation: Carboxylate-type molecules have pKa around 3 to 5, with examples including ethanoic acid at 4.75 and aspirin at 3.5. Amine-type bases are around 9.
questions.title: Acids & Bases

questions.q: Which drug is given as an example with both acid and base functional groups?
options: Benzyl penicillin only
Atropine only
Norfloxacin with pKa1 5.9 and pKa2 8.2
Procaine with a single pKa of 9
Ethanol with pKa 16
questions.explanation: Benzyl penicillin is listed as an acid (pKa 2.8), atropine as a base (pKa 9.7), and norfloxacin as both acid and base with pKa1 5.9 and pKa2 8.2.
questions.title: Acids & Bases

questions.q: In the acids and bases background slide, what is described as a proton-donating species?
options: A base such as R-NX
An acid such as AH or AnH
A salt such as sodium phenobarbital only
Water acting solely as solvent
A conjugate base A-
questions.explanation: An acid is AH or AnH, for example HNO3 or H2SO4, defined as a proton (H+ aq) donating species. A base accepts a proton.
questions.title: Acids & Bases

questions.q: The term pH derives from which French phrase meaning power of hydrogen?
options: pouvoir de Hydrogene or puissance de Hydrogene
pression de Hydrogene
proportion de Hydrogene
potentiel de Hydroxyde
point de Hydrogene
questions.explanation: pH comes from the French pouvoir de Hydrogene or puissance de Hydrogene. The pH scale was devised in 1909 by Sorensen.
questions.title: Acids & Bases

questions.q: Which feature of the glass electrode for pH measurement is emphasised on the slide?
options: It depends on redox processes at the membrane
It uses an ion selective glass electrode with a thin semi-permeable membrane
It measures only total dissolved solids
It requires boiling of the sample
It cannot distinguish H+ from Na+
questions.explanation: The glass electrode is ion selective, does not depend on redox processes, and makes use of a thin semi-permeable membrane allowing selective passage.
questions.title: Acids & Bases

questions.q: In the detailed pH electrode diagram, which ions does the hydrated gel bind?
options: Only chloride ions
H+ and Na+
Only hydroxide ions
Calcium and magnesium only
Potassium ions exclusively
questions.explanation: The hydrated gel binds H+ and Na+, while the non-hydrated gel allows only Na+ passage. Ion-specific liganding to silicate occurs at the membrane.
questions.title: Acids & Bases

questions.q: Why are buffering systems important for aspirin according to the hydrolysis data?
options: Buffers increase the rate of hydrolysis at all pH values
To retain drug suitability and stability by controlling pH-dependent hydrolysis
Aspirin does not hydrolyse in aqueous solution
Buffers eliminate the need for storage temperature control
Hydrolysis is fastest at neutral pH only
questions.explanation: The slide shows aspirin hydrolysis rate varies strongly with pH and states that a buffering system is used to retain drug suitability and stability.
questions.title: Acids & Bases

questions.q: Which topic is NOT listed among the part 1 lecture key takeaways?
options: pKa, pKb and pKw
Henderson-Hasselbalch equation
PSA and log P/D titrations
pH measurement and the glass electrode
Buffers and buffering
questions.explanation: Part 1 key points include pKa/pKb/pKw, acids and bases, pH basis, pH measurement/glass electrode, Henderson-Hasselbalch, and buffers. PSA and log P/D belong to part 2.
questions.title: Acids & Bases

questions.q: In the example SAQ, what Henderson-Hasselbalch input values are given for drug HA?
options: log10(base/acid) = -0.80, pKa = 7.00, pH = 6.20
log10(base/acid) = +0.80, pKa = 6.20, pH = 7.00
pKa = 8.3 and pH = 10.9
Ka = 1.8 x 10^-5 only
pKw = 14 with no drug data
questions.explanation: The SAQ asks for unionised versus ionised drug percentage when log10(base/acid) is -0.80 with pKa 7.00 and solution pH 6.20 for weak acid HA.
questions.title: Acids & Bases

questions.q: Lecture part 2 on partition coefficient, pK values, acids, bases and buffering is labelled as which part?
options: Part 1 only
Part 2
Part 3
A revision session with no part number
An independent study module
questions.explanation: The second title slide lists partition coefficient, pK values, acids, bases and buffering with the label (#2), indicating part 2 of the material.
questions.title: Acids & Bases

questions.q: According to the thermodynamics slide, what does chemical potential depend on?
options: Only the temperature of the system
The concentration of active species and links to free energy minimised at equilibrium
The colour of the indicator used
The density of the titrant alone
The molecular weight of water only
questions.explanation: Chemical potential is the likelihood of a reaction depending on the concentration of active species. It links to free energy, which is minimised at equilibrium.
questions.title: Acids & Bases

questions.q: Which attributes are listed as key in defining drug and excipient molecules?
options: Dissolution profile in water, log P, RMM, substituents, pKa and partial charges
Only melting point and refractive index
Boiling point and vapour pressure exclusively
Crystal colour and odour
Molecular symmetry and isotope mass only
questions.explanation: Key defining attributes include dissolution profile in aquo, log P, RMM, substituents, pKa-ionisation, and partial charges.
questions.title: Acids & Bases

questions.q: In experimental log P determination, what do the octanol and aqueous phases model?
options: Crystal lattice energies in solids
Fatty structures of the body
Ionic strength of blood plasma only
The pH of gastric fluid exclusively
Enzyme binding sites in the liver
questions.explanation: Experimental log P uses octanol or organic phase versus aqueous phase and is designed to model the fatty structures of the body.
questions.title: Acids & Bases

questions.q: Which log P modelling methods are named on the brain capillary permeability slide?
options: A log P, C log P, M log P and X log P
Only Hamaker and Traube methods
Nernst and Henderson methods
Fick and Stokes methods
Arrhenius and van't Hoff methods
questions.explanation: Computer simulation methods listed are A log P and X log P (atom-based contributions) and C log P and M log P (fragment-based or atom-based contributions).
questions.title: Acids & Bases

questions.q: Why is the dissociation constant very important in pharmaceutical science?
options: It determines only the colour of a titration indicator
Drugs may need to dissolve in polar or apolar tissues and suitable solvents for analysis
It replaces the need for any pH measurement
It applies only to strong electrolytes
It is irrelevant for salt forms of drugs
questions.explanation: The dissociation constant is very important because drugs may need to dissolve in polar or apolar body tissues and fluids, and suitable solvents are needed for analytical testing.
questions.title: Acids & Bases

questions.q: Which item is listed among essential apparatus for acid-base titrations?
options: Burette, pipettes, conical flask and volumetric flask
Ultracentrifuge and Coulter counter
SEM microscope only
NMR spectrometer
Freeze dryer
questions.explanation: Essential apparatus includes burette, range of pipettes, conical flask, volumetric flask with stopper, solutions, indicator, sample and titrant.
questions.title: Acids & Bases

questions.q: Which relationship correctly expresses number of moles n from volume and molarity?
options: n = V / M x 1000
n = M / V only
n = density x volume
n = pKa x pH
questions.explanation: Key formulae give number of moles n = (V x M)/1000, along with C1V1 = C2V2, molarity = weight per litre over MW, and w = n x MW.
questions.title: Acids & Bases

questions.q: What does stoichiometry mean according to the lecture?
options: A fixed ratio of quantities of a substance involved in a reaction
The rate at which equilibrium is reached
The colour change at an indicator end point
The activity coefficient of an ion
The partition coefficient between phases
questions.explanation: Stoichiometry derives from stoicheon (simple parts) and metiri (measurement) and means a fixed ratio of quantities of a substance involved in a reaction.
questions.title: Acids & Bases

questions.q: In a titration with an indicator, what is the analyte?
options: The molecule or atom you are trying to measure
The indicator dye only
The burette wall material
The volumetric flask stopper
The excess titrant deliberately added
questions.explanation: The analyte is what molecule or atom you are trying to measure. The indicator exists in two forms depending on environment and ideally has affinity less than the analyte.
questions.title: Acids & Bases

questions.q: Which topics are listed in the part 2 lecture key takeaways?
options: PSA, solubility and log P/D, titrations, accuracy, indicators, potentiometry and peptisation
Only cis-trans isomerism
Micelle formation and CMC
DNA replication only
Young's modulus of metals
questions.explanation: Part 2 key points include PSA, solubility and log P/D, titrations, accuracy, indicators, potentiometry, and the peptisation process.
questions.title: Acids & Bases

questions.q: What does the END slide encourage students to practise?
options: Calculations, trying not to look at provided answers
Memorising only lecture titles
Skipping all titration questions
Ignoring Henderson-Hasselbalch problems
Focusing solely on potentiometry theory
questions.explanation: The END slide says to have a try at some of these calculations and try not to look at the answers where provided.
questions.title: Acids & Bases

questions.q: In the stoichiometry worked example, 1.50 ml of 0.1 M solution A reacts with 10.5 ml of B in a 2:1 molar ratio. What is the concentration of B before stoichiometric correction?
options: 92 wt %
questions.explanation: Using C1V1 = C2V2 gives 0.1 x 1.5 = C2 x 10.5, so C2 = 0.0143 M before halving for the 2:1 stoichiometry to give 7.15 x 10^-3 M.
questions.title: Acids & Bases

questions.q: What volume of 0.47 M NaNO3 stock is required to prepare 200 cm3 at 0.01 M?
options: 10 cm3
92 cm3
questions.explanation: Question 1 asks what volume of 0.47 M stock is needed for 200 cm3 at 0.01 M. The answer given is V1 = (0.01 x 200) / 0.47 = 4.26 cm3.
questions.title: Acids & Bases

questions.q: When 5 cm3 of 0.0253 M NaCl is diluted to 250 cm3, what is the new concentration?
questions.explanation: Answer 2 uses 0.0253 x 5 = C2 x 250, giving C2 = 5.06 x 10^-4 mol dm^-3.
questions.title: Acids & Bases

questions.q: In the CaCO3 back-titration example, what reaction is given for the excipient analysis?
options: CaCO3(s) + 2H+(aq) -> Ca2+ + CO2 + H2O
CaCO3(s) + NaOH -> Ca(OH)2 + Na2CO3
CaCO3 dissolves without acid
HCl is not consumed in the reaction
Only one mole of HCl reacts per mole CaCO3
questions.explanation: The titrimetry question gives the reaction CaCO3(s) + 2H+(aq) -> Ca2+ + CO2 + H2O and asks for percentage weight of CaCO3 in the excipient.
questions.title: Acids & Bases

questions.q: What percentage by weight of CaCO3 is calculated in the titrimetry worked answer?
options: 92 wt %
76 wt %
50 wt %
questions.explanation: The worked answer gives HCl consumed, stoichiometry 1 mole CaCO3 per half mole HCl consumed, 0.498 g CaCO3, and Wt % = (0.498 / 0.5413) x 100 = 92 wt %.
questions.title: Acids & Bases

questions.q: For a weak acid with Ka 1.7783 x 10^-7 at pH 6.32, what ratio of unionised to ionised species is given?
options: 1:1 only
questions.explanation: Answer 2 calculates pKa = 6.75, log b/a = -0.43, b/a = 0.3715, and the ratio of unionised to ionised = 0.73:0.27.
questions.title: Acids & Bases

questions.q: What pKa is calculated for a drug with Ka of 1.254 x 10^-7 M in the practice calculations?
questions.explanation: The practice slide shows pKa = -log(1.254 x 10^-7) = 6.9 for the given Ka value.
questions.title: Acids & Bases

questions.q: In question 1 of the dilemmas set, drug Z is a weak acid with which pKa at pH 6.4?
options: pKa 6.9
pKa 3.2
pKa 8.3
pKa 14.0
questions.explanation: Question 1 asks for the percentage of unionised species of drug Z, a weak acid with pKa 6.9, in buffer at pH 6.4.
questions.title: Acids & Bases

questions.q: What percentage of unionised drug Z is calculated in the worked answer for pH 6.4 and pKa 6.9?
questions.explanation: Rearranging Henderson-Hasselbalch gives log(b/a) = -0.5, b/a = 0.3162, and the unionised fraction is 1/1.3162 = 76%.
questions.title: Acids & Bases

questions.q: How does a formulation differ from a dosage form?
options: A formulation contains no excipients whereas a dosage form does
A formulation is the specific mixture of ingredients making a specific product, while the dosage form is the drug product type such as tablet or capsule
A formulation is the marketed pack; a dosage form is the unlicensed preparation
A formulation applies only to liquids and a dosage form only to solids
They are two words for exactly the same thing
questions.explanation: The dosage or medicinal form is the drug product containing drug plus excipients, such as a tablet or cream. The formulation is the specific mixture of ingredients that makes a specific product; tablets can use different formulations to give immediate release, effervescent or slow release.
questions.title: Biopharmaceutics: ADME

questions.q: What is biopharmaceutics concerned with?
options: The manufacture of biological medicines from living cells
The relationship between a drug's physicochemical properties, its dosage form and route of administration, and the rate and extent of absorption
The measurement of drug purity and quality in the finished product
The design of clinical trials for new medicines
The interaction of a drug with its receptor at the site of action
questions.explanation: Biopharmaceutics is the relationship between the physicochemical properties of the drug, its dosage forms and its route of administration, and the rate and extent of drug absorption, that is bioavailability.
questions.title: Biopharmaceutics: ADME

questions.q: How is bioavailability defined?
options: The total dose administered to the patient
The fraction of drug bound to plasma proteins
The rate and extent to which an active agent is absorbed and becomes available at its site of action, giving a clinical response
The proportion of drug excreted unchanged in urine
The time taken for plasma concentration to fall by half
questions.explanation: Bioavailability is the rate and extent to which an active agent is absorbed and becomes available at its site of action and therefore gives a clinical response.
questions.title: Biopharmaceutics: ADME

questions.q: Which of these is listed as a factor affecting bioavailability?
options: Pre-systemic metabolism
The colour of the tablet coating
The patient's blood group
The storage temperature of the pack
The batch size of manufacture
questions.explanation: Bioavailability is affected by release of drug from the dosage form, stability in biological fluids, permeability (how much drug can diffuse through intestinal epithelial cells), and pre-systemic metabolism.
questions.title: Biopharmaceutics: ADME

questions.q: What does ADME stand for, and what is the study of these processes called?
options: Absorption, Distribution, Metabolism, Elimination; pharmacokinetics
Absorption, Dissolution, Metabolism, Excretion; pharmacodynamics
Administration, Distribution, Metabolism, Elimination; biopharmaceutics
Absorption, Distribution, Modification, Excretion; pharmacokinetics
Adsorption, Dispersion, Metabolism, Elimination; pharmaceutics
questions.explanation: ADME is Absorption, Distribution, Metabolism and Elimination. The study of these four processes is called pharmacokinetics.
questions.title: Biopharmaceutics: ADME

questions.q: Why is plasma drug concentration used to assess bioavailability?
options: It directly measures drug at the site of action
It is an indirect indicator of drug at the site of action and is the easiest to determine, through a blood test
It is the only method accepted by regulators
It requires no assumptions about distribution
It gives a quantitative clinical response for every drug
questions.explanation: Bioavailability could be assessed by a quantitative clinical response, or by detecting drug at the site of action which is very difficult, but measurement of plasma concentration is easiest via a blood test and is an indirect indicator of drug at the site of action.
questions.title: Biopharmaceutics: ADME

questions.q: On a plasma concentration-time curve, what does the area under the curve (AUC) indicate?
options: The rate of absorption only
The extent of absorption
The half-life of the drug
The minimum effective dose
The degree of plasma protein binding
questions.explanation: AUC is an indication of the extent of absorption. Cmax is the peak concentration, Tmax the time to peak, and the therapeutic window lies between the minimum effective dose and the maximum safe dose.
questions.title: Biopharmaceutics: ADME

questions.q: Which route gives 100 per cent bioavailability by definition, with F = 1?
options: Oral
Intramuscular
Subcutaneous
Intravenous
Rectal
questions.explanation: With intravenous administration all the drug reaches the systemic circulation, so bioavailability is 100 per cent and F = 1. All other routes are compared against it.
questions.title: Biopharmaceutics: ADME

questions.q: The AUC of a 400 mg oral tablet of drug X is 50 microgram.h/mL, and the AUC of the same 400 mg dose given IV is 200 microgram.h/mL. What is the absolute bioavailability?
options: 4 per cent
20 per cent
25 per cent
40 per cent
400 per cent
questions.explanation: Absolute bioavailability = (AUC oral / AUC IV) x 100 = (50/200) x 100 = 25 per cent. No dose correction is needed because the same dose was given by both routes.
questions.title: Biopharmaceutics: ADME

questions.q: The AUC of a 400 mg oral tablet is 50 microgram.h/mL and the AUC of a 20 mg IV dose is also 50 microgram.h/mL. What is the absolute bioavailability?
options: 5 per cent
12.5 per cent
20 per cent
25 per cent
100 per cent
questions.explanation: When the doses differ, each AUC must be divided by its dose. Oral gives 50/400 = 0.125 and IV gives 50/20 = 2.5, so bioavailability = (0.125/2.5) x 100 = 5 per cent.
questions.title: Biopharmaceutics: ADME

questions.q: When is relative rather than absolute bioavailability used?
options: When the drug is given to healthy volunteers only
When the IV route is not available, so a test formulation is compared with a standard formulation of the same drug
When the drug has a half-life of less than one hour
When only a single dose can be administered
When the drug is more than 90 per cent protein bound
questions.explanation: If the IV route is not available, so 100 per cent bioavailability cannot be established, only relative bioavailability can be used. It compares the rate and extent of absorption of different formulations of the same drug.
questions.title: Biopharmaceutics: ADME

questions.q: A 500 mg tablet gives an AUC of 100 microgram.h/mL and a 100 mg capsule of the same drug gives 25 microgram.h/mL. What is the relative bioavailability of the tablet compared with the capsule?
options: 20 per cent
25 per cent
80 per cent
125 per cent
400 per cent
questions.explanation: Tablet: 100/500 = 0.2. Capsule: 25/100 = 0.25. Relative bioavailability = (0.2/0.25) x 100 = 80 per cent, so the tablet is 20 per cent less effective than the capsule at the same dose.
questions.title: Biopharmaceutics: ADME

questions.q: Which condition is NOT required for an oral drug to achieve 100 per cent bioavailability?
options: Complete release from the dosage form
Full dissolution in GI fluids
Stability in solution in GI fluids
Extensive binding to plasma albumin
Passage through the liver into the systemic circulation unchanged
questions.explanation: The drug must be completely released, fully dissolved, stable in GI fluids, pass the GI barrier into the mesenteric circulation without being metabolised, and pass through the liver unchanged. Plasma protein binding is unrelated to reaching the circulation.
questions.title: Biopharmaceutics: ADME

questions.q: Alendronate sodium has an oral bioavailability of about 0.64 per cent, compared with verapamil at 90 per cent. What does this mean practically?
options: Alendronate is more potent than verapamil
Only a tiny fraction of an oral alendronate dose reaches the systemic circulation intact
Alendronate must be given intravenously in all cases
Verapamil has a longer half-life than alendronate
Alendronate is completely destroyed by first-pass metabolism in the liver
questions.explanation: Bioavailability is the fraction of the administered dose reaching the systemic circulation unchanged, so at 0.64 per cent almost none of an oral alendronate dose gets there, compared with 90 per cent for verapamil.
questions.title: Biopharmaceutics: ADME

questions.q: Two formulations are considered bioequivalent when they do not differ significantly in which parameters?
options: Dose, dosage form and route
Cmax, Tmax and AUC
Half-life, clearance and volume of distribution
Disintegration time, dissolution rate and hardness
Protein binding, metabolism and excretion
questions.explanation: Two formulations are bioequivalent if their plasma concentration-time curves can be superimposed, that is they do not differ significantly in Cmax, Tmax or AUC, and there is no significant difference in therapeutic efficacy.
questions.title: Biopharmaceutics: ADME

questions.q: Morphine solution requires 30 mg orally but only 10 mg intravenously for the same effect. What does this illustrate?
options: That bioavailability varies with route even for the same dosage form
That the oral solution has a different formulation from the IV one
That morphine is unstable in solution
That the oral dose is distributed more widely in the body
That morphine binds more strongly to plasma proteins when given orally
questions.explanation: Morphine is made as a solution for both IV and oral use, so the dosage form is the same. The higher oral dose is needed because bioavailability differs by route, principally because of first-pass hepatic metabolism.
questions.title: Biopharmaceutics: ADME

questions.q: How is absorption defined in this lecture?
options: The transfer of drug from blood to other body locations
The passage of a drug in solution, in molecular form, across one or more barrier membranes or tissues
The biotransformation of a drug to a more water-soluble product
The release of drug from its dosage form into GI fluids
The binding of a drug to its receptor at the site of action
questions.explanation: Absorption is the passage of a drug in solution, in a molecular form, across one or more barrier membranes or tissues. With appropriate physicochemical properties the drug passes by passive diffusion from high to low concentration.
questions.title: Biopharmaceutics: ADME

questions.q: In the absorption equation dC/dt = DA(C GIT - C blood)/h, why can this simplify to dC/dt = k.C GIT?
options: Because the membrane thickness h is always zero
Because C blood is almost zero due to sink conditions, the drug being carried away by the circulation
Because the surface area A varies with concentration
Because the diffusion coefficient changes during absorption
Because C GIT equals C blood at equilibrium
questions.explanation: C GIT is far greater than C blood, which is almost zero because circulating blood carries drug away, creating sink conditions. Since D, A and h are constant for a given drug and membrane, diffusion rate is driven solely by the concentration in the GI lumen.
questions.title: Biopharmaceutics: ADME

questions.q: Which of the ADME processes is described as the only reversible one?
options: Absorption
Distribution
Metabolism
Elimination
Excretion
questions.explanation: Distribution is the transfer of drug from blood to other body locations and is reversible, with an equilibrium between drug in blood and in other locations. Metabolism to an inactive product is generally irreversible.
questions.title: Biopharmaceutics: ADME

questions.q: Which plasma protein is the main one that drugs bind to, and what is the consequence of binding?
options: Haemoglobin; the drug is transported faster to tissues
Albumin; the bound drug is inactive and not subject to metabolism or filtration, acting as a reservoir
Globulin; the drug is metabolised more rapidly
Fibrinogen; the drug is excreted unchanged in bile
Transferrin; the drug becomes more lipid soluble
questions.explanation: Drugs bind mainly to albumin by van der Waals, hydrogen and ionic bonds. Binding is saturable and reversible, makes the drug inactive, protects it from metabolism and filtration, and creates a reservoir or depot.
questions.title: Biopharmaceutics: ADME

questions.q: Warfarin is more than 97 per cent protein bound and naproxen more than 99 per cent. Why does this matter clinically?
options: Both drugs are eliminated unchanged in the urine
They compete for the same binding proteins, so a drug interaction occurs
Both are inactivated by first-pass hepatic metabolism
High binding means both have very short half-lives
Protein binding prevents either drug from reaching the liver
questions.explanation: Because both are extensively bound and compete for the same binding proteins, an interaction occurs; displacement raises the free, active concentration of the displaced drug.
questions.title: Biopharmaceutics: ADME

questions.q: Metabolism generally biotransforms a drug into products with which set of properties?
options: More lipid soluble, less ionised and more readily stored in fat
More water soluble, more ionised, less protein bound and more readily excreted in urine
More potent pharmacologically and more toxic
Less water soluble but more able to penetrate cell membranes
Identical in properties but present at lower concentration
questions.explanation: Metabolism produces substances that are more water soluble, more ionised, less able to bind plasma proteins, less able to be stored in fatty tissue, less able to penetrate membranes, generally less pharmacologically active, less toxic and more readily excreted in urine.
questions.title: Biopharmaceutics: ADME

questions.q: Which enzyme class is correctly matched to its metabolic pathway and main location?
options: Oxidases carrying out oxidation, found in the liver
Reductases carrying out hydrolysis, found in the kidney
Esterases carrying out conjugation, found in the GIT
Oxidases carrying out reduction, found in the gut wall
Glucuronidases carrying out oxidation, found in plasma
questions.explanation: The main pathways are oxidation by oxidases in the liver, reduction by reductases in the GIT and liver, hydrolysis by esterases in the liver, and conjugation including glucuronide conjugation, methylation and acylation.
questions.title: Biopharmaceutics: ADME

questions.q: Why is first-pass hepatic metabolism a problem for oral administration only?
options: Because oral drugs are always given at lower doses
Because blood from the gut always drains to the liver via the portal vein before entering the systemic circulation
Because liver enzymes are only active on drugs that have been swallowed
Because oral drugs are unstable in gastric acid
Because the oral route bypasses the mesenteric circulation
questions.explanation: Blood from the gut always drains to the liver via the portal vein before reaching the systemic circulation, so orally absorbed drug is exposed to hepatic metabolism first. It is significant for certain drugs such as propranolol and aspirin.
questions.title: Biopharmaceutics: ADME

questions.q: Which strategy is given for overcoming extensive first-pass metabolism?
options: Add an enzyme inhibitor to the tablet formulation
Use an alternative route such as rectal, which bypasses the liver
Reduce the oral dose to avoid saturating the enzymes
Give the drug with food to slow gastric emptying
Formulate the drug as an enteric coated tablet
questions.explanation: The solutions given are to find an alternative route of administration, for example the rectal route which bypasses the liver, or to give a much larger dose orally than would be required intravenously, as with morphine.
questions.title: Biopharmaceutics: ADME

questions.q: Which route of excretion is described as significant only when re-absorption is minimal?
options: Urine via the kidney
Faeces, as unabsorbed drug from the GIT
Bile
Expired breath via the lungs
Sweat and saliva
questions.explanation: Bile is significant only when re-absorption is minimal, because metabolised drug stored in bile empties into the intestine and may be re-absorbed rather than eliminated. This is entero-hepatic recycling.
questions.title: Biopharmaceutics: ADME

questions.q: What is the half-life of a drug?
options: The time taken for the plasma concentration to fall by half
