The time taken for half the dose to be absorbed
The time at which peak plasma concentration is reached
Half the interval between successive doses
The time for which the drug remains within the therapeutic window
questions.explanation: Half-life is the time taken for a drug's plasma concentration to fall by half. It reflects the rate of metabolic and excretory processes, can be determined after an IV dose, varies from minutes to days and influences the dosing interval.
questions.title: Biopharmaceutics: ADME

questions.q: After three half-lives, what percentage of the drug has been eliminated?
options: 50 per cent
75 per cent
87.5 per cent
93.8 per cent
99.2 per cent
questions.explanation: After one half-life 50 per cent remains, after two 25 per cent, after three 12.5 per cent. So 87.5 per cent has been eliminated after three half-lives, rising to 99.2 per cent after seven.
questions.title: Biopharmaceutics: ADME

questions.q: Digoxin has a half-life of 1.5 to 2 days, prolonged to 4 to 6 days in renal impairment. What should be done to avoid toxicity?
options: Increase the dose to overcome slower absorption
Reduce the dose or increase the dosing interval
Change to the intravenous route
Give the drug with food
Add a second drug that competes for protein binding
questions.explanation: If kidney function is impaired the half-life of digoxin is greatly prolonged, so the drug accumulates. The dose must be reduced or the dosing interval increased to avoid toxicity.
questions.title: Biopharmaceutics: ADME

questions.q: Absolute bioavailability is measured by comparing the AUC of a test formulation with that of which other formulation of the same drug?
options: An intravenous injection
An intramuscular injection
A subcutaneous injection
An oral solution
A tablet
questions.explanation: Absolute bioavailability compares the test formulation against an intravenous injection, since only the IV route delivers all the drug to the systemic circulation and is therefore 100 per cent bioavailable.
questions.title: Biopharmaceutics: ADME

questions.q: For a drug given orally, why do absorption and elimination occur at the same time, but not after an IV bolus?
options: Because IV drugs are not eliminated at all
Because with IV administration there is no absorption phase, the drug being placed directly in the circulation
Because IV drugs are given at much lower doses
Because elimination begins only once absorption is complete for all routes
Because IV drugs bypass the kidney
questions.explanation: Except for intravenous administration, absorption and elimination occur simultaneously but at different rates. With IV there is no absorption step because the drug is delivered straight into the systemic circulation.
questions.title: Biopharmaceutics: ADME

questions.q: Paracetamol is available as an oral suspension, capsules and tablets. Which would you expect to act fastest, and why?
options: The tablet, because compression aids dissolution
The capsule, because the shell protects the drug from acid
The suspension, because the drug is already finely dispersed and needs no disintegration
All three act at exactly the same rate
The tablet, because it contains the largest dose
questions.explanation: Bioavailability may vary with dosage form by the same route. A suspension already presents finely divided drug requiring no tablet disintegration or deaggregation, so dissolution and hence absorption are faster.
questions.title: Biopharmaceutics: ADME

questions.q: For systemic drug action after non-IV administration, the drug must first:
options: Be absorbed into the blood
Be excreted unchanged in urine
Bind irreversibly to albumin
Remain at the site of administration permanently
Be metabolised before reaching any membrane
questions.explanation: Drugs acting systemically must reach the blood and distribute to their site of action. Unless injected intravenously, the drug needs to be absorbed into the blood to work.
questions.title: Biopharmaceutics: ADME

questions.q: In the ADME diagram, Ka represents:
options: Absorption rate constant
Metabolism rate only
Distribution to tissues only
Excretion via bile only
Protein synthesis rate
questions.explanation: The distribution diagram labels absorption as Ka, with metabolism (Km), elimination/excretion (Ke) and distribution (Kd) as separate processes linking administration site, blood and site of action.
questions.title: Biopharmaceutics: ADME

questions.q: When Ka is greater than Ke on a plasma concentration-time curve, the curve shows:
options: A distinct absorption phase before elimination
No absorption phase at all
Immediate zero concentration
Only protein binding
No elimination phase
questions.explanation: The plasma concentration-time curve illustrates absorption and elimination phases. When Ka > Ke, absorption dominates early, producing a rising phase before elimination.
questions.title: Biopharmaceutics: ADME

questions.q: Bioavailability may vary for the same drug when:
options: Oral aqueous suspensions contain different excipients
The drug name is changed
The patient reads the leaflet
The colour of packaging differs
The prescriber's handwriting varies
questions.explanation: For a given drug, bioavailability may vary with the same route and dosage form type but different formulations, such as oral aqueous suspensions with different excipients.
questions.title: Biopharmaceutics: ADME

questions.q: Three oral formulations of the same drug and dose may produce different:
options: Plasma concentration-time profiles
Molecular weights of the API
Receptor structures
Bile production rates only
DNA sequences
questions.explanation: The slide shows three different oral formulations (A, B, C) of the same drug and dose producing different blood/plasma concentration-time curves, reflecting differing bioavailability.
questions.title: Biopharmaceutics: ADME

questions.q: Concentration of drug at the site of action depends on:
options: Absorption, distribution, metabolism and elimination (ADME)
Only the tablet colour
Only the prescriber's specialty
Only storage humidity of the pharmacy
Only the patient's age
questions.explanation: Magnitude of clinical response relates to concentration at the site of action, which depends on dose, extent of absorption, distribution, metabolism and elimination, all influenced by physicochemical properties.
questions.title: Biopharmaceutics: ADME

questions.q: Passive diffusion absorption across the GI membrane involves:
options: Partition of drug between GI fluids and the membrane, then diffusion
Active transport requiring ATP at all times
Endocytosis of whole tablets
Direct IV injection
Excretion before crossing the membrane
questions.explanation: Absorption by passive diffusion involves drug in solution in the intestinal lumen partitioning into the GI cell membrane, diffusing through it, then partitioning into blood and being carried away by circulation.
questions.title: Biopharmaceutics: ADME

questions.q: In the membrane diffusion quiz, diffusion is faster when:
options: The concentration gradient across the membrane is larger
Both sides have equal concentrations
No membrane is present
The drug is permanently protein-bound
Metabolism occurs before contact with membrane
questions.explanation: Fick's law shows rate of diffusion is proportional to the concentration difference across the membrane, so a steeper gradient gives faster diffusion.
questions.title: Biopharmaceutics: ADME

questions.q: The ADME diagram with 'Pain case' links distribution to:
options: Clinical effect at the site of action
Tablet disintegration only
Manufacture of excipients
Gram staining
Fischer projections
questions.explanation: The distribution diagram including the pain case connects absorption, distribution, metabolism and elimination to unbound drug and drug at the site of action, leading to clinical effect.
questions.title: Biopharmaceutics: ADME

questions.q: Crystallographic studies of HSA show ligand binding sites occupied by:
options: Fatty acids, endogenous ligands and drugs
Only water molecules
Only DNA
Peptidoglycan
Flagellin
questions.explanation: The HSA ligand-binding summary depicts fatty acids (myristic acid), other endogenous ligands (hemin, thyroxin) and drugs in distinct binding regions defined by crystallographic studies.
questions.title: Biopharmaceutics: ADME

questions.q: Drug binding to plasma albumin is important because:
options: Bound drug can be displaced by other drugs, altering free concentration
It always increases free active drug
It prevents all distribution
It replaces hepatic metabolism
It only occurs with IV drugs
questions.explanation: The supplementary material on drugs binding to albumin explains how bound drugs can displace other bound drugs, affecting free drug concentration and pharmacological effect.
questions.title: Biopharmaceutics: ADME

questions.q: Drug metabolism generally produces metabolites that are:
options: More water soluble and more readily excreted
More lipid soluble and stored in fat permanently
Always more pharmacologically active
Unable to ionise
Less excreted in urine
questions.explanation: Metabolism biotransforms drugs to more water-soluble, more ionised products that are generally less active (unless prodrugs), less toxic and more readily excreted in urine.
questions.title: Biopharmaceutics: ADME

questions.q: Pre-systemic metabolism can occur in:
options: The GI lumen, gut wall and liver (first-pass)
Only the kidneys after excretion
Only the lungs after inhalation
Nowhere before systemic circulation
Only during tablet compression
questions.explanation: Sites of metabolism include pre-systemic locations such as the GI lumen, membrane passage across the gut wall, and first-pass hepatic metabolism, as well as systemic metabolism mainly in the liver.
questions.title: Biopharmaceutics: ADME

questions.q: The Biopharmaceutical Classification System applies to which route of administration?
options: Intravenous
Oral
Transdermal
Pulmonary
All routes equally
questions.explanation: The BCS applies to the oral route. Drugs are classified into four classes according to dose, aqueous solubility across the GI pH range, and permeability across the GI mucosa.
questions.title: Biopharmaceutics Classification System (BCS)

questions.q: On which three properties is the BCS classification based?
options: Dose, aqueous solubility across the GI pH range, and permeability across the GI mucosa
Molecular weight, log P and pKa
Half-life, clearance and volume of distribution
Melting point, crystal form and particle size
Cmax, Tmax and AUC
questions.explanation: Drugs are classified according to dose, aqueous solubility across the GI pH range, and permeability across the GI mucosa.
questions.title: Biopharmaceutics Classification System (BCS)

questions.q: What is the BCS definition of a highly soluble drug substance?
options: The highest dose strength dissolves in 900 mL or less of water at 25 degrees C
The highest dose strength is soluble in 250 mL or less of water over pH 1 to 7.5 at 37 degrees C
More than 85 per cent dissolves within 30 minutes
The drug has a solubility greater than 1 mg/mL at any pH
More than 90 per cent of the dose is absorbed in humans
questions.explanation: A drug substance is highly soluble when its highest dose strength dissolves in 250 mL or less of water over the pH range 1 to 7.5 at 37 degrees C, reflecting a glass of water, the GI pH range and body temperature.
questions.title: Biopharmaceutics Classification System (BCS)

questions.q: What is the BCS definition of a highly permeable drug substance?
options: It crosses Caco-2 cells with a Papp above 2.0 x 10^-6 cm/s
Its log P is greater than zero
The extent of absorption in humans is greater than 90 per cent of an administered dose
It reaches Cmax within 30 minutes of dosing
It dissolves in 250 mL or less of water
questions.explanation: A drug substance is highly permeable when the extent of absorption in humans is greater than 90 per cent of an administered dose, based on mass balance or compared with an intravenous reference dose.
questions.title: Biopharmaceutics Classification System (BCS)

questions.q: When is a drug product considered rapidly dissolving?
options: When 85 per cent or more dissolves within 30 minutes in 900 mL or less of buffer using USP Apparatus 1 or 2
When 100 per cent dissolves within 60 minutes in 250 mL of water
When 50 per cent dissolves within 15 minutes at pH 1.0
When it disintegrates within 5 minutes in gastric fluid
When the whole dose dissolves in 250 mL at 37 degrees C
questions.explanation: Rapid dissolution means 85 per cent or more of the labelled amount dissolves within 30 minutes using USP Apparatus 1 (rotating basket) or 2 (paddle) in a volume of 900 mL or less of buffer solutions.
questions.title: Biopharmaceutics Classification System (BCS)

questions.q: Which combination defines a BCS Class II drug?
options: High solubility, high permeability
High solubility, low permeability
Low solubility, high permeability
Low solubility, low permeability
High solubility, variable permeability
questions.explanation: Class I is high solubility and high permeability, Class II low solubility and high permeability, Class III high solubility and low permeability, and Class IV low solubility and low permeability.
questions.title: Biopharmaceutics Classification System (BCS)

questions.q: Levothyroxine sodium has a solubility of 105 micrograms/mL and a highest dose of 200 micrograms. What volume is needed to dissolve the highest dose, and is it highly soluble?
options: 0.5 mL; yes, highly soluble
1.9 mL; yes, highly soluble
19 mL; yes, highly soluble
190 mL; yes, highly soluble
525 mL; no, low solubility
questions.explanation: If 105 micrograms dissolve in 1 mL, then 200 micrograms need 200/105 = 1.9 mL. This is far below 250 mL, so levothyroxine sodium counts as highly soluble.
questions.title: Biopharmaceutics Classification System (BCS)

questions.q: A drug has a highest dose strength of 160 mg and a solubility of 0.27 mg/mL. Is it highly soluble by BCS criteria?
options: Yes, it needs only 43 mL
Yes, it needs 160 mL
No, it needs about 593 mL
No, it needs about 250 mL exactly
Cannot be determined without the permeability data
questions.explanation: Volume required = 160/0.27 = about 593 mL, which exceeds 250 mL, so this drug has low solubility. In the worked example it is drug C, which combined with low permeability makes it Class IV.
questions.title: Biopharmaceutics Classification System (BCS)

questions.q: Why is permeability described as the most difficult BCS criterion to establish?
options: Because it changes with the batch of drug substance
Because it requires human mass-balance or absolute bioavailability studies, or extensive validated in vitro cell permeability data
Because no in vitro models exist for it
Because it can only be measured at 37 degrees C
Because it depends on the dosage form rather than the drug substance
questions.explanation: Establishing permeability requires fundamental human mass-balance studies, absolute bioavailability studies, or extensive in vitro cell permeability data using a properly validated system.
questions.title: Biopharmaceutics Classification System (BCS)

questions.q: Which in vitro cell line is used to model the small intestine when measuring permeability?
options: HeLa
Caco-2
CHO
Vero
HEK293
questions.explanation: Caco-2 cells model the small intestine in cell culture permeability studies; HT29 is also mentioned. A typical Papp value is 2.0 x 10^-6 cm/s, and Papp correlates with percentage absorption in humans.
questions.title: Biopharmaceutics Classification System (BCS)

questions.q: Which is an example of an in silico approach to predicting permeability?
options: Calculated log P (clog P)
Caco-2 cell monolayers
In situ intestinal perfusion
The InteliSite capsule in humans
Excised tissue membrane vesicles
questions.explanation: Computational or in silico prediction uses clog P. Physicochemical methods use the partition coefficient or an immobilised artificial membrane; biological methods run from cell culture and excised tissue through in situ perfusion to human studies such as Loc-I-Gut and the InteliSite capsule.
questions.title: Biopharmaceutics Classification System (BCS)

questions.q: What formulation approach is appropriate for a BCS Class I drug?
options: A lipid-based delivery vehicle
A simple solid oral dosage form, since good oral bioavailability is expected
A permeation enhancer to aid absorption
Particle size reduction to speed dissolution
An alternative non-oral route
questions.explanation: Class I drugs have high solubility so dissolve rapidly, and high permeability so are rapidly absorbed. Good oral bioavailability is expected and a simple solid oral dosage form can be used. Propranolol and metoprolol are examples.
questions.title: Biopharmaceutics Classification System (BCS)

questions.q: For a BCS Class II drug, which step limits bioavailability and how should the formulator respond?
options: Permeability limits it; add a permeation enhancer
Dissolution limits it; increase dissolution rate by particle size reduction or solid dispersions
Metabolism limits it; use an enzyme inhibitor
Release from the dosage form limits it; use a controlled release matrix
Solubility limits it; the drug cannot be given orally
questions.explanation: Class II drugs have low solubility so dissolve slowly, making dissolution the rate-limiting step, but are highly permeable. Formulation should focus on increasing dissolution rate, for example by particle size reduction or solid dispersions. Ketoprofen and carbamazepine are examples.
questions.title: Biopharmaceutics Classification System (BCS)

questions.q: Why should a BCS Class III drug generally not be formulated as a controlled release product?
options: Because the drug would dissolve too quickly and cause toxicity
Because permeability is rate-limiting, so the drug should be released early to give maximum time for absorption in the GIT
Because Class III drugs are unstable in gastric acid
Because controlled release would reduce the dissolution rate below the BCS limit
Because Class III drugs are always given intravenously
questions.explanation: Class III drugs are highly soluble but poorly permeable, so absorption is the rate-limiting step. Dosage forms should release drug early to maximise the time available for absorption, so controlled release is probably inappropriate. A permeation enhancer could be included. Ranitidine and atenolol are examples.
questions.title: Biopharmaceutics Classification System (BCS)

questions.q: Which strategies are suggested for improving the bioavailability of a BCS Class IV drug?
options: Reduce the dose and increase the dosing frequency
Add a disintegrant and a wetting agent to the tablet
Make prodrugs, use lipid-based delivery vehicles, or choose an alternative route
Increase particle size to slow dissolution
Formulate as a controlled release matrix tablet
questions.explanation: Class IV drugs dissolve slowly and are absorbed slowly, giving poor oral bioavailability, and may not be usable orally at all. Options are prodrugs, lipid-based delivery vehicles such as those used for saquinavir and ritonavir, or an alternative route.
questions.title: Biopharmaceutics Classification System (BCS)

questions.q: Which BCS class of drug would be expected to show improved bioavailability if the particle size were reduced?
options: Class I
Class I and Class II
Class II
Class III
Class IV
questions.explanation: Particle size reduction increases surface area and therefore dissolution rate. This only helps when dissolution is rate-limiting, which is the case for Class II drugs: low solubility but high permeability.
questions.title: Biopharmaceutics Classification System (BCS)

questions.q: A drug has a highest dose of 0.2 mg and a solubility of 0.0005 mg/mL, with low permeability read from the Caco-2 correlation. Which BCS class is it?
options: Class I
Class II
Class III
Class IV
Cannot be classified
questions.explanation: Volume needed = 0.2/0.0005 = 400 mL, which exceeds 250 mL, so solubility is low. In the worked SAQ this drug has high permeability and is Class II; a drug with both low solubility and low permeability, such as drug C needing 593 mL, is Class IV.
questions.title: Biopharmaceutics Classification System (BCS)

questions.q: Besides guiding formulation, what regulatory benefit does the BCS provide?
options: It removes the need for stability testing of the product
It can provide assurance of in vivo bioequivalence from in vitro characterisation, avoiding unnecessary human studies
It replaces the requirement for a marketing authorisation
It allows a drug to be sold without dissolution testing
It guarantees the drug will be 100 per cent bioavailable
questions.explanation: The BCS is a scientific framework that aids candidate selection in discovery, guides design of immediate and controlled release dosage forms, and can provide assurance of in vivo bioequivalence from extensive in vitro comparative characterisation, offering a pathway to avoid unnecessary human studies.
questions.title: Biopharmaceutics Classification System (BCS)

questions.q: Which pair of apparatus is specified for BCS dissolution testing?
options: USP Apparatus 1 (rotating basket) and USP Apparatus 2 (paddle)
The Franz diffusion cell and the Ussing chamber
The cone and plate viscometer and the Ostwald viscometer
The Caco-2 transwell and the excised tissue chamber
USP Apparatus 3 (reciprocating cylinder) and 4 (flow-through cell)
questions.explanation: Rapid dissolution is assessed with USP Apparatus 1, the rotating basket, or USP Apparatus 2, the paddle method, in 900 mL or less of buffer.
questions.title: Biopharmaceutics Classification System (BCS)

questions.q: Atorvastatin has a highest dose of 80 mg and a solubility of 0.00063 mg/mL, described as practically insoluble. Roughly what volume would be needed to dissolve the highest dose?
options: About 130 mL, so it is highly soluble
About 1,270 mL, so it has low solubility
About 12,700 mL, so it has low solubility
About 127,000 mL, so it has low solubility
About 50 mL, so it is highly soluble
questions.explanation: Volume = 80/0.00063 = approximately 127,000 mL, vastly more than the 250 mL limit, confirming atorvastatin as a low solubility drug consistent with its pharmacopoeial description of practically insoluble.
questions.title: Biopharmaceutics Classification System (BCS)

questions.q: Why does the BCS solubility test specify 37 degrees C and pH 1.0 to 7.5?
options: To match standard laboratory conditions used for all pharmacopoeial tests
To reflect body temperature and the range of pH values a drug meets along the GI tract
Because solubility cannot be measured outside these conditions
Because these are the conditions inside the dissolution apparatus by default
To match the conditions used to measure log P
questions.explanation: The conditions are physiologically based: 37 degrees C is body temperature, pH 1.0 to 7.5 spans the range from stomach to intestine, and 250 mL approximates the glass of water taken with an oral dose.
questions.title: Biopharmaceutics Classification System (BCS)

questions.q: Metformin hydrochloride has a highest dose of 2 g and a solubility of 1.38 mg/mL. What does this indicate?
options: It needs about 1,450 mL, so despite being freely soluble it fails the BCS high solubility criterion at its highest dose
It needs about 145 mL, so it is highly soluble
It needs about 14 mL, so it is highly soluble
Solubility is irrelevant because the drug is given at a high dose
It cannot be classified because it is a hydrochloride salt
questions.explanation: Volume = 2000/1.38 = about 1,450 mL, well above the 250 mL limit. This shows why dose matters as much as intrinsic solubility: a freely soluble drug given at a 2 g dose can still fail the BCS high solubility test.
questions.title: Biopharmaceutics Classification System (BCS)

questions.q: Levothyroxine sodium has a solubility of 105 micrograms per mL. How much dissolves in 250 mL, and does this meet BCS high solubility for a highest dose of 200 micrograms?
options: Only 105 micrograms dissolves, so it fails
250 x 105 micrograms = 26,250 micrograms dissolves, which exceeds the 200 microgram highest dose and meets high solubility in 250 mL
No drug dissolves in 250 mL
Exactly 200 micrograms dissolves with none in excess
Solubility cannot be calculated from these data
questions.explanation: If 105 micrograms dissolves in 1 mL, then 250 mL can dissolve 250 x 105 = 26,250 micrograms. This exceeds the 200 microgram highest dose, so the highest dose is soluble in 250 mL.
questions.title: Biopharmaceutics Classification System (BCS)

questions.q: Which processes are involved as a drug moves from the intestinal lumen into the blood during absorption?
options: Only active transport with no partitioning
Diffusion and partition between GI fluids, the GI cell membrane and circulating blood
Only filtration through the stomach wall
Only metabolism in the liver before any membrane contact
Only dissolution with no membrane crossing
questions.explanation: The permeability slide illustrates drug in solution in the intestinal lumen partitioning into the GI cell membrane and then into blood, where it is carried away by circulation. Diffusion and partition govern this movement.
questions.title: Biopharmaceutics Classification System (BCS)

questions.q: Which BCS boundary definitions are correct?
options: High solubility requires dissolution in 10 mL at any temperature
High solubility: highest dose strength soluble in 250 mL or less over pH 1-7.5 at 37 degrees C; high permeability: greater than 90% absorption; rapidly dissolving: 85% or more within 30 min
High permeability means less than 10% absorption
Rapidly dissolving requires 100% dissolution within 5 minutes
Solubility is assessed only at pH 7.4
questions.explanation: BCS class boundaries define high solubility when the highest dose dissolves in 250 mL or less over pH 1-7.5 at 37 degrees C, high permeability when absorption exceeds 90% of the dose, and rapidly dissolving when 85% or more dissolves within 30 minutes using USP Apparatus 1 or 2.
questions.title: Biopharmaceutics Classification System (BCS)

questions.q: How does a substandard medicine differ from a falsified one?
options: Substandard medicines fail their quality standards or specifications; falsified medicines deliberately misrepresent their identity, composition or source
Substandard medicines are unlicensed; falsified medicines are licensed but poorly made
Substandard medicines are always generics; falsified medicines are always innovator products
Substandard medicines are sold online; falsified medicines are sold in pharmacies
There is no meaningful difference between the two terms
questions.explanation: Substandard medicines fail to meet their quality standards or specifications, or both. Falsified medicines, also called fake or counterfeit, deliberately or fraudulently misrepresent their identity, composition or source.
questions.title: Drug and Medicine Quality

questions.q: What is an unregistered or unlicensed medical product?
options: One that has expired but is still on sale
One that has not undergone evaluation or approval by the national or regional regulatory authority for the market in which it is used
One made by a company without a manufacturing licence
One that has failed a pharmacopoeial assay
One sold without a prescription
questions.explanation: Unregistered or unlicensed medical products are those that have not undergone evaluation and/or approval by the national or regional regulatory authority for the market in which they are marketed, distributed or used.
questions.title: Drug and Medicine Quality

questions.q: Which therapeutic categories are among the most commonly reported substandard and falsified medical products?
options: Antihypertensives and statins
Anti-malarials and antibiotics
Insulins and anticoagulants
Vaccines and in vitro diagnostics only
Analgesics and antidepressants
questions.explanation: Anti-malarials and antibiotics are among the most commonly reported substandard and falsified products, although reports to WHO span all main therapeutic categories including medicines, vaccines and in vitro diagnostics.
questions.title: Drug and Medicine Quality

questions.q: What proportion of medical products in low- and middle-income countries is estimated to be substandard or falsified?
options: About 1 in 100
About 1 in 50
About 1 in 20
About 1 in 10
About 1 in 3
questions.explanation: An estimated 1 in 10 medical products in low- and middle-income countries is substandard or falsified. They are found in illegal street markets and unregulated websites but also in pharmacies, clinics and hospitals.
questions.title: Drug and Medicine Quality

questions.q: How is pharmaceutical analysis defined?
options: The study of how drugs are absorbed, distributed, metabolised and eliminated
The branch of practical chemistry involving purification, separation, identification and qualification of pharmaceutical components
The design of clinical trials to test drug efficacy
The process of turning an API into a dosage form
The legal registration of a medicine with a regulatory authority
questions.explanation: Pharmaceutical analysis is the branch of practical chemistry involving a series of processes for purification, separation, identification and qualification of pharmaceutical components. Testing product quality involves chemical, physical and microbiological analysis.
questions.title: Drug and Medicine Quality

questions.q: What is the difference between qualitative and quantitative analysis?
options: Qualitative reveals the identity of elements and compounds; quantitative indicates the amount or concentration of each substance
Qualitative measures concentration; quantitative measures identity
Qualitative is done in the laboratory; quantitative is done in silico
Qualitative applies to raw materials; quantitative applies to finished products
Qualitative uses spectroscopy; quantitative uses chromatography
questions.explanation: Qualitative analysis reveals the identity of the elements and compounds in a sample. Quantitative analysis indicates the amount or concentration of each substance present.
questions.title: Drug and Medicine Quality

questions.q: Why is a state of absolute 100 per cent chemical purity described as virtually unattainable?
options: Because analytical methods cannot detect impurities below 1 per cent
Because chemical purity means complete freedom from foreign matter, which cannot be fully achieved in practice
Because pharmacopoeias forbid purity above 99 per cent
Because all drugs decompose immediately on manufacture
Because purity is only ever measured as a relative value
questions.explanation: Chemical purity is complete freedom from foreign matter, and absolute purity is virtually unattainable. The acceptable level is set by the purification methods available, the stability of the product, the toxicity of the impurities and the dose of the active ingredient.
questions.title: Drug and Medicine Quality

questions.q: Which criterion helps determine the acceptable level of purity for a drug substance?
options: The toxicity of the impurities and the dose of the active ingredient
The retail price of the finished medicine
The country in which the drug is manufactured
The colour of the raw material
The number of dosage forms available
questions.explanation: The criteria determining acceptable purity are the purification methods, the stability of the product, the toxicity of the impurities and the dose of the active ingredient.
questions.title: Drug and Medicine Quality

questions.q: Which of these is a manufacturing process source of impurities?
options: Isolation of the chemical from a plant source
Air oxidation during storage in the pharmacy
Reagents, solvents and catalysts used in the process, and traces of metallic ions from the reaction vessel
A change in crystal size and form over time
Microbial contamination introduced by the patient
questions.explanation: Manufacturing process sources include the starting material and its impurities, intermediates, reagents, solvents and catalysts, and the reaction vessel with traces of metallic ions. Raw material origin, chemical and physical instability, and manufacturing hazards are separate categories.
questions.title: Drug and Medicine Quality

questions.q: A change in crystal size and form during storage is an example of which source of impurity?
options: Raw materials
Manufacturing process
Chemical instability
Physical instability
Manufacturing hazards
questions.explanation: Physical instability covers changes in crystal size and form and changes in particle size. Chemical instability is decomposition under non-ideal storage from light, acids or alkalis, air oxidation, water vapour or carbon dioxide.
questions.title: Drug and Medicine Quality

questions.q: What is a pharmacopoeia?
options: A commercial catalogue of medicines available for sale
A public document giving specifications for the purity and properties of pharmaceutical materials, and official methods of testing
A textbook of pharmacology for prescribers
A register of licensed pharmaceutical manufacturers
A database of adverse drug reactions
questions.explanation: Pharmacopoeias are public documents giving specifications for the purity and properties of pharmaceutical materials, and official methods of testing. The British Pharmacopoeia reproduces many European Pharmacopoeia monographs.
questions.title: Drug and Medicine Quality

questions.q: Why do pharmacopoeias matter so much in practice?
options: They are advisory guidance that manufacturers may follow if they choose
They have legal status, and any material intended for medicinal purposes subject to a BP monograph must comply with all its specifications
They set the retail price of every licensed medicine
They list which medicines can be sold without prescription
They record the patent status of each drug substance
questions.explanation: Pharmacopoeias have legal status. Any material intended for medicinal purposes that is subject to a monograph in the BP must comply with all the specifications in that monograph.
questions.title: Drug and Medicine Quality

questions.q: Which volumes of the British Pharmacopoeia cover largely raw materials?
options: Volumes I and II
Volume III
Volume IV
Volume V
Volumes III and IV
questions.explanation: BP Volumes I and II cover largely raw materials, Volume III largely formulated products, Volume IV other products such as herbal and radiological, and Volume V infrared spectra and supplementary chapters.
questions.title: Drug and Medicine Quality

questions.q: Which section of a monograph gives the chemical name and the purity required?
options: Characters
Identification
Definition
Assay
Action and use
questions.explanation: The Definition gives the chemical name and the purity required, for example paracetamol as N-(4-hydroxyphenyl)acetamide with a content of 99.0 to 101.0 per cent of the dried substance. Characters describes the nature of the material.
questions.title: Drug and Medicine Quality

questions.q: The BP monograph for paracetamol gives its content as 99.0 to 101.0 per cent. Why can the upper limit exceed 100 per cent?
options: Because impurities are counted as active drug
Because the figure includes the excipients in the tablet
Because it reflects the tolerance of the assay method applied to the dried substance
Because paracetamol gains mass on drying
Because the monograph limit is set by the manufacturer
questions.explanation: Content limits of 99.0 to 101.0 per cent of the dried substance define an acceptable band around the nominal value, allowing for the analytical tolerance of the titrimetric assay rather than implying more than complete purity.
questions.title: Drug and Medicine Quality

questions.q: The paracetamol monograph specifies a melting point of 168 to 172 degrees C. In which section of the monograph does this appear?
options: Definition
Characters
Identification
Tests
Assay
questions.explanation: Melting point 168 to 172 degrees C is Identification test A. Other identification tests use ultraviolet absorbance at 249 nm, infrared spectrophotometry, a colour reaction with potassium dichromate, and the reaction of acetyl.
questions.title: Drug and Medicine Quality

questions.q: In the paracetamol monograph, what is the maximum permitted level of heavy metals?
options: 1 ppm
10 ppm
20 ppm
50 ppm
0.1 per cent
questions.explanation: Heavy metals are limited to a maximum of 20 ppm. Loss on drying is limited to a maximum of 0.5 per cent determined at 105 degrees C, and sulfated ash to a maximum of 0.1 per cent.
questions.title: Drug and Medicine Quality

questions.q: The related substances test in the paracetamol monograph uses which analytical technique?
options: Infrared spectrophotometry
Liquid chromatography
Titration with cerium sulfate
Atomic absorption spectroscopy
Gravimetric analysis
questions.explanation: Related substances are determined by liquid chromatography, with detection at 245 nm, an octylsilyl silica gel column and defined limits for impurities J, K and F and for any other impurity.
questions.title: Drug and Medicine Quality

questions.q: Impurity K in paracetamol is 4-aminophenol, limited to 50 ppm. What does this limit represent?
options: The concentration of paracetamol in the reference solution
The maximum permitted amount of that specific impurity in the substance
The detection limit of the chromatographic method
The signal-to-noise ratio required for system suitability
The relative retention of the impurity
questions.explanation: The Limits section sets maximum permitted amounts for named impurities: impurity J at 10 ppm, impurity K at 50 ppm, impurity F at 0.05 per cent, any other impurity at 0.05 per cent and total other impurities at 0.1 per cent.
questions.title: Drug and Medicine Quality

questions.q: The paracetamol assay titrates with 0.1 M cerium sulfate, where 1 mL is equivalent to 7.56 mg of C8H9NO2. What kind of measurement is this?
options: A qualitative identification test
A quantitative determination of content
A test for heavy metals
A measurement of loss on drying
A determination of melting point
questions.explanation: The assay is the quantitative determination of how much active substance is present, using titration with cerium sulfate and ferroin indicator against a blank titration.
questions.title: Drug and Medicine Quality

questions.q: Which key terms are used to describe results in pharmaceutical analysis?
options: Accuracy, precision, selectivity, sensitivity, linear range, limit of detection, limit of quantitation and error
Solubility, permeability, dissolution and bioavailability
Cmax, Tmax, AUC and half-life
Identity, purity, potency and stability only
Viscosity, density, refractive index and pH
questions.explanation: The key terms listed are accuracy, precision, selectivity, sensitivity, linear range, limit of detection, limit of quantitation and error.
questions.title: Drug and Medicine Quality

questions.q: What does relative standard deviation (RSD), also called the coefficient of variation, express?
options: The difference between the measured value and the true value
The standard deviation expressed as a percentage of the mean
The number of repeat measurements taken
The smallest concentration that can be detected
The range over which the response is linear
questions.explanation: Standard deviation measures how tightly the data are packed around the mean; relative standard deviation or coefficient of variation expresses that result as a percentage of the mean.
questions.title: Drug and Medicine Quality

questions.q: Ibuprofen tablet absorbances of 0.25, 0.36, 0.85, 0.62 and 0.88 are measured against a standard of 0.65. How should these results be interpreted?
options: They are accurate, but not precise
They are accurate but have bias
They are both accurate and precise
They are neither accurate nor precise
They are precise, but not accurate
questions.explanation: The values are widely scattered from 0.25 to 0.88, so they are not precise. They also do not cluster around the standard value of 0.65, so they are not accurate either.
questions.title: Drug and Medicine Quality

questions.q: A set of measurements clusters very tightly but sits well away from the true value. How is this described?
options: Accurate but not precise
Precise but not accurate
Both accurate and precise
Neither accurate nor precise
Selective but not sensitive
questions.explanation: Precision describes how tightly repeat values agree with each other; accuracy is closeness to the true value. Tight clustering away from the true value is precise but not accurate, and indicates systematic error or bias.
questions.title: Drug and Medicine Quality

questions.q: In analytical method development, which competing factors are being optimised together?
options: Accuracy, precision, number of steps, time and cost
Solubility, permeability and dissolution
Purity, potency and stability
Sensitivity and selectivity only
Temperature, pressure and pH
questions.explanation: The analyst is optimising accuracy, precision, the number of steps, time and cost together, which is why efficient analytical decisions matter.
questions.title: Drug and Medicine Quality

questions.q: Using Grade A rather than Grade B glassware in a dilution would have what effect?
options: It would reduce the uncertainty contributed by the glassware
It would increase the sensitivity of the detector
It would improve the selectivity of the method
It would remove the need for a calibration curve
It would have no effect on the measurement
questions.explanation: Grade A glassware has tighter volumetric tolerances than Grade B, so the error contributed by the pipette and volumetric flask is smaller, reducing the overall uncertainty of the measurement.
questions.title: Drug and Medicine Quality

questions.q: Which groups are identified as sharing responsibility for medicine quality?
options: Regulatory authorities alone
Pharmaceutical companies alone
Regulatory authorities, pharmaceutical companies, doctors and other prescribers, pharmacists and patients
Pharmacists and patients only
The World Health Organization alone
questions.explanation: Medicine quality is presented as the shared responsibility of the regulatory authority, pharmaceutical companies, doctors and other prescribers, pharmacists and patients.
questions.title: Drug and Medicine Quality

questions.q: Which question is pharmaceutical analysis used to answer?
options: Which patients should receive the medicine
What is the correct dose for a child
What are the concentrations of specified impurities in the product
How should the medicine be marketed
Which prescriber wrote the prescription
questions.explanation: Pharmaceutical analysis answers questions about drug identity, the presence of impurities and their concentrations, stability, rate of drug release, whether purity meets specification, plasma concentrations, and physicochemical properties such as pKa, partition coefficient and solubility.
questions.title: Drug and Medicine Quality

questions.q: According to the British Pharmacopoeia monograph extract, what is the action and use of paracetamol?
options: Antibacterial for systemic infection
Analgesic and antipyretic
Anticoagulant for thrombosis
Antihypertensive for cardiovascular disease
Antifungal for dermatophyte infection
questions.explanation: The paracetamol monograph lists its action and use as analgesic and antipyretic. The monograph also details numerous preparations including tablets, capsules, suspensions and combination products.
questions.title: Drug and Medicine Quality

questions.q: When reviewing an analytical procedure, which steps are most likely to reduce accuracy if performed carelessly?
options: Using calibrated reference standards and Grade A glassware throughout
Using low-grade glassware, imprecise weighing or pipetting, and poorly prepared calibration standards
Repeating measurements and calculating a mean
Following the pharmacopoeial monograph method exactly
Documenting all raw data immediately
questions.explanation: The identifying error exercises ask students to highlight process steps that reduce accuracy. Poor volumetric technique with lower-grade glassware, inaccurate weighing or pipetting, and inadequate calibration preparation all introduce systematic error into the measurement.
questions.title: Drug and Medicine Quality

questions.q: In a multi-step quantitative analysis, which factors most commonly introduce error that reduces accuracy?
options: Using a single calibrated instrument with no dilutions
Multiple transfer and dilution steps, incorrect meniscus reading, and cumulative volumetric tolerances
Reading the result at the same wavelength for all samples
Using freshly prepared mobile phase within its stability period
Applying the same extraction time to all samples
questions.explanation: The second identifying error exercise focuses on parts of a process that reduce accuracy. Each transfer, dilution and volumetric measurement can compound error, especially with lower-grade glassware or inconsistent technique.
questions.title: Drug and Medicine Quality

questions.q: Which key points summarise the drug and medicine quality lecture?
options: Medicine quality is unimportant if the drug is cheap
Medicine quality is essential for safe effective medicines; the pharmacopoeia is a critical legal document; accuracy and precision matter; uncertainty must be understood and addressed
Only pharmaceutical companies are responsible for quality
Impurity limits are optional recommendations
Calibration curves are never needed in pharmaceutical analysis
questions.explanation: Key points state that medicine quality is essential, the pharmacopoeia provides legal methodology to test drug and medicine purity, analysts must understand accuracy and precision, and uncertainty in measurement must be recognised and addressed.
questions.title: Drug and Medicine Quality

questions.q: When measuring codeine concentration in a tablet by UV-visible spectroscopy using a five-point calibration, where might error be introduced?
options: Only when printing the final report
During preparation of calibration standards, tablet extraction, dilution, pipetting and spectrophotometer measurement
Only during storage of the finished tablets before analysis
Only when selecting the colour of laboratory coats
Only when choosing the brand of laboratory notebook
questions.explanation: The example SAQ asks students to highlight experimental steps where error could be introduced during calibration and suggest strategies to minimise it. Errors can arise when preparing standards, extracting the tablet, diluting, pipetting and reading absorbance.
questions.title: Drug and Medicine Quality

questions.q: Peptides and proteins are polymers of amino acids joined by which type of bond?
options: Ester bonds
Amide bonds
Glycosidic bonds
Disulphide bonds
Hydrogen bonds
questions.explanation: Amino acids are joined by amide bonds, known as peptide bonds. The peptide bond forms between the carboxylic acid of one amino acid and the alpha-amino group of a second.
questions.title: Lecture 16 - Chemistry of Amino Acids, Carbohydrates and Lipids

questions.q: What ultimately dictates the properties of a peptide or protein?
options: Its total molecular weight
The sequence of amino acids and their functional groups
The temperature at which it was synthesised
The number of peptide bonds alone
The solvent used to dissolve it
questions.explanation: The properties of peptides and proteins are dictated ultimately by the sequence of amino acids and their functional groups.
questions.title: Lecture 16 - Chemistry of Amino Acids, Carbohydrates and Lipids

questions.q: Water-soluble proteins typically have which amino acids on their surface?
options: Non-polar amino acids such as valine and leucine
A mix of polar (hydrophilic) and charged amino acids
Only cysteine residues forming disulphide bridges
Exclusively glycine, which is the smallest residue
Aromatic residues capable of pi-stacking
questions.explanation: Proteins that are water soluble typically have a mix of polar (hydrophilic) and charged amino acids on their surface, since solubility is a fundamental protein property.
questions.title: Lecture 16 - Chemistry of Amino Acids, Carbohydrates and Lipids

questions.q: Which set of amino acids has non-polar side chain groups?
options: Phenylalanine, proline, valine, leucine and alanine
Asparagine, cysteine, glutamine, serine and threonine
Aspartic acid and glutamic acid
Lysine, arginine and histidine
Tyrosine, tryptophan and threonine
questions.explanation: The non-polar side chain amino acids listed are phenylalanine, proline, valine, leucine, isoleucine, glycine, alanine and methionine. Asparagine, cysteine, glutamine, serine, threonine, tryptophan and tyrosine are polar but neutral; aspartic and glutamic acids are acidic.
questions.title: Lecture 16 - Chemistry of Amino Acids, Carbohydrates and Lipids

questions.q: Why does the amine group of an amino acid behave as a Bronsted-Lowry base?
options: It donates a proton from the N-H bond
It has a lone pair on the nitrogen, so it can act as a proton acceptor
It carries a permanent negative charge
It is stabilised by resonance with the carboxyl group
It has a high electronegativity
questions.explanation: The amine group has a lone pair on the nitrogen, which means it can act as a proton acceptor and therefore behaves as a Bronsted-Lowry base. The carboxyl group loses a proton from the -OH and acts as an acid.
questions.title: Lecture 16 - Chemistry of Amino Acids, Carbohydrates and Lipids

questions.q: Why are amino acids described as zwitterions?
options: Because they contain both an acidic carboxylic acid group and a basic amine group
Because they exist as two enantiomers
Because they can form both cyclic and open chain structures
Because they contain two chiral centres
Because they can polymerise in either direction
questions.explanation: Amino acids have both acidic (carboxylic acid) and basic (amine) groups, so they carry both charges simultaneously. They have at least two pKa values, and the side chain may add a further acidic or basic group.
questions.title: Lecture 16 - Chemistry of Amino Acids, Carbohydrates and Lipids

questions.q: What is the isoelectric point of an amino acid?
options: The pH at which the carboxyl group is fully protonated
The pH at which the net charge is zero
The pH equal to the pKa of the amine group
The pH at which the amino acid is least soluble in lipid
The pH at which the side chain becomes ionised
questions.explanation: The isoelectric point of an amino acid is the pH at which the net charge is zero.
questions.title: Lecture 16 - Chemistry of Amino Acids, Carbohydrates and Lipids

questions.q: Under which conditions are the carboxylic acid and amine groups of an amino acid ionised?
options: Carboxylic acids ionise under acidic conditions; amines under alkaline conditions
Carboxylic acids ionise under alkaline conditions; amines under acidic conditions
Both ionise only under acidic conditions
Both ionise only under alkaline conditions
Neither ionises at physiological pH
questions.explanation: Carboxylic acids are ionised under alkaline conditions and amines are ionised under acidic conditions. The extent of ionisation depends on the pKa values and the pH of the environment.
questions.title: Lecture 16 - Chemistry of Amino Acids, Carbohydrates and Lipids

questions.q: Which protein amino acid is the exception to the rule that the alpha-carbon is chiral?
options: Alanine
Cysteine
Glycine
Proline
Serine
questions.explanation: All protein amino acids are alpha-amino acids and the alpha-carbon is chiral with one exception: glycine, which has two hydrogens attached to the alpha-carbon.
questions.title: Lecture 16 - Chemistry of Amino Acids, Carbohydrates and Lipids

questions.q: In the Fischer and CIP conventions, how are the protein amino acids designated?
options: All are D-, and all are R- under CIP
All are L-, and all are S- under CIP except cysteine which is R-
All are L-, and all are R- under CIP except glycine
Half are D- and half are L-, depending on the side chain
All are D-, and all are S- under CIP except cysteine
questions.explanation: Fischer designated the protein alpha-amino acids as D- or L-, and all the protein amino acids are L-. Under the CIP convention they are all S- except cysteine, which is R-.
questions.title: Lecture 16 - Chemistry of Amino Acids, Carbohydrates and Lipids

questions.q: Peptide bond formation between two amino acids involves which process?
options: Addition of water (hydration)
Exclusion of water (dehydration)
Oxidation of the carboxyl group
Reduction of the amine group
Transfer of a phosphate group
questions.explanation: The reaction of two amino acids to form a peptide bond involves the exclusion of water, that is a dehydration or condensation reaction.
questions.title: Lecture 16 - Chemistry of Amino Acids, Carbohydrates and Lipids

questions.q: Why does the peptide bond have restricted rotation?
options: Because it is a full double bond
Because it is resonance hybridised
Because of steric clash between adjacent side chains
Because of hydrogen bonding to water
Because the alpha-carbon is chiral
questions.explanation: The peptide bond is resonance hybridised, which gives restricted rotation to the bond and contributes to the overall shape of the molecule.
questions.title: Lecture 16 - Chemistry of Amino Acids, Carbohydrates and Lipids

questions.q: Most drug targets are proteins. What determines the strength of binding between a drug and its protein target?
options: The molecular weight of the drug alone
Complementary functional groups for bonding, and complementary shape of both molecules
The concentration of the drug in plasma
The number of peptide bonds in the protein
The isoelectric point of the protein
questions.explanation: Drug targets are mostly proteins with a three-dimensional shape. Binding strength is determined by complementary functional groups for bonding and complementary shape of both molecules, giving a stabilising interaction.
questions.title: Lecture 16 - Chemistry of Amino Acids, Carbohydrates and Lipids

questions.q: What is the empirical formula of a carbohydrate, and what does the name mean?
options: Cn(H2O)n; hydrates of carbon
CnH2nOn; carbon-oxygen polymers
CnH2n+2; saturated carbon chains
CnHnOn; equal parts of each element
C6H12O6 in every case; six-carbon sugars
questions.explanation: Carbohydrates have the empirical formula Cn(H2O)n and are literally hydrates of carbon. They supply about 55 per cent of dietary calories.
questions.title: Lecture 16 - Chemistry of Amino Acids, Carbohydrates and Lipids

questions.q: Which grouping of carbohydrates is correct?
options: Monosaccharides: maltose, sucrose, lactose
Disaccharides: glucose, fructose, galactose
Polysaccharides: starch, glycogen, cellulose
Monosaccharides: starch and glycogen
Disaccharides: cellulose and amylose
questions.explanation: Monosaccharides are glucose, fructose and galactose; disaccharides are maltose, sucrose and lactose; polysaccharides are starch, glycogen and cellulose.
questions.title: Lecture 16 - Chemistry of Amino Acids, Carbohydrates and Lipids

questions.q: Why can glucose be used directly for energy while fructose and galactose cannot?
options: Glucose is the only sugar absorbed from the gut
Glucose is the primary energy source, whereas fructose and galactose must first be converted to glucose or other forms
Fructose and galactose are not present in the human diet
Fructose and galactose are D- sugars while glucose is L-
Only glucose can form a cyclic hemiacetal
questions.explanation: Glucose is readily used for energy and is the primary energy source, while fructose and galactose must be converted into glucose or other forms before they can be used.
questions.title: Lecture 16 - Chemistry of Amino Acids, Carbohydrates and Lipids

questions.q: In aqueous solution, which form of a monosaccharide predominates?
options: The open chain form, because it is more stable
The cyclic form, which is generally more stable
Neither, because they do not interconvert
The fully oxidised acid form
The dimeric form
questions.explanation: Monosaccharides exist in open chain and cyclic isomeric forms which are in equilibrium in aqueous solution. The cyclic form is generally more stable and therefore the more likely structure.
questions.title: Lecture 16 - Chemistry of Amino Acids, Carbohydrates and Lipids

questions.q: How does glucose form its cyclic hemiacetal?
options: The hydroxy group on C5 attacks the carbonyl carbon on C1
The hydroxy group on C1 attacks the carbonyl carbon on C6
Two glucose molecules condense with loss of water
The carboxyl group reacts with the amine group
A phosphate group bridges C1 and C5
questions.explanation: In glucose the hydroxy group on C5 attacks the carbonyl carbon on C1 to form a cyclic hemiacetal, introducing a new chiral carbon called the anomeric carbon.
questions.title: Lecture 16 - Chemistry of Amino Acids, Carbohydrates and Lipids

questions.q: What distinguishes the alpha and beta anomers of glucose?
options: Alpha has the anomeric hydroxyl beneath the plane, beta above the plane
Alpha is the open chain form, beta the cyclic form
Alpha is D- and beta is L-
Alpha contains six carbons and beta contains five
Alpha is an aldose and beta a ketose
questions.explanation: The hemiacetal introduces a new chiral centre, the anomeric carbon, with two possible configurations: alpha beneath the plane and beta above the plane.
questions.title: Lecture 16 - Chemistry of Amino Acids, Carbohydrates and Lipids

questions.q: What is mutarotation?
options: The conversion of a D- sugar into its L- form
The interconversion between the alpha and beta anomers via the aldehyde form
The hydrolysis of a disaccharide into two monosaccharides
The rotation of a peptide bond through 180 degrees
The conversion of glucose into fructose
questions.explanation: Mutarotation is the interconversion between the alpha and beta forms via the aldehyde form. The two anomers have different physicochemical properties, the beta form is more stable, and the equilibrium specific rotation is +54.
questions.title: Lecture 16 - Chemistry of Amino Acids, Carbohydrates and Lipids

questions.q: Why are monosaccharides water soluble?
options: Because they carry a permanent negative charge
Because they have a large number of hydroxyl groups that hydrogen bond to water
Because they are ionised at physiological pH
Because they have low molecular weight only
Because they exist in the open chain form
questions.explanation: Monosaccharides are water soluble because of their large number of hydroxyl groups, which hydrogen bond to water molecules.
questions.title: Lecture 16 - Chemistry of Amino Acids, Carbohydrates and Lipids

questions.q: Why do monosaccharides act as reducing sugars?
options: Because the cyclic hemiacetal is highly reactive
Because the aldehyde form is present in small amounts at equilibrium
Because they carry a free carboxylic acid group
Because the anomeric carbon is chiral
Because they can be oxidised at C6
questions.explanation: Although monosaccharides exist in solution mainly as cyclic hemiacetals, the aldehyde form is present in small amounts, which explains the reactions of reducing sugars.
questions.title: Lecture 16 - Chemistry of Amino Acids, Carbohydrates and Lipids

questions.q: What is a glycoside?
options: The full acetal of glucose plus another molecule
The cyclic hemiacetal form of a monosaccharide
A polymer of two or more monosaccharides only
An amino acid linked to a sugar
A fatty acid ester of glycerol
questions.explanation: Glycosides are the full acetals of glucose plus another molecule, and can form from -OH, -NH or -SH groups. The non-sugar part is the aglycone, joined through the glycosidic bond.
questions.title: Lecture 16 - Chemistry of Amino Acids, Carbohydrates and Lipids

questions.q: Lactose is which of the following?
options: An alpha-1,4 linked glucose-glucose dimer
A beta-1,4 linked galactose-glucose dimer, cleaved by lactase
A dimer of alpha-D-glucose and beta-D-fructose
A homopolymer of glucose with alpha-1,6 branches
A beta-1,4 linked glucose polymer
questions.explanation: Lactose, milk sugar, is a beta-1,4 linked galactose-glucose dimer cleaved by the enzyme lactase (beta-galactosidase). Lactose intolerance is a lack of lactase.
questions.title: Lecture 16 - Chemistry of Amino Acids, Carbohydrates and Lipids

questions.q: What is galactosaemia?
options: A lack of the enzyme lactase
An inability to epimerise galactose to glucose
An allergy to milk proteins
An excess of galactose in the diet
An inability to absorb galactose from the gut
questions.explanation: Galactosaemia is the inability to epimerise galactose to glucose. This is distinct from lactose intolerance, which is a lack of the enzyme lactase.
questions.title: Lecture 16 - Chemistry of Amino Acids, Carbohydrates and Lipids

questions.q: Sucrose is unusual among disaccharides because of which structural feature?
options: It contains two identical monosaccharide units
The link is between the anomeric centres of both sugars
It has a beta-1,4 linkage
It contains a nitrogen atom in the glycosidic bond
It cannot be hydrolysed by any enzyme
questions.explanation: Sucrose is a disaccharide of alpha-D-glucose and beta-D-fructose in which the link is between the anomeric centres of both sugars, so neither anomeric carbon is free.
questions.title: Lecture 16 - Chemistry of Amino Acids, Carbohydrates and Lipids

questions.q: How do amylose and amylopectin differ?
options: Amylose has only alpha-1,4 links; amylopectin also has alpha-1,6 branches
Amylose has beta-1,4 links; amylopectin has alpha-1,4 links
Amylose is a heteropolymer; amylopectin is a homopolymer
Amylose is found in animals; amylopectin in plants
Amylose is branched; amylopectin is linear
questions.explanation: Starch consists of amylose and amylopectin. Amylose has only alpha-1,4 glucose-glucose links, while amylopectin also has some alpha-1,6 linked branches.
questions.title: Lecture 16 - Chemistry of Amino Acids, Carbohydrates and Lipids

questions.q: Why can humans not use cellulose as food, even though it is a homopolymer of glucose?
options: Cellulose is not absorbed from the gut
We lack the enzymes to hydrolyse its beta-1,4 links
Cellulose is chemically inert and cannot be hydrolysed by anything
Cellulose contains no glucose in a usable form
Cellulose is too soluble to remain in the gut
questions.explanation: Cellulose has beta-1,4 links with secondary structure held by hydrogen bonds. Humans do not have enzymes to hydrolyse beta-1,4 links, although some microorganisms, for example in ruminants, can.
questions.title: Lecture 16 - Chemistry of Amino Acids, Carbohydrates and Lipids

questions.q: Which is the primary energy storage carbohydrate in mammals?
options: Starch
Cellulose
Glycogen
Amylose
Sucrose
questions.explanation: Glycogen is the primary energy storage carbohydrate in mammals. Starch is the primary energy storage substance in plants and cellulose the primary structural material in plants; all three are homopolymers of glucose.
questions.title: Lecture 16 - Chemistry of Amino Acids, Carbohydrates and Lipids

questions.q: Many plant-derived drugs such as digoxin are glycosides. What effect do the sugar hydroxy groups have?
options: They increase the polarity of the molecule and make the drug water soluble
They increase lipid solubility and aid membrane crossing
They protect the drug from hepatic metabolism
They allow the drug to bind covalently to its receptor
They reduce the molecular weight of the drug
questions.explanation: Many bioactive substances from plants are glycosides, including digoxin and the anthraquinone glycosides. Their many hydroxy groups increase the polarity of the molecule and make the drug water soluble.
questions.title: Lecture 16 - Chemistry of Amino Acids, Carbohydrates and Lipids

questions.q: Fatty acids are described as which type of molecule?
options: Amino derivatives of long-chain hydrocarbons
Carboxylic acids of long-chain hydrocarbons, CH3-(CH2)n-COOH
Esters of glycerol with three sugar units
Cyclic hemiacetals of hexoses
Polymers of glucose linked by ester bonds
questions.explanation: Fatty acids are the monomer units of lipids and are carboxylic acids of long-chain hydrocarbons, CH3-(CH2)n-COOH. They are important dietary and biochemical molecules and are found in some drug molecules.
questions.title: Lecture 16 - Chemistry of Amino Acids, Carbohydrates and Lipids

questions.q: How does the solubility behaviour of a fatty acid change on dissociation?
options: The undissociated form is water soluble; the dissociated form is not
The undissociated form is not water soluble, while the dissociated form is a surfactant that can form micelles
Both forms are equally insoluble in water
The dissociated form precipitates from solution
Dissociation has no effect on solubility
questions.explanation: Fatty acids are not soluble in water in the undissociated form. The dissociated forms are surfactants: they interact with both water and lipid, can form micelles and can solubilise fatty substances.
questions.title: Lecture 16 - Chemistry of Amino Acids, Carbohydrates and Lipids

questions.q: Lauric acid (12:0) melts at 44 degrees C and stearic acid (18:0) at 69 degrees C. What general rule does this illustrate?
options: Melting point decreases as chain length increases
Melting point increases as chain length increases
Melting point depends only on the degree of unsaturation
Melting point is unrelated to chain length in saturated fatty acids
Melting point increases only above 16 carbons
questions.explanation: As chain length increases, so does the melting point: lauric 12:0 at 44 degrees C, myristic 14:0 at 58, palmitic 16:0 at 63 and stearic 18:0 at 69 degrees C.
questions.title: Lecture 16 - Chemistry of Amino Acids, Carbohydrates and Lipids

questions.q: Which physicochemical property of monosaccharides allows them to rotate plane-polarised light?
options: Molecular weight
Stereoisomerism
Degree of saturation
Solubility
Ionisation
questions.explanation: Optical activity arises from chirality, so it is the stereoisomerism of monosaccharides, arising from their chiral carbons, that allows them to rotate plane-polarised light.
questions.title: Lecture 16 - Chemistry of Amino Acids, Carbohydrates and Lipids

questions.q: The carboxyl group of an amino acid can:
options: Lose a proton from –OH and act as a Brønsted-Lowry acid
Never ionise in water
Act only as a base
Form peptide bonds without a carboxylate
Remain neutral at all pH values
questions.explanation: Amino acid chemistry: the carboxyl group can lose a proton from the –OH group, behaving as a Brønsted-Lowry acid and leaving a negative carboxylate ion.
questions.title: Lecture 16 - Chemistry of Amino Acids, Carbohydrates and Lipids

questions.q: Amino acid chirality arises from:
options: A chiral α-carbon between the amine and carboxyl groups
Chirality of the carboxylate oxygen only
Random thermal motion
Glycosidic bond rotation
Fatty acid saturation only
questions.explanation: Amino acids can have a chiral carbon situated between the amine and carboxyl groups, depending on the identity of the four groups bonded to that carbon.
questions.title: Lecture 16 - Chemistry of Amino Acids, Carbohydrates and Lipids

questions.q: Protein amino acids in Fischer projection are:
options: L α-amino acids with both carboxylic acid and amine groups
D sugars only
Fatty acids with no amine
Nucleotides with phosphate
Only glycine with no functional groups
questions.explanation: Amino acids have both a carboxylic acid and an amine in their structure and are represented as L α-amino acids in Fischer projection.
questions.title: Lecture 16 - Chemistry of Amino Acids, Carbohydrates and Lipids

questions.q: According to the amino acid summary, side chains may be:
options: Acidic, basic, neutral polar or neutral non-polar
Only hydrocarbons with no functionality
Only phosphate esters
Only disaccharide units
Absent in all amino acids
questions.explanation: Proteins are made of amino acids with carboxylic acid (acidic) and amino (basic) groups plus side chain functionality that may be acidic, basic, neutral polar or neutral non-polar.
questions.title: Lecture 16 - Chemistry of Amino Acids, Carbohydrates and Lipids

questions.q: Why should pharmacists note carbohydrate excipients in medicines?
options: Some patients have allergies or dietary restrictions to sugars
Sugars always prevent drug absorption
Carbohydrates are never used in tablets
Sugars replace all active ingredients
Excipients never affect patients
questions.explanation: Some medications such as oral contraceptives may contain sugars as excipients; pharmacists should be aware for patients with allergies or dietary restrictions.
questions.title: Lecture 16 - Chemistry of Amino Acids, Carbohydrates and Lipids

questions.q: The name 'glucose' was coined from Greek glycos meaning:
options: Sugar or sweet
Fat or lipid
Protein chain
Amino nitrogen
Phosphate group
questions.explanation: IUPAC vs Fischer notes that glucose was named in 1838 by Jean Dumas from Greek glycos, meaning sugar or sweet; fructose comes from Latin fructus (fruit) plus -ose.
questions.title: Lecture 16 - Chemistry of Amino Acids, Carbohydrates and Lipids

questions.q: In the Fischer convention, D-glyceraldehyde is:
options: The reference dextrorotatory enantiomer for assigning D configuration
Always an L-sugar
A ketose with no chirality
A fatty acid with 18 carbons
A polysaccharide of glucose only
questions.explanation: Dextrorotatory glyceraldehyde is designated D in the Fischer convention, and chirality of other molecules is assigned relative to this reference (absolute configuration confirmed in 1951).
questions.title: Lecture 16 - Chemistry of Amino Acids, Carbohydrates and Lipids

questions.q: In a Fischer projection, a molecule is designated D when:
options: The substituent on the chiral carbon furthest from the top is to the right
The lowest carbon is always on the left
The molecule cannot rotate light
It contains only ketones
It has no chiral centres
questions.explanation: Fischer projection rules place the most highly oxidised carbon at the top; if the substituent on the chiral carbon furthest from the top is to the right, the molecule is D.
questions.title: Lecture 16 - Chemistry of Amino Acids, Carbohydrates and Lipids

questions.q: Which monosaccharide name must be known according to the D-aldose series slide?
options: Glucose
All eight names must be memorised with no exceptions
Only ribose
Only fructose
Only galactose without glucose
questions.explanation: The D-aldose series includes allose through galactose, but the slide states glucose must be known while other monosaccharide names can be looked up as required.
questions.title: Lecture 16 - Chemistry of Amino Acids, Carbohydrates and Lipids

questions.q: Major homopolysaccharides are made of which monomer?
options: Glucose units linked by glycosidic bonds
Amino acids only
Fatty acids only
Nucleotides only
Cholesterol only
questions.explanation: Polysaccharides are made of sugar monomer units; glucose forms the major homopolysaccharides starch, glycogen and cellulose, linked by glycosidic bonds that can be hydrolysed.
questions.title: Lecture 16 - Chemistry of Amino Acids, Carbohydrates and Lipids

questions.q: A fundamental structural difference between monosaccharides and disaccharides is:
options: Disaccharides contain two monosaccharide units joined by a glycosidic bond
Monosaccharides always have higher molecular weight
Disaccharides lack any chiral centres
Monosaccharides cannot form rings
Disaccharides are always proteins
questions.explanation: The example SAQ asks for a fundamental difference: disaccharides consist of two monosaccharide units linked by a glycosidic bond, whereas monosaccharides are single sugar units.
questions.title: Lecture 16 - Chemistry of Amino Acids, Carbohydrates and Lipids

questions.q: What is the correct order of increasing complexity in biological structures?
options: Polymers build monomers, which build macromolecules, which build cells
Monomers build polymers, which build macromolecules, which build cells
Macromolecules build polymers, which build monomers, which build cells
Cells build macromolecules, which build polymers, which build monomers
Monomers build macromolecules, which build polymers, which build cells
questions.explanation: Monomers are the building blocks that build polymers; polymers build macromolecules; and macromolecules build cells.
questions.title: Lecture 17 - Macromolecules 1

questions.q: Which four macromolecule types are described as the building blocks of life?
options: Carbohydrates, lipids, nucleic acids and proteins
Sugars, starches, fats and vitamins
DNA, RNA, ATP and NADH
Enzymes, hormones, receptors and channels
Cellulose, glycogen, cholesterol and haemoglobin
questions.explanation: The key macromolecules found in most cells are carbohydrates, lipids, nucleic acids and proteins, described as the building blocks of life.
questions.title: Lecture 17 - Macromolecules 1

questions.q: What is the general formula of a monosaccharide?
options: CnH2n+2
(CH2O)n
CnH2nO
C6H12O6 only
CnHnOn
questions.explanation: Monosaccharides are simple organic compounds with the general formula (CH2O)n. Examples are the trioses glyceraldehyde and dihydroxyacetone, both C3H6O3, and the hexoses glucose and fructose, both C6H12O6.
questions.title: Lecture 17 - Macromolecules 1

questions.q: What distinguishes an aldose from a ketose?
options: An aldose has an aldehyde group; a ketose has a ketone group
An aldose is cyclic; a ketose is linear
An aldose has five carbons; a ketose has six
An aldose is a D- sugar; a ketose is an L- sugar
An aldose can polymerise; a ketose cannot
questions.explanation: Aldoses have an aldehyde group and ketoses have a ketone group. Glyceraldehyde is an aldose and dihydroxyacetone a ketose; glucose is an aldose and fructose a ketose.
questions.title: Lecture 17 - Macromolecules 1

questions.q: What is a hemiacetal?
options: A carbon connected to two oxygens, one an alcohol and the other an ether
A carbon connected to two nitrogens
A carbon double bonded to oxygen in a ring
Two sugars joined by a glycosidic bond
A phosphate ester of a sugar hydroxyl
questions.explanation: A hemiacetal is a carbon connected to two oxygens where one is an alcohol (OH) and the other an ether (OR). Hemiacetals form when an alcohol group reacts with an aldehyde; in sugars this reaction is intramolecular.
questions.title: Lecture 17 - Macromolecules 1

questions.q: Monosaccharides with how many carbons can exist in both linear and cyclic forms?
options: Three or more
Four or more
Five or more
Six or more
Only exactly six
questions.explanation: Monosaccharides composed of 5 or more carbons can exist in both linear and cyclic forms.
questions.title: Lecture 17 - Macromolecules 1

questions.q: Which pair of reactions builds and breaks down biological macromolecules?
options: Oxidation adds water; reduction removes water
Condensation (polymerisation) removes water; hydrolysis adds water
Condensation adds water; hydrolysis removes water
Phosphorylation removes water; dephosphorylation adds water
Both condensation and hydrolysis remove water
questions.explanation: Condensation or polymerisation removes water to build polymers, while hydrolysis or hydrolytic degradation adds water to break them down. Enzymes catalyse both reactions.
questions.title: Lecture 17 - Macromolecules 1

questions.q: Which bond links monosaccharides together to form disaccharides and polysaccharides?
options: Peptide bond
Ester bond
Phosphodiester bond
Glycosidic bond
Disulphide bond
questions.explanation: The glycosidic bond links monosaccharides together to form disaccharides and polysaccharides.
questions.title: Lecture 17 - Macromolecules 1

questions.q: Glycogen, the animal energy store, has which structural features and location?
options: Unbranched alpha-1,4 links, stored in plant granules
Highly branched alpha-1,4 and alpha-1,6 links, stored in liver and muscle
Beta-1,4 links, found in plant cell walls
Highly branched beta-1,4 and beta-1,6 links, stored in adipocytes
Alpha-1,6 links only, stored in the bloodstream
questions.explanation: Glycogen is the animal energy store, kept in the liver and muscle, and is highly branched with alpha-1,4 and alpha-1,6 glycosidic bonds.
questions.title: Lecture 17 - Macromolecules 1

questions.q: Why is cellulose classed as dietary fibre?
options: It contains no glucose units
Its beta-1,4 glycosidic bonds are indigestible to humans
It is too large to enter the small intestine
It dissolves completely in water and passes straight through
It is chemically identical to starch but in a different physical form
questions.explanation: Cellulose forms plant cell walls and has indigestible beta-1,4 glycosidic bonds, which is why it functions as dietary fibre. Starch and glycogen use digestible alpha links.
questions.title: Lecture 17 - Macromolecules 1

questions.q: Peptidoglycan is built from which disaccharide unit, and why does it matter pharmacologically?
options: Glucose-fructose; it is the target of insulin
NAG-NAM (N-acetylglucosamine and N-acetylmuramic acid); it is central to the action of beta-lactam and glycopeptide antibiotics
Galactose-glucose; it is cleaved by lactase
NAG-NAM; it is the target of antifungal azoles
Glucose-glucose; it is the store of bacterial energy
questions.explanation: Peptidoglycans are polysaccharides with peptides attached, built from the N-acetylglucosamine (NAG) and N-acetylmuramic acid (NAM) disaccharide. This is very important for the mechanism of action of beta-lactam and glycopeptide antibiotics.
questions.title: Lecture 17 - Macromolecules 1

questions.q: In lipopolysaccharide (LPS), which component is toxic and which is immunogenic?
options: Lipid A is toxic; the O-polysaccharide is immunogenic
The O-polysaccharide is toxic; lipid A is immunogenic
Both parts are toxic and neither is immunogenic
The core sugar is toxic; lipid A is immunogenic
Lipid A is immunogenic; the peptide chain is toxic
questions.explanation: In lipopolysaccharide, lipid A is the toxic component and the O-polysaccharide is the immunogenic component.
questions.title: Lecture 17 - Macromolecules 1

questions.q: Which set of properties describes lipids?
options: Largely hydrocarbon with more oxygen than carbohydrates, and high water solubility
Largely hydrocarbon with generally less oxygen than carbohydrates, low water solubility and high solubility in organic solvents
Highly polar molecules with many hydroxyl groups
Charged polymers that dissolve readily in water
Nitrogen-containing compounds with low solubility in organic solvents
questions.explanation: Lipids are organic compounds, largely hydrocarbon but generally with less oxygen than carbohydrates, with low solubility in water and high solubility in organic solvents. They may be open chain or fused ring.
questions.title: Lecture 17 - Macromolecules 1

questions.q: Why are lipids described as not being true polymers?
options: They contain no repeating units at all
Fatty acids act as building blocks but generally do not polymerise alone
They are too small to be polymers
They are held together only by hydrogen bonds
They cannot be hydrolysed
