questions.explanation: Lipids are not true polymers because fatty acids, although they often act as lipid building blocks, generally do not polymerise alone. Fatty acid chain length varies from 4 to 22 carbons.
questions.title: Lecture 17 - Macromolecules 1

questions.q: What does amphipathic mean when applied to a fatty acid?
options: It contains both saturated and unsaturated bonds
It contains both hydrophilic and hydrophobic ends
It can exist as both D- and L- isomers
It can act as both an acid and a base
It is soluble in neither water nor organic solvents
questions.explanation: An amphipathic lipid contains both hydrophilic and hydrophobic ends, which is why dissociated fatty acids behave as surfactants and why phospholipids form membranes.
questions.title: Lecture 17 - Macromolecules 1

questions.q: How is a triglyceride constructed?
options: Glycerol linked by three ester bonds to three fatty acids
Glycerol linked by two ester bonds to two fatty acids and a phosphate
Three glycerol molecules linked to one fatty acid
Three fatty acids linked to each other by ester bonds
A steroid nucleus with three hydrocarbon rings
questions.explanation: Triglycerides, also called triacylglycerols, are simple lipids made of glycerol linked by three ester bonds to three fatty acids.
questions.title: Lecture 17 - Macromolecules 1

questions.q: How does the energy content of triglycerides compare with carbohydrates?
options: About 17 kJ/g versus 39 kJ/g for carbohydrates
About 39 kJ/g versus 17 kJ/g for carbohydrates
Both provide about 39 kJ/g
About 4 kJ/g versus 17 kJ/g for carbohydrates
Triglycerides provide no usable energy
questions.explanation: Triglycerides are high energy at about 39 kJ/g compared with 17 kJ/g for carbohydrates, which is why they are the predominant storage lipid in adipocytes.
questions.title: Lecture 17 - Macromolecules 1

questions.q: Besides energy storage, what other functions does adipose tissue serve?
options: Oxygen transport and pH buffering
Heat insulation and mechanical protection
Antibody production and phagocytosis
Bile secretion and drug metabolism
Nerve conduction and muscle contraction
questions.explanation: Adipose tissue also has functions in heat insulation and mechanical protection, in addition to storing triglycerides.
questions.title: Lecture 17 - Macromolecules 1

questions.q: How does a phospholipid differ from a triglyceride?
options: It has three fatty acid chains rather than two
It has only two fatty acid chains, being a diacylglycerol, and is amphipathic
It contains no glycerol backbone
It contains four hydrocarbon rings
It is entirely hydrophobic with no polar region
questions.explanation: Phospholipids resemble fats but have only two fatty acid chains, making them diacylglycerols. They are amphipathic lipids and a major component of cell membranes.
questions.title: Lecture 17 - Macromolecules 1

questions.q: Which statements about cholesterol are correct?
options: Formed via cyclisation of squalene, has four hydrocarbon rings, is amphiphilic and is the basis of steroid hormones
Formed from three fatty acids and glycerol, and stored in adipocytes
Formed from two fatty acids and a phosphate, and forms the membrane bilayer
A polysaccharide of glucose with beta-1,4 links
A nucleotide derivative that carries energy in cells
questions.explanation: Cholesterol is formed via cyclisation of squalene, has four hydrocarbon rings, is amphiphilic, is an important component of lipid membranes and is the basis of the steroid hormones such as androgens and oestrogens.
questions.title: Lecture 17 - Macromolecules 1

questions.q: Which nucleic acid holds the genetic information in all cellular organisms?
options: RNA
DNA
ATP
Peptidoglycan
Both DNA and RNA equally
questions.explanation: DNA holds the genetic information in all cellular organisms and some viruses. RNA holds the genetic material in some viruses and is also required for protein synthesis.
questions.title: Lecture 17 - Macromolecules 1

questions.q: What are the three parts of a nucleotide?
options: A phosphate group, a five-carbon sugar and a nitrogenous base
An amino group, a carboxyl group and a side chain
Two sugars and a phosphate
A glycerol backbone, a fatty acid and a phosphate
A purine, a pyrimidine and a sugar
questions.explanation: Each nucleotide consists of a phosphate group, a five-carbon sugar and a nitrogenous base. The sugar plus base alone, without the phosphate, is a nucleoside.
questions.title: Lecture 17 - Macromolecules 1

questions.q: Which bases are purines and which are pyrimidines?
options: Purines: cytosine, thymine, uracil; pyrimidines: guanine, adenine
Purines: guanine, adenine; pyrimidines: cytosine, thymine, uracil
Purines: adenine, thymine; pyrimidines: guanine, cytosine
Purines: guanine, cytosine; pyrimidines: adenine, thymine
All five bases are purines
questions.explanation: The purines are guanine (G) and adenine (A). The pyrimidines are cytosine (C), thymine (T) and uracil (U).
questions.title: Lecture 17 - Macromolecules 1

questions.q: Why are polynucleotide chains directional?
options: Because the bases can only pair in one orientation
Because a phosphodiester linkage forms between the 5' and 3' carbons of the sugar ring, giving different ends
Because the phosphate groups carry a negative charge
Because DNA is always read left to right
Because the major and minor grooves run in opposite directions
questions.explanation: Nucleotides polymerise via their phosphate groups, forming a phosphodiester linkage between the 5' and 3' carbons of the sugar ring. This means the chain has two different ends, called 5' and 3'.
questions.title: Lecture 17 - Macromolecules 1

questions.q: How does the usual structure of DNA compare with that of RNA?
options: DNA is usually a single helix; RNA is usually a double helix
DNA is usually a double helix of two antiparallel strands; RNA is usually a single helix
Both are usually double helices
Both are usually single helices
DNA is linear and RNA is always circular
questions.explanation: DNA is usually a double helix made of two antiparallel polynucleotide strands, whereas RNA is usually a single helix. Functional groups on each strand allow hydrogen bonding between them.
questions.title: Lecture 17 - Macromolecules 1

questions.q: Which base pairs form in DNA, and which pairing is stronger?
options: A-T and G-C, with G-C bound more strongly
A-T and G-C, with A-T bound more strongly
A-G and C-T, with A-G bound more strongly
A-C and G-T, with G-T bound more strongly
A-U and G-C, with A-U bound more strongly
questions.explanation: Hydrogen bonding occurs between complementary bases A-T and G-C. G-C pairs are bound more strongly than A-T pairs.
questions.title: Lecture 17 - Macromolecules 1

questions.q: Why does base pairing enable faithful copying of DNA?
options: Because the sugar-phosphate backbone is identical in both strands
Because each strand can act as a template for its complementary strand
Because the major and minor grooves guide the polymerase
Because G-C pairs resist separation during replication
Because DNA is asymmetrical
questions.explanation: Because of complementary base pairing, each DNA strand can act as a template for its complementary strand, which is the basis of faithful copying.
questions.title: Lecture 17 - Macromolecules 1

questions.q: Why does DNA have major and minor grooves?
options: Because the strands are of unequal length
Because DNA is slightly asymmetrical
Because G-C pairs occupy more space than A-T pairs
Because the sugar-phosphate backbone is charged
Because the two strands run in the same direction
questions.explanation: DNA is slightly asymmetrical, so the double helix has major and minor grooves. A sugar-phosphate backbone runs along each strand, with the paired bases hydrogen bonded in the centre.
questions.title: Lecture 17 - Macromolecules 1

questions.q: How many nucleotides are converted to a single amino acid during translation?
options: One
Two
Three
Four
Six
questions.explanation: The DNA sequence of a gene is read by transcription into RNA, and the RNA is translated into protein with every set of 3 nucleotides converted to a single corresponding amino acid.
questions.title: Lecture 17 - Macromolecules 1

questions.q: How does ATP act as an energy carrier?
options: Its breakdown to ADP releases energy, and energy input is needed to reconstitute ATP
Its breakdown to ADP requires energy, which is stored as heat
It stores energy in the adenine base rather than the phosphates
It carries energy by transferring electrons rather than phosphate
It releases energy only when converted to DNA
questions.explanation: ATP is adenosine 5'-triphosphate. Breakdown to ADP releases energy, and energy input is needed to reconstitute ATP from ADP.
questions.title: Lecture 17 - Macromolecules 1

questions.q: Which medicinal macromolecule is correctly matched to its class and use?
options: Hydrocortisone, a carbohydrate, used to reduce constipation
Ispaghula, a lipid steroid hormone, used to reduce immune response
Lactulose, a non-absorbable disaccharide sugar, used to reduce constipation
Lactulose, a lipid, used to reduce the immune response
Hydrocortisone, a soluble fibre, used to reduce constipation
questions.explanation: Hydrocortisone is a lipid steroid hormone that reduces the immune response. Ispaghula is a high soluble fibre carbohydrate and lactulose a non-absorbable disaccharide sugar, both used to reduce constipation.
questions.title: Lecture 17 - Macromolecules 1

questions.q: If a monomer has an asymmetric carbon at its centre, what follows?
options: It can exist as two optical isomers or enantiomers, often labelled D and L
It cannot form polymers
It must be a carbohydrate
It will always be water soluble
It will have two different melting points
questions.explanation: A monomer with an asymmetric carbon at its centre can exist as two optical isomers or enantiomers, commonly known as the D (right, dextro) and L (left, levo) forms.
questions.title: Lecture 17 - Macromolecules 1

questions.q: Glucose and fructose are both hexoses. How do they differ in their linear and cyclic forms?
options: Glucose is an aldose hexose; fructose is a ketose hexose
Glucose is a ketose; fructose is an aldose
Both are aldoses with identical structures
Both are ketoses that cannot cyclise
Only fructose can exist in linear form
questions.explanation: Both glucose and fructose are six-carbon sugars (hexoses) that exist in linear and cyclic forms. Glucose is an aldose and fructose a ketose, reflecting their aldehyde versus ketone groups.
questions.title: Lecture 17 - Macromolecules 1

questions.q: Why are monosaccharides and polysaccharides collectively called carbohydrates?
options: They have the general formula Cx(H2O)y, meaning hydrated carbon
They contain only carbon and hydrogen
They cannot be polymerised from monomer subunits
They are synthesised only from lipids
They lack oxygen in their structure
questions.explanation: Monosaccharide subunits can polymerise to form polysaccharides. Both are called carbohydrates because they fit the general formula Cx(H2O)y, literally hydrated carbon.
questions.title: Lecture 17 - Macromolecules 1

questions.q: A protein with carbohydrate attached is called what?
options: A lipoprotein
A glycoprotein
A multimer
A proteoglycan monomer
A nucleoprotein
questions.explanation: Proteins are polymers of amino acid monomers that may also have carbohydrates attached, making glycoproteins, or lipids attached, making lipoproteins.
questions.title: Lecture 18 - Macromolecules 2

questions.q: What are the four levels of protein structure, in order?
options: Primary (amino acid sequence), secondary (local hydrogen bonding), tertiary (3D shape), quaternary (subunit interactions)
Primary (3D shape), secondary (sequence), tertiary (hydrogen bonding), quaternary (folding)
Primary (folding), secondary (subunits), tertiary (sequence), quaternary (bonding)
Primary (hydrogen bonding), secondary (sequence), tertiary (subunits), quaternary (3D shape)
Primary (sequence), secondary (3D shape), tertiary (subunits), quaternary (hydrogen bonding)
questions.explanation: Primary structure is the amino acid sequence; secondary structure arises from local hydrogen bonding giving alpha helices and beta-pleated sheets; tertiary is the 3D shape of the protein; quaternary describes interactions between protein subunits.
questions.title: Lecture 18 - Macromolecules 2

questions.q: Which protein type is correctly matched with its example?
options: Structural protein: haemoglobin
Transport protein: haemoglobin, which carries oxygen in the blood
Motor protein: ferritin, which stores iron in the liver
Storage protein: myosin in skeletal muscle
Signal protein: alpha-keratin in hair and horn
questions.explanation: Transport proteins carry molecules through the bloodstream and across membranes, with haemoglobin carrying oxygen and bacteriorhodopsin transporting H+ out of bacterial cells. Alpha-keratin is structural, myosin a motor protein, and ferritin a storage protein.
questions.title: Lecture 18 - Macromolecules 2

questions.q: Insulin controlling blood glucose and epidermal growth factor stimulating cell division are examples of which protein class?
options: Receptor proteins
Signal proteins
Gene regulatory proteins
Motor proteins
Immune proteins
questions.explanation: Signal proteins such as hormones and growth factors carry messages from cell to cell to coordinate physiological function. Receptor proteins, such as rhodopsin and the insulin receptor, detect signals and transmit information.
questions.title: Lecture 18 - Macromolecules 2

questions.q: The bacterial lactose repressor, which silences genes for lactose processing enzymes when lactose is absent, is an example of which protein class?
options: Receptor protein
Gene regulatory protein
Enzyme
Storage protein
Structural protein
questions.explanation: Gene regulatory proteins effect changes in gene expression and may increase or decrease it. The bacterial lactose repressor is the example given.
questions.title: Lecture 18 - Macromolecules 2

questions.q: Why is knowing a protein's shape critical to understanding its function?
options: Because shape determines its molecular weight
Because proteins are machines that act by changing their shape, usually using ATP
Because shape determines the protein's amino acid sequence
Because only spherical proteins are biologically active
Because shape determines how many genes encode it
questions.explanation: Proteins are machines that do things in the body by changing their shape, which requires energy, usually ATP. Knowing their shape and how it changes is therefore critical to their function.
questions.title: Lecture 18 - Macromolecules 2

questions.q: How many standard amino acids are there, and what varies between them?
options: 20, differing in their variable R-group side chain
20, differing in their backbone structure
22, differing in their carboxyl group
64, differing in their codon
4, differing in their nitrogenous base
questions.explanation: There are 20 standard amino acids, all with a common structure, differing in their variable R-group side chain. The side chain can be polar or nonpolar, and polar side chains can be charged or uncharged.
questions.title: Lecture 18 - Macromolecules 2

questions.q: In which optical isomeric form do amino acids naturally occur?
options: The D form
The L form
A racemic mixture of both
Neither, because amino acids are achiral
The meso form
questions.explanation: Amino acids have an asymmetric carbon at their centre so exist as two optical isomers, and they naturally occur in the L form.
questions.title: Lecture 18 - Macromolecules 2

questions.q: Where does polypeptide assembly occur, and what determines the sequence?
options: In the nucleus, determined by DNA directly
In the ribosome, with the sequence determined by mRNA
In the mitochondria, determined by ATP availability
In the endoplasmic reticulum, determined by tRNA alone
In the cytoplasm, determined at random
questions.explanation: Polypeptide assembly is a condensation reaction that occurs in the ribosome, with the sequence determined by mRNA, forming a polypeptide chain.
questions.title: Lecture 18 - Macromolecules 2

questions.q: Which of these can be predicted by in silico analysis of a protein's primary structure?
options: Sites of post-translational modification such as glycosylation and phosphorylation
The rate at which the protein will be degraded in the stomach
The exact melting point of the crystallised protein
The number of subunits in the final multimer with certainty
The concentration of the protein in plasma
questions.explanation: Primary structure analysis can predict sites of post-translational modification such as glycosylation and phosphate attachment, internal disulphide bonds, signal peptides or localisation sequences, and other motifs such as protease cleavage sites.
questions.title: Lecture 18 - Macromolecules 2

questions.q: In HIV-1 envelope glycoprotein gp160, what is the role of the signal peptide?
options: It directs the protein to the surface membrane
It marks the protein for degradation
It provides the sites of sugar attachment
It forms the disulphide bonds between domains
It anchors the protein in the membrane
questions.explanation: In gp160 the signal peptide directs the protein to the surface membrane. Separately, sites of glycosylation, disulphide bonds separating the glycoprotein into domains, and a hydrophobic transmembrane region can all be identified from the sequence.
questions.title: Lecture 18 - Macromolecules 2

questions.q: What molecular force gives rise to secondary structure?
options: Covalent disulphide bonds
Hydrogen bonds between adjacent amino acids
Ionic bonds between charged side chains
Hydrophobic interactions between R-groups
Van der Waals forces between subunits
questions.explanation: Secondary structure is the conformation of parts of the polypeptide chain as it folds, with hydrogen bonds between adjacent amino acids forming structural motifs such as the alpha helix and beta sheet.
questions.title: Lecture 18 - Macromolecules 2

questions.q: In an alpha helix, between which amino acids do hydrogen bonds form?
options: Between every 2nd amino acid
Between every 3rd amino acid
Between every 4th amino acid
Between side-by-side segments of the chain
Between the first and last amino acids only
questions.explanation: The alpha helix is a helical conformation around a central axis forming a rigid cylinder, with hydrogen bonds formed between every 4th amino acid, linking the O of one carboxylic acid group to the H of another monomer's amino group.
questions.title: Lecture 18 - Macromolecules 2

questions.q: How do the hydrogen bonds in a beta sheet differ in arrangement from those in an alpha helix?
options: They form between side-by-side segments of polypeptide rather than within a single coiled run
They link side chains rather than backbone groups
They are covalent rather than hydrogen bonds
They form only between identical amino acids
They form between separate protein subunits
questions.explanation: Beta sheets form hydrogen bonds between side-by-side segments of polypeptide. Like the alpha helix, the bonds link the O of one carboxylic acid group to the H of another monomer's amino group, giving strong pleated structures at the core of many proteins.
questions.title: Lecture 18 - Macromolecules 2

questions.q: Which pair of examples correctly illustrates the two main secondary structures?
options: Alpha-keratin in hair for the alpha helix; spider silk for the beta sheet
Spider silk for the alpha helix; alpha-keratin for the beta sheet
Haemoglobin for the alpha helix; insulin for the beta sheet
Collagen for the alpha helix; cellulose for the beta sheet
Myosin for the alpha helix; ferritin for the beta sheet
questions.explanation: Alpha-keratin in hair is the example given of an alpha helix protein, and spider silk the example of a beta sheet protein.
questions.title: Lecture 18 - Macromolecules 2

questions.q: At what point is a polypeptide considered a functional protein?
options: As soon as the peptide bonds form in the ribosome
When the first alpha helix has formed
When all side chain interactions are complete and the chain folds into its 3D tertiary structure
Only once it has joined with other subunits
Once it has been glycosylated
questions.explanation: When all side chain interactions are complete, the polypeptide folds into a 3D tertiary structure, and it is at that point that the polypeptide is considered a functional protein.
questions.title: Lecture 18 - Macromolecules 2

questions.q: Which techniques give the most accurate determination of tertiary structure?
options: X-ray crystallography or cryo-electron microscopy
Mass spectrometry or gel electrophoresis
Ultraviolet spectroscopy or HPLC
Light scattering or ultracentrifugation
Titration or potentiometry
questions.explanation: The most accurate way to determine tertiary structure is currently X-ray crystallography or cryo-electron microscopy, both slow, laborious and specialised, although in silico prediction models are catching up.
questions.title: Lecture 18 - Macromolecules 2

questions.q: What role do disulphide bonds play, particularly in extracellular proteins?
options: They form the backbone of the polypeptide chain
They are covalent cross-linkages that help stabilise a favoured protein conformation
They are hydrogen bonds that create secondary structure
They join separate subunits into a multimer only
They mark the protein for degradation
questions.explanation: Extracellular proteins are often stabilised by covalent cross-linkages, and disulphide bonds help stabilise a favoured protein conformation.
questions.title: Lecture 18 - Macromolecules 2

questions.q: Haemoglobin, with its alpha and beta globin subunits and haem groups, illustrates which level of protein structure?
options: Primary
Secondary
Tertiary
Quaternary
Domain organisation
questions.explanation: Quaternary structure refers to proteins composed of subunits. Such multimers can be formed of identical or different subunits, for example homodimers, heterodimers and tetramers; haemoglobin is the example given.
questions.title: Lecture 18 - Macromolecules 2

questions.q: What is a protein domain?
options: The region of the protein that binds the substrate only
One of two or more distinct regions of a protein, each of which can have distinct functions and properties
A single alpha helix within a folded protein
The interface between two subunits in a multimer
The carbohydrate portion of a glycoprotein
questions.explanation: Domains occur when proteins are composed of two or more distinct regions. Each domain can have distinct functions and properties such as binding, anchoring or providing structure.
questions.title: Lecture 18 - Macromolecules 2

questions.q: How is a biologic defined?
options: Any medicine given by injection
A biological product such as a vaccine, cell or blood serum used in medicine
Any drug with a molecular weight above 1 kDa
A medicine made entirely by chemical synthesis
A medicine derived only from human tissue
questions.explanation: A biologic is a biological product such as a vaccine, cell or blood serum used in medicine. Biologics are isolated from natural sources (human, animal or microorganism) and are often produced by biotechnology using a DNA template from a living organism.
questions.title: Lecture 18 - Macromolecules 2

questions.q: Which characteristics make antibodies valuable as therapeutic tools?
options: They are small and easily absorbed orally
They are highly targeted and specific, and bind strongly
They are chemically synthesised at low cost
They are non-immunogenic in all patients
They can cross the blood-brain barrier freely
questions.explanation: Antibodies occur normally in the immune system, where an individual can make billions of different ones. Their value as tools comes from being highly targeted and specific, and from binding strongly.
questions.title: Lecture 18 - Macromolecules 2

questions.q: How does trastuzumab (Herceptin) work in HER2-positive metastatic breast cancer?
options: It blocks the production of epidermal growth factor
It locks on to the HER2 receptor so there is no signalling through HER2, reducing proliferation
It binds directly to the tumour DNA and prevents replication
It neutralises the spike protein preventing cell entry
It binds overproduced inflammatory signal molecules
questions.explanation: HER2-positive metastatic breast cancer cells have excess HER2 on their surface, and EGF stimulation of HER2 triggers abnormal proliferation. Trastuzumab locks on to the HER2 receptor, blocking signalling and reducing proliferation.
questions.title: Lecture 18 - Macromolecules 2

questions.q: Ronapreve (casirivimab and imdevimab) works by which mechanism?
options: A single monoclonal antibody binding the viral polymerase
A cocktail of two neutralising monoclonal antibodies binding two different sites on the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein
An mRNA vaccine encoding the spike protein
A fusion protein of a soluble receptor and IgG Fc
A small molecule protease inhibitor
questions.explanation: Ronapreve is a cocktail of two neutralising monoclonal antibodies that bind two different sites on the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein, neutralising the virus's ability to enter and infect cells. It was approved for COVID-19 in adults in August 2021.
questions.title: Lecture 18 - Macromolecules 2

questions.q: How do biologic disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs such as infliximab and adalimumab work?
options: By binding overproduced signal molecules, so inflammatory signalling is reduced
By destroying the joint tissue that produces inflammation
By blocking the HER2 receptor
By replacing a missing enzyme
By stimulating antibody production against the joint
questions.explanation: bDMARDs such as infliximab, adalimumab and rituximab ablate inflammation by binding to overproduced signal molecules, reducing inflammatory signalling.
questions.title: Lecture 18 - Macromolecules 2

questions.q: What kind of molecule is insulin, and where is it produced?
options: A steroid hormone produced by the adrenal cortex
A peptide hormone produced by the beta cells of the pancreas
A glycoprotein produced by the liver
A monoclonal antibody produced by B cells
A nucleotide produced by the pancreas
questions.explanation: Insulin is a peptide hormone produced by the beta cells of the pancreas, and it regulates blood glucose levels.
questions.title: Lecture 18 - Macromolecules 2

questions.q: How does the underlying defect differ between Type 1 and Type 2 diabetes?
options: In Type 1 the immune system destroys the pancreatic beta cells; in Type 2 the body does not produce enough insulin or cells do not react to it
In Type 1 the cells do not react to insulin; in Type 2 the beta cells are destroyed
Both are caused by immune destruction of beta cells
In Type 1 the liver overproduces glucose; in Type 2 the pancreas is destroyed
In Type 1 insulin is chemically abnormal; in Type 2 it is absent
questions.explanation: In Type 1 diabetes the immune system attacks and destroys the pancreatic beta cells that produce insulin. In Type 2 the body does not produce enough insulin, or the body's cells do not react to insulin. Type 1 patients usually require insulin injections.
questions.title: Lecture 18 - Macromolecules 2

questions.q: What is the structure of insulin?
options: 51 amino acids, 5.8 kDa, in two linked peptide chains of 21 and 30 amino acids
153 amino acids in a single chain with a haem group
Four identical subunits of 51 amino acids each
30 amino acids in a single chain, 5.8 kDa
A glycoprotein of 160 kDa with multiple domains
questions.explanation: Insulin is relatively small at 51 amino acids and 5.8 kDa, composed of two linked peptide chains: an alpha chain of 21 amino acids and a beta chain of 30. It normally forms inactive hexamers, giving delayed onset and long duration of action.
questions.title: Lecture 18 - Macromolecules 2

questions.q: Which was the first FDA-approved biologic, and in what year?
options: Herceptin, in 1996
Humulin (human insulin), in 1982
Humira, in 2002
Ronapreve, in 2021
Keytruda, in 1987
questions.explanation: Humulin, human insulin, was the first FDA-approved biologic in 1982. Many synthetic insulins were produced in bacteria from 1982 and in yeasts from 1987, and from 1996 insulin analogues were developed by DNA engineering to be rapid, delayed or long acting.
questions.title: Lecture 18 - Macromolecules 2

questions.q: Which statements about enzymes are correct?
options: They are nearly always proteins, act as highly specific catalysts, and are often reusable and unchanged before and after use
They are nearly always carbohydrates and are consumed during the reaction
They are non-specific catalysts that speed up any reaction
They are permanently altered by the reactions they catalyse
They function only outside living organisms
questions.explanation: Enzymes are nearly always proteins, often reusable and unchanged before and after use. They act as highly specific catalysts, binding one or more substrates and converting them into chemically modified products, and facilitate virtually all functions in living organisms.
questions.title: Lecture 18 - Macromolecules 2

questions.q: What are DNA polymers made of?
options: A sugar-phosphate backbone plus hexose bases
Hydrogen-bonded nucleosides
Nucleotides held together by phosphodiester linkages
Poly-adenylated ribose chains
Amino acids held together by peptide bonds
questions.explanation: DNA polymers are made of nucleotides held together by phosphodiester linkages between the 5' and 3' carbons of the sugar rings. A nucleoside lacks the phosphate, so cannot form the backbone.
questions.title: Lecture 18 - Macromolecules 2

questions.q: Why must pharmacists understand protein structure?
options: Because it determines the price of the biologic
Because proteins only show optimal biological and pharmacological activity in a specific stable 3D structure, which matters for manufacture, storage and drug design
Because protein structure determines the route of administration alone
Because all proteins have identical structures
Because structure determines which patients can be prescribed the drug
questions.explanation: Proteins have defined, stable 3D structures in which they are optimally biologically and pharmacologically active, which matters for manufacture and storage. Knowledge of structure also allows the design of new therapies.
questions.title: Lecture 18 - Macromolecules 2

questions.q: According to the lecture, which roles do proteins perform in the body?
options: Catalyse reactions, transport molecules such as oxygen, and contribute to the immune system
Store genetic information and replicate DNA
Form the lipid bilayer of the plasma membrane only
Serve only as energy storage molecules
Act exclusively as hormones in the bloodstream
questions.explanation: Proteins are macromolecules made of amino acids. In the body they catalyse reactions, transport molecules like oxygen, and keep us healthy as part of the immune system. Skin, muscles, bones and organs are made largely of protein.
questions.title: Lecture 18 - Macromolecules 2

questions.q: Which molecular interactions primarily stabilise secondary protein structure?
options: Hydrogen bonds between backbone groups in alpha helices and beta sheets
Disulfide bridges between side chains only
Ionic bonds between quaternary subunits
Hydrophobic interactions in the core only
Peptide bonds between adjacent amino acids
questions.explanation: Secondary structure is formed by alpha helices and beta sheets. The revision slide asks what molecular forces determine secondary structure: hydrogen bonding between backbone groups is the key interaction.
questions.title: Lecture 18 - Macromolecules 2

questions.q: Which statement about top-selling pharmaceutical biologics is correct?
options: Many leading products are monoclonal antibodies or fusion proteins used in cancer and autoimmune disease
All top sellers are small-molecule tablets
Biologics have negligible market share compared with generics
mRNA vaccines are not classified as biologics
Humira is a small-molecule statin
questions.explanation: The 2022 top pharmaceutical products by worldwide sales include many biologics such as adalimumab (Humira) and pembrolizumab (Keytruda), mostly monoclonal antibodies or fusion proteins for rheumatoid arthritis, Crohn's disease, psoriasis and cancer.
questions.title: Lecture 18 - Macromolecules 2

questions.q: How are most therapeutic proteins now manufactured?
options: By recombinant DNA technology
By chemical synthesis from amino acids in the laboratory only
By extraction from animal tissues alone
By fermentation of bacteria without genetic modification
By crushing plant tissues
questions.explanation: Most therapeutic proteins are now made by recombinant DNA technology, as introduced further in the gene-to-biologic lecture. Recombinant proteins constructed by genetic engineering form a very important class of drugs.
questions.title: Lecture 18 - Macromolecules 2

questions.q: Which resource is recommended as the key text for protein structure in this lecture?
options: Alberts et al., Essential Cell Biology (5th ed.), Garland Science, Chapter 4
Rang and Dale's Pharmacology, Chapters 1-3
Goodman and Gilman's Pharmacology, Chapter 18 only
Martindale's Drug Reference
The British National Formulary only
questions.explanation: The guided reading lists Alberts et al. (2019) Essential Cell Biology (5th ed.), Garland Science, Chapter 4 as the key text, alongside videos on protein folding and Khan Academy resources on orders of protein structure.
questions.title: Lecture 18 - Macromolecules 2

questions.q: In the example SAQ on secondary structure, which features should be included in the answer?
options: The types of secondary structure, the bonds involved, and how structure affects protein properties
Only the amino acid sequence of the protein
Only the quaternary subunit arrangement
Only post-translational modifications
Only the DNA sequence encoding the protein
questions.explanation: The example SAQ asks students to describe two common types of secondary protein structure, including what structures are formed, what types of bonds are involved, and how these structures can affect protein properties.
questions.title: Lecture 18 - Macromolecules 2

questions.q: By roughly what factor can enzymes accelerate biological reactions?
options: About 10 fold
About 100 fold
About 1,000 fold
About 1,000,000 fold
They do not change reaction rate, only yield
questions.explanation: Enzymes are biological catalysts that accelerate reactions by around a million fold.
questions.title: Lecture 19 - Enzymes

questions.q: The term ligand derives from the Latin ligare. What does it mean, and what can a ligand be?
options: To bind; an ion, small organic molecule or macromolecule
To break; only a small organic molecule
To bind; only a protein
To catalyse; any charged particle
To fold; only a metal ion
questions.explanation: Ligand comes from the Latin ligare, to bind. A ligand can be an ion, a small organic molecule or a macromolecule, and it associates at the enzyme's binding site or active site.
questions.title: Lecture 19 - Enzymes

questions.q: Which forces hold a substrate at an enzyme's binding site?
options: Covalent bonds only
Weak non-covalent interactions: hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, van der Waals interactions and some hydrophobic forces
Disulphide bridges formed on binding
Peptide bonds between substrate and enzyme
Metallic bonding through cofactors
questions.explanation: Binding site specificity arises from weak non-covalent interactions: hydrogen bonds, ionic (electrostatic) bonds, van der Waals interactions and some hydrophobic forces. Many form simultaneously because of the close fit of ligand to enzyme.
questions.title: Lecture 19 - Enzymes

questions.q: How is the substrate converted into product by an enzyme?
options: By the breaking or formation of covalent bonds
By the breaking of hydrogen bonds only
By raising the temperature of the local environment
By transferring the substrate to another enzyme
By changing the pH at the active site
questions.explanation: The substrate binds through weak non-covalent bonds, and is converted into one or more products by the breaking or formation of covalent bonds.
questions.title: Lecture 19 - Enzymes

questions.q: Which digestive enzyme is correctly matched with its substrate and product?
options: Amylase: protein to amino acids
Trypsin: starch to glucose
Lipase: fats to fatty acids and glycerol
DNAse: carbohydrate to glucose
Amylase: fats to fatty acids
questions.explanation: Lipase acts in the small intestine on butter, fats and oils to give fatty acids and glycerol, absorbed by the villi. Amylase acts on carbohydrate and starch to give glucose, trypsin on protein to amino acids, and DNAse on DNA to nucleotides.
questions.title: Lecture 19 - Enzymes

questions.q: Which metabolic enzyme class is correctly described?
options: Hydrolases break down material by the addition of water
Lyases break molecules by hydrolysis
Ligases split molecules into two or more parts
Isomerases oxidise substances to alcohols or ketones
Reductases remove hydrogen from substrates
questions.explanation: Hydrolases break down material by the addition of water. Lyases break molecules without hydrolysis or oxidation, ligases bring about bonding of two or more molecules, isomerases convert a molecule from one form to another, and reductases add hydrogen.
questions.title: Lecture 19 - Enzymes

questions.q: Which enzyme adds glucuronic acid to non-water-soluble substances so they can be excreted in urine?
options: Transaminase
Glycogen synthase
Glucuronyl transferase
Aminoacyl tRNA synthetase
Carboxypeptidase
questions.explanation: Glucuronyl transferase is the key enzyme that adds glucuronic acid to non-water-soluble substances, converting them to water soluble forms for excretion in urine.
questions.title: Lecture 19 - Enzymes

questions.q: What does one molecule of glucose yield during glycolysis?
options: Pyruvate, plus 2 ATP and 2 NADH
Lactate, plus 4 ATP and 1 NADH
Oxaloacetate, plus 2 ATP only
Pyruvate, plus 36 ATP
Glycogen, plus 2 NADH
questions.explanation: In glycolysis one molecule of glucose is metabolised to pyruvate, generating 2 ATP and 2 NADH as energy carriers. Pyruvate then enters the Krebs or citric acid cycle where more enzymes produce more energy.
questions.title: Lecture 19 - Enzymes

questions.q: How do enzymes speed up chemical reactions?
options: By raising the activation energy of the reaction
By lowering the activation energy, the barrier needed to get the reaction started
By increasing the concentration of substrate
By changing the equilibrium position of the reaction
By supplying ATP directly to the substrate
questions.explanation: Enzymes lower the activation energy of a chemical reaction, the energy barrier needed to get the reaction started, and so greatly enhance the speed of the reaction.
questions.title: Lecture 19 - Enzymes

questions.q: What is the turnover number of an enzyme?
options: The number of substrate molecules bound at equilibrium
The maximum number of substrate molecules per second that a single active site can convert to product
The number of active sites per enzyme molecule
The number of times an enzyme is recycled before degradation
The ratio of Vmax to km
questions.explanation: The turnover number is the maximum number of substrate molecules per second that a single active site can convert to product, and can range from 1 to 100,000 molecules per second.
questions.title: Lecture 19 - Enzymes

questions.q: Which are the five factors that affect enzyme activity?
options: Temperature, pH, substrate concentration, binding of small molecules and covalent modification
Temperature, pressure, volume, pH and concentration
Substrate, product, enzyme, cofactor and inhibitor concentrations
Primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary structure plus temperature
Km, Vmax, turnover number, activation energy and pH
questions.explanation: The five factors affecting enzyme activity are temperature, pH, substrate concentration, the binding of small molecules such as cofactors and coenzymes, and covalent modification such as phosphorylation.
questions.title: Lecture 19 - Enzymes

questions.q: Why does reaction velocity plateau at Vmax as substrate concentration increases?
options: The substrate begins to inhibit the enzyme
The enzyme becomes denatured at high substrate concentrations
All enzyme molecules are fully occupied by substrate, so the enzyme is saturated
The product accumulates and reverses the reaction
The activation energy rises with substrate concentration
questions.explanation: At low substrate concentration all substrate is rapidly bound; as it increases more is bound and rate rises; at high concentration all enzyme molecules are fully occupied, so no more can bind and rate remains constant at Vmax. The enzyme is said to be saturated.
questions.title: Lecture 19 - Enzymes

questions.q: What does km, the Michaelis-Menten constant, equal in terms of substrate concentration?
options: The substrate concentration at which V equals Vmax
The substrate concentration at which V equals half of Vmax
The substrate concentration at which the enzyme denatures
Twice the substrate concentration at Vmax
The product concentration at equilibrium
questions.explanation: Setting V equal to half Vmax in the Michaelis-Menten equation gives km = [S]. So km is the substrate concentration at half maximal velocity, with units of moles per litre.
questions.title: Lecture 19 - Enzymes

questions.q: What does a low km value tell you about an enzyme?
options: It has weak binding for its ligand
It has strong binding for its ligand
It has a high turnover number
It is allosteric
It requires a cofactor
questions.explanation: km is a measure of ligand binding strength: the lowest value implies the strongest binding, because half maximal velocity is reached at a lower substrate concentration.
questions.title: Lecture 19 - Enzymes

questions.q: What is the purpose of the Lineweaver-Burk transformation?
options: It converts the Michaelis-Menten equation into a linear equation so Vmax and km can be read from the axis intercepts
It corrects the Michaelis-Menten equation for allosteric enzymes
It converts substrate concentration into product concentration
It removes the need to measure reaction velocity
It accounts for the backward reaction E + P to ES
questions.explanation: The Lineweaver-Burk transformation rearranges the Michaelis-Menten equation into the linear form y = mx + c, allowing Vmax to be calculated from the y-axis intercept and km from the x-axis intercept of plotted experimental data.
questions.title: Lecture 19 - Enzymes

questions.q: Why is the Michaelis-Menten framework important beyond enzymology?
options: It also describes receptor-ligand interactions, so it is useful for designing drugs that bind and inhibit enzymes or receptors
It predicts the rate at which a drug is excreted in urine
It determines the solubility of a drug in plasma
It sets the shelf life of biologic medicines
It calculates the dose needed for a given body weight
questions.explanation: A modification of the Michaelis-Menten equations also describes receptor-ligand interactions, where the receptor becomes saturated with ligand. This makes it very useful in designing drugs that bind specifically to and inhibit enzyme or receptor activity.
questions.title: Lecture 19 - Enzymes

questions.q: Why are medical enzymes, as biologics, stored at 4 degrees C?
options: Because enzymes have an optimal temperature range and are heat sensitive
Because cold increases their turnover number
Because refrigeration prevents pH change
Because they must be kept below their km
Because cold prevents cofactor binding
questions.explanation: Enzymes have an optimal temperature range. Viral enzymes are very susceptible to heat, which is why fever helps control infection, while thermophilic bacterial enzymes work at 100 degrees C and are used in PCR. Medical enzymes as biologics are stored at 4 degrees C.
questions.title: Lecture 19 - Enzymes

questions.q: How does pH affect enzyme activity?
options: It changes the covalent bonds of the polypeptide backbone
It influences the ionisation of functional groups, altering 3D structure and function, and extreme pH can denature proteins
It alters the turnover number without affecting structure
It only affects enzymes that require metal cofactors
It changes the substrate concentration required for saturation
questions.explanation: pH influences the ionisation of functional groups, which alters 3D structure and function. For example at low pH the COO- of glutamic acid may take up H+ to form uncharged COOH. Extreme pH can denature proteins, so care is needed in formulating medicines.
questions.title: Lecture 19 - Enzymes

questions.q: What are apoenzymes and holoenzymes?
options: An apoenzyme is the active form; a holoenzyme is the inactive form
An apoenzyme is the inactive enzyme without its cofactor; a holoenzyme is the active enzyme with cofactor bound
An apoenzyme is a competitive inhibitor; a holoenzyme a non-competitive inhibitor
An apoenzyme has one active site; a holoenzyme has several
An apoenzyme is monomeric; a holoenzyme is multimeric
questions.explanation: Without its cofactor or coenzyme the enzyme is inactive and called an apoenzyme, and the substrate does not bind the active site. With the cofactor bound it becomes the active holoenzyme, the substrate fits and the reaction proceeds.
questions.title: Lecture 19 - Enzymes

questions.q: Carboxypeptidase requires zinc to function. What term describes such an enzyme?
options: An allosteric enzyme
A metalloenzyme
A transaminase
A holoenzyme without cofactor
An isomerase
questions.explanation: Carboxypeptidase, which cleaves polypeptide chains, is a metalloenzyme because it needs zinc to function. Pyruvate carboxylase is another cofactor example, binding biotin in the citric acid cycle.
questions.title: Lecture 19 - Enzymes

questions.q: How does phosphorylation regulate enzyme activity?
options: It adds a PO3 group with two negative charges, altering the enzyme's shape
It removes an amino group from the enzyme
It cleaves the enzyme into two active fragments
It permanently destroys the active site
It adds a sugar chain to the enzyme surface
questions.explanation: Phosphorylation adds a PO3 group carrying two negative charges, which alters the enzyme's shape and can stimulate or inhibit activity. The terminal phosphate is transferred from ATP to the -OH group usually on serine, threonine or tyrosine side chains.
questions.title: Lecture 19 - Enzymes

questions.q: Which enzymes carry out phosphorylation and dephosphorylation respectively?
options: Protein kinase and protein phosphatase
Protein phosphatase and protein kinase
Transaminase and ligase
Oxidase and reductase
Synthase and synthetase
questions.explanation: Phosphorylation is catalysed by protein kinases, of which there are hundreds, and dephosphorylation by protein phosphatases.
questions.title: Lecture 19 - Enzymes

questions.q: Statins act by inhibiting which enzyme?
options: Dihydrofolate reductase
HMG-CoA reductase
Acetylcholinesterase
Transpeptidase
Cytochrome c oxidase
questions.explanation: Statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, which is involved in the synthesis of cholesterol in the liver. Methotrexate, by contrast, inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, essential for DNA synthesis.
questions.title: Lecture 19 - Enzymes

questions.q: Streptokinase is a drug that IS an enzyme. How does it work?
options: It oxidises uric acid to allantoin
It is a bacterial protease that digests fibrin, a component of blood clots
It removes dead tissue from wounds and ulcers
It inhibits transpeptidase in bacterial cell walls
It breaks down acetylcholine at the synapse
questions.explanation: Streptokinase is a bacterial protease used to treat heart attack patients. It digests fibrin, an important component of blood clots, restoring normal blood flow and preventing excessive damage to heart tissue.
questions.title: Lecture 19 - Enzymes

questions.q: How does uricase prevent gout?
options: It dissolves existing urate crystals directly
It oxidises uric acid to highly soluble allantoin, which is readily excreted in urine
It inhibits the enzyme that makes uric acid
It binds uric acid in the gut to prevent absorption
It reduces inflammation in the affected joint
questions.explanation: Uricase prevents deposition of uric acid in joints by oxidising uric acid to highly soluble allantoin, which is readily excreted in the urine.
questions.title: Lecture 19 - Enzymes

questions.q: How do beta-lactam antibiotics such as penicillins inhibit their target enzyme?
options: By competing reversibly with the peptidoglycan substrate
By covalently bonding to penicillin-binding proteins (transpeptidases), preventing their normal action
By binding an allosteric site on the transpeptidase
By chelating the zinc cofactor of the enzyme
By phosphorylating the enzyme active site
questions.explanation: Transpeptidase enzymes, the penicillin-binding proteins, catalyse crosslinking of peptidoglycan strands in bacterial cell walls. Beta-lactam antibiotics inhibit PBPs by covalently bonding to them, which makes them irreversible inhibitors.
questions.title: Lecture 19 - Enzymes

questions.q: Edrophonium is an example of which type of inhibitor, and what is its effect?
options: An irreversible inhibitor that destroys acetylcholinesterase
A reversible inhibitor that binds acetylcholinesterase with temporary ionic bonds, prolonging the acetylcholine signal
A non-competitive inhibitor of cytochrome c oxidase
A competitive inhibitor of dihydropteroate synthetase
An allosteric activator of acetylcholine release
questions.explanation: Edrophonium binds acetylcholinesterase with temporary ionic bonds at the anionic site, a reversible inhibition. This prevents the enzyme breaking down acetylcholine and so prolongs the neurotransmitter signal.
questions.title: Lecture 19 - Enzymes

questions.q: What characterises a competitive inhibitor?
options: It is a structural analogue of the substrate, occupies the catalytic site, and can be reversed by increasing substrate concentration
It binds a site separate from the catalytic site and cannot be overcome by more substrate
It covalently modifies the enzyme permanently
It removes the cofactor required for activity
It changes the pH of the local environment
questions.explanation: Competitive inhibitors are structural analogues of the substrate that occupy the catalytic site. Their effect can be reversed by increasing the substrate concentration.
questions.title: Lecture 19 - Enzymes

questions.q: Why is sulfanilamide an effective antibacterial?
options: It is structurally similar to PABA and competes with it, inhibiting dihydropteroate synthetase
It irreversibly binds bacterial ribosomes
It chelates the iron needed for bacterial respiration
It is structurally similar to folate and blocks its uptake
It inhibits dihydrofolate reductase in bacteria only
questions.explanation: p-aminobenzoic acid (PABA) is an essential precursor for bacterial DNA and RNA synthesis. Sulfanilamide is structurally similar to PABA and competes with it, inhibiting dihydropteroate synthetase which normally incorporates PABA into 7,8-dihydropteroic acid.
questions.title: Lecture 19 - Enzymes

questions.q: How does cyanide act as a non-competitive inhibitor?
options: It competes with oxygen for the active site of Complex IV
It binds to iron in Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase), preventing electron transport so the chain stalls
It phosphorylates Complex IV, changing its shape
It removes the haem cofactor from Complex IV
It denatures all mitochondrial enzymes by lowering pH
questions.explanation: Cyanide non-competitively inhibits Complex IV, cytochrome c oxidase, of the mitochondrial electron transport chain. CN- binds to iron in the complex, preventing electron transport so the chain stalls, respiration is prevented and cellular hypoxia results.
questions.title: Lecture 19 - Enzymes

questions.q: On a Lineweaver-Burk plot, how do competitive and non-competitive inhibition differ?
options: Competitive inhibition changes Vmax but not km; non-competitive changes km but not Vmax
Competitive inhibition leaves Vmax unchanged since more substrate overcomes it; non-competitive leaves km unchanged but reduces Vmax
Both reduce Vmax and increase km equally
Neither affects Vmax or km, only the slope
Competitive inhibition abolishes the reaction entirely
questions.explanation: In competitive inhibition there is competition for active site access, and increasing substrate can overcome it, so Vmax does not change. In non-competitive inhibition binding is elsewhere, binding strength is unchanged so km does not change, but Vmax is reduced.
questions.title: Lecture 19 - Enzymes

questions.q: Why must enzyme activity be regulated rather than run continuously at full speed?
options: To prevent cells depleting energy reserves, wasting critical substrates or accumulating toxic products
To prevent enzymes from being degraded by heat
Because enzymes are consumed during each reaction
Because the activation energy rises over time
To maintain a constant intracellular pH
questions.explanation: Enzymes do not operate continuously at full speed; activities are regulated so molecules are produced as required. This ensures cells do not deplete energy reserves, waste stockpiles of critical substrates, or accumulate toxic products.
questions.title: Lecture 19 - Enzymes

questions.q: Which is a mechanism by which enzyme activity is regulated?
options: Controlling gene expression, regulating protein degradation rate, confining production to specific cell areas, and feedback inhibition
Altering the activation energy of the reaction directly
Changing the turnover number of the active site
Increasing the number of substrate molecules produced
Adjusting the body temperature of the organism
questions.explanation: Regulation may occur by controlling gene expression as an on/off switch, regulating the rate at which the protein product is degraded, confining production to specific areas of the cell such as mitochondria, and feedback inhibition by the protein product.
questions.title: Lecture 19 - Enzymes

questions.q: In feedback inhibition, which enzyme in a pathway is usually inhibited and by what?
options: The last enzyme, inhibited by the starting substrate
The first enzyme in the pathway, inhibited by the end product, forming a negative feedback loop
Every enzyme equally, inhibited by ATP
The rate-limiting enzyme, inhibited by its own substrate
A randomly selected enzyme, inhibited by a cofactor
questions.explanation: In metabolic pathways an enzyme may be inhibited by the product of a downstream reaction. The end product usually inhibits the first enzyme in the pathway, forming a negative feedback loop.
questions.title: Lecture 19 - Enzymes

questions.q: What defines an allosteric enzyme?
options: It has two binding sites, one for the substrate and one for the inhibitor or regulator
It has only one binding site but very high affinity
It requires a metal cofactor to function
It can only be inhibited irreversibly
It works exclusively in the mitochondria
questions.explanation: An allosteric enzyme has two types of binding site: one binds the substrate and makes product, and the other regulates the enzyme's activity. Allosteric enzymes are usually multimeric and their binding sites can affect each other.
questions.title: Lecture 19 - Enzymes

questions.q: Why do allosteric enzymes with multiple active sites not obey Michaelis-Menten kinetics?
options: Because they have no measurable Vmax
Because substrate binding at one catalytic site increases the affinity of the others, giving sigmoidal curves through positive co-operativity
Because they are irreversibly inhibited by their substrate
Because their km is always zero
Because they operate only at very high pH
questions.explanation: In enzymes with multiple active sites, substrate binding to one catalytic site can increase the affinity of the other sites for substrate. This positive co-operativity gives sigmoidal reaction curves rather than the hyperbolic Michaelis-Menten form.
questions.title: Lecture 19 - Enzymes

questions.q: How does ADP act as a cofactor activator in the example given?
options: It binds the open form of the enzyme and inactivates it
It binds the closed active form, locking it in the active mode, so at high ligand concentration nearly all such enzymes are activated
It is consumed by the enzyme as a substrate
It phosphorylates the enzyme's serine residues
It competes with the substrate for the active site
questions.explanation: The example enzyme is active in the closed form, with about 10 per cent active by chance from random thermal motion. ADP binds the closed form and locks it in the active mode, so at high enough ligand concentration activity increases towards 100 per cent.
questions.title: Lecture 19 - Enzymes

questions.q: GTP-binding proteins regulate enzymes by acting as what?
options: Molecular switches, often stimulated in response to cell signalling
Permanent covalent modifiers of the active site
Competitive inhibitors of downstream enzymes
Structural scaffolds with no regulatory role
Energy carriers equivalent to ATP in glycolysis
questions.explanation: GTP-binding proteins act as molecular switches. They are often stimulated in response to cell signalling and can then regulate other proteins and their activities.
questions.title: Lecture 19 - Enzymes

questions.q: How do competitive inhibitors affect enzymes?
options: By altering the shape of the binding site
By forcing conversion of GDP to GTP
By irreversibly binding to the enzyme's target
By occupying the enzyme binding site
By permanently removing phosphorylation sites
questions.explanation: Competitive inhibitors are structural analogues of the substrate that occupy the enzyme binding site, blocking substrate access. Altering the shape of the enzyme at a separate site describes non-competitive inhibition.
questions.title: Lecture 19 - Enzymes

questions.q: Trypsin is used therapeutically for which purpose?
options: To dissolve blood clots after a heart attack
To oxidise uric acid in gout
For digestion if the patient lacks enzymes, with bromelain and rutin for osteoarthritis, and to remove dead tissue from wounds
To inhibit cholesterol synthesis in the liver
To prolong acetylcholine signalling at the neuromuscular junction
questions.explanation: Trypsin, a protease, may be given for digestion if the patient lacks the necessary enzymes, in combination with bromelain and rutin for osteoarthritis, and applied directly to wounds and ulcers to remove dead tissue and improve healing.
questions.title: Lecture 19 - Enzymes

questions.q: In an enzyme-catalysed reaction, which definitions are correct?
options: Substrate is a reactant; the active site is where substrate binds; product is the resultant molecule
Substrate is the enzyme; the active site is the product; product is the reactant
Substrate is a cofactor; the active site is on the product; product is always water
Substrate is the inhibitor; the active site is the whole enzyme surface; product is unchanged substrate
Substrate and product are identical; the active site is optional
questions.explanation: The lecture defines substrate as a reactant, the active (binding) site as the small portion of the enzyme surface where substrate becomes bound, and product as the resultant molecule(s).
questions.title: Lecture 19 - Enzymes

questions.q: In the notation E + S → ES → E + P, what do S and P represent?
options: S is substrate (a reactant/ligand) and P is product
S is enzyme and P is substrate
S is product and P is inhibitor
S is cofactor and P is enzyme
S is active site and P is binding energy
questions.explanation: Enzymes convert substrates (S) to products (P). S is a reactant that binds at the active site on enzyme E.
questions.title: Lecture 19 - Enzymes

questions.q: What is the turnover number of an enzyme?
options: The maximum substrate molecules converted to product per second by one active site
The minimum activation energy of the reaction
The ratio of enzyme to substrate at Vmax
The number of enzymes in a cell
The temperature at which the enzyme denatures
questions.explanation: Turnover number is the maximum number of substrate molecules per second that a single active site can convert to product, ranging from about 1 to 100,000.
questions.title: Lecture 19 - Enzymes

questions.q: What happens to reaction velocity V as substrate concentration [S] increases at fixed enzyme concentration?
options: V increases until a maximum Vmax is reached when all enzyme active sites are saturated
V decreases linearly with increasing [S]
V remains constant regardless of [S]
V increases without limit as [S] rises
Vmax is reached only when enzyme concentration is doubled
questions.explanation: At a given enzyme concentration, increasing substrate concentration increases reaction speed until a maximum, Vmax, is reached when all active sites are occupied.
questions.title: Lecture 19 - Enzymes

questions.q: In deriving the Michaelis-Menten equation, what assumption is made about the reverse reaction E + P → ES?
options: There is no significant rate for the backward reaction
The backward reaction is faster than the forward reaction
Product always rebinds irreversibly to enzyme
The reverse reaction determines Vmax
E and P form a covalent complex
questions.explanation: Michaelis-Menten kinetics assume there is no significant rate for the backward reaction E + P → ES.
questions.title: Lecture 19 - Enzymes

questions.q: What does the Michaelis constant Km represent?
options: A constant derived from the rates of ES formation and breakdown: Km = (k-1 + k2) / k1
The maximum reaction velocity Vmax
The total enzyme concentration in the cell
The inhibitor concentration at 50% inhibition
The activation energy of the catalysed reaction
questions.explanation: At equilibrium, rates of ES formation and breakdown are equal. From these rates Km is defined as (k-1 + k2) / k1, leading to the Michaelis-Menten equation V = Vmax[S] / (Km + [S]).
questions.title: Lecture 19 - Enzymes

questions.q: Which five factors affect enzyme activity according to the lecture?
options: Substrate concentration, temperature, pH, binding of small molecules, and covalent modification
Light, pressure, gravity, magnetism, and sound
DNA replication, transcription, translation, splicing, and methylation
Membrane fluidity, cholesterol, porins, aquaporins, and pumps
Competitive inhibition only, with no other regulators
questions.explanation: The lecture lists five factors: substrate concentration, temperature, pH, binding of small molecules, and covalent modification.
questions.title: Lecture 19 - Enzymes

questions.q: How does reversible non-competitive inhibition differ from competitive inhibition?
options: It binds a separate site from the catalytic site, does not compete with substrate, and cannot be reversed simply by increasing substrate
It binds the catalytic site and is overcome by more substrate
It permanently destroys the enzyme active site
It only occurs with allosteric enzymes at high pH
It increases Vmax while decreasing Km
questions.explanation: Non-competitive inhibitors bind a site separate from the catalytic site. There is no competition with substrate and the block cannot simply be reversed by increasing substrate concentration.
questions.title: Lecture 19 - Enzymes

questions.q: Which set correctly names three factors that affect enzyme activity?
options: Temperature, pH, and substrate concentration
DNA sequence, ribosome number, and Golgi size
Blood pressure, heart rate, and lung volume
Membrane thickness, cholesterol only, and cell diameter
Antibiotic class, MIC, and zone diameter only
questions.explanation: The example SAQ asks students to name three factors affecting enzyme activity; the lecture's five factors include substrate concentration, temperature, pH, binding of small molecules, and covalent modification.
questions.title: Lecture 19 - Enzymes

questions.q: In the Michaelis-Menten derivation, what condition allows Km to be defined from rate constants?
options: At equilibrium, the rate of ES formation equals the rate of ES breakdown
The enzyme is permanently saturated with inhibitor
Substrate concentration is always zero
Product concentration exceeds substrate concentration
The reaction runs only in reverse
questions.explanation: At equilibrium the rate of ES formation equals the dissociation and conversion rate. Rearranging these rates defines Km = (k-1 + k2) / k1.
questions.title: Lecture 19 - Enzymes

questions.q: What holds the cell membrane together?
options: Covalent bonds between adjacent phospholipids
Non-covalent interactions
Disulphide bridges between membrane proteins
Peptide bonds within the bilayer
Ionic bonds with extracellular calcium
questions.explanation: The cell membrane is a closed boundary of lipids, protein and carbohydrates, primarily a phospholipid bilayer that is fluid-like and non-symmetrical, held together by non-covalent interactions.
questions.title: Lecture 21 - Cell Membranes

questions.q: Why do amphipathic lipids spontaneously form bilayers in aqueous environments?
options: Because the hydrophilic regions stay in contact with water while the hydrophobic regions stay inside where water is excluded
Because they are covalently linked head to tail
Because water forces them into a single monolayer
Because they are more dense than water
Because proteins push them into position
questions.explanation: Membrane lipids are amphipathic. In water, hydrophilic regions stay in contact with water and hydrophobic regions stay inside where water is excluded, so bilayers form spontaneously and seal into compartments.
questions.title: Lecture 21 - Cell Membranes

questions.q: Which type of lipid movement within a membrane is hardest and requires enzymes?
options: Rotation
Lateral diffusion
Transverse movement between leaflets
Vertical oscillation within a leaflet
All three occur equally easily
questions.explanation: Membranes are 2D fluids. Rotation is easy and lateral diffusion is rapid, but transverse movement from one leaflet to the other is harder and requires enzymes.
questions.title: Lecture 21 - Cell Membranes

questions.q: Besides protection, which three functions of the membrane are highlighted?
options: Transport, signal transduction and energy storage as an electrical potential
Protein synthesis, DNA replication and cell division
Digestion, absorption and excretion
Photosynthesis, respiration and fermentation
Immunity, clotting and inflammation
questions.explanation: As well as protection, the membrane is important for transport through channels or pumps, signal transduction as hormones interact with receptors, and energy storage as an electrical potential across the membrane.
questions.title: Lecture 21 - Cell Membranes

questions.q: Which are the three major groups of membrane lipid?
options: Triglycerides, waxes and terpenes
Glycerophospholipids, sphingolipids and sterols
Fatty acids, glycerol and phosphate
Glycolipids, lipoproteins and lipopolysaccharides
Ceramides, cholesterol and cardiolipin
questions.explanation: The three major groups are glycerophospholipids (phosphoglycerides), sphingolipids and sterols. The term phospholipid can cover either of the first two. A typical membrane contains over 100 different lipid species.
questions.title: Lecture 21 - Cell Membranes

questions.q: What do most phospholipids contain?
options: A platform backbone, one or more fatty acids, a phosphate group and an alcohol component
Three fatty acids esterified to glycerol
A steroid ring system and a single hydroxyl group
A sugar backbone and two phosphate groups
An amino acid backbone with a lipid tail
questions.explanation: Most phospholipids contain a platform molecule as backbone, one or more hydrophobic fatty acids, a hydrophilic phosphate group and a hydrophilic alcohol component. The platform, glycerol or a sphingoid, determines the subtype.
questions.title: Lecture 21 - Cell Membranes

questions.q: Which alcohol head groups can be linked to the phosphate of a glycerophospholipid?
options: Choline, ethanolamine, serine or inositol
Glucose, galactose, mannose or fructose
Glycine, alanine, valine or leucine
Sphingosine, sphinganine or phytosphingosine
Cholesterol, ergosterol or hopanoid
questions.explanation: In a glycerophospholipid, glycerol has two carbons esterified to fatty acids and one to a phosphate. The phosphate is often linked to an alcohol: choline, ethanolamine, serine or inositol.
questions.title: Lecture 21 - Cell Membranes

questions.q: Which glycerophospholipid makes up roughly 50 per cent of total membrane phospholipid?
options: Phosphatidylserine
Phosphatidylinositol
Phosphatidylcholine
Phosphatidylglycerol
Cardiolipin
questions.explanation: Phosphatidylcholine makes up about 50 per cent of total membrane phospholipid. Phosphatidylethanolamine is second most abundant and important to bacteria, phosphatidylserine about 10 per cent for cell signalling and phosphatidylinositol about 5 per cent for intracellular signalling.
questions.title: Lecture 21 - Cell Membranes

questions.q: Cardiolipin, formed from two phosphatidylglycerol units, is important in which organelle?
options: The nucleus
The lysosome
The Golgi apparatus
The mitochondrion
The endoplasmic reticulum
questions.explanation: Cardiolipin (DPG) is formed from two phosphatidylglycerol units and is important in mitochondria. Phosphatidylglycerol itself is important in the lungs.
questions.title: Lecture 21 - Cell Membranes

questions.q: How is a sphingolipid constructed?
options: A glycerol backbone with three ester-linked fatty acids
A sphingoid backbone with an amide bond to a fatty acid and an ester bond to a phosphate or sugar group
A steroid ring with a polar hydroxyl head
Two fatty acids joined directly to a phosphate
A protein backbone with attached lipid chains
questions.explanation: Sphingolipids have a sphingoid backbone, an amide bond between the nitrogen group and a fatty acid, and an ester bond between the alcohol group and either a phosphate group or a sugar group, the latter making a glycolipid.
questions.title: Lecture 21 - Cell Membranes

questions.q: Which is the most abundant sphingolipid, important in membranes and lipid rafts?
options: Ceramide
Sphingomyelin
Glucosylceramide
Galactosylceramide
Ceramide phosphoethanolamine
questions.explanation: Sphingomyelin, with a phosphocholine head group, is the most abundant sphingolipid and is important in signalling, membranes and lipid rafts.
questions.title: Lecture 21 - Cell Membranes

questions.q: Misregulation of glucosylceramide leads to which disease state?
options: Cataracts
Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus
Gaucher disease
Long QT syndrome
Epilepsy
questions.explanation: Glucosylceramide misregulation leads to disease states such as Gaucher disease. Cataracts and nephrogenic diabetes insipidus arise from aquaporin mutations, and long QT syndrome and epilepsy from voltage-gated channel mutations.
questions.title: Lecture 21 - Cell Membranes

questions.q: How is the lipid bilayer asymmetrical?
options: All glycolipids and most PC and SM sit in the external monolayer, while most PS and PE and almost all PI sit in the cytosolic leaflet
All glycolipids sit in the cytosolic leaflet and cholesterol only in the external leaflet
PC and PS are confined to the cytosolic leaflet and PE to the external
The two leaflets have identical composition but different thickness
Cholesterol is found only in the external monolayer
questions.explanation: The external monolayer holds all glycolipids and most phosphatidylcholine and sphingomyelin. The cytosolic leaflet holds most phosphatidylserine and phosphatidylethanolamine, with phosphatidylinositol almost exclusively there. Cholesterol is distributed equally in both.
questions.title: Lecture 21 - Cell Membranes

questions.q: Why do most plasma membranes have a negatively charged interior face?
options: Because cholesterol carries a negative charge
Because phosphatidylserine has a slight negative charge and phosphatidylinositol can be phosphorylated, and both sit on the cytosolic side
Because glycolipids accumulate on the inner leaflet
Because sphingomyelin is negatively charged
Because chloride ions bind the inner leaflet
questions.explanation: Phosphatidylserine has a slight negative charge and phosphatidylinositol can be phosphorylated. Since both are concentrated in the cytosolic leaflet, most plasma membranes have a negatively charged interior compared with the exterior.
questions.title: Lecture 21 - Cell Membranes

questions.q: Which features describe a sterol?
options: Larger than phospholipids, with two polar head groups
Smaller than phospholipids, with a single polar hydroxyl head, a rigid steroid ring structure and a short non-polar hydrocarbon tail
A sphingoid backbone with two fatty acid chains
A glycerol backbone with a phosphate and a sugar
A cyclic molecule with no hydrophobic region
questions.explanation: Sterols are smaller than phospholipids, with a single polar hydroxyl head group, a rigid steroid ring structure and a short non-polar hydrocarbon tail.
questions.title: Lecture 21 - Cell Membranes

questions.q: What is the melting temperature (Tm) of a membrane?
options: The temperature at which lipids are chemically degraded
The temperature at which the transition from rigid state to fluid state occurs
The temperature at which cholesterol crystallises out
The temperature at which membrane proteins denature
The temperature at which lipid rafts dissolve completely
questions.explanation: The melting temperature Tm is the temperature at which the transition from rigid state to fluid state occurs. Fluidity is determined by fatty acid length, fatty acid saturation and cholesterol content.
questions.title: Lecture 21 - Cell Membranes

questions.q: What evidence shows that cholesterol stabilises the cell membrane?
options: Mutant cells unable to synthesise cholesterol lyse easily
Cholesterol-rich membranes have a lower protein content
Cholesterol makes membranes impermeable to water
Cholesterol prevents lateral diffusion of all lipids
Cholesterol only appears in bacterial membranes
questions.explanation: Cholesterol stiffens and stabilises cell membranes. Mutant cells that are unable to synthesise cholesterol lyse easily, demonstrating its stabilising role.
questions.title: Lecture 21 - Cell Membranes

questions.q: What are lipid rafts made of, and how big are they?
options: Unsaturated phospholipids only, about 500 nm across
Glycosphingolipids, sphingomyelin, saturated glycerophospholipids and cholesterol, forming microdomains about 70 nm in diameter
Pure cholesterol patches about 5 nm across
Integral proteins alone, about 20 nm across
Glycolipids and unsaturated fatty acids, about 1 micron across
questions.explanation: Lipid rafts are regions of increased density formed of glycosphingolipids, sphingomyelin, saturated glycerophospholipids and cholesterol. Long tails give thicker regions and saturation gives denser packing, forming microdomains about 70 nm in diameter with some protein enrichment.
questions.title: Lecture 21 - Cell Membranes

questions.q: Phosphatidylinositol bisphosphate (PIP2) contributes to signalling by which mechanism?
options: It transports ions directly across the membrane
External signals trigger its cleavage into second messengers that transduce signals to intracellular effects
It binds hormones at the cell surface
It forms the pore of a voltage-gated channel
It anchors the cytoskeleton to the membrane
questions.explanation: Signals outside cells can trigger cleavage of phosphatidylinositol (PIP2) into second messengers, which transduces the signal to have intracellular effects.
questions.title: Lecture 21 - Cell Membranes

questions.q: Aminoglycoside antibiotics are actively transported into bacterial cells by carriers that human cells lack. What principle does this illustrate?
options: Feedback inhibition
Selective toxicity
Facilitated diffusion
Competitive inhibition
Bioequivalence
questions.explanation: Bacteria have different membrane compositions and transport mechanisms from eukaryotes. Carrier molecules actively transport aminoglycoside antibiotics into bacterial cells with no such system in human cells, a good example of selective toxicity.
questions.title: Lecture 21 - Cell Membranes

questions.q: How do siderophores work, and why do they matter for drug design?
options: They sequester and solubilise iron for uptake; adding iron-binding groups to drugs can increase potency
They pump antibiotics out of bacterial cells; blocking them restores drug activity
They degrade beta-lactam antibiotics; inhibiting them protects penicillins
They form pores in the fungal membrane; they are used as antifungals
They transport water across the membrane; they are targets in diabetes insipidus
questions.explanation: Bacteria release siderophores that sequester and solubilise iron. Receptors recognise them and transport them into the cell, where Fe3+ is reduced to Fe2+ to release it. Adding iron-binding groups to drugs can increase potency by exploiting this route.
questions.title: Lecture 21 - Cell Membranes

questions.q: What is the function of the bacterial cell wall, and what is it made of?
options: It withstands hydrostatic pressure preventing the cell bursting, and is made of peptidoglycan
It stores energy for the cell, and is made of glycogen
It regulates ion balance, and is made of phospholipid
It provides motility, and is made of flagellin
It prevents antibiotic entry, and is made of lipopolysaccharide alone
questions.explanation: The bacterial cell wall withstands hydrostatic pressure, preventing the cell from bursting. It is made of peptidoglycan: a mesh-like polymer of sugar and amino acids, with amino sugars connected by beta-1,4 linkages and polysaccharide chains cross-linked between amino acids.
questions.title: Lecture 21 - Cell Membranes

questions.q: Why do Gram positive bacteria appear purple after Gram staining?
options: They have two phospholipid bilayers that trap the dye
They have a thick layer of peptidoglycan that prevents the stain leaking out
Their lipopolysaccharides bind the dye covalently
They contain lipoteichoic acids that are naturally purple
Their thin peptidoglycan retains the counterstain
questions.explanation: Gram positive bacteria have a thick layer of peptidoglycan which prevents the stain leaking out, so they appear purple. Their cell wall also includes negatively charged lipoteichoic acids.
questions.title: Lecture 21 - Cell Membranes

questions.q: Which features characterise the Gram negative cell envelope?
options: Thick peptidoglycan and a single bilayer
Thin peptidoglycan, two phospholipid bilayers, wall attached to the outer membrane by Braun's lipoproteins, and protruding lipopolysaccharides
No peptidoglycan at all and one bilayer
Thick peptidoglycan with lipoteichoic acids and no outer membrane
Two bilayers with hopanoids replacing all peptidoglycan
questions.explanation: Gram negative bacteria have thin peptidoglycan walls so the dye leaks out. They have two phospholipid bilayers, the cell wall attached to the outer membrane by Braun's lipoproteins, and negatively charged lipopolysaccharides protruding, which can protect against hydrophobic drugs.
questions.title: Lecture 21 - Cell Membranes

questions.q: In bacteria, sterols are replaced by which molecules?
