options: Hopanoids, cyclic molecules also derived from squalene
Ergosterol, a fungal sterol
Cardiolipin, an anionic phospholipid
Lipoteichoic acids
Ceramides
questions.explanation: Sterols are replaced by hopanoids in bacteria, cyclic molecules that like sterols are derived from squalene.
questions.title: Lecture 21 - Cell Membranes

questions.q: Which lipids predominate in bacterial membranes?
options: Phosphatidylcholine as the main zwitterionic lipid and phosphatidylserine as the main anionic lipid
Phosphatidylethanolamine as the main zwitterionic lipid, with phosphatidylglycerol and cardiolipin as the main anionic lipids
Sphingomyelin and cholesterol
Glycosphingolipids and ceramide
Triglycerides and free fatty acids
questions.explanation: Bacterial lipid composition varies widely between species but usually phosphatidylethanolamine is the main zwitterionic lipid, with phosphatidylglycerol and cardiolipin the main anionic lipids. The presence of LPS and LTA anionic lipids confers selective toxicity of cationic antimicrobials.
questions.title: Lecture 21 - Cell Membranes

questions.q: Which membrane has the highest protein content by weight?
options: Myelin membrane, at under 25 per cent
Plasma membrane, at about 50 per cent
Inner mitochondrial membrane, at about 75 per cent
All membranes contain the same 50 per cent
Nuclear membrane, at about 90 per cent
questions.explanation: Protein content varies with function: the myelin membrane which insulates nerves is under 25 per cent protein, plasma membranes about 50 per cent, and the inner mitochondrial membrane, which carries out energy transduction, about 75 per cent.
questions.title: Lecture 21 - Cell Membranes

questions.q: Porins in bacterial outer membranes are built from which structural motif?
options: A single alpha helix spanning the membrane
Multiple alpha helices forming a hydrophilic pore
Antiparallel beta sheets forming a beta sheet barrel
A cholesterol-lined channel
A lipid raft microdomain
questions.explanation: Transmembrane proteins can use beta sheet structures, especially the porins of bacterial outer membranes, which form a beta sheet barrel of antiparallel beta sheets. They are also found in eukaryotic mitochondria and chloroplasts.
questions.title: Lecture 21 - Cell Membranes

questions.q: How do porins contribute to antibiotic resistance?
options: By actively pumping antibiotics out of the cell
By enzymatically destroying antibiotics as they pass
By changing their physical parameters under selective pressure, lowering antibiotic permeability and preventing penetration
By binding antibiotics irreversibly in the periplasm
By thickening the peptidoglycan layer
questions.explanation: Porins have a significant role in antibiotic resistance. Under selective pressure, changes in their physical parameters alter function, lowering antibiotic permeability and preventing penetration of antibiotics.
questions.title: Lecture 21 - Cell Membranes

questions.q: Amphotericin B works as an antifungal by which mechanism?
options: Inhibiting fungal cell wall synthesis
Interacting with the fungal sterol ergosterol to create channels in the membrane, interfering with ionic balance
Blocking fungal DNA replication
Inhibiting fungal protein synthesis at the ribosome
Chelating iron needed for fungal growth
questions.explanation: Polyene antifungals such as amphotericin B interact with the fungal sterol ergosterol, creating channels in the cell membrane and interfering with the cell's ionic balance.
questions.title: Lecture 21 - Cell Membranes

questions.q: What distinguishes simple diffusion from transport requiring integral proteins?
options: Small, uncharged ions and molecules can move down their concentration gradient unaided, whereas charged or large molecules need assistance from integral proteins
Simple diffusion requires ATP whereas protein-mediated transport does not
Simple diffusion only occurs in bacteria
Simple diffusion moves molecules against their gradient
Only water can cross by simple diffusion
questions.explanation: Small, uncharged ions and molecules can move down their concentration gradient towards equilibrium by simple diffusion, described as passive transport. Charged or large molecules need assistance from integral proteins.
questions.title: Lecture 21 - Cell Membranes

questions.q: What is the role of aquaporins, and what happens when they are mutated?
options: They allow passage of water and regulate osmolarity; mutations can cause cataracts and nephrogenic diabetes insipidus
They allow passage of sodium; mutations cause long QT syndrome
They allow passage of chloride; mutations disrupt neuronal excitability
They pump protons into lysosomes; mutations cause Gaucher disease
They transport iron; mutations cause anaemia
questions.explanation: Aquaporins allow the passage of water and regulate osmolarity, and are important for the kidneys. They are highly alpha-helical with significant structural conservation across kingdoms, and mutations can lead to cataracts and nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.
questions.title: Lecture 21 - Cell Membranes

questions.q: How does the GABA-A receptor function as a ligand-gated ion channel?
options: GABA binding closes a sodium channel
GABA binding allows Cl- ions through a selective channel, and unbinding closes it
GABA binding pumps chloride against its gradient using ATP
GABA binding depolarises the membrane by admitting calcium
GABA binding triggers phosphorylation of the channel
questions.explanation: GABA is an inhibitory neurotransmitter. Binding to the GABA-A receptor allows Cl- ions through a selective channel and unbinding closes it. Mutations disrupt neuronal excitability, and benzodiazepines and alcohol increase Cl- conductance.
questions.title: Lecture 21 - Cell Membranes

questions.q: How does the voltage sensing domain of a voltage-gated ion channel work?
options: The S4 segment carries positive amino acids and is repelled by positive charges outside the cell; depolarisation draws S4 upwards, pulling the S4-5 linker so S5 and S6 pull apart and the channel opens
A ligand binds S4 and pulls the pore open
Phosphorylation of S6 opens the pore directly
Calcium binding to S1 collapses the pore
The pore domain senses voltage and the S4 segment forms the pore
questions.explanation: Each subunit has a pore domain and a voltage-sensing domain. The S4 segment, carrying positive amino acids, is repelled by positive charges outside the cell. Membrane depolarisation draws S4 upwards, pulling the S4-5 linker and causing S5 and S6 to pull apart so the channel opens.
questions.title: Lecture 21 - Cell Membranes

questions.q: How do uniporters, symporters and antiporters differ?
options: Uniporters move a single ion type by facilitated diffusion; symporters use one ion's gradient to pull a different ion in the same direction; antiporters move the two ions in opposite directions
Uniporters use ATP; symporters and antiporters use facilitated diffusion
Uniporters move two ions; symporters one; antiporters three
All three require ATP hydrolysis to function
Uniporters work only in bacteria; the others only in eukaryotes
questions.explanation: These are electrochemical potential-driven transporters. A uniporter moves a single ion type by facilitated diffusion down its gradient. A symporter uses facilitated diffusion of one ion to pull a different ion with it; an antiporter does the same but in opposite directions.
questions.title: Lecture 21 - Cell Membranes

questions.q: What does the sodium-potassium pump, a P-type ATPase, transport and in which direction?
options: 2 Na+ out and 3 K+ in, down their concentration gradients
3 Na+ out of the cell and 2 K+ into the cell, against their concentration gradients
3 K+ out and 2 Na+ in, against their gradients
Equal numbers of Na+ and K+ in opposite directions
Protons out of the cell in exchange for sodium
questions.explanation: The sodium-potassium pump, a P-type ATPase where P stands for phosphorylation, transports 3 Na+ out of the cell and brings 2 K+ into the cell, against their concentration gradients. It is very important in muscles, nerves, stomach and kidney.
questions.title: Lecture 21 - Cell Membranes

questions.q: Which active transporter type is correctly described?
options: V-ATPases pump protons across the membranes of lysosomes and endosomes using a rotary motor
F-ATPases pump protons into lysosomes
ABC transporters are driven by a proton gradient
P-type ATPases use rotational catalysis
V-ATPases synthesise ATP in mitochondria
questions.explanation: V-ATPases pump protons across the membranes of lysosomes and endosomes using a rotary motor. F-ATPases use a proton gradient to drive ATP synthesis by rotational catalysis, and ABC transporters use ATP hydrolysis to move substrates, including removing foreign chemicals from cells.
questions.title: Lecture 21 - Cell Membranes

questions.q: Why are ABC transporters of interest in cancer chemotherapy?
options: They synthesise ATP needed by tumour cells
They remove foreign chemicals from cells, which can include chemotherapeutic agents
They import chemotherapy drugs selectively into tumours
They regulate the resting membrane potential of tumour cells
They form the pores through which drugs diffuse passively
questions.explanation: ABC transporters move substrates using energy from ATP hydrolysis and remove foreign chemicals from cells, which raises the question of their role in removing chemotherapeutic agents.
questions.title: Lecture 21 - Cell Membranes

questions.q: What determines the resting membrane potential of a cell?
options: The concentration of ATP inside the cell
Summing the equilibrium balance points for each cellular ion, where each ion balances its chemical gradient against the electrical force
The total protein content of the membrane
The thickness of the lipid bilayer
The number of aquaporins present
questions.explanation: Electrochemical balance depends on both concentration and charge. Potassium, for example, tends to leave down its chemical gradient but is drawn in by electrical charge, reaching an equilibrium point. Summing the balance points for each ion gives the resting membrane potential, about -70 mV for neurons.
questions.title: Lecture 21 - Cell Membranes

questions.q: Why does an action potential propagate directionally along a nerve?
options: Because the membrane is thicker at one end
Because channels in the wave's wake must reset before they can open again
Because sodium is only present at one end of the axon
Because ATP is consumed only in the forward direction
Because myelin blocks backward conduction entirely
questions.explanation: A wave of depolarisation flips the charge across the membrane, and ion channels allow directional propagation of the signal because channels in the wave's wake must reset before they can open again.
questions.title: Lecture 21 - Cell Membranes

questions.q: What key properties do biological membranes provide as closed boundaries?
options: Selective permeability for protection and containment, allowing different environments on each side
Complete impermeability to all ions and nutrients at all times
Rigid crystalline structure that never changes
Exclusive transport of DNA between cells
Uniform composition with no associated proteins
questions.explanation: Biological membranes are selectively permeable boundaries that protect and contain cells, permit different environments on each side, and allow regulated movement and signalling.
questions.title: Lecture 21 - Cell Membranes

questions.q: What is the basic structure of all cell membranes described in the lecture?
options: A lipid bilayer barrier with associated proteins for transport and membrane functions
A single layer of cholesterol with no proteins
A protein sheet with no lipid component
A carbohydrate mesh surrounding the nucleus only
A rigid peptidoglycan wall like bacteria
questions.explanation: All membranes share a lipid bilayer providing barrier properties plus associated proteins that permit transport and perform membrane functions—the fluid mosaic model.
questions.title: Lecture 21 - Cell Membranes

questions.q: What are the two main platform molecules for phospholipids?
options: Glycerol or a sphingoid complex alcohol
Glucose or fructose only
Cholesterol or steroid hormones only
Amino acids or nucleotides
RNA or DNA backbones
questions.explanation: Phospholipids are built on either glycerol, a small simple alcohol, or a sphingoid complex alcohol such as sphingosine.
questions.title: Lecture 21 - Cell Membranes

questions.q: What holds lipid bilayers together and what determines their fluidity?
options: Non-covalent bonds; fluidity depends on relative lipid movement and factors that alter those bonds
Covalent peptide bonds between fatty acids
Ionic bonds to the nucleus only
Hydrogen bonds that are unaffected by temperature
Metallic bonds between cholesterol molecules
questions.explanation: Bilayers are held by non-covalent bonds. Fluidity reflects relative lipid movement; increasing temperature raises kinetic energy until intermolecular bonds can no longer maintain a packed structure.
questions.title: Lecture 21 - Cell Membranes

questions.q: How can transmembrane proteins span a membrane?
options: As a single alpha-helix or as multiple alpha-helices forming a hydrophilic pore
Only as beta-sheets on the cytoplasmic face with no membrane crossing
Exclusively as peripheral proteins that never enter the bilayer
As carbohydrate chains attached to the outer leaflet only
As DNA loops embedded in the membrane
questions.explanation: Transmembrane proteins may consist of a single alpha-helix across the membrane or multiple alpha-helices interacting to form a transmembrane hydrophilic pore.
questions.title: Lecture 21 - Cell Membranes

questions.q: Why do larger or more charged molecules need more assistance crossing membranes?
options: Simple diffusion alone is insufficient; they may require facilitated diffusion or active transport
They are too small to fit through any channel
They always enter by endocytosis regardless of size
They dissolve directly in the hydrophobic core without help
They can only cross during mitosis
questions.explanation: Larger or more charged molecules need more assistance crossing the membrane, moving beyond simple diffusion to facilitated diffusion or active transport.
questions.title: Lecture 21 - Cell Membranes

questions.q: Which ion channel types are highlighted in the lecture?
options: Porins, aquaporins, voltage-gated ion channels, and ligand-gated ion channels
Only sodium-potassium ATPase pumps
Gap junctions and desmosomes only
Nuclear pores exclusively
Ribosomal channels for protein export
questions.explanation: The lecture groups ion channels into porins, aquaporins, voltage-gated ion channels, and ligand-gated ion channels among many subtypes.
questions.title: Lecture 21 - Cell Membranes

questions.q: What are the three main mechanisms of membrane transport?
options: Simple diffusion, facilitated diffusion, and active transport
Osmosis, dialysis, and filtration only
Endocytosis, exocytosis, and apoptosis
Replication, transcription, and translation
Phagocytosis, pinocytosis, and binary fission
questions.explanation: Membrane transport occurs by simple diffusion, facilitated diffusion, and active transport, maintaining concentrations and moving required molecules and waste.
questions.title: Lecture 21 - Cell Membranes

questions.q: Why are ion channels and transporters important for the resting membrane potential?
options: They control membrane permeability, creating concentration differences that determine electrical charge across the membrane
They store ATP for muscle contraction only
They synthesise neurotransmitters in the Golgi
They replicate mitochondrial DNA
They prevent all ion movement so the membrane is always neutral
questions.explanation: Different ionic environments exist on each side of the membrane. Channels and transporters control permeability; concentration differences determine the resting membrane potential.
questions.title: Lecture 21 - Cell Membranes

questions.q: Which statement about cell membranes is a key point from the lecture?
options: Phospholipid bilayers are fluid and non-symmetrical; transporters can use ATP or electrochemical gradients
Membranes are identical on both faces with no integral proteins
All transport is passive with no energy requirement
Bacterial and eukaryotic membranes are identical so drugs cannot be selective
Ion channels are formed only from beta-sheets in all organisms
questions.explanation: Key points include a fluid, non-symmetrical phospholipid bilayer, ion channels of alpha-helices or beta-sheets, and transporters moving molecules with or against gradients using ATP or electrochemical energy.
questions.title: Lecture 21 - Cell Membranes

questions.q: What do the roots of the word eukaryote mean?
options: 'eu' meaning true and 'karyon' meaning kernel or nucleus
'eu' meaning before and 'karyon' meaning cell
'eu' meaning many and 'karyon' meaning organelle
'eu' meaning outer and 'karyon' meaning membrane
'eu' meaning complex and 'karyon' meaning body
questions.explanation: Eukaryote comes from 'eu' meaning true and 'karyon' meaning kernel or nucleus. Prokaryote uses 'pro' meaning before, that is before the nucleus.
questions.title: Lecture 22 - Eukaryotic Cells

questions.q: Which structures make up the endomembrane system?
options: The nuclear membrane, endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi apparatus, vesicles and lysosomes
The mitochondria, peroxisomes and cytoskeleton
The plasma membrane, cell wall and nuclear envelope
The ribosomes, nucleolus and chromatin
The microtubules, actin filaments and intermediate filaments
questions.explanation: The endomembrane system comprises the nuclear membrane, endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi apparatus, vesicles and lysosomes. Peroxisomes and mitochondria are membrane-enclosed organelles but are considered separately.
questions.title: Lecture 22 - Eukaryotic Cells

questions.q: What is chromatin?
options: DNA plus proteins, stored in the nucleus in the nucleoplasm
The double membrane boundary of the nucleus
The site of ribosome assembly only
RNA plus histones in the cytoplasm
The gel-like substance filling the nucleus
questions.explanation: Chromatin is DNA plus proteins, stored in the nucleus in a gel-like substance called the nucleoplasm.
questions.title: Lecture 22 - Eukaryotic Cells

questions.q: What happens in the nucleolus?
options: DNA replication
rRNA transcription and processing, and ribosome assembly
Protein glycosylation
Lipid synthesis
ATP production
questions.explanation: The nucleolus is a condensed region of chromatin where rRNA transcription and processing take place, along with ribosome assembly.
questions.title: Lecture 22 - Eukaryotic Cells

questions.q: Which describes the nuclear envelope?
options: A single phospholipid bilayer with no pores
Two phospholipid bilayers whose outer membrane is continuous with the ER, with pores allowing substances to enter and exit
A rigid protein shell surrounding the chromatin
A single bilayer continuous with the Golgi apparatus
Two bilayers with no connection to any other organelle
questions.explanation: The nuclear envelope has two phospholipid bilayers, inner and outer. The outer membrane is continuous with the endoplasmic reticulum, and pores allow substances such as newly synthesised ribosomes to enter and exit the nucleus.
questions.title: Lecture 22 - Eukaryotic Cells

questions.q: What is a nucleosome?
options: About 1.7 turns of DNA, roughly 200 bp, wrapped around 8 histone proteins
A single turn of DNA around one histone protein
A 30 nm chromatin fibre
The condensed region of the nucleus where ribosomes assemble
A pore in the nuclear envelope
questions.explanation: The nucleosome is the fundamental subunit of chromatin: about 1.7 turns of DNA, roughly 200 base pairs, wrapped around 8 histone proteins, with the energy for coiling provided by electrostatic interactions.
questions.title: Lecture 22 - Eukaryotic Cells

questions.q: Which histone is required for the second level of DNA folding?
options: H2A
H2B
H3
H4
H1
questions.explanation: The first level of folding is the nucleosome. The second level of folding requires histone H1.
questions.title: Lecture 22 - Eukaryotic Cells

questions.q: For most of the cell cycle, how is DNA organised?
options: As iconic four-armed chromosomes
As 30 nm diameter chromatin fibres, like balls of unravelled string
As free naked DNA in the nucleoplasm
As circular plasmids
As single nucleosomes not joined together
questions.explanation: The iconic four-armed chromosome exists only for a brief part of the cell cycle. Most of the time DNA is simply organised into 30 nm diameter chromatin fibres.
questions.title: Lecture 22 - Eukaryotic Cells

questions.q: How does rough ER differ from smooth ER in appearance and function?
options: Rough ER is tubular and makes lipids; smooth ER is flattened and makes proteins
Rough ER consists of flattened sacs studded with ribosomes for protein synthesis; smooth ER is more tubular and handles lipid production, carbohydrate metabolism, detoxification and calcium storage
Rough ER handles detoxification; smooth ER assembles ribosomes
Rough ER is found only in the nucleus; smooth ER only near the Golgi
They are separate organelles with no connection
questions.explanation: Rough ER is highly convoluted, flattened sealed sacs studded on the outer surface with ribosomes. Smooth ER is contiguous with it but more tubular, and handles lipid production and metabolism, carbohydrate metabolism, detoxification and Ca2+ storage for signalling.
questions.title: Lecture 22 - Eukaryotic Cells

questions.q: What distinguishes proteins made on rough ER ribosomes from those made on free cytoplasmic ribosomes?
options: RER proteins typically contain a signal sequence destination label and translocate into the ER; free ribosomes synthesise all other proteins encoded by the nuclear genome
RER proteins are always enzymes; free ribosome proteins are always structural
RER proteins are smaller than those from free ribosomes
Free ribosome proteins always contain a signal sequence
There is no functional difference, only location
questions.explanation: Ribosomes attached to the rough ER synthesise proteins that translocate into the ER and on to other compartments after quality control; these typically contain a specific destination label or signal sequence. Free cytoplasmic ribosomes synthesise all other nuclear-encoded proteins.
questions.title: Lecture 22 - Eukaryotic Cells

questions.q: What is a cisterna, and what does each one contain?
options: A flattened sac of the Golgi stack, each containing different protein modification enzymes
A vesicle budding from the plasma membrane
A fold of the inner mitochondrial membrane
A pore in the nuclear envelope
A compartment of the lysosome
questions.explanation: The Golgi apparatus is a stack of flattened, pancake-like sacs called cisternae. Each cisterna contains different protein modification enzymes.
questions.title: Lecture 22 - Eukaryotic Cells

questions.q: How is the polarity of the Golgi apparatus arranged?
options: The cis side faces the plasma membrane where proteins enter; the trans side faces the nucleus where they exit
The cis side faces the nucleus where proteins enter; the trans side faces the plasma membrane where proteins exit
Both sides face the nucleus and proteins enter and exit at the same point
The Golgi has no polarity; entry and exit are random
Proteins enter and leave through the lateral edges only
questions.explanation: The Golgi has polarity: the cis side faces the nucleus where proteins enter, and the trans side faces away towards the plasma membrane where proteins exit. In the trans-Golgi network they are packaged for transport to other organelles or for secretion.
questions.title: Lecture 22 - Eukaryotic Cells

questions.q: Defects in Golgi function can result in which conditions?
options: Congenital glycosylation disorders and some forms of muscular dystrophy
Cataracts and nephrogenic diabetes insipidus
Long QT syndrome and epilepsy
Gaucher disease only
Sickle cell anaemia and thalassaemia
questions.explanation: Defects in Golgi function can result in congenital glycosylation disorders and some forms of muscular dystrophy, and may contribute to diabetes, cancer and cystic fibrosis.
questions.title: Lecture 22 - Eukaryotic Cells

questions.q: How are vesicles formed and what do they do?
options: By pinching off a small portion of lipid membrane; they store and transport biomolecules and fuse with membranes to deliver contents
By assembly of free proteins in the cytosol; they degrade unwanted molecules
By division of lysosomes; they generate ATP
By budding from mitochondria; they carry oxygen
By condensation of chromatin; they carry DNA
questions.explanation: Vesicles are small membrane-bound organelles formed by pinching off a small portion of a lipid membrane. They store and transport biomolecules and can fuse with other cellular membranes to deliver their contents, within a cell, out of cells or between cells.
questions.title: Lecture 22 - Eukaryotic Cells

questions.q: Why does the low pH inside lysosomes matter?
options: It activates ATP synthesis
It protects cells from accidental release of the degradative enzymes
It allows DNA to be stored safely
It maintains the resting membrane potential
It permits oxygen storage
questions.explanation: Lysosomes are the recycling centres of the cell, containing at least 50 different enzymes capable of breaking down all biological polymers. Their low pH requirement protects cells from accidental release, since the enzymes need acidic conditions to work.
questions.title: Lecture 22 - Eukaryotic Cells

questions.q: How are lysosomes formed, and in which processes do they participate?
options: By budding from mitochondria; in respiration and ATP production
By fusion of endosomes with transport vesicles budded from the trans-Golgi network; in phagocytosis, endocytosis and autophagy
By pinching off from the nuclear envelope; in transcription
By assembly from free ribosomes; in protein synthesis
By division of peroxisomes; in lipid metabolism
questions.explanation: Lysosomes are formed by fusion of endosomes with transport vesicles budded from the trans-Golgi network, and they play roles in phagocytosis, endocytosis and autophagy.
questions.title: Lecture 22 - Eukaryotic Cells

questions.q: Which describes mitochondrial membrane structure?
options: A permeable outer membrane and a far less permeable inner membrane, heavily folded into cristae, enclosing the matrix
A single membrane enclosing the matrix
A less permeable outer membrane and a highly permeable inner membrane
Two identical membranes with no folding
A membrane continuous with the endoplasmic reticulum
questions.explanation: The mitochondrion has a permeable outer membrane and an inner membrane which is far less permeable. The inner membrane is heavily folded to create cristae, and inside it lies the matrix.
questions.title: Lecture 22 - Eukaryotic Cells

questions.q: Of the roughly 3000 genes needed to make a mitochondrion, how many are encoded by mtDNA?
options: All 3000
About 1500
About 300
None
questions.explanation: Of the 3000 genes needed to make a mitochondrion, mtDNA encodes only 37. Other required proteins are made elsewhere and trafficked to developing mitochondria. Only about 3 per cent of the genes are allocated to making ATP.
questions.title: Lecture 22 - Eukaryotic Cells

questions.q: What is endosymbiosis?
options: One organism living inside another to their mutual benefit
The fusion of two identical cells into one
The engulfment of a cell followed by its destruction
The exchange of genetic material between bacteria
The division of an organelle by binary fission
questions.explanation: Endosymbiosis is one organism living inside another to their mutual benefit. In obligate endosymbiosis the host cannot survive alone. Some eukaryotic organelles are thought to have evolved through symbiosis with single-celled prokaryotes.
questions.title: Lecture 22 - Eukaryotic Cells

questions.q: Which is evidence for the endosymbiotic origin of mitochondria?
options: They contain 80S ribosomes like the cytoplasm
They have their own circular DNA genome, multiply by binary fission and have 70S ribosomes
They are much larger than any known prokaryote
They have a single membrane like other organelles
Their rRNA genes group with those of archaea
questions.explanation: The evidence includes mitochondria being similar in size to prokaryotes, having their own cell membranes, having their own circular DNA genome, multiplying by binary fission independent of the cell, having 70S ribosomes, and their rRNA genes grouping with modern proteobacteria (Rickettsiales).
questions.title: Lecture 22 - Eukaryotic Cells

questions.q: Chloroplasts are thought to be related to which group of organisms?
options: Rickettsiales proteobacteria
Nitrogen-fixing filamentous cyanobacteria
Archaea
Yeasts
Mycobacteria
questions.explanation: Phylogenetic studies group mitochondrial rRNA genes with proteobacteria (Rickettsiales), while chloroplasts are thought to be related to nitrogen-fixing filamentous cyanobacteria.
questions.title: Lecture 22 - Eukaryotic Cells

questions.q: What are the two main fundamental processes carried out by peroxisomes?
options: ATP synthesis and calcium storage
Defence systems for in situ scavenging of peroxides and reactive oxygen species, and diverse reactions involved in lipid metabolism
Protein synthesis and glycosylation
DNA replication and repair
Phagocytosis and autophagy
questions.explanation: Peroxisomes carry out defence against peroxides and reactive oxygen species by in situ scavenging, and diverse reactions in lipid metabolism. They contain about 60 different oxidative enzymes.
questions.title: Lecture 22 - Eukaryotic Cells

questions.q: Which peroxisomal role is tissue specific?
options: Oxidation of long chain fatty acids
Scavenging of reactive oxygen species
Bile acid synthesis and alcohol detoxification in the liver
Oxidative deamination of D-amino acids
Cholesterol biosynthesis
questions.explanation: Peroxisomes oxidise long chain fatty acids as a source of metabolic energy, carry out some lipid biosynthesis such as cholesterol and plasmalogens, degrade amino acids by oxidative deamination of D-amino acids, and have tissue specific roles such as bile acid synthesis and alcohol detoxification in the liver.
questions.title: Lecture 22 - Eukaryotic Cells

questions.q: Where does the peroxisomal membrane originate, and how are peroxisomes assembled?
options: From the ER, but assembled like mitochondria using proteins imported from free ribosomes
From the Golgi, and assembled from vesicles
From the plasma membrane, and assembled by endocytosis
From the nuclear envelope, and assembled in the nucleus
They arise only by division of existing lysosomes
questions.explanation: The peroxisomal membrane originates from the ER. Peroxisomes have similar morphology to lysosomes but are assembled more like mitochondria, using proteins synthesised and imported from free ribosomes.
questions.title: Lecture 22 - Eukaryotic Cells

questions.q: Which is a function of the cytoskeleton?
options: Synthesising ATP for the cell
Supporting the plasma membrane, controlling cell shape, enabling movement, guiding intracellular traffic and pulling chromosomes apart during division
Degrading biological polymers
Transcribing rRNA and assembling ribosomes
Storing calcium for signalling
questions.explanation: The cytoskeleton supports the plasma membrane, controls cell shape, enables some cells to move, drives and guides intracellular traffic of organelles, proteins and RNA, and pulls the chromosomes apart during cell division.
questions.title: Lecture 22 - Eukaryotic Cells

questions.q: What are the roles of intermediate filaments, and what is their diameter?
options: About 10 nm; provide tensile strength, maintain cell shape and anchor organelles
About 25 nm; form the mitotic spindle
About 5 to 9 nm; provide the motive force for muscle contraction
About 50 nm; transport cargo along the cell
About 2 nm; form the cell cortex
questions.explanation: Intermediate filaments are about 10 nm in diameter, made of bundles of monomers twisted into ropes. They provide tensile strength, maintain cell shape and anchor organelles.
questions.title: Lecture 22 - Eukaryotic Cells

questions.q: Which intermediate filament type is correctly matched to its location?
options: Keratin in nerve cells
Vimentin in epithelial cells
Neurofilaments in connective tissue
Nuclear lamins in all animal cells
Keratin in glial cells
questions.explanation: The four main types are keratin in epithelial cells, vimentin and related proteins in connective tissue, muscle and glial cells, neurofilaments in nerve cells, and nuclear lamins in all animal cells.
questions.title: Lecture 22 - Eukaryotic Cells

questions.q: What are microtubules made of, and what is their diameter?
options: Polymers of actin, about 5 to 9 nm
Polymers of tubulin heterodimers, about 25 nm, as rigid hollow rods
Bundles of keratin monomers, about 10 nm
Polymers of myosin, about 25 nm
Polymers of tubulin, about 10 nm
questions.explanation: Microtubules are about 25 nm in diameter, rigid hollow rods and dynamic structures. They are polymers of the single protein tubulin, as heterodimers of the alpha and beta forms, and are important in cell shape, movement and internal cargo transport.
questions.title: Lecture 22 - Eukaryotic Cells

questions.q: What is the role of gamma-tubulin?
options: It forms the bulk of the microtubule wall
It is specifically localised to the centrosome and initiates microtubule assembly
It caps the plus end to stop growth
It carries cargo along the microtubule
It hydrolyses GTP to GDP within the protofilament
questions.explanation: Alpha and beta tubulin form the heterodimers of the microtubule. A third type, gamma-tubulin, is specifically localised to the centrosome where it initiates microtubule assembly.
questions.title: Lecture 22 - Eukaryotic Cells

questions.q: How many protofilaments make up a microtubule, and what is the significance of its ends?
options: 13 protofilaments; the structure is polar with a plus end where growth and shrinkage occur rapidly
8 protofilaments; both ends behave identically
13 protofilaments; the minus end is the more dynamic
4 protofilaments; the plus end is static
26 protofilaments; the ends are chemically identical
questions.explanation: Microtubules are composed of 13 protofilaments, head-to-tail arrays of tubulin dimers arranged in parallel. They are polar with two distinct ends, plus and minus, and the plus end is the more dynamic where growth and shrinkage occur rapidly.
questions.title: Lecture 22 - Eukaryotic Cells

questions.q: How does GTP regulate microtubule polymerisation, and what is treadmilling?
options: GTP-bound beta-tubulin adds to the growing filament and is hydrolysed to GDP shortly after, weakening binding; the tube can grow at one end while shrinking at the other
GDP-bound tubulin adds to the filament and is converted to GTP, strengthening binding
ATP rather than GTP drives assembly, and treadmilling means both ends grow equally
GTP hydrolysis stops all polymerisation permanently
Treadmilling is the movement of motor proteins along the microtubule
questions.explanation: Beta-tubulin bound to GTP joins the growing protofilaments, and hydrolysis to GDP occurs shortly after polymerisation, weakening binding affinity for adjacent molecules. Polymerisation continues while free GTP-bound tubulin is high and is faster at the plus end, while GDP-bound tubulin is more easily lost from the minus end, so tubes can grow at one end while shrinking at the other.
questions.title: Lecture 22 - Eukaryotic Cells

questions.q: Which motor protein travels in which direction along a microtubule?
options: Kinesins travel anterograde from minus to plus; dyneins travel retrograde from plus to minus
Kinesins travel retrograde from plus to minus; dyneins travel anterograde
Both kinesins and dyneins travel from minus to plus
Myosins travel along microtubules in both directions
Direction depends only on the cargo, not the motor
questions.explanation: Microtubule polarity matters for direction of travel: kinesins travel in the anterograde direction from minus to plus, and dyneins travel in the retrograde direction from plus to minus.
questions.title: Lecture 22 - Eukaryotic Cells

questions.q: Which describes actin?
options: A 42 kDa structural protein about 5 to 9 nm in diameter, whose filaments (F-actin) are polymers of monomers (G-actin), with polymerisation driven by ATP
A 25 nm hollow rod polymerised from tubulin using GTP
A 10 nm rope of twisted monomers providing tensile strength
A motor protein that walks along microtubules
A membrane protein that forms ion channels
questions.explanation: Actin is a highly abundant 42 kDa structural protein about 5 to 9 nm in diameter, found in all eukaryotic cells with a highly conserved primary structure. Filaments, F-actin, are polymers of G-actin monomers, and polymerisation is driven by ATP.
questions.title: Lecture 22 - Eukaryotic Cells

questions.q: What is the cell cortex?
options: The outermost layer of the plasma membrane
The region of highest actin density near the plasma membrane, determining shape, stiffness and movement of the cell surface
The dense region of microtubules around the centrosome
The layer of intermediate filaments lining the nucleus
The junction between the ER and the Golgi
questions.explanation: The actin cytoskeleton consists of bundles of actin filaments with associated motor proteins. The highest actin density is near the plasma membrane, called the cell cortex, which determines the shape, stiffness and movement of the cell surface.
questions.title: Lecture 22 - Eukaryotic Cells

questions.q: How do myosins generate movement?
options: By using energy from ATP hydrolysis to move and exert tension on actin filaments
By hydrolysing GTP to slide along microtubules
By contracting intermediate filaments
By pumping ions across the membrane
By polymerising and depolymerising tubulin
questions.explanation: Myosins are a large multigene family of actin-based molecular motors, with 13 classes in humans, that use energy from ATP hydrolysis to move and exert tension on actin filaments.
questions.title: Lecture 22 - Eukaryotic Cells

questions.q: Which myosin class is typically involved in muscle contraction?
options: Myosin-I
Myosin-II
Myosin-V
Kinesin
Dynein
questions.explanation: Myosin-I, a monomer, is mostly involved in membrane dynamics and vesicle trafficking. Myosin-II is typically involved in muscle, pulling on actin to cause contraction. Myosin-V is a dimeric cargo-carrying isoform and a highly processive motor.
questions.title: Lecture 22 - Eukaryotic Cells

questions.q: Myosins are also involved in which pathological process?
options: The rapid entry of certain microbial pathogens into eukaryotic host cells
The degradation of misfolded proteins
The accumulation of reactive oxygen species
The mutation of mitochondrial DNA
The formation of amyloid plaques
questions.explanation: Besides growth, tissue formation, metabolism, reproduction, communication, reshaping and movement of cells, myosins are also involved in the rapid entry of certain microbial pathogens into eukaryotic host cells.
questions.title: Lecture 22 - Eukaryotic Cells

questions.q: Which elements of the endomembrane system are physically contiguous?
options: The Golgi apparatus and lysosomes
The mitochondria and nucleolus
The nuclear membrane and the endoplasmic reticulum
The peroxisomes and vesicles
The lysosomes and peroxisomes
questions.explanation: The outer membrane of the nuclear envelope is continuous with the endoplasmic reticulum, so these two are physically contiguous. The Golgi is closely associated with the ER but connected by vesicle traffic rather than continuous membrane.
questions.title: Lecture 22 - Eukaryotic Cells

questions.q: Why is understanding the molecular and cell biology of eukaryotes important for pharmacy?
options: Because all drugs are made from eukaryotic cells
Because cell composition, metabolism, cell cycle and communication can all be origins of disease and potential therapeutic targets
Because eukaryotic cells cannot be studied in the laboratory
Because only eukaryotes are susceptible to antibiotics
Because eukaryotic cells have no membranes to cross
questions.explanation: Molecular biology allows understanding of cellular structure and function at the molecular level, essential for understanding the physiology and pathology of cells and drug mechanisms. Cell composition and biochemistry, metabolism, cell cycle and communication can all be origins of problems and potential therapeutic targets.
questions.title: Lecture 22 - Eukaryotic Cells

questions.q: Roughly 2 metres of DNA must fit into a nucleus about 0.001 mm across. Which sequence describes how this is achieved?
options: DNA wraps around histones to form nucleosomes, folding requires H1, then chromatin fibres of 30 nm form and supercoil further
DNA is cut into fragments and reassembled during division
DNA is dehydrated to reduce its volume
DNA is wound around microtubules in the nucleoplasm
DNA remains linear but is compressed by nuclear pressure
questions.explanation: DNA condenses around histone proteins to form nucleosomes, the first level of folding. The second level requires histone H1, then multiple levels of coiling and supercoiling produce 30 nm chromatin fibres and, at division, condensed chromosomes.
questions.title: Lecture 22 - Eukaryotic Cells

questions.q: In biological classification, which sequence runs from the broadest to the most specific level?
options: Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species
Species, Genus, Family, Order, Class, Phylum, Kingdom
Domain, Molecule, Atom, Cell, Tissue, Organ
Genus, Species, Family, Order, Class only
Phylum, Kingdom, Class, Order, Species
questions.explanation: The lecture illustrates the taxonomic hierarchy from Kingdom through Phylum, Class, Order, Family and Genus to Species, with the mnemonic Kings Play Chess On Finely Grained Sand.
questions.title: Lecture 22 - Eukaryotic Cells

questions.q: How is evolutionary distance between living things determined?
options: By nucleotide sequence comparisons
By body mass alone
By counting membrane-bound organelles
By membrane lipid content only
By the number of chromosomes only
questions.explanation: All living things are classified into three major domains, and evolutionary distance between them is based on nucleotide sequence comparisons.
questions.title: Lecture 22 - Eukaryotic Cells

questions.q: Which molecules can easily cross the plasma membrane without help from membrane proteins?
options: Relatively small, non-polar materials
Large polar proteins
Charged ions such as Na+ and K+
Glucose without a transporter
All macromolecules equally
questions.explanation: All eukaryotic and prokaryotic cells have a surrounding plasma membrane. Only relatively small, non-polar materials can easily move through; other molecules need help from membrane proteins.
questions.title: Lecture 22 - Eukaryotic Cells

questions.q: What represents the first level of DNA folding in the nucleus?
options: Nucleosomes, with DNA wrapped around histone proteins
The 30 nm chromatin fibre
Condensed metaphase chromosomes
The nuclear pore complex
The replication fork
questions.explanation: Nucleosomes are the first level of folding, with DNA wrapped around histone proteins. Further levels of coiling and supercoiling follow.
questions.title: Lecture 22 - Eukaryotic Cells

questions.q: How is the cell cycle defined?
options: The process by which a single mother cell gives rise to two identical daughter cells
The process by which a cell increases in size without dividing
The sequence of events leading to programmed cell death
The replication of DNA within the nucleus only
The differentiation of a stem cell into a specialised cell
questions.explanation: The cell cycle is the process by which a single mother cell gives rise to two identical daughter cells.
questions.title: The Cell Cycle

questions.q: In which phase of the cell cycle does DNA replication occur?
options: G1 phase
G2 phase
G2/M phase
M phase
S phase
questions.explanation: S phase is the synthesis phase, in which all DNA in the cell's genome is replicated while cell growth continues.
questions.title: The Cell Cycle

questions.q: What happens during G2 phase?
options: DNA is replicated
Chromosomes are partitioned into daughter cells
Cell growth continues and the cell checks for replication errors
The cell enters a quiescent state
The nuclear envelope disintegrates
questions.explanation: G2 is the second gap phase, in which cell growth continues and the cell checks for replication errors before entering mitosis.
questions.title: The Cell Cycle

questions.q: What controls entry into the cell cycle, and at which point?
options: The availability of growth factors, at the restriction point in late G1
The availability of nutrients, at the start of S phase
The level of p53, at the M phase checkpoint
The number of chromosomes, during G2
The concentration of cyclin B, at the end of mitosis
questions.explanation: The availability of growth factors controls the cell cycle at a point in late G1 called the restriction point.
questions.title: The Cell Cycle

questions.q: What happens to cells if growth factors are not available during G1?
options: They undergo apoptosis immediately
They enter a quiescent stage called G0
They proceed directly to S phase
They arrest in metaphase
They fuse with neighbouring cells
questions.explanation: If growth factors are not available during G1, cells enter a quiescent stage of the cycle called G0.
questions.title: The Cell Cycle

questions.q: What is replicative senescence?
options: The permanent entry into G0 once a cell's limited proliferation capacity is exhausted
The rapid degradation of cyclins at the end of mitosis
The arrest of cells at the G2 checkpoint following DNA damage
The fragmentation of DNA during apoptosis
The failure of chromosomes to align on the spindle
questions.explanation: Cells have a limited proliferation capacity and will eventually enter G0 permanently, a state referred to as replicative senescence.
questions.title: The Cell Cycle

questions.q: How many chromosomes do humans have?
options: 23 chromosomes in 23 pairs
46 chromosomes in 23 pairs
46 chromosomes in 46 pairs
22 chromosomes in 11 pairs
92 chromosomes in 46 pairs
questions.explanation: Humans have 23 pairs of chromosomes, for a total of 46 chromosomes. Each chromosome is made of protein and a single molecule of DNA wrapped tightly around spool-like histone proteins.
questions.title: The Cell Cycle

questions.q: Which sequence correctly describes the early stages of M phase?
options: Chromosomes condense, mitotic spindles form, the nuclear membrane disintegrates, spindles attach to kinetochores
The nuclear membrane disintegrates, chromosomes align at the equator, spindles form
Sister chromatids separate, then chromosomes condense and spindles form
Cytoplasm divides, then chromosomes condense and align
Spindles attach to kinetochores before chromosomes condense
questions.explanation: In the early stages of M phase, chromosomes condense, mitotic spindles form, the nuclear membrane disintegrates and spindles attach to the kinetochores.
questions.title: The Cell Cycle

questions.q: What happens after chromosomes align at the equator during mitosis?
options: The nuclear envelope reforms immediately
Sister chromatids separate and are pulled towards the spindle poles
The chromosomes condense further
DNA replication begins
The cell enters G0
questions.explanation: After chromosomes align at the equator, the sister chromatids separate and are pulled towards the spindle poles. The chromosomes then arrive at the poles, nuclear envelopes reform, and the cytoplasm divides.
questions.title: The Cell Cycle

questions.q: What are cyclin-dependent kinases (Cdks)?
options: Protein kinases whose activity rises and falls during the cell cycle, activated by cyclins
Structural proteins that form the mitotic spindle
Transcription factors that bind damaged DNA
Enzymes that replicate DNA during S phase
Inhibitors that prevent cell cycle progression
questions.explanation: Cdks are protein kinases whose activity rises and falls during the cell cycle. They produce cyclical changes in the phosphorylation of intracellular proteins that initiate or regulate the major events of the cell cycle, and are activated by cyclins.
questions.title: The Cell Cycle

questions.q: How many CDK family members are there in human cells?
questions.explanation: In human cells the CDK family consists of 20 different members that play key roles in regulation of the cell cycle and transcription.
questions.title: The Cell Cycle

questions.q: How do cyclin and Cdk levels differ across the cell cycle?
options: Cyclin levels are constant while Cdk levels rise and fall
Cyclins accumulate through interphase and are rapidly degraded towards the end of mitosis, while Cdk levels are constant
Both cyclins and Cdks are degraded at the end of each cycle
Both remain constant throughout the cycle
Cyclins are degraded during S phase and Cdks during M phase
questions.explanation: Cyclins were identified as proteins that accumulate throughout interphase and are rapidly degraded towards the end of mitosis, whereas Cdk levels remain constant. It is cyclin availability that controls Cdk activity.
questions.title: The Cell Cycle

questions.q: Which CDK-cyclin pairing drives the M phase transition?
options: CDK1 with cyclin B
CDK2 with cyclin E
CDK4 and CDK6 with cyclin D
CDK2 with cyclin A
CDK7 with cyclin H
questions.explanation: CDK1 with cyclin B drives the M phase transition. CDK2-cyclin A drives the S/G2 transition, CDK2-cyclin E the G1/S transition, CDK4 and CDK6 with cyclin D the G1/S transition, and CDK7-cyclin H acts in CAK and RNAPII transcription.
questions.title: The Cell Cycle

questions.q: Which CDK-cyclin complex phosphorylates the retinoblastoma gene product (Rb)?
options: CDK1 with cyclin B
CDK2 with cyclin A
CDK3 with cyclin C
CDK4 and CDK6 with cyclin D
CDK7 with cyclin H
questions.explanation: CDK4 and CDK6 with cyclin D drive the G1/S transition and phosphorylate the retinoblastoma gene product, Rb.
questions.title: The Cell Cycle

questions.q: What is a CKI, and which two families exist in animal cells?
options: A cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor; the INK4 family and the CIP/KIP family
A cyclin kinase initiator; the Ras and Raf families
A checkpoint kinase inhibitor; the p53 and p21 families
A cyclin kinase intermediate; the CDK4 and CDK6 families
A chromosome kinetochore inhibitor; the MAP and ERK families
questions.explanation: A cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor (CKI) interacts with a cyclin-CDK complex to inhibit activity, for example during G1 or in response to DNA damage. The two primary families are INK4 and CIP/KIP.
questions.title: The Cell Cycle

questions.q: How do the INK4 and CIP/KIP families of inhibitors differ in their action?
options: INK4 proteins bind and inhibit CDK4 and CDK6; CIP/KIP proteins prevent activation of CDK-cyclin heterodimers, disrupting both cyclin binding and kinase activity
INK4 proteins degrade cyclins; CIP/KIP proteins degrade CDKs
INK4 proteins act only in M phase; CIP/KIP only in S phase
INK4 proteins activate CDKs; CIP/KIP proteins inhibit them
Both act identically but in different tissues
questions.explanation: INK4 family proteins bind to and inhibit CDK4 and CDK6 by D-type cyclins. The CIP/KIP family prevents activation of CDK-cyclin heterodimers, disrupting both cyclin binding and kinase activity.
questions.title: The Cell Cycle

questions.q: The Cdk1/cyclin B complex is also known by which name?
options: PCNA
MPF, maturation promotion factor
MAPK
CAK
Rb
questions.explanation: The Cdk1/cyclin B complex catalyses multiple phosphorylation events, initiating several events required during mitosis. It is also called MPF, maturation promotion factor.
questions.title: The Cell Cycle

questions.q: Growth factors acting as mitogens induce the synthesis of D-type cyclins through which signalling pathway?
options: The p53/p21 pathway
The Ras/Raf/ERK pathway, known as the MAPK pathway
The apoptosis signalling pathway
The PIP2 second messenger pathway
The INK4/CIP-KIP pathway
questions.explanation: Growth factors regulate cell cycle progression through the G1 restriction point, acting as mitogens. They induce the synthesis of D-type cyclins via the Ras/Raf/ERK signalling pathway, the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway.
questions.title: The Cell Cycle

questions.q: What is the purpose of cell cycle checkpoints?
options: To ensure that complete genomes are transmitted to daughter cells
To speed up progression through the cycle
To trigger apoptosis in all dividing cells
To increase the number of chromosomes before division
To synthesise cyclins at the correct time
questions.explanation: Several checkpoints function to ensure that complete genomes are transmitted to daughter cells.
questions.title: The Cell Cycle

questions.q: What triggers arrest at the M phase checkpoint?
options: Damaged or unreplicated DNA
Absence of growth factors
Daughter chromosomes not properly aligned on the mitotic spindle
Excess cyclin B
Low levels of p53
questions.explanation: One major checkpoint arrests cells in G2 in response to damaged or unreplicated DNA, damaged DNA also causes arrest at a G1 checkpoint, and a checkpoint in M phase arrests mitosis if the daughter chromosomes are not properly aligned on the mitotic spindle.
questions.title: The Cell Cycle

questions.q: Which transcription factor mediates the G1 checkpoint?
options: Rb
PCNA
Cyclin D
questions.explanation: The G1 checkpoint is mediated by a transcription factor called p53. In response to DNA damage, levels of p53 increase.
questions.title: The Cell Cycle

questions.q: By what two mechanisms does p53 halt cell cycle progression?
options: It causes transcription of p21, a cdk inhibitor, and p21 also binds PCNA, blocking DNA replication machinery
It degrades all cyclins and destroys the mitotic spindle
It phosphorylates Rb and activates CDK4
It removes growth factors from the environment
It fragments the DNA directly
questions.explanation: p53 causes the transcription of p21, a cdk inhibitor, and cdk inhibition prevents cell cycle progression. p21 also binds PCNA, a component of the DNA replication machinery, preventing its activity.
questions.title: The Cell Cycle

questions.q: What does p53 do when DNA damage is irreparable?
options: It allows the cell to continue dividing
It initiates signalling pathways leading to programmed cell death, apoptosis
It reverses the damage by direct repair
It converts the cell into a stem cell
It permanently arrests the cell in S phase
questions.explanation: p53 stops cell division to allow DNA repair. Where DNA damage is irreparable, p53 initiates signalling pathways that lead to programmed cell death, or apoptosis.
questions.title: The Cell Cycle

questions.q: How does apoptosis differ from necrosis?
options: Apoptosis affects groups of cells and causes inflammation; necrosis affects individual cells

Apoptosis affects individual cells, the cell rounds and shrinks, DNA is systematically fragmented and contents are packed into apoptotic bodies and phagocytosed; necrosis affects groups of cells with swelling, lysis and inflammation
Apoptosis causes cell swelling and vacuolisation; necrosis causes shrinking
Both cause an inflammatory response equally
Apoptosis is caused by acute cell injury; necrosis is programmed
questions.explanation: Necrosis affects groups of cells following acute injury, with cell swelling, vacuolisation and lysis, causing an inflammatory response. Apoptosis affects individual cells: the cell rounds and shrinks, DNA is systematically fragmented, and contents are packed into apoptotic bodies phagocytosed by adjacent cells.
questions.title: The Cell Cycle

questions.q: In what proportion of human cancers is the p53 gene mutated?
options: Fewer than 10 per cent
About 25 per cent
More than 50 per cent, and in almost every type of human cancer
Exactly 100 per cent
Only in blood cancers
questions.explanation: p53 is a key tumour suppressor and loss of its function is frequently a prerequisite for cancer development. It is the most frequently mutated gene in human cancers, with mutations in more than 50 per cent of all human cancers and in almost every type.
questions.title: The Cell Cycle

questions.q: Why do pharmacists need to know about CDKs?
options: Because abnormal activation of CDKs results in uncontrolled cancer cell proliferation
Because CDKs determine drug absorption from the gut
Because CDKs control the shelf life of biologic medicines
Because CDKs are the target of all antibiotics
Because CDKs are only found in bacteria
questions.explanation: CDK expression is controlled by a complex regulatory network of genetic and epigenetic mechanisms, which is dysregulated during cancer progression. Abnormal activation of CDKs results in uncontrolled cancer cell proliferation.
questions.title: The Cell Cycle

questions.q: How do most cancer chemotherapeutic agents work at the level of the cell cycle?
options: By stopping cancer cell division through blocking DNA replication, and some by blocking mitosis, causing growth arrest by triggering checkpoints
By increasing the availability of growth factors
By restoring functional p53 to the cell
By preventing cells from entering G0
By accelerating progression through S phase
questions.explanation: Most chemotherapeutic agents stop cancer cell division by blocking DNA replication, and some by blocking mitosis. This causes growth arrest by triggering cell cycle checkpoints. Conventional cytotoxics therefore act at S or M phase.
questions.title: The Cell Cycle

questions.q: Why is understanding the cell cycle relevant to pharmacy practice?
options: Because diseases such as diabetes, cancer and Alzheimer's disease are caused by problems at the cell level
Because the cell cycle determines how quickly tablets dissolve
Because all medicines are manufactured in dividing cells
Because the cell cycle sets the half-life of every drug
Because only dividing cells can absorb drugs
questions.explanation: Diseases such as diabetes, cancer and Alzheimer's disease are all caused by problems at the cell level. Understanding how cells work in healthy and diseased states allows development of new and more effective treatments and vaccines.
questions.title: The Cell Cycle

questions.q: What is the role of the kinetochore during mitosis?
options: It is the site where mitotic spindles attach to the chromosome
It is the region where DNA replication begins
It is the protein that degrades cyclin B
It is the structure that divides the cytoplasm
It is the site of ribosome assembly
questions.explanation: Following chromosome condensation, mitotic spindle formation and nuclear membrane disintegration, the spindles attach to the kinetochores of the chromosomes.
questions.title: The Cell Cycle

questions.q: Which statement about the outcome of mitosis and cytokinesis is correct?
options: The cytoplasm divides, resulting in two genetically near-identical cells
The cytoplasm divides, giving two genetically distinct cells
Four daughter cells are produced from each division
The nuclear envelope does not reform after division
The daughter cells each contain half the parental DNA content
questions.explanation: After chromosomes arrive at the poles and nuclear envelopes reform, the cytoplasm divides, resulting in two genetically near-identical cells.
questions.title: The Cell Cycle

questions.q: In most cells most of the time, what does mitosis accomplish within the cell cycle?
options: Division of the nucleus, following interphase growth and DNA replication
Replication of DNA in the S phase only
Permanent entry into G0 senescence
Apoptosis of damaged cells
Fusion of two daughter cells into one
questions.explanation: Panel 18-1 shows the processes of mitosis as division of the nucleus, which in most cells occurs most of the time after growth phases in the cell cycle.
questions.title: The Cell Cycle

questions.q: Which chapter of Alberts Essential Cell Biology is recommended for guided reading on the cell cycle?
options: Chapter 18
Chapter 4
Chapter 7
Chapter 1
Chapter 50
questions.explanation: The guided reading recommends Alberts et al. (2013) Essential Cell Biology (4th ed.), Garland Science, Chapter 18, alongside animations on cell cycle phases, checkpoints and mitosis.
questions.title: The Cell Cycle

questions.q: What role do cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs) play in cell cycle progression?
options: They drive cell cycle progression and are important in diseases such as cancer
They degrade DNA at the replication fork
They assemble ribosomes during translation
They synthesise ATP during G0
They prevent all cell division permanently
questions.explanation: The example SAQ asks students to describe the role of CDKs in cell cycle progression and explain in which diseases these may be important, such as cancer where cell cycle control is disrupted.
questions.title: The Cell Cycle

questions.q: What are the three essential parts of a cell signalling system?
options: A signal molecule, a target cell and a response
A receptor, a kinase and a phosphatase
A hormone, a nerve and a muscle
A ligand, a channel and an ion
A gene, an mRNA and a protein
questions.explanation: The essential parts of a signalling system are a signal molecule, a target cell and a response. A good signal must be able to reach its target readily, be made or altered quickly, and be controllable.
questions.title: Lecture 24 - Cell Signalling

questions.q: Why do cells need to signal to each other?
options: Because each cell contains a complete copy of the genome
Because cell specialisation limits the activities of any one cell, so co-ordination of several cells achieves a single end result benefiting the whole organism
Because cells cannot survive in isolation for more than a few minutes
Because signalling is required for DNA replication
Because signalling prevents mutations from accumulating
questions.explanation: Cell specialisation means each cell has a limited array of activities, so co-ordination of several cells is needed to achieve a single end result that benefits the whole organism.
questions.title: Lecture 24 - Cell Signalling

questions.q: Which features characterise endocrine signalling?
options: Messages travel via the circulation, are long range, can affect multiple targets at once, and are potent because of dilution
Messages act only on the cell that released them
Messages travel only between directly touching cells
Messages travel along axons to a limited number of target sites
Messages diffuse only a few cell diameters
questions.explanation: Endocrine messages travel via the circulation, are long range, can affect multiple targets at the same time, and must be potent because of dilution. Examples include adrenaline, cortisol, oestradiol, glucagon, insulin, testosterone and thyroid hormone.
questions.title: Lecture 24 - Cell Signalling

questions.q: Which two chemical classes of endocrine hormone are described, and how do they differ?
options: Peptides, proteins and amino acid derivatives which are usually hydrophilic; and steroids which are usually lipophilic
Peptides which are lipophilic; and steroids which are hydrophilic
Carbohydrates which are hydrophilic; and lipids which are lipophilic
Nucleotides and fatty acids, both hydrophilic
All hormones are hydrophilic
questions.explanation: Endocrine hormone types are peptides, proteins and amino acid derivatives, usually hydrophilic, and steroids, usually lipophilic. They are often self-regulating via feedback loops, as with insulin and glucose.
questions.title: Lecture 24 - Cell Signalling

questions.q: What is autocrine signalling?
options: A signal travelling through the circulation to distant cells
A local mediator released by a cell that affects the cell itself
A signal passed only by direct cell-to-cell contact
A signal released at a synapse onto a target cell
A signal that moves along the cytoskeleton within one cell
questions.explanation: Autocrine signalling is where a local mediator released by a cell affects the cell itself. It is relevant to the immune system, signal reinforcement and cancer.
questions.title: Lecture 24 - Cell Signalling

questions.q: What is paracrine signalling?
options: Signals on the surface of a cell affect nearby cells through direct contact
Signals released by one cell affect nearby cells
Signals released by one cell travel through the blood and affect far away cells
Signals within a cell travel along the cytoskeleton to affect another part of the cell
Signals travel along a nerve axon to a distant target
questions.explanation: Paracrine signalling is where signals released by one cell act locally on nearby cells, for example in blood clotting. Examples of local mediators include EGF, PDGF, NGF, TGF-beta, histamine and nitric oxide.
questions.title: Lecture 24 - Cell Signalling

questions.q: Which features distinguish neuronal signalling?
options: Messages travel very fast, can be very long range, and a limited number of target sites localises the effect
Messages travel slowly but reach every cell in the body
Messages act only on the releasing cell
Messages require direct membrane contact between cells
Messages are carried in the bloodstream to multiple targets
questions.explanation: In neuronal signalling, messages travel very fast and can be very long range, but the limited number of target sites localises the effect. Examples of neurotransmitters are acetylcholine, GABA and dopamine.
questions.title: Lecture 24 - Cell Signalling

questions.q: What is distinctive about contact-dependent (juxtacrine) signalling?
options: Direct contact makes the signal extremely targeted, and unlike other signalling it can be bidirectional
It is the slowest form of signalling and always unidirectional
It requires the signal to travel through the bloodstream first
It only occurs between cells of different tissue types
It uses only steroid hormones
questions.explanation: Contact-dependent or juxtacrine signalling uses direct contact, which makes the signal extremely targeted, and unlike other forms of signalling it can be bidirectional. Examples include PD-L1, CTLA4, Delta, ions and cadherins.
questions.title: Lecture 24 - Cell Signalling

questions.q: Gap junctions allow which type of exchange between cells?
options: Exchange of whole organelles
Exchange of small molecules such as ions, water and cAMP
Exchange of DNA between nuclei
Exchange of membrane lipids only
Exchange of complete proteins such as antibodies
questions.explanation: Gap junctions are channels between cells allowing exchange of small molecules such as ions, water and cAMP. Cardiac tissue cells connected this way are electrically continuous.
questions.title: Lecture 24 - Cell Signalling

questions.q: How can a small hydrophobic hormone such as cortisol act on a cell?
options: By binding a ligand-gated ion channel at the surface
By directly activating a transcriptional regulator inside the cell
By triggering adenylyl cyclase at the membrane
Only via a G-protein coupled receptor
By passing through gap junctions to neighbouring cells
questions.explanation: Signal molecules may bind cell-surface receptors, or intracellular enzymes or receptors. Small hydrophobic hormones such as cortisol can cross the membrane and directly activate a transcriptional regulator.
questions.title: Lecture 24 - Cell Signalling

questions.q: Why do some extracellular signals act rapidly and others slowly?
options: Fast responses usually involve altering protein function, whereas slow processes usually involve synthesis of new proteins by transcription and translation
Fast responses involve steroid hormones and slow ones involve peptides
Fast responses occur only in nerve cells
Slow responses involve altering protein function and fast ones new protein synthesis
The speed depends only on the distance the signal travels
questions.explanation: Fast responses usually involve altering the function of proteins already present, while slow processes usually involve the synthesis of new proteins by transcription and translation.
questions.title: Lecture 24 - Cell Signalling

questions.q: What can intracellular signalling proteins do to an incoming signal?
options: Relay, amplify, integrate and distribute it
Only relay it unchanged to the nucleus
Only terminate it
Convert it into a hormone for secretion
Store it for later use
questions.explanation: Via intracellular signalling proteins, incoming signals can be relayed, amplified, integrated and distributed, forming an intricate system.
questions.title: Lecture 24 - Cell Signalling

questions.q: What are the three main types of cell-surface receptor?
options: Ion channel receptors, GPCRs and enzyme-linked receptors
Nuclear receptors, cytoplasmic receptors and membrane receptors
Agonist, antagonist and partial agonist receptors
Alpha, beta and gamma receptors
Kinases, phosphatases and GTPases
questions.explanation: Cell-surface or transmembrane receptors fall into three main types: ion channel receptors, G-protein coupled receptors and enzyme-linked receptors.
questions.title: Lecture 24 - Cell Signalling

questions.q: What are the three general domains of a cell-surface receptor?
options: External ligand-binding, transmembrane hydrophobic, and internal domain that triggers second messengers
Nuclear, cytoplasmic and membrane-bound
Catalytic, regulatory and structural
Alpha helix, beta sheet and random coil
Agonist site, antagonist site and allosteric site
questions.explanation: Cell-surface receptors have three general domains: an external ligand-binding domain, a transmembrane hydrophobic domain, and an internal domain that triggers second messengers.
questions.title: Lecture 24 - Cell Signalling

questions.q: What do ligand-gated ion channels do, and how fast do they act?
options: Convert chemical signals to electrical signals, giving rapid depolarisation or hyperpolarisation in milliseconds
Convert electrical signals to chemical signals over minutes
Trigger gene transcription over hours
Generate second messengers over seconds
Activate Ras and the MAPK pathway
questions.explanation: Ion-channel coupled receptors, also known as ligand-gated ion channels, convert chemical signals to electrical signals, producing rapid depolarisation or hyperpolarisation on a millisecond timescale.
questions.title: Lecture 24 - Cell Signalling

questions.q: Which is an example of a ligand-gated ion channel receptor?
options: Beta-adrenoceptor
Epidermal growth factor receptor
Nicotinic acetylcholine receptor
Muscarinic acetylcholine receptor
Oestrogen receptor
questions.explanation: Examples of ligand-gated ion channels include the 5-HT, nicotinic acetylcholine, GABA-A, glycine, AMPA and NMDA receptors. The muscarinic acetylcholine receptor is a GPCR and EGFR an enzyme-linked receptor.
questions.title: Lecture 24 - Cell Signalling

questions.q: The nicotinic acetylcholine receptor at skeletal neuromuscular junctions is permeable to which ions, and what is its antagonist?
options: Cl- only; antagonist atropine
Na+ and K+ (and Ca2+); antagonist tubocurarine
K+ only; antagonist propranolol
Ca2+ only; antagonist cetuximab
Na+ only; antagonist salbutamol
questions.explanation: Nicotinic acetylcholine receptors at skeletal neuromuscular junctions are permeable to Na+ and K+ (and Ca2+). The agonist is acetylcholine, requiring two molecules, and the antagonist is tubocurarine.
questions.title: Lecture 24 - Cell Signalling

questions.q: Why are GPCRs also known as 7-TM receptors, and what happens when a signalling molecule binds?
options: Because of their seven transmembrane structure; binding causes a conformational change that stimulates the G-protein to exchange GDP for GTP, becoming active
Because they have seven ligand-binding sites; binding causes them to dimerise
Because they need seven molecules of agonist; binding opens a channel
Because they have seven subunits; binding triggers phosphorylation directly
Because they span seven membranes; binding releases calcium
questions.explanation: GPCRs are called 7-TM receptors because of their seven transmembrane structure. Binding of a signalling molecule causes a conformational change, and the G-protein is stimulated to exchange GDP for GTP, becoming active.
questions.title: Lecture 24 - Cell Signalling

questions.q: Beta-adrenoceptors in bronchial smooth muscle trigger which enzyme, and what are their agonist and antagonist?
options: Phospholipase C; agonist atropine, antagonist acetylcholine
Adenylate cyclase; agonist salbutamol, antagonist propranolol
Tyrosine kinase; agonist EGF, antagonist cetuximab
Protein kinase A; agonist propranolol, antagonist salbutamol
Guanylate cyclase; agonist nitric oxide, antagonist atropine
questions.explanation: Beta-adrenoceptors, for example in bronchial smooth muscle, are GPCRs that trigger adenylate cyclase. Their agonist is salbutamol and their antagonist propranolol.
questions.title: Lecture 24 - Cell Signalling

questions.q: Muscarinic acetylcholine receptors in the heart are permeable to which ion, and what is their antagonist?
options: Na+; antagonist tubocurarine
Cl-; antagonist propranolol
K+; antagonist atropine
Ca2+; antagonist salbutamol
K+; antagonist cetuximab
questions.explanation: Muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, for example in the heart, are GPCRs coupled to K+ permeability. The agonist is acetylcholine and the antagonist atropine.
questions.title: Lecture 24 - Cell Signalling

questions.q: How are enzyme-linked receptors activated?
options: They dimerise in response to signal molecule binding, activating their catalytic domain
They open a pore to allow ion flow
They exchange GDP for GTP on a coupled G-protein
They are cleaved by a protease at the membrane
They move into the nucleus to bind DNA
questions.explanation: Enzyme-linked receptors dimerise in response to signal molecule binding, thus activating their catalytic domain. The dimers may be homodimers or heterodimers.
questions.title: Lecture 24 - Cell Signalling

questions.q: What do receptor tyrosine kinases do once activated?
options: They dimerise to activate their kinase domain, which phosphorylates a range of further intracellular signalling proteins
They generate cAMP from ATP
They open a chloride channel
They bind directly to DNA to alter transcription
They hydrolyse GTP to GDP
questions.explanation: Receptor tyrosine kinases are the largest group of enzyme-coupled receptors. They dimerise to activate their kinase domain, which in turn phosphorylates a range of further intracellular signalling proteins.
questions.title: Lecture 24 - Cell Signalling

questions.q: The epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) has which agonist and antagonist?
options: Agonist acetylcholine, antagonist atropine
Agonist EGF, antagonist cetuximab
Agonist salbutamol, antagonist propranolol
Agonist 17-beta-oestradiol, antagonist raloxifene
Agonist EGF, antagonist tubocurarine
questions.explanation: EGFR is a tyrosine kinase receptor that activates transcription for cell division. Its agonist is EGF and its antagonist is cetuximab.
questions.title: Lecture 24 - Cell Signalling

questions.q: How do the response timescales of the three receptor types compare?
options: Ligand-gated channels act in milliseconds, GPCRs in seconds, and enzyme-linked receptors over minutes to hours
All three act within milliseconds
Enzyme-linked receptors are fastest and ligand-gated channels slowest
GPCRs act in milliseconds and ligand-gated channels over hours
All three act over minutes to hours
questions.explanation: Ligand-gated ion channels give rapid depolarisation or hyperpolarisation in milliseconds; GPCRs produce ion changes or second messengers and cellular processes over seconds; enzyme-linked receptors activate signal pathways and gene transcription over minutes to hours.
questions.title: Lecture 24 - Cell Signalling

questions.q: How is cyclic AMP formed and removed?
options: Formed by cyclisation of ATP by adenylyl cyclase, and hydrolysed by specific enzymes acting as an off switch
Formed by phosphorylation of AMP by protein kinase A, and removed by GTPases
Formed by cleavage of phosphatidylinositol, and removed by phospholipase C
Formed by hydrolysis of GTP, and removed by adenylyl cyclase
Formed in the nucleus and exported to the cytoplasm
questions.explanation: cAMP, the archetypal second messenger, is formed by cyclisation of ATP by adenylyl cyclase (also called adenylate or adenyl cyclase) and is hydrolysed by specific enzymes which act as the off switch.
questions.title: Lecture 24 - Cell Signalling

questions.q: How is the cAMP signal mediated?
options: By protein kinase A, which phosphorylates many targets
By phospholipase C, which cleaves membrane lipids
By Ras, which activates the MAPK pathway
By calmodulin binding cAMP directly
By protein kinase C acting on DAG
questions.explanation: The cAMP signal is mediated by PKA, cAMP-dependent protein kinase A, which phosphorylates many downstream targets.
questions.title: Lecture 24 - Cell Signalling

questions.q: Which amino acid side chains are phosphorylated in regulatory phosphorylation, and why does it change protein behaviour?
options: Serine, threonine or tyrosine; each phosphate carries two negative charges which can cause a major conformational change
Lysine, arginine or histidine; the added positive charge alters folding
Glycine, alanine or valine; the added bulk blocks the active site
Cysteine only; disulphide bonds are broken
Aspartate or glutamate; charge is neutralised
questions.explanation: Phosphorylation attaches a phosphate group to a serine, threonine or tyrosine side chain. Each phosphate carries two negative charges which can cause a major conformational change, acting as either an ON or an OFF switch. Kinases add phosphates and phosphatases reverse this.
questions.title: Lecture 24 - Cell Signalling

questions.q: How do GTPase switches work?
options: Inherent GTPase activity hydrolyses GTP to GDP, switching the protein off, modulated by GEFs and GAPs
GDP binding activates the protein and GTP binding inactivates it
They require ATP hydrolysis rather than GTP
They are switched on permanently and cannot be regulated
They are switched by phosphorylation of tyrosine residues
questions.explanation: Small G-proteins are regulated by guanine nucleotide binding. Inherent GTPase activity hydrolyses GTP to GDP, switching them from on to off. They can be modulated by guanine-nucleotide exchange factors (GEFs) and GTPase-activating proteins (GAPs).
questions.title: Lecture 24 - Cell Signalling

questions.q: Which small GTP-binding protein is activated by most RTKs and is mutated in many human cancers?
options: Rb
Ras
Myc
NF-kappa-B
questions.explanation: Most receptor tyrosine kinases activate Ras, a monomeric small GTP-binding protein. Ras is mutated in many human cancers.
questions.title: Lecture 24 - Cell Signalling

questions.q: The MAPK pathway is described as which kind of mechanism, and what are its three tiers?
options: A phosphorylation cascade, comprising Rafs, MEKs and ERKs
A GTPase cycle, comprising GEFs, GAPs and Ras
A second messenger cascade, comprising cAMP, PKA and calmodulin
An ion flux cascade, comprising Na+, K+ and Ca2+
A transcriptional cascade, comprising p53, p21 and Rb
