questions.explanation: Ras feeds into many intracellular signalling pathways, notably the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway, which is a phosphorylation cascade running through the Rafs, MEKs and ERKs, eventually altering target protein activity and gene expression.
questions.title: Lecture 24 - Cell Signalling

questions.q: What second messengers are produced when phosphatidylinositol is cleaved, and what does IP3 do?
options: cAMP and AMP; cAMP activates PKA
DAG and IP3; IP3 acts on ligand-gated ion channels on the ER to trigger calcium release
GTP and GDP; GTP activates Ras
DAG and cAMP; cAMP opens calcium channels
IP3 and cGMP; cGMP triggers calcium release
questions.explanation: The membrane lipid phosphatidylinositol is cleaved in response to an external signal, releasing the second messengers diacylglycerol (DAG) and inositol trisphosphate (IP3). Ligand-gated ion channels on the ER respond to IP3 and trigger calcium release.
questions.title: Lecture 24 - Cell Signalling

questions.q: The oestrogen receptor in breast tissue has which agonist and antagonist?
options: Agonist 17-beta-oestradiol, antagonist raloxifene in certain tissues
Agonist raloxifene, antagonist 17-beta-oestradiol
Agonist cortisol, antagonist cetuximab
Agonist EGF, antagonist tamoxifen
Agonist acetylcholine, antagonist atropine
questions.explanation: The oestrogen receptor is a nuclear receptor acting in breast tissue on growth, proliferation and maintenance. Its agonist is 17-beta-oestradiol and raloxifene acts as an antagonist, though notably only in certain tissues.
questions.title: Lecture 24 - Cell Signalling

questions.q: How do transcription factors exert their effect?
options: They bind DNA upstream from a gene and act either as activators promoting RNA polymerase activity or as repressors blocking it
They bind directly to mRNA and prevent translation
They phosphorylate RNA polymerase to switch it off permanently
They cleave DNA at the promoter site
They transport proteins out of the nucleus
questions.explanation: Transcription factors bind to DNA upstream from a gene, sometimes at a distance, and can act either as activators by promoting RNA polymerase activity, or as repressors by blocking RNA polymerase activity.
questions.title: Lecture 24 - Cell Signalling

questions.q: Which transcription factor is described as constantly active unless it is held in a complex, and is important in inflammation and cancer?
options: Myc
E2F
NF-kappa-B
Rb
questions.explanation: NF-kappa-B is a constantly active transcription factor unless it is in a complex, and is important in inflammation and cancer. Other examples of transcription factors in signalling are p53 in DNA damage sensing and steroid hormone receptors.
questions.title: Lecture 24 - Cell Signalling

questions.q: What happens once a cell passes the restriction point in G1?
options: The cell is irreversibly committed to dividing, even if the growth factor signal is removed
The cell can still return to G0 if growth factors are withdrawn
The cell immediately enters mitosis
The cell begins apoptosis
The cell requires a second growth factor signal to continue
questions.explanation: Cell signalling by growth factors determines whether a cell enters the division cycle. Without growth factors during G1, cells enter quiescence (G0). Once past the restriction point the cell is irreversibly committed to dividing, even if the growth factor signal is removed.
questions.title: Lecture 24 - Cell Signalling

questions.q: How do growth factors trigger cell division through the MAPK pathway?
options: An RTK interacts with the growth factor, the MAP kinase phosphorylation cascade leads to expression of transcription factors such as Myc, and Myc causes transcription activating the G1-CDK complex
The growth factor enters the nucleus directly and binds DNA
The growth factor activates p53, which drives the cell into S phase
The growth factor opens calcium channels which trigger mitosis
The growth factor inhibits Ras, releasing the cell cycle brake
questions.explanation: An RTK interacts with the growth factor and the MAP kinase phosphorylation cascade leads to expression of transcription factors such as Myc. Myc then causes transcription that activates the G1-CDK complex.
questions.title: Lecture 24 - Cell Signalling

questions.q: How does the G1-CDK complex allow the cell cycle to continue via Rb?
options: Rb normally binds and inactivates the E2F transcription factor; phosphorylation of Rb frees E2F, which acts on many genes leading to cell cycle entry and DNA synthesis
Rb normally activates E2F; phosphorylation of Rb inhibits E2F and stops division
Rb is degraded by the CDK complex and E2F is synthesised anew
Rb phosphorylates E2F directly to switch it on
Rb binds DNA and is released by calcium influx
questions.explanation: The retinoblastoma protein Rb is an important tumour suppressor that usually binds to and inactivates the E2F transcription factor. When the cell is ready to divide, phosphorylation of Rb frees E2F, which then acts on many genes leading to cell cycle entry and DNA synthesis.
questions.title: Lecture 24 - Cell Signalling

questions.q: According to the key points, which pathway is described as one of the most important in cancer?
options: The cAMP/PKA pathway
The MAPK pathway
The IP3/DAG pathway
The nuclear receptor pathway
The gap junction pathway
questions.explanation: Many complex signalling pathways are important in cancer, mediating cell survival, division, differentiation and cell death, and the MAPK pathway is described as one of the most important.
questions.title: Lecture 24 - Cell Signalling

questions.q: Many extracellular signalling pathways disturbed in cancer are described as:
options: Hallmarks of cancer
Only gap junction defects
Only lipid digestion pathways
Only Gram stain errors
Only tablet disintegration failures
questions.explanation: Animal cells depend on multiple extracellular signals, and many of these pathways are highly disturbed in human cancers as part of the hallmarks of cancer.
questions.title: Lecture 24 - Cell Signalling

questions.q: Extracellular signals acting via cell-surface receptors can:
options: Alter protein behaviour or cause protein synthesis inside the cell
Only change cell size without any intracellular effect
Never cross the plasma membrane
Only destroy DNA immediately
Only function in prokaryotes
questions.explanation: Many extracellular signals act via cell-surface receptors to change cell behaviour; the signal is transmitted to the interior where it can alter protein behaviour or cause protein synthesis.
questions.title: Lecture 24 - Cell Signalling

questions.q: The three key components of signalling pathways are:
options: Cell-surface receptors, intracellular signalling molecules and effector/transcriptional regulators
Only DNA polymerase
Only the Golgi apparatus
Only peptidoglycan and LPS
Only fatty acid melting points
questions.explanation: Key components listed are cell-surface receptors, intracellular signalling molecules, and effector proteins or transcriptional regulators.
questions.title: Lecture 24 - Cell Signalling

questions.q: Which is an example of a G-protein coupled receptor ligand?
options: Dopamine
Epidermal growth factor
Insulin at the tyrosine kinase receptor
Toll-like receptor ligand only
DNA directly
questions.explanation: GPCR examples include bradykinin, GABA B, opioids, dopamine, serotonin, glutamate and acetylcholine.
questions.title: Lecture 24 - Cell Signalling

questions.q: Which is an example of an enzyme-linked receptor ligand?
options: Epidermal growth factor
Opioids at GPCRs
GABA B
Bradykinin at GPCRs
Serotonin at GPCRs
questions.explanation: Enzyme-linked receptor examples include epidermal growth factor, glial cell-derived neurotrophic factor, natriuretic peptide, tyrosine kinase receptors and Toll-like receptors.
questions.title: Lecture 24 - Cell Signalling

questions.q: Intracellular signalling pathways commonly include which second messengers or molecules?
options: cAMP, IP3/DAG and phosphorylation cascades
Only peptidoglycan monomers
Only fatty acid carboxylates
Only tablet binders
Only crystal violet dye
questions.explanation: After cell-surface receptors, intracellular signalling involves molecules such as cAMP/PKA pathways and PLC-generated IP3/DAG, alongside phosphorylation cascades.
questions.title: Lecture 24 - Cell Signalling

questions.q: Phosphorylation is important in signalling because:
options: It is the most commonly used molecular switch in intracellular proteins
It only occurs in the nucleus during mitosis
It permanently destroys all enzymes
It prevents all GTP binding
It replaces transcription entirely
questions.explanation: Many intracellular signalling proteins act as molecular switches, and phosphorylation is the most commonly used switch, occurring directly or indirectly.
questions.title: Lecture 24 - Cell Signalling

questions.q: GTP versus GDP binding affects signalling proteins by:
options: Changing protein conformation, acting as a molecular switch
Preventing all enzyme activity permanently
Converting DNA to RNA directly
Dissolving the cell membrane
Blocking all receptor dimerisation
questions.explanation: The GDP vs GTP slide shows how GTP versus GDP binding alters the conformation of a CKI protein; GTP and GDP are guanosine tri- and di-phosphate forms of the guanine base.
questions.title: Lecture 24 - Cell Signalling

questions.q: Effector proteins in signalling pathways may include:
options: Transcription factors that regulate gene expression
Only bacterial flagella
Only tablet disintegrants
Only LPS lipid A
Only contact angle measurements
questions.explanation: Key components include effector proteins and transcriptional regulators as the third stage after receptors and intracellular signalling molecules.
questions.title: Lecture 24 - Cell Signalling

questions.q: Transcription factors alter gene expression by:
options: Binding DNA and regulating the rate of transcription to RNA
Translating proteins without RNA
Destroying all receptors at the cell surface
Synthesising peptidoglycan
Blocking all phosphorylation permanently
questions.explanation: Gene expression proceeds from DNA transcription to RNA to protein; transcription factors (transcriptional regulators) alter the rate of transcription.
questions.title: Lecture 24 - Cell Signalling

questions.q: Transcription factors exert their effect by:
options: Binding DNA upstream of genes to promote or repress RNA polymerase activity
Catalysing β-lactam ring opening
Forming bacterial capsules
Measuring dissolution rate directly
Determining Gram stain colour
questions.explanation: The example SAQ asks students to describe transcription factors in cell signalling, including binding DNA and acting as activators or repressors of RNA polymerase to control gene expression.
questions.title: Lecture 24 - Cell Signalling

questions.q: How is a drug defined in this lecture?
options: A chemical substance of known structure that has a biological effect when administered to a living organism
Any substance that cures disease
A protein produced by a living cell
Any compound that binds a receptor, whether or not it has an effect
A formulated product containing an active ingredient and excipients
questions.explanation: A drug is a chemical substance of known structure that has a biological effect when administered to a living organism.
questions.title: Lecture 25 - Drug-Receptor Interactions 1

questions.q: What are the three linked areas of pharmacology?
options: Pharmacodynamics, pharmacokinetics and toxicology
Pharmaceutics, pharmacognosy and pharmacology
Absorption, distribution and excretion
Affinity, efficacy and potency
Agonism, antagonism and inverse agonism
questions.explanation: Pharmacology is the study of the effects of drugs on living systems and has three linked areas: pharmacodynamics, the mechanism of the drug and its effect on the body; pharmacokinetics, the effect of the body on the drug; and toxicology, the harmful effects of drugs.
questions.title: Lecture 25 - Drug-Receptor Interactions 1

questions.q: Which definition is correct?
options: Affinity is how small a concentration of drug produces a given effect
Efficacy is the selectiveness with which a drug binds its target
Potency is how small a concentration of drug is required to produce a given effect
Specificity is the ability of a drug to bind its target
Potency is the ability of a drug to produce an effect on its target
questions.explanation: Specificity is the selectiveness with which a drug binds its target, affinity the ability of a drug to bind its target, efficacy the ability or strength of a drug to produce an effect on its target, and potency how small a concentration is required to produce a given effect.
questions.title: Lecture 25 - Drug-Receptor Interactions 1

questions.q: What is a drug target?
options: A molecule in the body, usually a protein, intrinsically associated with a particular disease
The organ in which the drug accumulates
The site at which the drug is metabolised
The route by which the drug is administered
The plasma protein to which the drug binds
questions.explanation: A target is a molecule in the body, usually a protein, that is intrinsically associated with a particular disease. Such proteins can be receptors, enzymes, ion channels, transporters or signalling molecules.
questions.title: Lecture 25 - Drug-Receptor Interactions 1

questions.q: Which of these is NOT listed as a type of drug target protein?
options: Receptors
Enzymes
Ion channels
Transporters
Ribosomal RNA
questions.explanation: The protein targets listed are receptors, enzymes, ion channels, transporters and signalling molecules.
questions.title: Lecture 25 - Drug-Receptor Interactions 1

questions.q: Which receptor type produces its effect over minutes to hours via gene transcription?
options: Ligand-gated ion channels
G protein coupled receptors
Enzyme-linked receptors
Voltage-gated ion channels
Transporters
questions.explanation: Ligand-gated ion channels give rapid depolarisation or hyperpolarisation within milliseconds, GPCRs produce ion changes or second messengers and cellular processes within seconds, and enzyme-linked receptors activate signal pathways leading to gene transcription over minutes to hours.
questions.title: Lecture 25 - Drug-Receptor Interactions 1

questions.q: Which of these is a recognised class of receptor agonist?
options: Competitive agonist
Non-competitive agonist
Inverse agonist
Allosteric agonist
Reversible agonist
questions.explanation: The classes of agonist listed are endogenous agonist, super agonist, full agonist, partial agonist, inverse agonist and irreversible agonist. Competitive and non-competitive describe antagonists.
questions.title: Lecture 25 - Drug-Receptor Interactions 1

questions.q: Histamine acting on H1 receptors in smooth muscle and H2 receptors in stomach parietal cells produces different effects. What does this illustrate?
options: That different receptor subtypes can respond to the same agonist with different effects
That histamine is a partial agonist at both receptors
That receptor subtypes always produce the same effect
That H1 and H2 receptors bind different endogenous ligands
That histamine has no efficacy at H2 receptors
questions.explanation: Different receptors for the same agonist can produce different effects. Histamine on H1 receptors in smooth muscle causes contraction, while on H2 receptors in stomach parietal cells it causes acid secretion.
questions.title: Lecture 25 - Drug-Receptor Interactions 1

questions.q: According to lock and key theory, what determines the size of the response?
options: The number of receptors ligated, with maximal response achieved once all receptors are occupied
The rate at which the drug is metabolised
The concentration of the endogenous agonist alone
The affinity of the drug regardless of receptor occupancy
The number of receptors expressed, independent of binding
questions.explanation: Ligand-receptor binding is a dynamic equilibrium. The more receptors ligated, the bigger the response, with the maximal response achieved once all receptors are occupied.
questions.title: Lecture 25 - Drug-Receptor Interactions 1

questions.q: In the binding equilibrium D + R giving DR, what are the units of the dissociation constant Kd?
options: M (molar)
Dimensionless
mol/s
questions.explanation: The forward rate constant alpha has units M^-1 s^-1 and the backward rate constant beta has units s^-1. Kd is defined as beta divided by alpha, so it has units of M.
questions.title: Lecture 25 - Drug-Receptor Interactions 1

questions.q: Which equation gives the fraction of receptors occupied?
options: Kd/([D] + Kd)
[D] x Kd
Kd/[D]
questions.explanation: Rearranging the equilibrium expression gives [DR]/[Rt] = [D]/(Kd + [D]), which is the fraction of receptors occupied.
questions.title: Lecture 25 - Drug-Receptor Interactions 1

questions.q: Morphine has a Kd of 1.7 microM at the mu opioid receptor. What percentage of receptors is occupied at 1 microM?
options: 6 per cent
15 per cent
37 per cent
64 per cent
85 per cent
questions.explanation: Fraction occupied = [D]/(Kd + [D]) = 1/(1.7 + 1) = 0.37, that is 37 per cent. At 0.1 microM it is 6 per cent, at 0.3 microM 15 per cent, at 3 microM 64 per cent and at 10 microM 85 per cent.
questions.title: Lecture 25 - Drug-Receptor Interactions 1

questions.q: Morphine has a Kd of 1.7 microM. Roughly what percentage of receptors is occupied at 10 microM?
options: 37 per cent
50 per cent
64 per cent
85 per cent
100 per cent
questions.explanation: Fraction occupied = 10/(1.7 + 10) = 0.855, that is about 85 per cent. Even at nearly six times the Kd, occupancy does not reach 100 per cent, illustrating the hyperbolic nature of the binding curve.
questions.title: Lecture 25 - Drug-Receptor Interactions 1

questions.q: What does Kd equal, in terms of receptor occupancy?
options: The drug concentration at which half of all receptors are occupied
The drug concentration at which all receptors are occupied
The drug concentration at which no receptors are occupied
The number of receptors present in the tissue
The rate at which the drug dissociates from the receptor
questions.explanation: Setting the occupancy fraction to one half gives Kd = [D]. Kd is therefore the drug concentration at which half of all receptors are occupied.
questions.title: Lecture 25 - Drug-Receptor Interactions 1

questions.q: Drug A has a Kd of 0.1 microM and drug B a Kd of 10 microM at the same receptor. What can you conclude?
options: Drug A has the higher affinity because the smaller the Kd, the more tightly bound the ligand
Drug B has the higher affinity because the larger the Kd, the tighter the binding
Both have equal affinity but drug A has greater efficacy
Drug B is a partial agonist
Nothing can be concluded without knowing Emax
questions.explanation: Kd is commonly used to describe the affinity between a ligand and its receptor. The smaller the Kd, the more tightly bound the ligand and therefore the higher the affinity. A high Kd indicates more drug is required to occupy 50 per cent of the receptors.
questions.title: Lecture 25 - Drug-Receptor Interactions 1

questions.q: What does Clark's occupancy theory assume?
options: That the more receptors ligated the larger the response, and that maximal response is achieved once all receptors are occupied, so E/Emax equals the fraction of receptors occupied
That only 50 per cent of receptors need to be occupied for a maximal response
That efficacy and affinity are the same property
That the response is independent of receptor occupancy
That partial agonists occupy fewer receptors than full agonists
questions.explanation: Clark's occupancy theory holds that the more receptors ligated by a drug, the larger the response, and assuming maximal response is achieved when all receptors are occupied, the fraction of receptors occupied equals E/Emax.
questions.title: Lecture 25 - Drug-Receptor Interactions 1

questions.q: Besides half-maximal occupancy, what else does Kd equal?
options: The drug concentration at which the drug attains its half-maximal effect, the EC50
The maximum effect the drug can produce
The efficacy of the drug expressed as a percentage
The total receptor concentration in the tissue
The rate constant for the forward binding reaction
questions.explanation: Since Kd is the concentration at which half of all receptors are occupied, and under Clark's theory occupancy is proportional to effect, Kd is also the drug concentration at which the drug attains its half-maximal effect, the EC50.
questions.title: Lecture 25 - Drug-Receptor Interactions 1

questions.q: In the Clark equation E/Emax = [D]/(Kd + [D]), what does [Rt] represent?
options: The concentration of occupied receptor
The total receptor concentration
The rate of receptor turnover
The response at time t
The residual drug concentration
questions.explanation: In the Clark equation, E is the effect or response, Emax the maximum effect, [D] the drug concentration, Kd the dissociation constant, [DR] the concentration of occupied receptor and [Rt] the total receptor concentration.
questions.title: Lecture 25 - Drug-Receptor Interactions 1

questions.q: How does efficacy differ from affinity?
options: Efficacy is the relative ability of a drug-receptor complex to produce a maximum functional response, whereas affinity is a measure of the drug's ability to bind the receptor
Efficacy measures binding strength and affinity measures response
They are two names for the same property
Efficacy applies only to antagonists and affinity only to agonists
Efficacy is measured in molar units and affinity as a percentage
questions.explanation: Efficacy refers to the relative ability of a drug-receptor complex to produce a maximum functional response. It is not the same as affinity, which is a measure of a drug's ability to bind to the receptor.
questions.title: Lecture 25 - Drug-Receptor Interactions 1

questions.q: A ligand has affinity for the receptor but no efficacy. What is it?
options: A full agonist
A partial agonist
An antagonist
An inverse agonist
A super agonist
questions.explanation: An antagonist has affinity but no efficacy, so e = 0. A full agonist has efficacy equal to the endogenous agonist (e = 100), a partial agonist less (0 < e < 100), a super agonist more (e > 100) and an inverse agonist has inverse efficacy (e < 0).
questions.title: Lecture 25 - Drug-Receptor Interactions 1

questions.q: What defines a super agonist?
options: Efficacy higher than the endogenous agonist, e greater than 100
Efficacy equal to the endogenous agonist, e equal to 100
Efficacy less than the endogenous agonist, e between 0 and 100
Affinity but no efficacy, e equal to 0
Inverse efficacy, e less than 0
questions.explanation: A super agonist has efficacy higher than the endogenous agonist, with e greater than 100 per cent.
questions.title: Lecture 25 - Drug-Receptor Interactions 1

questions.q: What defines an inverse agonist in terms of efficacy?
options: Efficacy of exactly zero
Inverse efficacy, e less than 0
Efficacy between 0 and 100
Efficacy greater than 100
Efficacy that cannot be measured
questions.explanation: An inverse agonist has inverse efficacy, that is e less than 0, meaning it produces the opposite effect to the endogenous agonist rather than simply blocking it.
questions.title: Lecture 25 - Drug-Receptor Interactions 1

questions.q: Salbutamol acting at the beta-2 adrenergic receptor, where the natural ligands are norepinephrine and epinephrine, is an example of what?
options: An endogenous agonist
An exogenous mimic acting as a receptor agonist
A competitive antagonist
An inverse agonist
A non-competitive antagonist
questions.explanation: Receptor agonists can be endogenous substances or exogenous mimics. Salbutamol is an exogenous mimic at the beta-2 adrenergic receptor, where norepinephrine and epinephrine are the endogenous agonists.
questions.title: Lecture 25 - Drug-Receptor Interactions 1

questions.q: In the binding equilibrium, why is the backward rate constant beta independent of concentration while the forward rate depends on agonist concentration?
options: Because dissociation depends only on the existing drug-receptor complexes, whereas association requires drug and receptor to meet
Because the receptor concentration changes over time
Because beta is measured at a different temperature
Because the forward reaction is irreversible
Because beta describes metabolism rather than binding
questions.explanation: The forward rate depends on rate constant alpha and on agonist concentration, with units M^-1 s^-1, because association requires drug and receptor to encounter each other. The backward rate beta, with units s^-1, is independent of concentration because it depends only on the complexes already formed.
questions.title: Lecture 25 - Drug-Receptor Interactions 1

questions.q: Which three receptor classes are shown as the main cell-surface receptor types?
options: Ligand-gated ion channels, G protein coupled receptors and enzyme-linked receptors
Nuclear, cytoplasmic and mitochondrial receptors
Agonist, antagonist and inverse agonist receptors
H1, H2 and beta-2 receptors
Transporters, enzymes and signalling molecules
questions.explanation: The three main receptor classes shown are ligand-gated ion channels, G protein coupled receptors and enzyme-linked receptors, alongside intracellular receptors which are considered separately.
questions.title: Lecture 25 - Drug-Receptor Interactions 1

questions.q: According to the lecture key points, which topics should you now be able to discuss after this lecture?
options: Drug targets and receptor types, agonist classes, binding theories, receptor occupancy, dissociation constant and efficacy
Antibiotic resistance mechanisms and MIC testing only
Gram stain technique and culture media preparation
DNA replication, transcription and translation exclusively
Colloid stability and surfactant HLB values only
questions.explanation: Key points summarise: what a drug is, pharmacology's importance, receptor types and characteristics, agonist classes, lock-and-key/two-state binding, occupancy, dissociation constant (Kd) and efficacy defining agonist types.
questions.title: Lecture 25 - Drug-Receptor Interactions 1

questions.q: Two drugs act at the same receptor. Drug A has an EC50 of 10^-6 M and drug B an EC50 of 10^-3 M. Which is more potent?
options: Drug A, because a lower concentration is needed for half-maximal effect
Drug B, because a higher concentration is needed
They are equally potent because they act at the same receptor
Drug B, because higher EC50 means greater efficacy
Potency cannot be judged from EC50
questions.explanation: Potency is how small a concentration of drug is required to produce a given effect. The drug with the lower EC50, drug A here, is the more potent.
questions.title: Lecture 26 - Drug-Receptor Interactions 2

questions.q: How is a partial agonist defined?
options: It binds and activates a receptor but has only partial efficacy relative to a full agonist
It binds the receptor but produces no effect at all
It produces an effect opposite to the endogenous agonist
It binds irreversibly to a fraction of the receptors
It produces a greater effect than the endogenous agonist
questions.explanation: Partial agonists bind and activate a receptor but have only partial efficacy relative to a full agonist at that receptor.
questions.title: Lecture 26 - Drug-Receptor Interactions 2

questions.q: Why can a partial agonist be considered to display both agonist and antagonist behaviour?
options: Because it binds two different receptors simultaneously
Because when competing with a full agonist for receptor occupancy it produces a net decrease in receptor activation
Because it becomes an antagonist at high concentration
Because it has negative efficacy at some receptors
Because it binds irreversibly after initial activation
questions.explanation: A partial agonist can display both agonist and antagonist behaviour because, when competing with a full agonist for receptor occupancy, it produces a net decrease in receptor activation.
questions.title: Lecture 26 - Drug-Receptor Interactions 2

questions.q: What conditions must exist for an inverse agonist to produce a response?
options: The receptor must have a constitutive level of activity
The endogenous agonist must be present at high concentration
The receptor must be irreversibly bound
Spare receptors must be present
The receptor must be an enzyme-linked receptor
questions.explanation: For an inverse agonist response the receptor must have a constitutive level of activity. The inverse agonist then suppresses that baseline receptor activity, producing a response opposite to that of the agonist.
questions.title: Lecture 26 - Drug-Receptor Interactions 2

questions.q: Which receptor is given as an example where inverse agonists act?
options: The beta-2 adrenergic receptor
The mu opioid receptor
The GABA-A receptor
The H2 histamine receptor
The epidermal growth factor receptor
questions.explanation: GABA-A receptors are given as an example of receptors at which inverse agonists act. An inverse agonist binds the same receptor as the endogenous agonist but induces the opposite pharmacological response, and can be blocked by a receptor antagonist.
questions.title: Lecture 26 - Drug-Receptor Interactions 2

questions.q: What characterises an irreversible agonist, and what is the example given?
options: It binds permanently so the receptor is permanently activated; oxymorphazone at the mu opioid receptor, binding covalently
It binds reversibly but with very high affinity; morphine at the mu opioid receptor
It blocks the receptor permanently; tubocurarine at the nicotinic receptor
It activates then destroys the receptor; salbutamol at beta-2 receptors
It binds two receptors at once; histamine at H1 and H2
questions.explanation: Irreversible agonists are very rare. They bind permanently to a receptor which is then permanently activated. The example is the opioid mu receptor agonist oxymorphazone, which binds via a covalent bond.
questions.title: Lecture 26 - Drug-Receptor Interactions 2

questions.q: When spare receptors are present, what is the relationship between EC50 and Kd?
options: EC50 is less than Kd
EC50 is greater than Kd
EC50 equals Kd exactly
EC50 becomes zero
Kd becomes undefined
questions.explanation: If EC50 is less than Kd, spare receptors exist. This gives increased sensitivity to the agonist and amplifies signal duration and intensity.
questions.title: Lecture 26 - Drug-Receptor Interactions 2

questions.q: With spare receptors present, which statement remains true and which breaks down?
options: Kd still equals 50 per cent receptor occupancy, but EC50 no longer equals Kd
EC50 still equals Kd, but Kd no longer corresponds to 50 per cent occupancy
Both relationships still hold exactly
Neither relationship holds
Kd becomes equal to Emax
questions.explanation: Without spare receptors, Clark's equation holds: Kd equals 50 per cent occupancy and also equals EC50. With spare receptors, Kd still equals 50 per cent receptor occupancy, but EC50 is no longer equal to Kd because the relationship between occupancy and response becomes non-linear.
questions.title: Lecture 26 - Drug-Receptor Interactions 2

questions.q: What is the practical consequence of spare receptors for the tissue?
options: Increased sensitivity to the agonist, with amplified signal duration and intensity
Reduced sensitivity requiring higher agonist concentrations
Loss of the maximal response
Conversion of full agonists into partial agonists
Elimination of the need for the endogenous agonist
questions.explanation: Where spare receptors exist, EC50 is less than Kd. This produces increased sensitivity to the agonist and amplifies signal duration and intensity, so a maximal response is achieved without occupying all receptors.
questions.title: Lecture 26 - Drug-Receptor Interactions 2

questions.q: Under the Bliss independence model, what is the total response to drugs A and B given together?
options: Fa + Fb
Fa x Fb
Fa + Fb(100 - Fa)
Fa - Fb(100 - Fa)
(Fa + Fb)/2
questions.explanation: The Bliss independence model assumes compounds act independently. If drug A is already in the system, the additional response to drug B is Fb x (100 - Fa), so the total response is Fa + Fb(100 - Fa). Data fitting this prediction is said to be additive.
questions.title: Lecture 26 - Drug-Receptor Interactions 2

questions.q: What does the Bliss independence model assume about the two compounds?
options: That they act independently of one another
That they bind the same receptor site
That one is always a partial agonist
That their effects cancel out
That they have identical EC50 values
questions.explanation: The Bliss independence model assumes the compounds act independently, and models the prediction from the single agent response curves. Data that fits this prediction is described as additive; a greater than predicted effect indicates synergy.
questions.title: Lecture 26 - Drug-Receptor Interactions 2

questions.q: What is drug titration?
options: The process of adjusting the dose of a medication to achieve the desired beneficial effect while minimising adverse effects
The measurement of drug concentration by chemical titration
The determination of the dissociation constant experimentally
The comparison of two formulations of the same drug
The gradual conversion of a drug into its metabolite
questions.explanation: Drug titration is the process of adjusting the dose of a medication to achieve the desired beneficial effect while minimising adverse effects.
questions.title: Lecture 26 - Drug-Receptor Interactions 2

questions.q: How is the therapeutic index calculated?
options: LD50 divided by EC50
EC50 divided by LD50
LD50 minus EC50
EC50 multiplied by LD50
Kd divided by EC50
questions.explanation: The therapeutic index compares the toxic dose with the effective dose: it is LD50 divided by EC50. A larger index means a wider margin between effect and toxicity.
questions.title: Lecture 26 - Drug-Receptor Interactions 2

questions.q: Digoxin has an EC50 of 1.2 ng/mL and an LD50 of 2.4 ng/mL. What is its therapeutic index?
questions.explanation: Therapeutic index = LD50/EC50 = 2.4/1.2 = 2. This is a very narrow therapeutic index, meaning toxicity occurs at only twice the effective concentration.
questions.title: Lecture 26 - Drug-Receptor Interactions 2

questions.q: Morphine has an EC50 of 5 mg/kg and an LD50 of 350 mg/kg. What is its therapeutic index?
questions.explanation: Therapeutic index = 350/5 = 70. Of the three examples, morphine has the largest therapeutic index, paracetamol is 150/10 = 15, and digoxin the smallest at 2.
questions.title: Lecture 26 - Drug-Receptor Interactions 2

questions.q: Paracetamol has an EC50 of 10 mg/kg and an LD50 of 150 mg/kg. How does its therapeutic index compare with digoxin's?
options: Paracetamol 15, considerably wider than digoxin's 2
Paracetamol 15, narrower than digoxin's 70
Paracetamol 1.5, narrower than digoxin's 2
Both are the same at 15
Paracetamol 150, wider than digoxin's 24
questions.explanation: Paracetamol's therapeutic index is 150/10 = 15, considerably wider than digoxin's 2.4/1.2 = 2. Digoxin had the smallest therapeutic index of the three examples.
questions.title: Lecture 26 - Drug-Receptor Interactions 2

questions.q: What is the clinical implication of a narrow therapeutic index?
options: Titration of the dose is important to avoid side effects; examples include insulin and blood thinners
The drug can be given at any dose without monitoring
The drug is more potent than others
The drug should always be given intravenously
The drug has no toxic effects at all
questions.explanation: For drugs with a narrow therapeutic index, titration of the dose is important to avoid side effects. Examples of drugs requiring titration include insulin and blood thinners.
questions.title: Lecture 26 - Drug-Receptor Interactions 2

questions.q: Besides achieving the right dose, where else is drug titration important?
options: In some situations titrating a drug dose downwards is recommended over stopping it abruptly
In choosing between oral and intravenous routes
In deciding which excipients to include
In determining the drug's dissociation constant
In selecting the manufacturing method
questions.explanation: In some situations titrating a drug dose downwards is recommended over stopping it abruptly.
questions.title: Lecture 26 - Drug-Receptor Interactions 2

questions.q: Morphine has a dissociation constant of 1.7 microM. What percentage of receptors is occupied at 5 microM?
options: 25 per cent
50 per cent
65 per cent
75 per cent
85 per cent
questions.explanation: Fraction occupied = [D]/(Kd + [D]) = 5/(1.7 + 5) = 5/6.7 = 0.746, that is about 75 per cent.
questions.title: Lecture 26 - Drug-Receptor Interactions 2

questions.q: If the pharmacological response of a tissue to drug X is larger than the effect of the endogenous agonist, how is drug X described?
options: Antagonist
Full agonist
Inverse agonist
Partial agonist
Super agonist
questions.explanation: A super agonist has efficacy higher than the endogenous agonist, so its response exceeds that of the natural ligand. A full agonist matches the endogenous agonist and a partial agonist produces less.
questions.title: Lecture 26 - Drug-Receptor Interactions 2

questions.q: For a partial agonist, what is the typical relationship between EC50 and Kd?
options: EC50 is approximately equal to Kd
EC50 is always ten times Kd
EC50 is always zero
EC50 cannot be measured for a partial agonist
EC50 is always much greater than Kd
questions.explanation: For partial agonists the EC50 is approximately equal to the Kd, in contrast to a full agonist in a tissue with spare receptors where EC50 is less than or equal to Kd.
questions.title: Lecture 26 - Drug-Receptor Interactions 2

questions.q: Can the effect of an inverse agonist be prevented?
options: Yes, it can be blocked by a receptor antagonist
No, its action is irreversible
Only by removing all endogenous agonist
Only by increasing constitutive receptor activity
No, because it binds a different site from antagonists
questions.explanation: An inverse agonist binds the same receptor as the endogenous agonist but induces the opposite pharmacological response, and it can be blocked by a receptor antagonist.
questions.title: Lecture 26 - Drug-Receptor Interactions 2

questions.q: Why is the relationship between occupancy and response non-linear when spare receptors are present?
options: Because a maximal response is reached before all receptors are occupied, so E/Emax no longer equals the occupied fraction
Because the drug is metabolised faster at high concentrations
Because the receptor changes its Kd during binding
Because the endogenous agonist competes for the same sites
Because spare receptors have a different Kd from the others
questions.explanation: Without spare receptors there is a linear relationship between occupancy and response, so [D]/(Kd + [D]) = [DR]/[Rt] = E/Emax. With spare receptors the relationship becomes non-linear because a maximal response can be produced without full occupancy, so the occupancy fraction no longer equals E/Emax.
questions.title: Lecture 26 - Drug-Receptor Interactions 2

questions.q: When spare receptors are present, why is EC50 not equal to Kd?
options: Because a maximal response can be achieved without all receptors being occupied
Because Kd is undefined at low concentrations
Because the drug binds irreversibly to the receptor
Because receptors are always fully occupied at EC50
Because spare receptors have a higher affinity than others
questions.explanation: With spare receptors, EC50 is not equal to Kd. You do not need all receptors bound to a ligand to produce a maximal response, so the concentration giving 50% effect is lower than that giving 50% occupancy.
questions.title: Lecture 26 - Drug-Receptor Interactions 2

questions.q: Of the drugs compared on the therapeutic index slide, which had the largest and which the smallest index?
options: Morphine had the largest; digoxin had the smallest
Digoxin had the largest; morphine had the smallest
Paracetamol had the largest; morphine had the smallest
All three had identical therapeutic indices
Morphine had the smallest; digoxin the largest
questions.explanation: The therapeutic index slide asks which drug had the largest and smallest index. Morphine (LD50/EC50 = 70) had the largest, paracetamol 15, and digoxin (2.4/1.2 = 2) the smallest, meaning toxicity occurs at only twice the effective concentration.
questions.title: Lecture 26 - Drug-Receptor Interactions 2

questions.q: Which topics are included in the lecture key points on drug-receptor interactions?
options: Drug targets, agonist types, two-state receptor theory, Kd, and therapeutic index
Antibiotic resistance mechanisms only
Pharmacokinetics of hepatic metabolism only
BCS classification of drugs only
Drug formulation and excipients only
questions.explanation: Key points include describing drugs and pharmacology, understanding drug targets and receptors, discussing agonist types, describing two-state receptor theory with Kd and drug-receptor ligation, and understanding therapeutic index and drug safety.
questions.title: Lecture 26 - Drug-Receptor Interactions 2

questions.q: In the example SAQ, what must be explained when comparing full and partial agonists?
options: The two-state receptor theory and how it accounts for differences between full and partial agonists
Only the molecular weight of each drug
Only the route of administration
Only renal excretion rates
Only drug distribution volume
questions.explanation: The example SAQ asks students to describe the two-state receptor theory and use it to explain the differences between a full and partial agonist.
questions.title: Lecture 26 - Drug-Receptor Interactions 2

questions.q: How is an antagonist defined in terms of affinity and efficacy?
options: It displays affinity to bind but no efficacy to activate receptors
It displays efficacy but no affinity
It has both high affinity and high efficacy
It has negative affinity and negative efficacy
It has partial affinity and partial efficacy
questions.explanation: An antagonist opposes the action of an agonist by blocking receptors. It displays an affinity to bind to receptors but no efficacy to activate them, so it blocks agonist-mediated responses rather than causing a biological response itself.
questions.title: Lecture 27 - Physiological Antagonism & Antagonists

questions.q: What characterises a reversible competitive antagonist?
options: It binds via non-covalent intermolecular forces and eventually dissociates, freeing the receptor to be bound again
It binds covalently and never dissociates
It binds an allosteric site rather than the active site
It requires receptor activation before it can bind
It reduces the agonist concentration chemically
questions.explanation: Reversible competitive antagonists bind via non-covalent intermolecular forces. They eventually dissociate from the receptor, freeing it to be bound again. Naloxone at opioid receptors is the example given.
questions.title: Lecture 27 - Physiological Antagonism & Antagonists

questions.q: Which drug is given as the example of a reversible competitive antagonist at opioid receptors?
options: Morphine
Naloxone
Atropine
Memantine
Rilpivirine
questions.explanation: Naloxone at opioid receptors is the example of a reversible competitive antagonist. Atropine is the competitive antagonist example at muscarinic receptors.
questions.title: Lecture 27 - Physiological Antagonism & Antagonists

questions.q: What happens to an agonist concentration-response curve in the presence of a competitive antagonist?
options: The curve shifts to the right, the maximal response is not decreased, and the inhibition can be overcome by adding more agonist
The curve shifts to the left and the maximal response increases
The curve flattens and the maximal response falls
The curve is unchanged
The curve shifts to the right and the maximal response falls
questions.explanation: Competitive antagonists bind reversibly to the receptor. The inhibition can be overcome by adding more agonist, the maximal response of the agonist is not decreased, and the curve shifts to the right.
questions.title: Lecture 27 - Physiological Antagonism & Antagonists

questions.q: In the presence of a competitive antagonist B, what is the equation for the fraction of receptors occupied by drug D?
questions.explanation: With total receptors [Rt] = [R] + [DR] + [BR], and at equilibrium [D][R] = Kd[DR] and [B][R] = Kb[BR], rearrangement gives [DR]/[Rt] = [D]/([D] + Kd(1 + [B]/Kb)).
questions.title: Lecture 27 - Physiological Antagonism & Antagonists

questions.q: Morphine has Kd 1.7 microM and naloxone Kb 0.1 microM. What percentage of receptors is occupied by 1 microM morphine with no naloxone present?
options: 5 per cent
15 per cent
23 per cent
37 per cent
64 per cent
questions.explanation: With no antagonist the equation reduces to [D]/(Kd + [D]) = 1/(1.7 + 1) = 0.37, that is 37 per cent. Adding 0.1 microM naloxone reduces this to 23 per cent and 1 microM naloxone to 5 per cent.
questions.title: Lecture 27 - Physiological Antagonism & Antagonists

questions.q: With morphine at 3 microM (Kd 1.7 microM), occupancy falls from 64 per cent with no naloxone to 14 per cent with 1 microM naloxone (Kb 0.1 microM). What does this demonstrate?
options: That competitive antagonism markedly reduces agonist occupancy at a given agonist concentration
That naloxone reduces the maximal response achievable
That naloxone binds irreversibly
That morphine's Kd increases permanently
That naloxone acts at an allosteric site
questions.explanation: Because Kd is effectively multiplied by (1 + [B]/Kb), a competitive antagonist markedly reduces the fraction of receptors occupied by the agonist at any given agonist concentration, although higher agonist concentrations can still overcome it.
questions.title: Lecture 27 - Physiological Antagonism & Antagonists

questions.q: What percentage of receptors is occupied by 5 microM morphine (Kd 1.7 microM) in the presence of 0.1 microM naloxone (Kb 0.1 microM)?
options: 25 per cent
50 per cent
60 per cent
75 per cent
85 per cent
questions.explanation: Kd(1 + [B]/Kb) = 1.7 x (1 + 0.1/0.1) = 3.4. Occupancy = 5/(5 + 3.4) = 0.595, about 60 per cent. Without naloxone it would be 75 per cent.
questions.title: Lecture 27 - Physiological Antagonism & Antagonists

questions.q: What distinguishes an irreversible competitive antagonist?
options: It binds via covalent forces, and because there is insufficient free energy locally to break the covalent bonds, the receptor remains permanently antagonised until destroyed
It binds non-covalently but with very high affinity
It requires the agonist to bind first
It reduces the agonist concentration in plasma
It accelerates the metabolism of the agonist
questions.explanation: Irreversible competitive antagonists bind via covalent forces. Because there is not enough free energy in the local environment to break the covalent bonds, the receptor-antagonist complex never dissociates and the receptor remains permanently antagonised until it is destroyed.
questions.title: Lecture 27 - Physiological Antagonism & Antagonists

questions.q: How does a non-competitive antagonist act?
options: By binding an allosteric site on the receptor, or irreversibly binding the active site, reducing the maximum response attainable with any amount of agonist
By binding the active site reversibly and being displaced by more agonist
By requiring receptor activation before binding
By chemically inactivating the agonist in solution
By accelerating agonist elimination from the body
questions.explanation: Non-competitive antagonists bind to an allosteric site on the receptor or irreversibly bind the active site. They reduce the magnitude of the maximum response that can be attained with any amount of agonist. Rilpivirine, used in HIV infection, is the example.
questions.title: Lecture 27 - Physiological Antagonism & Antagonists

questions.q: What effect does a non-competitive antagonist have on the dose-response curve?
options: It flattens the curve, reducing the maximum response
It shifts the curve to the right without reducing the maximum
It shifts the curve to the left
It has no effect on the curve
It makes the curve steeper
questions.explanation: Non-competitive antagonists flatten the dose-response curve, because they reduce the maximum response attainable regardless of how much agonist is added.
questions.title: Lecture 27 - Physiological Antagonism & Antagonists

questions.q: Which drug is given as an example of a non-competitive antagonist?
options: Naloxone, used in opioid overdose
Rilpivirine, used to treat HIV infection
Memantine, used in Alzheimer's disease
Atropine, used as a muscarinic blocker
Salbutamol, used in asthma
questions.explanation: Rilpivirine, used to treat HIV infection, is given as the example of a non-competitive antagonist. Memantine is the example of an uncompetitive antagonist.
questions.title: Lecture 27 - Physiological Antagonism & Antagonists

questions.q: What defines an uncompetitive antagonist?
options: It requires receptor activation by an agonist before it can bind to a separate allosteric binding site
It binds the active site in competition with the agonist
It binds only in the absence of agonist
It has no affinity for the receptor at all
It binds covalently to the active site
questions.explanation: Uncompetitive antagonists require receptor activation by an agonist before they can bind to a separate allosteric binding site. Their kinetic profile shows the same amount of antagonist blocks higher agonist concentrations better than lower ones. Memantine, used in Alzheimer's disease, is the example.
questions.title: Lecture 27 - Physiological Antagonism & Antagonists

questions.q: What is unusual about the kinetic profile of an uncompetitive antagonist?
options: The same amount of antagonist blocks higher concentrations of agonist better than lower concentrations
The same amount of antagonist blocks lower concentrations better than higher ones
Its effect is independent of agonist concentration
Its effect diminishes over time regardless of agonist
It produces a rightward shift with no change in maximum
questions.explanation: Because uncompetitive antagonists need the receptor to be activated by agonist first, the same amount of antagonist blocks higher concentrations of agonist better than lower concentrations.
questions.title: Lecture 27 - Physiological Antagonism & Antagonists

questions.q: What is physiological antagonism?
options: Drug-based activation of a different compensatory mechanism to oppose the agonist activity
Drug-based reduction of the concentration of an agonist
Drugs that accelerate the pathways used to dispose of an agonist
Competition for the same receptor binding site
Covalent blockade of the receptor active site
questions.explanation: Physiological antagonism is drug-based activation of a different compensatory mechanism to oppose the agonist activity, rather than acting at the same receptor.
questions.title: Lecture 27 - Physiological Antagonism & Antagonists

questions.q: What is chemical antagonism?
options: Activation of a compensatory physiological mechanism
Drug-based reduction of the concentration of an agonist
Acceleration of the body's disposal pathways for an agonist
Binding to an allosteric receptor site
Blocking the receptor active site reversibly
questions.explanation: Chemical antagonism is drug-based reduction of the concentration of an agonist. Pharmacokinetic antagonism, by contrast, involves drugs that accelerate the pathways used by the body to dispose of an agonist.
questions.title: Lecture 27 - Physiological Antagonism & Antagonists

questions.q: What is pharmacokinetic antagonism?
options: Drugs that accelerate the pathways used by the body to dispose of an agonist
Drugs that chemically inactivate the agonist in the tissue
Drugs that block the agonist's receptor irreversibly
Drugs that activate an opposing physiological pathway
Drugs that reduce the agonist's affinity for its receptor
questions.explanation: Pharmacokinetic antagonism describes drugs that accelerate the pathways used by the body to dispose of an agonist, thereby reducing its effect without acting at the receptor.
questions.title: Lecture 27 - Physiological Antagonism & Antagonists

questions.q: Which statement about competitive and non-competitive antagonists is correct?
options: Competitive antagonists bind covalently to the receptor active site
Competitive antagonists bind to an allosteric site on the receptor
Non-competitive antagonists can be reversed by increasing agonist concentrations
Non-competitive antagonists shift the agonist dose-response curve to the right
Non-competitive antagonists when bound can change the structure of the active site, preventing agonist binding
questions.explanation: Non-competitive antagonists bind an allosteric site and can change the structure of the active site, preventing agonist binding. They cannot be overcome by more agonist and they flatten rather than shift the curve. Competitive antagonists bind the active site, usually non-covalently, and shift the curve rightwards.
questions.title: Lecture 27 - Physiological Antagonism & Antagonists

questions.q: Atropine acting against acetylcholine and muscarine at the muscarinic receptor is an example of what?
options: A competitive antagonist
A non-competitive antagonist
An uncompetitive antagonist
A physiological antagonist
An inverse agonist
questions.explanation: Atropine is shown as the competitive antagonist opposing acetylcholine and muscarine at the muscarinic receptor, competing for the same binding site.
questions.title: Lecture 27 - Physiological Antagonism & Antagonists

questions.q: Why does the term Kd(1 + [B]/Kb) capture the effect of a competitive antagonist?
options: Because the antagonist effectively raises the apparent Kd of the agonist in proportion to its own concentration relative to its Kb
Because the antagonist reduces the total number of receptors
Because the antagonist lowers the maximum response attainable
Because the antagonist changes the agonist's efficacy
Because the antagonist binds the agonist directly in solution
questions.explanation: In the presence of competitive antagonist B, occupancy is [D]/([D] + Kd(1 + [B]/Kb)). The antagonist effectively increases the apparent Kd of the agonist in proportion to [B]/Kb, which is why the curve shifts right but the maximum is unchanged.
questions.title: Lecture 27 - Physiological Antagonism & Antagonists

questions.q: One type of non-competitive antagonist allows agonist binding but no effect, another prevents agonist binding entirely. What does this illustrate?
options: That non-competitive antagonism can operate by more than one mechanism, but both reduce the maximum response
That non-competitive antagonists always prevent agonist binding
That non-competitive antagonists always allow agonist binding
That non-competitive antagonists behave identically to competitive ones
That the two types have opposite effects on the curve
questions.explanation: The non-competitive antagonist types shown include one where the agonist still binds but has no effect and one where agonist binding is prevented altogether. Either way the maximum response attainable is reduced and the curve flattens.
questions.title: Lecture 27 - Physiological Antagonism & Antagonists

questions.q: What happens to the concentration-response curve for Drug C in the presence of competitive antagonism?
options: The curve shifts to the right without a decrease in maximal response
The curve shifts to the left with increased maximal response
The maximal response is abolished at all agonist concentrations
The curve becomes flat with no change in potency
The curve disappears entirely
questions.explanation: In competitive antagonism the agonist concentration-response curve shifts to the right. The maximal response is not decreased because the inhibition can be overcome by adding more agonist.
questions.title: Lecture 27 - Physiological Antagonism & Antagonists

questions.q: In the receptor binding scheme with agonist D and competitive antagonist B, what does Kd equal?
options: Beta divided by alpha, the ratio of dissociation to association rate constants
Alpha divided by beta
The product of alpha and beta
The sum of agonist and antagonist concentrations
The total receptor concentration [Rt]
questions.explanation: In the binding equilibrium D + R ⇌ DR with rate constants alpha (association) and beta (dissociation), the dissociation constant Kd equals beta divided by alpha.
questions.title: Lecture 27 - Physiological Antagonism & Antagonists

questions.q: Which abilities are listed in the antagonism lecture key points?
options: Describe antagonists and their types, competitive effects on binding, and non-competitive mechanisms
Calculate hepatic clearance rates
Design dosage forms for sustained release
Classify bacteria by Gram stain only
Explain BCS permeability classes only
questions.explanation: Key points state that students should describe what an antagonist is and how it differs from an agonist, discuss different antagonist types, describe how competitive antagonists impact receptor binding, and discuss non-competitive antagonism mechanisms.
questions.title: Lecture 27 - Physiological Antagonism & Antagonists

questions.q: What are the four sub-classes of ion channel?
options: Ligand-gated, mechanically-gated, voltage-gated and leak channels
Sodium, potassium, calcium and chloride channels
Excitatory, inhibitory, mixed and silent channels
Fast, slow, intermediate and inactive channels
Pentameric, tetrameric, dimeric and monomeric channels
questions.explanation: Ion channels are classified into four sub-classes: ligand-gated ion channels, mechanically-gated ion channels, voltage-gated ion channels and leak channels.
questions.title: Basics of Ion Channels

questions.q: Which structural features characterise ligand-gated ion channels?
options: Pentameric proteins that typically require two molecules of a ligand to bind simultaneously to open, allowing fast responses
Tetrameric proteins with a voltage sensor and selectivity filter
Monomeric proteins activated by stretch
Dimeric proteins that are permanently open
Pentameric proteins requiring covalent ligand attachment
questions.explanation: Ligand-gated ion channels are pentameric proteins that typically require two molecules of a ligand to bind simultaneously to open the channel. They allow fast responses in the target cell; the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor is an example.
questions.title: Basics of Ion Channels

questions.q: What do voltage-gated ion channels respond to, and where are they crucial?
options: A change in voltage across the membrane; crucial for signalling in excitable tissues such as nerve cells and muscles
Binding of two ligand molecules; crucial in the gastrointestinal tract
Mechanical stretch; crucial in the ear
Changes in pH; crucial in the stomach
Changes in temperature; crucial in the skin
questions.explanation: Voltage-gated ion channels respond to a change in voltage across the membrane. They come in Na+, K+, Ca2+ and Cl- types and are crucial for signalling in excitable tissues such as nerve cells and muscles.
questions.title: Basics of Ion Channels

questions.q: Which structural features do voltage-gated ion channels have?
options: Four subunits, a voltage sensor and a selectivity filter, present in all electrically excitable cells
Five subunits and two ligand binding sites
A single subunit with a stretch-sensitive domain
Two subunits and a covalent gate
Four subunits but no selectivity filter
questions.explanation: Voltage-gated ion channels comprise four subunits, have a voltage sensor and a selectivity filter, and are present in all electrically excitable cells.
questions.title: Basics of Ion Channels

questions.q: What activates mechanically-gated ion channels, and where are they found?
options: Pressure or compression, stretch and shear stress; found in hair cells of the ear and enterochromaffin cells of the gastrointestinal tract
Voltage changes; found in cardiac muscle
Neurotransmitter binding; found at the neuromuscular junction
Light; found in the retina
Temperature change; found in the skin
questions.explanation: Mechanically-gated ion channels are activated by pressure or compression, stretch and shear stress. Examples of tissues include the hair cells of the ear and enterochromaffin cells of the gastrointestinal tract.
questions.title: Basics of Ion Channels

questions.q: What determines the effect an ion channel has on its target cell?
options: The ion it conducts
The number of subunits it has
Whether it is pentameric or tetrameric
How long it remains open
Its position in the membrane
questions.explanation: Most channels are closed at rest and open in response to a specific stimulus. They conduct a range of ions, and the effect on the target cell is dependent on the ion they conduct.
questions.title: Basics of Ion Channels

questions.q: What happens to an ion channel in the presence of continued similar stimulation, and what is the purpose?
options: It moves into a non-conducting inactive state, which can act as a filter for repetitive stimulations
It remains permanently open to maximise the signal
It is degraded and replaced by a new channel
It reverses the direction of ion flow
It changes the ion it conducts
questions.explanation: Ion channels are typically closed at rest and open in response to an appropriate stimulus. With continued similar stimulation they move into a non-conducting inactive state, and this process of inactivation can act as a filter for repetitive stimulations.
questions.title: Basics of Ion Channels

questions.q: Which ions make a channel excitatory, and which make it inhibitory?
options: Na+ and Ca2+ are excitatory as they depolarise the cell; K+ and Cl- are inhibitory as they hyperpolarise it
K+ and Cl- are excitatory; Na+ and Ca2+ are inhibitory
Na+ and K+ are excitatory; Ca2+ and Cl- are inhibitory
All cations are inhibitory and all anions excitatory
The ion does not determine excitatory or inhibitory effect
questions.explanation: Ions move down their concentration gradient. Channels conducting Na+ and Ca2+ are excitatory because they depolarise the cell, while channels conducting K+ and Cl- are inhibitory because they hyperpolarise it.
questions.title: Basics of Ion Channels

questions.q: The nicotinic acetylcholine receptor and the 5-HT3 receptor are non-specific cation channels. What is their usual effect?
options: They tend to be excitatory
They tend to be inhibitory
They have no net effect on membrane potential
They hyperpolarise the cell
Their effect depends on the ligand concentration
questions.explanation: Some ligand-gated channels are non-specific cation channels but tend to be excitatory, for example the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor and the 5-HT3 receptor.
questions.title: Basics of Ion Channels

questions.q: What two factors set the resting membrane potential?
options: The relative permeabilities of the cell at rest to Na+ and K+ ions, and the activity of the Na+/K+ ATPase pump
The number of ligand-gated channels and the concentration of neurotransmitter
The thickness of the membrane and its lipid composition
The rate of action potential firing and the axon diameter
The activity of mechanically-gated channels and shear stress
questions.explanation: The resting membrane potential is set by the relative permeabilities of the cell at rest to Na+ and K+ ions, and by the activity of the Na+/K+ ATPase pump.
questions.title: Basics of Ion Channels

questions.q: What is the typical range of the resting membrane potential?
options: Between -75 and -30 mV compared with the outside of the cell
Between +30 and +75 mV compared with the outside
Between -10 and 0 mV
Between -150 and -100 mV
Exactly -70 mV in all cells
questions.explanation: Typically, the resting membrane potential is between -75 and -30 mV compared with the outside of the cell.
questions.title: Basics of Ion Channels

questions.q: What is the sequence of events in an action potential?
options: Ligand-gated channels cause graded depolarisation, triggering voltage-gated Na+ channels to open causing depolarisation, then Na+ channels inactivate and voltage-gated K+ channels open causing repolarisation
Voltage-gated K+ channels open first causing depolarisation, then Na+ channels repolarise the cell
Ca2+ channels open first, then Cl- channels repolarise the membrane
Mechanically-gated channels open, then leak channels close
All channels open simultaneously and then close together
questions.explanation: Opening of ligand-gated ion channels causes a graded depolarisation. This triggers opening of voltage-gated Na+ channels leading to depolarisation. The Na+ channels then become inactive and voltage-gated K+ channels open, leading to repolarisation.
questions.title: Basics of Ion Channels

questions.q: Which ion channels are primarily responsible for the rapid depolarisation phase of the neuronal action potential?
options: Voltage-gated potassium channels
Ligand-gated chloride channels
Voltage-gated sodium channels
Calcium-activated potassium channels
Stretch-activated ion channels
questions.explanation: Voltage-gated sodium channels open in response to the initial graded depolarisation and produce the rapid depolarisation phase. Voltage-gated potassium channels open later and produce repolarisation.
questions.title: Basics of Ion Channels

questions.q: How does an arriving action potential lead to neurotransmitter release at the nerve terminal?
options: It opens voltage-gated Ca2+ channels, neurotransmitter is released and binds its receptor, which may be a ligand-gated ion channel, depolarising or hyperpolarising the target cell
It opens voltage-gated K+ channels which expel neurotransmitter
It closes all ion channels, forcing vesicle fusion
It activates mechanically-gated channels in the terminal membrane
It directly opens the postsynaptic channels without any transmitter
questions.explanation: The action potential opens voltage-gated Ca2+ channels at the terminal. Neurotransmitter is released and binds to its receptor, which could be a ligand-gated ion channel, and this either depolarises or hyperpolarises the target cell.
questions.title: Basics of Ion Channels

questions.q: For which therapeutic purposes are drugs that control ion movement across the membrane used?
options: Anxiety, arrhythmia, hypertension, ischaemic heart disease and local anaesthesia
Bacterial infection and fungal infection only
Diabetes and thyroid disease only
Cancer chemotherapy only
Constipation and diarrhoea only
questions.explanation: Ion movement across the cellular membrane can be controlled through different drugs used for many therapeutic purposes such as anxiety, arrhythmia, hypertension, ischaemic heart disease and local anaesthetics.
questions.title: Basics of Ion Channels

questions.q: How is the plasma membrane described in relation to ion channels?
options: A selectively permeable barrier separating the internal environment from the external surroundings
A fully permeable barrier allowing free ion movement
An impermeable barrier with no transport across it
A rigid structure that does not change with cell state
A barrier permeable only to water
questions.explanation: The plasma membrane is a selectively permeable barrier that separates the internal environment from the external surroundings, and ion channels provide the controlled routes across it.
questions.title: Basics of Ion Channels

questions.q: According to the key points, what creates the membrane potential?
options: Imbalanced distribution of ions and proteins across the membrane
The thickness of the phospholipid bilayer
The number of ligand-gated channels present
The rate of protein synthesis in the cell
The presence of cholesterol in the membrane
questions.explanation: Imbalanced distribution of ions and proteins creates the membrane potential. The action potential fires when the membrane threshold is reached, and neurons communicate with each other and other excitable cells through ion dynamics.
questions.title: Basics of Ion Channels

questions.q: Why does inactivation of voltage-gated sodium channels matter functionally?
options: It allows repolarisation to occur and acts as a filter limiting response to repetitive stimulation
It permanently switches off the neuron
It reverses the direction of the action potential
It releases neurotransmitter from the terminal
It converts the channel into a leak channel
questions.explanation: Voltage-gated Na+ channels become inactive after opening, allowing voltage-gated K+ channels to repolarise the cell. More generally, the inactivation of ion channels under continued stimulation acts as a filter for repetitive stimulations.
questions.title: Basics of Ion Channels

questions.q: The word homeostasis comes from which roots, and what does it actually describe?
options: 'Homeo' meaning similar to and 'stasis' meaning standing still; it describes a dynamic state
'Homeo' meaning same and 'stasis' meaning fixed; it describes an unchanging value
'Homeo' meaning human and 'stasis' meaning balance; it describes whole-body balance only
'Homeo' meaning together and 'stasis' meaning flow; it describes circulation
'Homeo' meaning constant and 'stasis' meaning state; it describes a single set value
questions.explanation: Homeo means similar to and stasis means standing still, but homeostasis is a dynamic state rather than adherence to a single specific value.
questions.title: Homeostasis

questions.q: What does dynamic equilibrium mean in the context of homeostasis?
options: Body systems constantly counteract any movement away from optimal set points, keeping the internal environment relatively stable within a narrow range
The internal environment is held at exactly one fixed value at all times
The body allows values to drift freely until symptoms appear
Internal and external factors are always equal
The body oscillates widely between two extremes
questions.explanation: Body systems constantly counteract any movement away from optimal conditions, the set points. Homeostasis does not mean adherence to a single specific value; the internal environment must be kept relatively stable within a narrow range against both internal and external factors.
questions.title: Homeostasis

questions.q: Why do pharmacists need to know about homeostasis?
options: Because all medical conditions can be traced to a failure in homeostatic control, and the goal of healthcare professionals is to stabilise the internal milieu
Because homeostasis determines drug solubility
Because it sets the shelf life of medicines
Because only diabetic patients are affected by it
Because it governs how tablets disintegrate
questions.explanation: All medical conditions can be traced to a failure in homeostatic control, and the goal of healthcare professionals is to stabilise the internal milieu. Examples include diabetes, hypertension, atherosclerosis, temperature dysregulation and dehydration.
questions.title: Homeostasis

questions.q: At which levels can homeostasis occur?
options: At cellular, tissue or organ, and whole body levels
At the whole body level only
At the cellular level only
At the organ level only
At the molecular level only
questions.explanation: Homeostasis can occur at a cellular level, at a tissue or organ level, and at the whole body level.
questions.title: Homeostasis

questions.q: Which of these is a homeostatically regulated factor listed in the lecture?
options: Blood volume and pressure
Height of the individual
Number of red blood cells produced per lifetime
Rate of hair growth
Skin pigmentation
questions.explanation: The regulated factors listed are glucose and other nutrient concentrations, body temperature, blood volume and pressure, waste product concentrations, pH, water, salt and electrolyte concentrations, and oxygen and carbon dioxide concentrations.
questions.title: Homeostasis

questions.q: What three things must a homeostatic regulatory system be able to do?
options: Detect deviations from normal, integrate this with other relevant information, and make appropriate adjustments
Store energy, release energy and conserve energy
Absorb, distribute and eliminate substances
Sense temperature, pH and pressure only
Produce hormones, transport them and destroy them
questions.explanation: Homeostatic regulation must be able to detect deviations from the normal, integrate this information with any other relevant information, and make appropriate adjustments.
questions.title: Homeostasis

questions.q: What is the optimum range given for blood glucose?
options: 1 to 2 mmol/L
4 to 6 mmol/L
8 to 10 mmol/L
10 to 15 mmol/L
0.5 to 1 mmol/L
questions.explanation: Blood glucose is maintained near an optimum value of 4 to 6 mmol/L, a range of only 2 mM.
questions.title: Homeostasis

questions.q: What are the three components of a homeostatic regulatory loop?
options: A sensor sensitive to an environmental change, a control centre that receives and processes the information, and an effector that responds
A stimulus, a hormone and a target organ
An input, an output and a feedback signal
A receptor, a ligand and a second messenger
A gene, a protein and an enzyme
questions.explanation: Homeostatic regulation requires a sensor sensitive to an environmental change or stimulus, a control centre which receives and processes the information supplied by the sensor, and an effector, a cell or organ that responds to the control centre and whose activity opposes or enhances the stimulus.
questions.title: Homeostasis

questions.q: Which type of feedback loop does homeostasis typically involve, and what does it do?
options: Negative feedback loops, which counteract changes of various properties from their set points
Positive feedback loops, which counteract changes from set points
Negative feedback loops, which amplify the initiating stimulus
Feedforward loops, which anticipate future changes
Neutral loops, which have no directional effect
questions.explanation: Homeostasis typically involves negative feedback loops that counteract changes of various properties from their target values, known as set points.
questions.title: Homeostasis

questions.q: How do positive feedback loops differ from negative feedback loops?
options: They amplify their initiating stimuli, moving the system away from its starting state
They return the system to its set point faster
They have no effect on the system
They operate only at the cellular level
They reduce the sensitivity of the sensor
questions.explanation: In contrast to negative feedback loops, positive feedback loops amplify their initiating stimuli, moving the system away from its starting state.
questions.title: Homeostasis

questions.q: Which process is given as the example of positive feedback control?
options: Homeostatic control of blood clotting
Homeostatic control of blood glucose
Homeostatic control of blood glucose variability
Homeostatic control of blood pressure
Homeostatic control of body temperature
questions.explanation: Blood clotting is given as the example of positive feedback, whereas body temperature regulation is the example of negative feedback.
questions.title: Homeostasis

questions.q: How does intrinsic regulation differ from extrinsic regulation?
options: Intrinsic is a direct automatic adjustment by the cell, tissue, organ or system to an environmental change (autoregulation); extrinsic involves interventions by the nervous and/or endocrine system in response to external change
Intrinsic involves the nervous system; extrinsic involves local chemical signals
Intrinsic occurs only in disease; extrinsic only in health
Intrinsic is slow and extrinsic is instantaneous
They are two names for the same process
questions.explanation: Intrinsic regulation, or autoregulation, is a direct automatic adjustment by a cell, tissue, organ or physiological system in response to some environmental change. Extrinsic regulation occurs in response to external change and involves interventions by the nervous and/or endocrine system.
questions.title: Homeostasis

questions.q: Decreased tissue oxygen leading to local release of nitric oxide and vasodilation is an example of what?
options: Intrinsic regulation (autoregulation)
Extrinsic regulation by the nervous system
Extrinsic regulation by the endocrine system
Positive feedback
A change in the set point
questions.explanation: This is intrinsic regulation: the symptom is decreased tissue oxygen levels, the response is that cells release chemicals such as nitric oxide causing local vasodilation, and the result is increased blood flow providing more oxygen to the region.
questions.title: Homeostasis

questions.q: When body temperature drops, which responses does the nervous system command?
options: Reduced blood flow to the skin to reduce heat loss, and a shivering response in skeletal muscle
Increased blood flow to the skin and sweating
Release of thyroid hormone to raise metabolic rate
Release of insulin to lower blood glucose
Local release of nitric oxide causing vasodilation
questions.explanation: For a drop in body temperature the nervous system issues commands including reduced blood flow to the skin to reduce heat loss and a shivering response in skeletal muscle. Separately the endocrine system releases thyroid hormone, increasing basal metabolic rate and heat production.
questions.title: Homeostasis

questions.q: How does the endocrine system contribute to correcting a fall in body temperature?
options: By releasing thyroid hormone, increasing basal metabolic rate and therefore heat production
By releasing insulin to raise glucose metabolism
By releasing glucagon to mobilise glycogen
By triggering shivering in skeletal muscle
By causing vasodilation in the skin
questions.explanation: The endocrine system releases thyroid hormone, and the resulting increase in basal metabolic rate produces increased heat production.
questions.title: Homeostasis

questions.q: Which cells of the islets of Langerhans secrete insulin and which secrete glucagon?
options: Beta cells secrete insulin in response to elevated blood glucose; alpha cells secrete glucagon in response to low blood glucose
Alpha cells secrete insulin; beta cells secrete glucagon
Delta cells secrete insulin; pp cells secrete glucagon
Beta cells secrete both insulin and glucagon
Alpha cells secrete both, depending on glucose level
questions.explanation: The islets of Langerhans are exquisitely sensitive to changes in blood glucose. Beta cells secrete insulin in response to elevated blood glucose and alpha cells secrete glucagon in response to low blood glucose.
questions.title: Homeostasis

questions.q: Which cell types make up the islets of Langerhans?
options: Alpha, beta, delta and pp cells
Alpha and beta cells only
Beta and delta cells only
Alpha, beta and gamma cells
Only beta cells
questions.explanation: The islets of Langerhans contain alpha cells, beta cells, delta cells and pp cells, and are exquisitely sensitive to changes in blood glucose.
questions.title: Homeostasis

questions.q: What determines how sensitive a homeostatic sensor needs to be?
options: The importance of the feature being regulated
The size of the organ containing it
The speed of the effector response
Whether the loop is positive or negative
The age of the individual
