questions.explanation: How sensitive the sensor needs to be in the body is determined by the importance of the feature being regulated. Blood glucose is held within a 2 mM range while ionised calcium is held within just 0.2 mM.
questions.title: Homeostasis

questions.q: Ionised calcium is regulated within 1.03 to 1.23 mM while blood glucose is regulated within 4 to 6 mM. What does this comparison show?
options: Calcium is held within a much narrower absolute range (0.2 mM) than glucose (2 mM), reflecting the tighter control its importance demands
Glucose is more tightly regulated than calcium
Both are regulated within identical ranges
Calcium regulation is less important than glucose regulation
Neither is under homeostatic control
questions.explanation: Blood glucose has a range of 2 mM (4 to 6 mM) whereas ionised calcium has a range of only 0.2 mM (1.03 to 1.23 mM), showing that more critical parameters require more sensitive sensors and tighter control.
questions.title: Homeostasis

questions.q: What is the purpose of all homeostatic systems, in terms of fluctuation?
options: To keep fluctuations small enough that they do not have an adverse effect
To eliminate all fluctuation completely
To maximise the range of tolerated values
To keep the value permanently above the set point
To allow the set point itself to drift freely
questions.explanation: The purpose of all homeostatic systems is to keep fluctuations small enough so that they do not have an adverse effect. If the control centre is effective, deviations either side of the set point will not compromise the internal environment.
questions.title: Homeostasis

questions.q: Body temperature varies for two distinct reasons. What are they?
options: Small oscillations around the set point, and changes in the set point itself
Sensor failure and effector failure
Positive feedback and negative feedback
Intrinsic regulation and disease
Measurement error and time of day only
questions.explanation: Body temperature can vary from moment to moment or day to day due to small oscillations around the set point and due to changes in the set point itself. Such variations occur in many extrinsic homeostatic systems, with the control centre in the higher brain centres.
questions.title: Homeostasis

questions.q: Where is the control centre for variations in extrinsic homeostatic systems?
options: In the higher brain centres
In the pancreas
In the peripheral tissues themselves
In the endocrine glands only
In the spinal cord
questions.explanation: Variations occur in many extrinsic homeostatic systems, and the control centre for these variations lies in the higher brain centres.
questions.title: Homeostasis

questions.q: According to the key points, which type of feedback do the vast majority of homeostatic regulatory systems use?
options: Negative feedback
Positive feedback
Feedforward control
Both equally
Neither; they use direct chemical control
questions.explanation: The vast majority of homeostatic regulatory systems utilise negative feedback, counteracting movement away from the set point. Positive feedback, such as in blood clotting, is the exception.
questions.title: Homeostasis

questions.q: In the example SAQ on blood glucose homeostasis, which pancreatic structure is central to the answer?
options: The Islets of Langerhans, with beta cells secreting insulin and alpha cells secreting glucagon
The exocrine acinar cells that release digestive enzymes
The hepatic portal vein only
The adrenal medulla
The hypothalamic thirst centre
questions.explanation: The example SAQ asks students to describe the role of the pancreatic Islets of Langerhans in regulating blood glucose. Beta cells secrete insulin in response to elevated glucose and alpha cells secrete glucagon in response to low glucose.
questions.title: Homeostasis

questions.q: A patient reports itching and swelling of the face after taking nitrofurantoin for a UTI. What is happening, and what is the treatment?
options: Life-threatening anaphylactic shock, treated with an epinephrine pen
A simple drug rash, treated with an oral antihistamine only
A urinary tract infection worsening, requiring a second antibiotic
Nitrofurantoin toxicity, treated by increasing fluid intake
An autoimmune reaction, treated with corticosteroids over several weeks
questions.explanation: This is life-threatening anaphylactic shock, an allergic reaction in which the immune system reacts to a substance as though it were harmful. An epi pen is administered, normally prescribed by a GP but in life-threatening cases administered by a pharmacist.
questions.title: Introduction to the Immune System

questions.q: Immunology is the discipline of medicine concerned with which areas?
options: The structure and function of the immune system, innate and acquired immunity, and the bodily distinction of self from non-self
The manufacture of vaccines only
The treatment of infectious disease with antibiotics
The genetics of inherited disease
The physiology of the lymphatic circulation only
questions.explanation: Immunology concerns the structure and function of the immune system, innate and acquired immunity, and the bodily distinction of self from non-self. Communication is key throughout.
questions.title: Introduction to the Immune System

questions.q: Which is an example of a physical or chemical barrier of innate immunity?
options: Lysozyme in tears, mucus membranes trapping microbes, and saliva and urine washing microbes away
Antibody secretion by plasma cells
T cell recognition of antigen
Complement fixation by IgM
Cytotoxic killing of virus-infected cells
questions.explanation: Physical and chemical barriers include skin, sebum, tears and sweat with lysozyme, mucus membranes lining the gastrointestinal, respiratory and genito-urinary tracts trapping microbes, ciliated epithelia, and saliva and urine washing microbes away.
questions.title: Introduction to the Immune System

questions.q: Which are the primary lymphoid tissues and what happens there?
options: Bone marrow for B cells and thymus for T cells; lymphocyte development and haematopoiesis
Spleen and lymph nodes; where adaptive responses are initiated
Tonsils and Peyer's patches; where antibody is secreted
Bone marrow and spleen; where antigen is presented
Thymus and lymph nodes; where lymphocytes congregate
questions.explanation: Primary lymphoid tissues are the bone marrow, for B cells, and the thymus, for T cells. They are the sites of lymphocyte development and haematopoiesis. Secondary lymphoid tissues, where lymphocytes congregate and adaptive responses are initiated, include spleen, lymph nodes, GALT with Peyer's patches, and tonsils.
questions.title: Introduction to the Immune System

questions.q: What are the two major roles of the thymus?
options: Secretion of growth factors to mature thymocytes into T-helper and T-cytotoxic cells, and exposure of thymocytes to self epitopes so that self-recognising T cells die by apoptosis
Production of antibodies and filtration of lymph
Storage of red blood cells and removal of old platelets
Secretion of complement proteins and acute phase proteins
Production of B cells and presentation of antigen to them
questions.explanation: The thymus secretes growth factors to mature thymocytes into T-helper and T-cytotoxic cells, and exposes thymocytes to self epitopes on the stroma so that T cells recognising self die via apoptosis. Its cortex is packed with immature thymocytes from the bone marrow.
questions.title: Introduction to the Immune System

questions.q: Which lymphoid organ is composed of red and white pulp?
options: Bursa of Fabricius
Lymph nodes
Spleen
Thymus
Mucosa associated lymphoid tissue
questions.explanation: The spleen is highly vascular and composed of red and white pulp. The white pulp is lymphoid tissue, with the periarterial sheath containing mostly T cells and the marginal zone containing many B cell follicles.
questions.title: Introduction to the Immune System

questions.q: How is a lymph node organised?
options: Cortex with dendritic cells presenting antigen and B cell follicles, paracortex with many T cells, and medulla where B cells secrete antibody
Red pulp and white pulp only
Cortex packed with thymocytes and a medulla of stroma
Follicles of lymphoid tissue with no defined regions
A single homogeneous mass of mixed lymphocytes
questions.explanation: Lymph nodes act as an immunological filter allowing contact between antigen and immune cells. They comprise a cortex with dendritic cells presenting antigen and B cell follicles where B cells proliferate, a paracortex with many T cells, and a medulla where B cells secrete antibody.
questions.title: Introduction to the Immune System

questions.q: Which structures are examples of mucosa associated lymphoid tissue (MALT)?
options: Tonsils, appendix and Peyer's patches
Thymus, bone marrow and spleen
Lymph nodes and lymphatic vessels
Skin, sebum and sweat glands
Liver, kidney and lung
questions.explanation: MALT consists largely of groupings of lymphoid follicles associated with mucosal tissue, and all MALT seems functionally linked. Examples are the tonsils, appendix and Peyer's patches.
questions.title: Introduction to the Immune System

questions.q: How do innate and adaptive immune responses differ?
options: Innate is inborn and non-specific; adaptive has memory and specificity and includes cell-mediated and antibody-mediated responses
Innate has memory and specificity; adaptive is non-specific
Innate acts only against viruses; adaptive only against bacteria
Innate involves only lymphocytes; adaptive only granulocytes
They are two names for the same response
questions.explanation: There are two main types of immune response: innate, which is inborn and non-specific, and adaptive, which has memory and specificity and includes cell-mediated and antibody-mediated responses.
questions.title: Introduction to the Immune System

questions.q: Which granulocyte is the predominant circulating cell and the first to arrive at a site of infection?
options: Neutrophil, about 60 per cent of circulating cells
Eosinophil, about 60 per cent of circulating cells
Basophil, about 40 per cent of circulating cells
Mast cell, about 30 per cent of circulating cells
Monocyte, about 60 per cent of circulating cells
questions.explanation: Neutrophils are the predominant cell, making up about 60 per cent of circulating cells. They are the first cells to arrive at the site of infection and engulf and destroy infectious agents.
questions.title: Introduction to the Immune System

questions.q: Which granulocyte contains major basic protein and eosinophil peroxidase and is important in parasitic infection?
options: Neutrophil
Eosinophil
Basophil
Mast cell
Monocyte
questions.explanation: Eosinophils contain cytoplasmic granules including major basic protein and eosinophil peroxidase, and are important for parasitic infections.
questions.title: Introduction to the Immune System

questions.q: Which cells contain histamines, cytokines and eicosanoids and are key to allergic reactions?
options: Neutrophils
Eosinophils
Mast cells
Natural killer cells
Plasma cells
questions.explanation: Mast cells contain histamines, cytokines and eicosanoids and are key to allergic reactions. Basophils are a minor population whose role is largely unknown but are thought to play a role in allergy through histamine release.
questions.title: Introduction to the Immune System

questions.q: Where do B lymphocytes develop and mature, and what happens after antigen exposure?
options: They develop in the bone marrow and mature in the spleen; after antigen exposure they proliferate and develop into plasma cells producing high levels of antibodies
They develop in the thymus and mature in lymph nodes; after antigen exposure they become cytotoxic
They develop in the spleen and mature in the bone marrow; they secrete antibody from birth
They develop in the liver and mature in the thymus; they present antigen to T cells
They develop in the tonsils and mature in Peyer's patches
questions.explanation: B lymphocytes, named after the bursa of Fabricius, develop in the bone marrow and mature in the spleen. Before antigen exposure they are naive or virgin and not yet producing antibody; after exposure they proliferate and develop into plasma cells producing high levels of antibody.
questions.title: Introduction to the Immune System

questions.q: What is the relationship between monocytes, macrophages and dendritic cells?
options: Monocytes are precursors of tissue macrophages and dendritic cells, infiltrating tissue at the site of infection and eliminating debris
Macrophages are precursors of monocytes and dendritic cells
Dendritic cells give rise to both monocytes and macrophages
They are unrelated lineages with no common precursor
Monocytes arise from mature macrophages in the tissues
questions.explanation: Monocytes are precursors of tissue macrophages and dendritic cells. They infiltrate tissue at the site of infection and eliminate debris. Macrophages phagocytose unwanted material and then present antigen to T cells.
questions.title: Introduction to the Immune System

questions.q: Why are dendritic cells described as highly efficient antigen presenting cells?
options: Because they have long dendrites that allow them to interact with numerous cells
Because they are the most abundant cell in the circulation
Because they secrete large amounts of antibody
Because they can kill target cells on contact
Because they mature in the thymus alongside T cells
questions.explanation: Dendritic cells have long dendrites and can interact with numerous cells, making them highly efficient antigen presenting cells. They may be derived from myeloid or lymphoid lineages.
questions.title: Introduction to the Immune System

questions.q: How do natural killer cells recognise their targets?
options: By low or absent MHC class I expression on the target cell
By high MHC class I expression on the target cell
By antibody bound to the target surface only
By the presence of a specific T cell receptor
By detecting bacterial peptidoglycan
questions.explanation: Natural killer cells are large lymphocyte-lineage cells that kill other cells on contact, killing tumour cells and some virus-infected cells. They recognise targets by low or no MHC class I expression.
questions.title: Introduction to the Immune System

questions.q: Which classes of mediator allow immune cells to communicate?
options: Lipid mediators such as eicosanoids, and polypeptide factors such as cytokines, complement and acute phase proteins
Only antibodies and complement
Only cytokines
Only direct cell-to-cell contact
Only nucleic acid signals
questions.explanation: For an effective immune system cells need to communicate. Mediators include lipid mediators such as eicosanoids (prostaglandins, leukotrienes, thromboxanes and platelet activating factors), and polypeptide factors including cytokines, complement and acute phase proteins.
questions.title: Introduction to the Immune System

questions.q: By which routes do cytokines signal?
options: Autocrine, paracrine or endocrine signalling
Only by direct cell contact
Only through the bloodstream
Only within the cell that produced them
Only via the lymphatic system
questions.explanation: Cytokines are critical elements of the immune response and act via autocrine, paracrine or endocrine signalling.
questions.title: Introduction to the Immune System

questions.q: How is an antigen defined?
options: An immunogen or hapten foreign to the body that evokes an immune response and can bind a product of that response such as an antibody or T cell
Any protein made by the body itself
A soluble protein that binds to a pathogen
The part of an antibody that binds the target
A cytokine released during inflammation
questions.explanation: An antigen is an immunogen or hapten foreign to the body that evokes an immune response, either alone or after forming a complex with a larger molecule such as a protein, and that is capable of binding a product of the immune response such as an antibody or T cell. It is the on-off switch of the immune system.
questions.title: Introduction to the Immune System

questions.q: What is an epitope?
options: The part of the antigen recognised by the immune response
The variable region of an antibody
The constant region of an antibody
The receptor on a B cell surface
A small antigen unable to provoke a response alone
questions.explanation: The parts of the antigen recognised by the immune response are called epitopes. The goodness of fit of the antigen to the antibody determines the strength of binding.
questions.title: Introduction to the Immune System

questions.q: Why does low affinity binding between an epitope and an antibody matter?
options: Because the antibody could then bind to another similar epitope, giving cross-reactivity
Because the antibody will be destroyed
Because it prevents any immune response occurring
Because the antigen becomes a hapten
Because the B cell will fail to mature
questions.explanation: If an epitope is a low affinity binder to an antibody, it is quite possible that antibody could bind to another, similar epitope, which is described as cross-reactivity.
questions.title: Introduction to the Immune System

questions.q: Which factors contribute to the immunogenicity of an antigen?
options: Size (greater than 1 kDa, otherwise a hapten), difference from self, dose, and class of molecule
Colour, solubility and melting point
Route of administration only
The patient's age and sex only
The presence of an adjuvant only
questions.explanation: Factors contributing to immunogenicity are size, needing to be greater than 1 kDa otherwise the molecule is a hapten, difference from self, dose, and class such as carbohydrate, lipid, nucleic acid or protein.
questions.title: Introduction to the Immune System

questions.q: Antibodies that vary in the variable region are called what?
options: Isotypes
Idiotypes
Epitopes
Haptens
Allotypes
questions.explanation: Antibodies which vary in the variable region are called idiotypes. Antibodies which vary in the constant region, such as the four IgG subtypes, are isotypes.
questions.title: Introduction to the Immune System

questions.q: Roughly how many amino acids do the variable regions of the heavy and light chains occupy?
options: About the first 11 amino acids
About the first 110 amino acids
About the first 500 amino acids
The entire chain
Only the last 20 amino acids
questions.explanation: The variable regions occupy about the first 110 amino acids of both the heavy and light chains.
questions.title: Introduction to the Immune System

questions.q: What is peculiar about the five antibody classes a B lymphocyte can produce?
options: It can produce all five classes but only one at a time, and switches in the order IgM, IgD, IgG, IgE, IgA
It can produce all five classes simultaneously
It can only ever produce one class for life
It switches randomly between classes
It produces IgG first and then reverts to IgM
questions.explanation: The different classes of antibody in humans are IgM, IgD, IgG, IgE and IgA. A B lymphocyte can produce all five classes, but only one at a time, and switches in that order.
questions.title: Introduction to the Immune System

questions.q: Which is the most abundant immunoglobulin in serum, and what are its functions?
options: IgG; transplacental transfer and milk, agglutination, complement activation, antibody dependent cytotoxicity, neutralisation and opsonisation
IgM; mucosal protection and neonatal defence
IgA; complement activation and opsonisation
IgE; transplacental transfer and agglutination
IgD; neutralisation and opsonisation
questions.explanation: IgG is the most abundant immunoglobulin in serum, with four subtypes. Its functions are transplacental transfer and transfer in milk, agglutination, activation of complement, antibody dependent cytotoxicity, neutralisation and opsonisation.
questions.title: Introduction to the Immune System

questions.q: In what two forms does IgM exist, and what is it particularly good at?
options: As a single IgG-like molecule on the B lymphocyte surface and as a pentamer in plasma; it is a very good agglutinator, perhaps 1000 times better than IgG
As a monomer and a dimer with a J chain; it protects the mucosa
Only as a pentamer; it mediates allergic responses
As a monomer in plasma and a trimer on cell surfaces; it opsonises bacteria
As two identical monomers; it crosses the placenta
questions.explanation: IgM exists on the surface of B lymphocytes as a single IgG-like molecule and in circulating plasma as a pentamer. It is a very good agglutinator of antigen, perhaps 1000 times better than IgG, and also provides foetal protection and activates complement.
questions.title: Introduction to the Immune System

questions.q: What is distinctive about IgA?
options: It exists as a monomer or dimer with a J-chain and is the only antibody secreted in any quantity across the mucosa, requiring a secretory piece that acts as a suicidal transporter
It is the most abundant antibody in serum
It exists as a pentamer and is the best agglutinator
It is the main antibody in asthma and allergy
It serves mainly as a B cell receptor and marker
questions.explanation: IgA exists as a monomer or a dimer with a J-chain. It protects the mucosa and is the only antibody which can be secreted in any quantity across the mucosa, requiring a secretory piece which acts as a suicidal transporter. It also provides neonatal protection from enteric pathogens.
questions.title: Introduction to the Immune System

questions.q: What is the major role of IgE?
options: A major role in asthma and allergy, and protection against parasitic infections such as helminths
Transplacental transfer to the foetus
Secretion across mucosal surfaces
Agglutination of antigen in plasma
Activation of basophils to release antimicrobial factors
questions.explanation: IgE is similar to IgG but longer. It has a major role in asthma and allergy and in protection against parasitic infections, particularly helminths.
questions.title: Introduction to the Immune System

questions.q: What roles does IgD have?
options: It is produced along with IgG, serves as a B cell receptor and marker, and activates basophils to release antimicrobial factors
It is the main antibody of the mucosal surfaces
It is the principal antibody of the allergic response
It is the most abundant serum immunoglobulin
It exists as a pentamer and fixes complement strongly
questions.explanation: IgD is produced along with IgG, also serves as a B cell receptor and marker, and activates basophils to release antimicrobial factors.
questions.title: Introduction to the Immune System

questions.q: How do lymphocytes recognise antigen?
options: Antigen binds to the B cell receptor or T cell receptor, allowing lymphocytes to proliferate and recognise the same antigen
Lymphocytes engulf antigen by phagocytosis
Antigen diffuses into the lymphocyte nucleus
Antigen is recognised only after complement binds it
Lymphocytes detect antigen by its molecular weight alone
questions.explanation: Antigen binds to the B cell receptor (BCR) or T cell receptor (TCR), allowing lymphocytes to proliferate and recognise the same antigen. Communication is central to the process.
questions.title: Introduction to the Immune System

questions.q: How does SARS-CoV-2 interfere with T cell-mediated immune responses?
options: By downregulating MHC class I and II molecules, restraining antigen presentation
By destroying all circulating B cells
By preventing IgA secretion at mucosal surfaces
By blocking complement activation
By inhibiting neutrophil migration
questions.explanation: SARS-CoV-2 restrains antigen presentation by downregulating MHC class I and II molecules, inhibiting T cell-mediated immune responses. Cytotoxic CD8+ T cells also exhibit functional exhaustion patterns.
questions.title: Introduction to the Immune System

questions.q: Which innate cell response is thought to contribute to excessive inflammation in COVID-19?
options: Macrophages showing significant production of IL-6
Neutrophils releasing major basic protein
Natural killer cells killing all infected cells
Mast cells releasing histamine
Eosinophils releasing peroxidase
questions.explanation: Innate immune cells such as macrophages may contribute to disease progression in COVID-19. Macrophages have shown significant production of IL-6, suggesting they may contribute to the excessive inflammation seen in the disease.
questions.title: Introduction to the Immune System

questions.q: Which arm of immunity is essential for SARS-CoV-2 virus clearance, and how do the humoral responses compare?
options: Adaptive immune responses are essential for clearance, and the specific IgA response appears stronger and more persistent than the IgM response
Innate immunity alone clears the virus, with IgM dominating
Adaptive immunity is irrelevant; clearance depends on macrophages
IgE responses are the most important for clearance
Complement alone is sufficient for clearance
questions.explanation: Adaptive immune responses are essential for SARS-CoV-2 virus clearance. Humoral immune responses play a role, and the specific IgA response appears to be stronger and more persistent than the IgM response.
questions.title: Introduction to the Immune System

questions.q: Which types of drug use the immune system to treat disease?
options: Monoclonal antibodies and anti-cytokine therapies
Beta-lactam antibiotics and antifungals
Diuretics and beta-blockers
Statins and antiplatelet agents
Proton pump inhibitors and antacids
questions.explanation: The immune system is important in many diseases and many drugs use it to treat conditions such as autoimmune diseases, cancer and allergic contact dermatitis. Such drugs include monoclonal antibodies and anti-cytokine therapies.
questions.title: Introduction to the Immune System

questions.q: Which topics are covered in the introduction to immunology lecture?
options: Only vaccine manufacture and antibiotic prescribing
Definition of immunology, function of the immune response, types of human immune responses, and principal components of the immune system
Genetics of inherited immunodeficiency only
Lymphatic drainage anatomy without immune function
Pharmacokinetics of monoclonal antibodies only
questions.explanation: The introduction covers the definition of immunology, the function of the immune response, the types of human immune responses, and the principal components of the immune system.
questions.title: Introduction to the Immune System

questions.q: Which cell groups are highlighted as requiring communication for an effective immune system?
options: Only erythrocytes and platelets
Granulocytes, mononuclear cells, macrophages, dendritic cells, natural killer cells and NK-T cells
Only B lymphocytes without other leucocytes
Only tissue fibroblasts and adipocytes
Only hepatocytes and renal tubular cells
questions.explanation: An effective immune system requires communication between many cells including granulocytes (neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils, mast cells), mononuclear cells (lymphocytes, monocytes), macrophages, dendritic cells, natural killer cells and NK-T cells.
questions.title: Introduction to the Immune System

questions.q: How are NK-T cells described in relation to other lymphocytes?
options: They are identical to plasma cells secreting IgG
They are similar to NK and T cells and are thought to react against microbial antigens
They are red blood cell precursors with no immune role
They are tissue macrophages that only phagocytose bacteria
They are exclusively involved in antibody class switching
questions.explanation: NK-T cells are similar to natural killer cells and T cells and are thought to react against microbial antigens, forming part of the communicating network of immune cells.
questions.title: Introduction to the Immune System

questions.q: Which summary points capture the core themes of the immune system lecture?
options: Only antibiotic resistance mechanisms in bacteria
Structure and function of the immune system, innate and acquired immunity, and the bodily distinction of self from non-self with communication as key
Only the pharmacology of antihistamines
Only the anatomy of the spleen without immune function
Only viral replication cycles in host cells
questions.explanation: The key points emphasise structure and function of the immune system, innate and acquired immunity, the bodily distinction of self from non-self, and that communication between immune cells is central.
questions.title: Introduction to the Immune System

questions.q: Innate immunity is described as targeting invading pathogens nonspecifically. Which type of defences does the example SAQ ask students to describe?
options: Five adaptive antibody responses only
Five physical barriers and mechanical defences protecting the human body against infection
Five cytotoxic T cell epitopes
Five complement cascade proteins
Five cytokine receptor subtypes
questions.explanation: The example SAQ asks students to describe five physical barriers and mechanical defences that protect the human body against infection, reflecting the nonspecific nature of innate immunity.
questions.title: Introduction to the Immune System

questions.q: Which of these is a way microbiology is relevant to pharmacy?
options: Manufacture of medicines, vaccine production, contamination of medicines and infection control
Only the treatment of infection with antibiotics
Only the production of vaccines
Only the calculation of drug doses
Only the storage temperature of medicines
questions.explanation: Microbiology is relevant to pharmacy through manufacture of medicines, vaccine production, assay organisms, mutagenic and carcinogenic activity, infection control, infection and fever, antibiotic resistance, contamination of medicines and product damage.
questions.title: Introduction to Microbiology 1

questions.q: Which historical figure disproved the theory of spontaneous generation and supported germ theory?
options: Robert Hooke
Antonie van Leeuwenhoek
Louis Pasteur
Carl Woese
Alexander Fleming
questions.explanation: Louis Pasteur supported germ theory and disproved the spontaneous generation theory. Robert Hooke was first to describe the microscopic world and van Leeuwenhoek first to describe single-celled organisms.
questions.title: Introduction to Microbiology 1

questions.q: Which agents are considered non-cellular and therefore non-living?
options: Bacteria and yeasts
Prions and viruses
Fungi and protozoa
Archaea and eubacteria
Mycoplasmas and chlamydiae
questions.explanation: Microbial agents are diverse, comprising cellular organisms such as bacteria and yeasts and non-cellular agents such as prions and viruses. Non-cellular agents are considered to be non-living.
questions.title: Introduction to Microbiology 1

questions.q: What size range do bacteria generally occupy, compared with red blood cells?
options: 0.2 to 2.0 microns in diameter and 2 to 8 microns long, against red cells at about 7.5 microns diameter
20 to 200 nm in diameter, against red cells at 7.5 microns
10 to 20 microns diameter, larger than red cells
0.2 to 2.0 nm diameter, far smaller than viruses
2 to 8 mm long, visible to the naked eye
questions.explanation: Red blood cells are approximately 7.5 microns in diameter. Bacteria generally range from 0.2 to 2.0 microns in diameter and 2 to 8 microns in length, while viruses range from 20 to 14,000 nm.
questions.title: Introduction to Microbiology 1

questions.q: What is the resolution of light microscopy?
options: Around 0.2 microns, or 200 nm
Around 0.002 microns, or 2 nm
Sub-nanometre resolution
Around 2 microns
Around 20 microns
questions.explanation: Light microscopy has a resolution of around 0.2 microns or 200 nm. Electron microscopy, of which various types are used depending on the sample, gives sub-nanometre resolution.
questions.title: Introduction to Microbiology 1

questions.q: Which statement about prions is correct?
options: They are small self-replicating proteins devoid of nucleic acid, derived from normal CNS membrane proteins with the same amino acid composition
They are the smallest known viruses, containing RNA only
They are bacteria lacking a cell wall
They are fungi that infect the nervous system
They are protein-coated DNA fragments
questions.explanation: Prions are small self-replicating proteins devoid of nucleic acid, derived from normal CNS membrane proteins with the same amino acid composition. They accumulate inside cells and cause diseases such as CJD and BSE.
questions.title: Introduction to Microbiology 1

questions.q: Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease is caused by which type of microbial agent?
options: Bacterium
Fungus
Protozoan
Prion
Virus
questions.explanation: CJD and variant CJD, along with BSE or mad cow disease, are caused by prions, self-replicating proteins devoid of nucleic acid.
questions.title: Introduction to Microbiology 1

questions.q: Which description of viruses is correct?
options: A nucleic acid genome packaged in a protein capsid, with no metabolic ability of their own, and not susceptible to antibiotics
Small cells with a plasma membrane and ribosomes but no nucleus
Self-replicating proteins with no nucleic acid
Organisms with both DNA and RNA genomes simultaneously
Cells that can only infect animals, not other microbes
questions.explanation: Viruses are not cellular. They are a nucleic acid genome packaged in a protective protein shell or capsid, with no metabolic ability of their own. The genome can be either DNA or RNA, all classes of organism including other microbes can be infected, and crucially they are not susceptible to antibiotics.
questions.title: Introduction to Microbiology 1

questions.q: What structural feature distinguishes enveloped from non-enveloped animal viruses?
options: Enveloped viruses such as HSV and VZV have a lipid envelope and tegument or matrix outside the capsid; non-enveloped viruses such as adenovirus and rhinovirus do not
Enveloped viruses have no capsid at all
Non-enveloped viruses carry a lipid bilayer around the genome
Enveloped viruses have DNA and non-enveloped have RNA
Enveloped viruses are always larger than 14,000 nm
questions.explanation: Enveloped animal viruses such as herpes simplex virus and varicella zoster virus have a viral genome in a protein capsid, surrounded by tegument or matrix and a lipid envelope. Non-enveloped viruses such as adenovirus and rhinovirus have only genome and capsid.
questions.title: Introduction to Microbiology 1

questions.q: What basic features do all cells possess?
options: A plasma membrane containing cytosol, chromosome(s) and ribosomes
A nucleus, mitochondria and a cell wall
A capsid, a genome and a lipid envelope
Peptidoglycan, flagella and pili
A nucleolus, histones and chloroplasts
questions.explanation: Cellular microorganisms consist of a single cell or clusters of cells. The basic features of all cells are a plasma membrane containing a semi-fluid substance called the cytosol, chromosome(s) and ribosomes.
questions.title: Introduction to Microbiology 1

questions.q: On what basis did Carl Woese devise the three domains of life classification?
options: Analysis of RNA genes, specifically 16S and 18S rRNA
Cell wall composition
Gram staining reaction
Cell size measured by electron microscopy
Whether the organism causes disease
questions.explanation: The three domains of life classification resulted from the work of Carl Woese and is based on analysis of RNA genes, specifically 16S and 18S rRNA. It is a widely accepted system.
questions.title: Introduction to Microbiology 1

questions.q: Which pair of features correctly distinguishes prokaryotes from eukaryotes?
options: Prokaryotes have nuclear material in the cytoplasm, no histones and usually one circular chromosome; eukaryotes have a membrane-enclosed true nucleus, histones and more than one chromosome
Prokaryotes have a true nucleus and histones; eukaryotes do not
Prokaryotes divide by mitosis; eukaryotes by binary fission
Prokaryotes have a nucleolus; eukaryotes do not
Prokaryotes have mitochondria; eukaryotes do not
questions.explanation: Prokaryotes keep nuclear material in the cytoplasm, lack histones and a nucleolus, divide by binary fission, reproduce asexually and usually have one circular chromosome with no mitochondria or chloroplasts. Eukaryotes have a true membrane-enclosed nucleus, histones, a nucleolus, mitosis and meiosis, and more than one chromosome.
questions.title: Introduction to Microbiology 1

questions.q: What is the ribosome size in prokaryotes compared with eukaryotes?
options: 70S in prokaryotes, 80S in eukaryotes (70S in organelles)
80S in prokaryotes, 70S in eukaryotes
70S in both
80S in both
60S in prokaryotes, 40S in eukaryotes
questions.explanation: Prokaryotes have 70S ribosomes, eukaryotes have 80S ribosomes with 70S in their organelles. This difference links directly to targets for antibiotics.
questions.title: Introduction to Microbiology 1

questions.q: How do prokaryotic and eukaryotic cell membranes and walls differ?
options: Prokaryote membranes lack sterols and their walls are usually peptidoglycan; eukaryote membranes contain sterols and their walls, when present, are cellulose or chitin
Prokaryote membranes contain sterols; eukaryote membranes do not
Both have peptidoglycan cell walls
Neither group has a cell wall
Prokaryote walls are cellulose; eukaryote walls are peptidoglycan
questions.explanation: Prokaryote cell membranes contain no sterols and their cell walls are usually peptidoglycan. Eukaryote membranes contain sterols and their cell walls, when present, are cellulose or chitin.
questions.title: Introduction to Microbiology 1

questions.q: How do prokaryotic and eukaryotic flagella differ?
options: Prokaryotic flagella are simple and composed of flagellin protein; eukaryotic flagella are complex with a 9 + 2 arrangement
Prokaryotic flagella have a 9 + 2 arrangement; eukaryotic are simple
Only eukaryotes have flagella
Only prokaryotes have flagella
Both are composed of flagellin in a 9 + 2 arrangement
questions.explanation: Prokaryotic flagella are simple, composed of flagellin protein. Eukaryotic flagella are complex with a 9 + 2 arrangement. Prokaryotes may have pili and fimbriae; eukaryotes have cilia instead.
questions.title: Introduction to Microbiology 1

questions.q: In the classification of Escherichia coli, which taxonomic levels are given?
options: Domain Bacteria, Kingdom Bacteria, Phylum Proteobacteria, Class gamma-Proteobacteria, Order Enterobacteriales, Family Enterobacteriaceae, Genus Escherichia, Species coli
Domain Eukarya, Kingdom Animalia, Phylum Chordata
Domain Archaea, Kingdom Bacteria, Phylum Firmicutes
Domain Bacteria, Kingdom Fungi, Phylum Proteobacteria
Domain Bacteria, Genus coli, Species Escherichia
questions.explanation: E. coli is classified as Domain Bacteria, Kingdom Bacteria, Phylum Proteobacteria, Class gamma-Proteobacteria, Order Enterobacteriales, Family Enterobacteriaceae, Genus Escherichia, Species coli, with genus and species being the most important levels to know.
questions.title: Introduction to Microbiology 1

questions.q: Which cell arrangement is correctly matched to its organism?
options: Clusters of Staphylococcus aureus, chains of Streptococcus, diplococci of Neisseria, tetrads of Micrococcus and octets of Sarcina
Chains of Staphylococcus and clusters of Streptococcus
Diplococci of Micrococcus and tetrads of Neisseria
Octets of Staphylococcus and clusters of Sarcina
All cocci occur only as single cells
questions.explanation: The arrangements given are clusters of Staphylococcus aureus, chains of Streptococcus sobrinus, Neisseria diplococci, tetrads of Micrococcus and octets of Sarcina.
questions.title: Introduction to Microbiology 1

questions.q: What determines whether bacteria are Gram-positive or Gram-negative?
options: The thickness of the peptidoglycan layer, which determines whether the crystal violet dye is retained
Whether the organism has flagella
The presence or absence of a capsule
The shape of the cell
Whether the organism forms endospores
questions.explanation: The Gram reaction reflects the ability of bacterial cells to retain or lose crystal violet dye, depending on the thickness of the peptidoglycan layer. A thick layer retains the dye and stains purple, designated Gram-positive; a thin layer does not retain it, designated Gram-negative.
questions.title: Introduction to Microbiology 1

questions.q: How is peptidoglycan constructed?
options: Alternating N-acetylglucosamine (NAG) and N-acetylmuramic acid (NAM) residues linked by beta-1,4 bonds, forming glycan chains cross-linked by short peptides
Alternating glucose and galactose linked by alpha-1,4 bonds
A single long chain of amino acids with no sugars
A lipid bilayer with embedded proteins
Repeating mycolic acid units cross-linked by sugars
questions.explanation: Peptidoglycan is a lattice-like polymeric macromolecule encasing the cytoplasmic membrane, with interlocking linear glycan chains cross-linked by short peptides. Its building block is the NAG-NAM monomer: alternating N-acetylglucosamine and N-acetylmuramic acid residues linked by beta-1,4 bonds.
questions.title: Introduction to Microbiology 1

questions.q: Which antibiotic classes and natural enzyme target peptidoglycan?
options: Beta-lactams and glycopeptides, and also lysozyme
Macrolides and aminoglycosides, and also amylase
Quinolones and rifamycins, and also lipase
Sulfonamides and trimethoprim, and also trypsin
Polyenes and azoles, and also protease
questions.explanation: Peptidoglycan is the target for some of the main classes of antibiotic, namely the beta-lactams and glycopeptides, and also for lysozyme.
questions.title: Introduction to Microbiology 1

questions.q: What is the role of penicillin-binding proteins in peptidoglycan synthesis?
options: They are enzymes catalysing the final steps of PGN synthesis, responsible for polymerisation and cross-linking into the existing cell wall
They transport PGN monomers across the membrane
They synthesise the NAG-NAM monomer in the cytosol
They degrade peptidoglycan during cell division
They bind penicillin and inactivate it
questions.explanation: Peptidoglycan monomers are synthesised in the cytosol and transported across the membrane by a lipid carrier. Penicillin-binding proteins are the enzymes catalysing the final steps of PGN synthesis, responsible for polymerisation and insertion into the existing cell wall by cross-linking.
questions.title: Introduction to Microbiology 1

questions.q: Why do beta-lactam antibiotics inhibit penicillin-binding proteins?
options: Because of the similarity between the natural substrate of PBPs, D-Ala-D-Ala, and the beta-lactam structure
Because beta-lactams dissolve the cell membrane
Because beta-lactams bind the NAG-NAM sugar directly
Because beta-lactams are transported by the same lipid carrier
Because beta-lactams inhibit ribosomal protein synthesis
questions.explanation: There is a similarity between the natural substrate of penicillin-binding proteins, D-Ala-D-Ala, and the beta-lactam antibiotics, which is why beta-lactams bind and inhibit these enzymes.
questions.title: Introduction to Microbiology 1

questions.q: Which statements about lipopolysaccharide in the Gram-negative outer membrane are correct?
options: LPS is synonymous with endotoxin, acts as a protective permeability barrier, and its lipid A is responsible for toxicity
LPS is found in the Gram-positive cell wall and is non-toxic
LPS is the same as peptidoglycan
The O antigen is responsible for toxicity and lipid A is immunogenic
LPS has an invariant structure across all species
questions.explanation: The Gram-negative outer membrane features lipopolysaccharide, synonymous with endotoxin. It has variable structure, forms a protective permeability barrier, and lipid A is responsible for toxicity. Lipid A links to core oligosaccharides via ketodeoxyoctonate, and the O antigen outer polysaccharide is highly variable, as in E. coli O157:H7.
questions.title: Introduction to Microbiology 1

questions.q: What is distinctive about the mycobacterial cell wall?
options: In addition to peptidoglycan it contains long chain fatty acids called mycolic acids, essential for growth, giving a waxy wall difficult to Gram stain
It contains no peptidoglycan at all
It is composed entirely of lipopolysaccharide
It has an unusually thin peptidoglycan layer that stains readily
It contains cellulose instead of peptidoglycan
questions.explanation: Mycobacteria cause diseases such as TB and leprosy. In addition to peptidoglycan, their cell wall contains long chain fatty acids called mycolic acids, essential for growth. The waxy cell wall is difficult to Gram stain and requires a specialist stain.
questions.title: Introduction to Microbiology 1

questions.q: How are bacterial flagella constructed and what is their function?
options: Helical filaments of flagellin protein, each with a rotary motor at its base, used for motility
Rigid protein tubes used to adhere to surfaces
Hair-like structures used for conjugation
Polysaccharide layers used for protection
Contractile fibres of actin used for crawling
questions.explanation: Flagella are used for motility and are helical filaments of the protein flagellin, each with a rotary motor at its base. They are found on some bacilli and spiral-form bacteria, with different arrangements such as polar monotrichous, amphitrichous and lophotrichous.
questions.title: Introduction to Microbiology 1

questions.q: How do fimbriae and pili differ in function?
options: Fimbriae are used to adhere to surfaces; pili are mainly involved in conjugation, such as the F pilus, and in movement via type IV pili
Fimbriae are used for conjugation; pili for adhesion
Both are used only for motility
Both are used only for conjugation
Fimbriae transport nutrients; pili anchor the cell wall
questions.explanation: Fimbriae and pili are fragile hair-like structures on prokaryotic cells, present on many Gram-negative and some Gram-positive bacteria. Fimbriae are used to adhere to surfaces, while pili are mainly involved in conjugation, for example the F pilus, and in movement through type IV pili.
questions.title: Introduction to Microbiology 1

questions.q: What is extracellular polymeric substance (EPS), and in what forms does it occur?
options: Material produced by many Gram-negative, some Gram-positive and most pathogenic mycobacteria, occurring as capsules, slime layers and biofilms with protective functions
The peptidoglycan layer of the cell wall
The lipid A component of endotoxin
The flagellin protein of flagella
The genetic material carried in plasmids
questions.explanation: Many Gram-negative bacteria, some Gram-positive bacteria and most pathogenic mycobacteria produce extracellular polymeric substance in the form of capsules, slime layers and biofilms. These have various protective functions and are sometimes associated with increased severity of disease.
questions.title: Introduction to Microbiology 1

questions.q: Which statement about bacterial endospores is correct?
options: They are resistant survival forms produced by genera such as Bacillus and Clostridium, more resistant than vegetative cells, and are not a means of reproduction
They are the normal means of bacterial reproduction
They are less resistant to heat than vegetative cells
They are produced by all bacterial species
They germinate only under unfavourable conditions
questions.explanation: Endospores are resistant survival forms produced by some bacteria such as Bacillus and Clostridium species. They show higher resistance to heat, some chemicals and UV than vegetative cells, surviving boiling for 15 minutes to 7 hours. Favourable conditions cause germination back into vegetative cells, and they are not a means of reproduction.
questions.title: Introduction to Microbiology 1

questions.q: Which structural components appear in the diagram of a bacterial cell?
options: Capsule, flagellum, plasmid, ribosomes, storage granule, nucleoid chromosome, plasma membrane, fimbria, cytoplasm, cell wall and pilus
Nucleus, mitochondria, Golgi apparatus and endoplasmic reticulum
Capsid, envelope and viral genome
Cortex, medulla and stroma
Cell cortex, microtubules and intermediate filaments
questions.explanation: The structural features of a bacterial cell shown are capsule, flagellum, plasmid, ribosomes, storage granule or other inclusion body, chromosome (nucleoid), plasma membrane, fimbria, cytoplasm, cell wall and pilus.
questions.title: Introduction to Microbiology 1

questions.q: In order of increasing complexity, how are microbial agents ranked?
options: Non-cellular agents (viroids, prions, then viruses), then prokaryotic organisms (chlamydiae, rickettsiae, mycoplasmas, other bacteria and archaea), then eukaryotic organisms (fungi and protozoa)
Eukaryotic organisms, then prokaryotic organisms, then non-cellular agents
Bacteria, then viruses, then prions
Fungi, then bacteria, then archaea
All microbial agents are of equal complexity
questions.explanation: Microbial diversity in order of increasing complexity runs from non-cellular agents (viroids and prions, then viruses), through prokaryotic organisms (chlamydiae, rickettsiae, mycoplasmas, other bacteria and archaea), to eukaryotic organisms (fungi and protozoa).
questions.title: Introduction to Microbiology 1

questions.q: What is the main function of the prokaryotic cell wall?
options: Structural integrity, though it also confers shape on the cell
Selective transport of nutrients
Storage of genetic material
Generation of ATP
Adhesion to host surfaces
questions.explanation: Prokaryotes fall into two groups, the true bacteria (eubacteria) and archaea. Most have a cell wall in addition to the plasma membrane, whose main function is structural integrity, though it also confers shape on the cells.
questions.title: Introduction to Microbiology 1

questions.q: Which four basic bacterial forms are described?
options: Cocci, rods (bacilli), spirals and curved rods
Cocci, cubes, spirals and stars
Rods, filaments, spheres and discs
Bacilli, hyphae, spores and cysts
Cocci, capsules, flagella and fimbriae
questions.explanation: The bacterial forms illustrated are cocci, rods (bacilli), spirals such as Borrelia burgdorferi, and curved rods.
questions.title: Introduction to Microbiology 1

questions.q: The 'Good, The Bad & The Ugly' slide illustrates that microorganisms can be:
options: Exclusively harmful parasites with no beneficial roles
Beneficial (e.g. gut microbiome), harmful parasites (e.g. hookworm) and dangerous pathogens (e.g. Ebola virus)
Only visible with electron microscopy
Only found in soil and never in humans
Always killed by standard antiseptics
questions.explanation: Microorganisms span beneficial roles such as the gut microbiome, harmful parasites such as hookworm, and dangerous pathogens such as the Ebola virus, illustrating the diversity of microbial impacts on health.
questions.title: Introduction to Microbiology 1

questions.q: Which patient-related aspects of microbiology are emphasised for pharmacists?
options: Only industrial fermentation economics
How infection occurs (pathogenicity, transmission), how to prevent infection (vaccines, infection control), and how to treat infection (antibiotics)
Only cosmetic formulation stability
Only plant taxonomy for herbal medicines
Only the history of spontaneous generation theory
questions.explanation: Microbiology and the patient covers how infection occurs through microbial pathogenicity and transmission, how to prevent infection with vaccines and infection control measures, and how to treat infection with antibiotics.
questions.title: Introduction to Microbiology 1

questions.q: How are micrometre and nanometre defined in relation to each other?
options: 1 micrometre equals 1000 nanometres; 1 nanometre is one thousandth of a micrometre (1 x 10^-9 m)
1 micrometre equals 1 nanometre
1 nanometre equals 1 millimetre
A micrometre is larger than a millimetre
A nanometre is one thousand times larger than a micrometre
questions.explanation: One micrometre is one thousandth of a millimetre (1 x 10^-6 m). One nanometre is one thousandth of a micrometre (1 x 10^-9 m), so 1 micrometre equals 1000 nanometres.
questions.title: Introduction to Microbiology 1

questions.q: If an Escherichia coli cell about 2 micrometres long divides every 20 minutes for 24 hours, what does the lecture illustrate about bacterial growth?
options: Bacteria cannot divide more than once per day
Exponential division can produce astronomical numbers of cells and vast cumulative length over 24 hours
E. coli always remains a single cell in culture
Division stops after exactly ten generations
Bacterial length shrinks with each division
questions.explanation: The E. coli thought experiment shows that repeated division every 20 minutes over 24 hours would produce an enormous number of cells whose end-to-end length could circle the Earth and reach the Moon many times, illustrating the power of exponential microbial growth.
questions.title: Introduction to Microbiology 1

questions.q: What distinguishes eukaryotic cells from prokaryotic cells?
options: Eukaryotic cells lack DNA entirely
Eukaryotic cells contain a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles; prokaryotic cells lack a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles
Prokaryotic cells always have a nucleus
Only prokaryotes possess ribosomes
Eukaryotic cells never have a cell membrane
questions.explanation: Eukaryotic cells contain a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles, whereas prokaryotic cells lack a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles. This fundamental distinction underpins microbial classification.
questions.title: Introduction to Microbiology 1

questions.q: Which key points summarise the microbiology lecture for pharmacy students?
options: Microbiology is irrelevant to pharmacy practice

Microbiology relates to medicine manufacture, product safety, infection prevention and treatment, and infection control; microorganisms are diverse; bacterial structures such as flagella and peptidoglycan influence treatment
Only viruses matter in pharmacy with no role for bacteria
All microorganisms are identical in structure and treatment
Peptidoglycan is found in human cell walls and is not an antibiotic target
questions.explanation: Key points include microbiology's role in manufacture, safety, prevention and treatment of infection, the diversity of microorganisms, bacterial structures for movement and adhesion, and peptidoglycan in the bacterial cell wall as a key antibiotic target.
questions.title: Introduction to Microbiology 1

questions.q: Which statements about fungi are correct?
options: They are eukaryotic organisms with a cell wall that contains no peptidoglycan, and only a few species are pathogenic to humans, mostly opportunists
They are prokaryotic organisms with a peptidoglycan cell wall
They are non-cellular agents like viruses
All 1.5 million species are pathogenic to humans
They have no cell wall at all
questions.explanation: Fungi are eukaryotic organisms with a cell wall but no peptidoglycan. There are over 1.5 million species including yeasts and moulds, but only a few are pathogenic to humans and most are opportunists rather than obligate parasites.
questions.title: Introduction to Microbiology 2

questions.q: Which are diseases caused by fungi (mycoses)?
options: Thrush, histoplasmosis and aspergillosis
Typhus, Q-fever and trench fever
Trachoma and non-specific urethritis
CJD and BSE
Cholera and the Black Death
questions.explanation: Fungi cause mycoses such as thrush, histoplasmosis and aspergillosis, often with predisposing conditions such as AIDS. They can also cause spoilage of pharmaceuticals and food.
questions.title: Introduction to Microbiology 2

questions.q: Which features characterise protozoa?
options: A large heterogeneous group of eukaryotic microorganisms with no cell wall, pleiomorphic, typically categorised by their method of locomotion
Prokaryotic organisms with a chitin cell wall
Non-cellular agents with a protein capsid
Organisms with a peptidoglycan cell wall and flagella
Obligate intracellular parasites with a dimorphic life cycle
questions.explanation: Protozoa are a large heterogeneous group of eukaryotic microorganisms with no cell wall and are pleiomorphic. They are typically categorised according to their method of locomotion.
questions.title: Introduction to Microbiology 2

questions.q: Which four groups of protozoa cause most human disease?
options: Amoeboid, flagellated, ciliated protozoa and sporozoans
Yeasts, moulds, dimorphic fungi and dermatophytes
Chlamydiae, rickettsiae, mycoplasmas and mycobacteria
Cocci, bacilli, spirals and curved rods
Prions, viroids, viruses and bacteriophages
questions.explanation: The four groups of protozoa that cause most human disease are amoeboid protozoa, flagellated protozoa, ciliated protozoa and sporozoans.
questions.title: Introduction to Microbiology 2

questions.q: What was the miasma theory of disease?
options: That disease such as cholera or the Black Death is caused by poisonous or bad air; it was the predominant theory before germ theory emerged
That disease is caused by demons possessing the victim
That disease is punishment from a vengeful god
That specific microorganisms cause specific diseases
That disease arises spontaneously from decaying matter
questions.explanation: The miasma theory held that disease such as cholera or the Black Death is caused by miasma, poisonous or bad air. It was the predominant theory of disease transmission before germ theory emerged, alongside the demonic and punitive theories.
questions.title: Introduction to Microbiology 2

questions.q: What is the germ theory of disease, and who proved it?
options: The concept that microorganisms cause disease and specific microorganisms cause specific diseases, proven by the laboratory work of Pasteur in the 1860s and Robert Koch in the 1870s
The concept that bad air causes disease, proven by Semmelweis
The concept that disease arises spontaneously, proven by Fracastoro
The concept that all microorganisms are pathogenic, proven by Henle
The concept that disease is inherited, proven by Koch
questions.explanation: The germ theory is the concept that microorganisms cause disease and that specific microorganisms cause specific diseases. It was proven by the laboratory work of Pasteur in the 1860s and Robert Koch in the 1870s, who observed the same microorganisms in all blood samples from infected animals.
questions.title: Introduction to Microbiology 2

questions.q: What was Ignaz Semmelweis's contribution?
options: He identified the cause of puerperal (childbed) fever and introduced antisepsis into medical practice
He first described single-celled organisms
He proposed that invisible particles transmit disease person to person
He wrote 'On Miasma and Contagia'
He devised the three domains of life
questions.explanation: Ignaz Semmelweis (1818-1865) identified the cause of puerperal or childbed fever and introduced antisepsis into medical practice. Fracastoro proposed transmission by minute invisible particles and Friedrich Henle wrote 'On Miasma and Contagia' in 1840.
questions.title: Introduction to Microbiology 2

questions.q: How does a pathogen differ from an opportunistic pathogen?
options: A pathogen can cause infection in individuals with normal host defences; an opportunist causes infection only in those with abnormal or compromised defences
A pathogen infects only compromised hosts; an opportunist infects healthy hosts
A pathogen is always a virus; an opportunist is always a bacterium
A pathogen is part of the normal flora; an opportunist is not
There is no meaningful difference between them
questions.explanation: A pathogen is an organism that can cause infection in individuals with normal host defences, such as Salmonella typhi or Chlamydia trachomatis. An opportunistic pathogen causes infection in individuals with abnormal or compromised host defences.
questions.title: Introduction to Microbiology 2

questions.q: What is a commensal?
options: An organism found normally on parts of the body exposed to, or communicating with, the external environment
An organism that always causes disease
An organism that lives only inside host cells
An organism that can survive only in the laboratory
An organism found only in the bloodstream
questions.explanation: A commensal is an organism found normally on parts of the body exposed to, or communicating with, the external environment, for example Bacteroides fragilis and Staphylococcus epidermidis.
questions.title: Introduction to Microbiology 2

questions.q: What proportion of microbes is pathogenic?
options: Very few are always pathogenic, many are potentially pathogenic opportunists, and most are never pathogenic
Most are always pathogenic and few are harmless
All microbes are potentially pathogenic
Exactly half are pathogenic and half are commensals
None are pathogenic unless the host is immunocompromised
questions.explanation: Very few microbes are always pathogenic. Many are potentially pathogenic, that is opportunistic pathogens, and most are never pathogenic.
questions.title: Introduction to Microbiology 2

questions.q: Which organisms are part of the normal skin microflora?
options: Staphylococcus epidermidis, Cutibacterium acnes and Pityrosporum ovale
Escherichia coli, Enterobacter and Bacteroides species
Streptococcus mitis and Haemophilus influenzae only
Lactobacillus species and Candida albicans only
Clostridium species and Bifidobacterium bifidum
questions.explanation: The normal skin microflora includes Staphylococcus epidermidis, Cutibacterium acnes and Pityrosporum ovale. The intestine carries organisms such as E. coli, Enterobacter and Bacteroides species, and the urogenital tract Lactobacillus species and Candida albicans.
questions.title: Introduction to Microbiology 2

questions.q: How can the normal microflora change over time?
options: With changes in hormonal physiology and development, when antibiotic usage selects for a resistant flora, and when new organisms are acquired
It is fixed from birth and never changes
Only through dietary change
Only through travel to other countries
Only in people who are immunocompromised
questions.explanation: Changes may occur with changes in hormonal physiology and development, when antibiotic usage selects for a resistant flora, and when new organisms are acquired, for example by neonates at birth, Gram-negative colonisation of gut and upper respiratory tract in hospitalised patients, and cross-infection with C. difficile, MRSA or VRE.
questions.title: Introduction to Microbiology 2

questions.q: Which is a benefit derived from the normal microflora?
options: Preventing colonisation by pathogenic species, known as colonisation resistance
Direct killing of all incoming viruses
Production of antibiotics that sterilise the gut
Absorption of drugs across the intestinal wall
Regulation of body temperature
questions.explanation: Benefits include preventing colonisation by pathogenic species (colonisation resistance), synthesis and excretion of some vitamins, stimulating development of certain tissues, and being antigenic, stimulating an immunological response with some cross-reactivity against pathogenic species.
questions.title: Introduction to Microbiology 2

questions.q: Which of these body sites is normally free of microflora?
options: Blood, cerebrospinal fluid, middle and inner ear, and urine in the kidneys and bladder
The mouth and upper respiratory tract
The skin and urogenital tract
The large intestine and rectum
The nasal sinuses and the oral cavity
questions.explanation: Areas normally free of a microflora include internal tissues and organs such as the middle and inner ear, sinuses, internal eye, bone marrow, muscles, glands, ovaries and testes, brain and spinal cord, and body fluids such as blood, cerebrospinal fluid, saliva before excretion, urine in the kidneys and bladder, and semen before entry to the urethra.
questions.title: Introduction to Microbiology 2

questions.q: Contamination of central venous catheters with S. epidermidis and Candida overgrowth after antibiotics both illustrate what?
options: That normal flora can be problematic if in the wrong location or if the balance is lost
That all commensals are actually pathogens
That antibiotics are ineffective against normal flora
That catheters should never be used
That Candida is always an obligate pathogen
questions.explanation: Examples of what happens when the normal microflora is lost or displaced include contamination of central venous catheters with S. epidermidis, E. coli biofilm on urinary catheters and overgrowth of Candida following antibiotic treatment. Normal flora can be problematic if in the wrong location.
questions.title: Introduction to Microbiology 2

questions.q: What is the difference between colonisation and infection?
options: In colonisation microorganisms are present at a body site but cause no harm or symptoms; in infection a microorganism invades and multiplies leading to signs and symptoms
In colonisation the organism is always pathogenic; in infection it is always a commensal
Colonisation occurs only in hospital; infection only in the community
Colonisation involves viruses and infection involves bacteria
They describe the same process at different times
questions.explanation: In colonisation microorganisms, which may be pathogenic, are present at a body site but no harm or symptoms of infection result. In infection a microorganism invades and multiplies in the host leading to signs and symptoms of infection.
questions.title: Introduction to Microbiology 2

questions.q: Which step is part of the infection cycle?
options: Maintaining a reservoir, transport to the host, adhering to and invading the host, evading host defences, multiplying, damaging the host, and leaving the host
Only entering the host and multiplying
Only producing toxins and leaving
Only adhering to surfaces
Only surviving outside the host
questions.explanation: The infection cycle requires the organism to maintain a reservoir, be transported to the host, adhere to, colonise or invade the host, initially evade host defences, multiply or complete its life cycle on or in the host, have the potential to damage the host, and leave the host to return to the reservoir or enter a new host.
questions.title: Introduction to Microbiology 2

questions.q: How do prions reproduce?
options: They accumulate and convert pre-existing normal forms of the protein to their abnormal form, so they reproduce without making new copies of themselves
They replicate their nucleic acid inside host cells
They divide by binary fission
They assemble new protein from amino acids in the cytosol
They insert their genome into host DNA
questions.explanation: Prions are non-cellular, derived from normal membrane proteins of the CNS. They accumulate and convert pre-existing normal forms of the protein to their abnormal form, so they reproduce without making new copies of themselves.
questions.title: Introduction to Microbiology 2

questions.q: What are the six steps of the viral infection process?
options: Attachment, fusion, uncoating, gene expression and replication, assembly, and release of new virus particles
Adhesion, invasion, multiplication, toxin release, damage and exit
Binding, endospore formation, germination, growth, division and lysis
Colonisation, infection, dissemination, latency, reactivation and clearance
Elementary body formation, entry, conversion, replication, reconversion and release
questions.explanation: To infect a host a virus must first enter cells at a body surface. The infection process comprises attachment, fusion, virus uncoating, gene expression and replication, assembly, and release of new virus particles, and requires the availability of relevant receptors.
questions.title: Introduction to Microbiology 2

questions.q: What are the three patterns of viral disease described?
options: Acute, where the virus rapidly kills cells; latent, a dormant infection with episodic reactivation; and chronic or persistent, a long-term infection without immediate cell death
Superficial, subcutaneous and systemic
Colonisation, infection and clearance
Elementary, reticulate and inclusion
Primary, secondary and tertiary
questions.explanation: Viral diseases can be acute, where the virus rapidly kills cells with rapid onset, often self-limiting but sometimes fatal; latent or reactivating, a dormant infection with episodic reactivation; or chronic and persistent, a long-term infection with no immediate cell death.
questions.title: Introduction to Microbiology 2

questions.q: What is virus tropism?
options: The tendency of viruses to exhibit cellular, tissue and host or species specificity
The rate at which a virus replicates
The ability of a virus to survive outside the host
The mechanism by which a virus releases new particles
The number of receptors a virus requires
questions.explanation: Viruses exhibit cellular, tissue and host or species tropisms, meaning they infect only particular cells, tissues and species, determined largely by the availability of relevant receptors.
questions.title: Introduction to Microbiology 2

questions.q: Which features describe Chlamydiae?
options: Obligate intracellular parasites with limited metabolic capabilities, small prokaryotic cells staining weakly Gram-negative, with an outer LPS membrane but no detectable peptidoglycan
Free-living prokaryotes with a thick peptidoglycan wall
Eukaryotic organisms with a chitin wall
Non-cellular agents with a protein capsid
Obligate intracellular organisms with abundant peptidoglycan
questions.explanation: Chlamydiae are obligate intracellular parasites that can only grow inside host cells, with limited metabolic capabilities. They are small prokaryotic cells staining weakly Gram-negative, with a cell wall containing an outer lipopolysaccharide membrane but no detectable peptidoglycan.
questions.title: Introduction to Microbiology 2

questions.q: In the dimorphic chlamydial life cycle, what is the role of the elementary body?
options: It is required for infection and can survive outside the host cell
It is required for replication inside the host cell but cannot survive outside
It is the mature inclusion within the host cell
It is the form that produces toxin
It is the extracellular resting spore
questions.explanation: Chlamydiae have a dimorphic life cycle. The elementary body is required for infection and can survive outside the host cell. The reticulate body is required for replication inside the host cell but cannot survive outside or initiate infection.
questions.title: Introduction to Microbiology 2

questions.q: Which chlamydial species is thought to be a very common cause of community-acquired pneumonia?
options: Chlamydia trachomatis
Chlamydia pneumoniae
Chlamydia psittaci
Rickettsia rickettsii
Mycoplasma pneumoniae
questions.explanation: Chlamydia pneumoniae causes respiratory tract infections and is thought to be a very common cause of community-acquired pneumonia. C. trachomatis causes urogenital and ocular infections including trachoma, and C. psittaci is a zoonotic cause of human respiratory infection.
questions.title: Introduction to Microbiology 2

questions.q: How do Rickettsiae differ from Chlamydiae?
options: Rickettsiae are obligate intracellular pathogens but are not dimorphic, can survive outside the cell, and contain peptidoglycan in their cell wall
Rickettsiae are free-living whereas Chlamydiae are intracellular
Rickettsiae lack peptidoglycan whereas Chlamydiae have it
Rickettsiae are eukaryotic whereas Chlamydiae are prokaryotic
Rickettsiae have a dimorphic life cycle whereas Chlamydiae do not
questions.explanation: Rickettsiae are obligate intracellular pathogens but are not dimorphic and can survive outside the cell. They are similar in structure to Gram-negative bacteria and contain peptidoglycan in their cell wall, unlike Chlamydiae.
questions.title: Introduction to Microbiology 2

questions.q: Which disease is correctly matched to its organism?
options: Rickettsia rickettsii causes Rocky Mountain spotted fever; Coxiella burnetii causes Q-fever; Bartonella species cause cat-scratch and trench fever
Rickettsia typhi causes Q-fever; Coxiella burnetii causes typhus
Bartonella causes scrub typhus; Orientia tsutsugamushi causes trench fever
Rickettsia prowazekii causes cat-scratch fever
Coxiella burnetii causes Rocky Mountain spotted fever
questions.explanation: Rickettsia typhi and R. prowazekii cause typhus, Orientia tsutsugamushi scrub typhus, and Rickettsia rickettsii Rocky Mountain spotted fever. Related organisms include Bartonella species (cat-scratch fever, trench fever) and Coxiella burnetii (Q-fever).
questions.title: Introduction to Microbiology 2

questions.q: How may Mycoplasmas be described?
options: Free-living microorganisms without peptidoglycan in the cell wall
Free-living microorganisms with a chitin-containing cell wall
Free-living microorganisms with peptidoglycan in the cell wall
Obligate intracellular microorganisms without peptidoglycan in the cell wall
Obligate intracellular microorganisms with peptidoglycan in the cell wall
questions.explanation: Mycoplasmas are the smallest free-living prokaryotic cells and most species are extracellular pathogens. Their cell walls lack peptidoglycan, consisting of single cell membranes coated in carbohydrates with sterols in the membrane.
questions.title: Introduction to Microbiology 2

questions.q: Why can Mycoplasma pneumoniae not be treated with cell wall active antibiotics?
options: Because its cell wall lacks peptidoglycan, so it can only be treated with agents such as tetracycline or erythromycin
Because it grows only inside host cells where antibiotics cannot reach
Because it has an unusually thick peptidoglycan layer
Because it forms endospores that resist antibiotics
Because it is a eukaryotic organism
questions.explanation: Mycoplasma cell walls lack peptidoglycan, so antibiotics acting on the cell wall are ineffective. Mycoplasma pneumoniae, which causes genital infections, atypical pneumonia and joint and inflammatory conditions, can be treated with some antibiotics such as tetracycline or erythromycin.
questions.title: Introduction to Microbiology 2

questions.q: Besides lacking peptidoglycan, which features characterise Mycoplasmas?
options: Fastidious nutritional requirements, gliding motility and a tip organelle facilitating adhesion
Flagella for swimming and endospores for survival
A dimorphic life cycle with elementary and reticulate bodies
Mycolic acids and a waxy cell wall
An outer lipopolysaccharide membrane with lipid A
questions.explanation: Mycoplasmas are fastidious in their nutritional requirements, show gliding motility and have a tip organelle to facilitate adhesion. They are also a problematic contaminant of cell culture.
questions.title: Introduction to Microbiology 2

questions.q: On what three factors does bacterial pathogenesis depend?
options: The immune status of the host, the nature of the species or strain (virulence factors), and the number of organisms in the initial exposure
The temperature, pH and oxygen level of the site
The age, sex and weight of the patient only
The antibiotic used, the dose and the duration
The Gram reaction, the cell shape and the arrangement
questions.explanation: A relatively limited number of bacterial species cause the majority of infectious diseases in healthy individuals. Pathogenesis is multifactorial, depending on the immune status of the host, the nature of the species or strain in terms of virulence factors, and the number of organisms in the initial exposure.
questions.title: Introduction to Microbiology 2

questions.q: Which are examples of virulence factors?
options: Adhesins, invasins and toxins
Ribosomes, plasmids and chromosomes
Peptidoglycan, sterols and chitin
Elementary bodies and reticulate bodies
Endospores and vegetative cells
questions.explanation: Virulence factors contribute to a pathogen's ability to cause disease, and examples given are adhesins, invasins and toxins.
questions.title: Introduction to Microbiology 2

questions.q: How is fungal disease classified by tissue involvement?
options: Superficial or mucocutaneous, subcutaneous, and systemic or invasive
Acute, latent and chronic
Colonisation, infection and dissemination
Primary, opportunistic and commensal
Elementary, reticulate and inclusion
questions.explanation: Fungal disease is often classified by tissue involvement and mode of entry: superficial or mucocutaneous, localised to skin, hair, nails and mucous membranes; subcutaneous, confined to dermis, subcutaneous tissue or adjacent structures; and systemic or invasive, deep infections of internal organs.
questions.title: Introduction to Microbiology 2

questions.q: Of approximately 1.5 million fungal species, about how many are known to cause human disease?
options: About 30
About 300
About 3,000
About 30,000
About 300,000
questions.explanation: There are around 1.5 million different species of fungi, but only about 300 are known to cause human disease, and rarely in healthy immunocompetent hosts.
questions.title: Introduction to Microbiology 2

questions.q: On what is resistance to fungal infection primarily based?
options: Cutaneous and mucosal physical barriers
Circulating antibody alone
Complement activation
Natural killer cell activity
The normal gut microflora
questions.explanation: Resistance to fungi is based primarily upon cutaneous and mucosal physical barriers. Fungal infections are often caused by fungi common in the environment and are often persistent and difficult to treat.
questions.title: Introduction to Microbiology 2

questions.q: Which bacterial morphological forms are described in the lecture?
options: Cocci, rods (bacilli), spirals and curved rods
Only cocci and bacilli
Only spirals and curved rods
Yeasts, moulds and dimorphic fungi
Prions and viroids
questions.explanation: The lecture illustrates bacterial forms including cocci, rods (bacilli), spirals and curved rods, with examples such as biofilm-forming rods and spiral Borrelia burgdorferi.
questions.title: Introduction to Microbiology 2

questions.q: Which cell arrangement is illustrated by chains of Streptococcus sobrinus?
options: Streptococcal chains
Staphylococcal clusters
Diplococci
Tetrads
Octets
questions.explanation: Slide 2 shows chains of Streptococcus sobrinus as an example of streptococcal chain arrangement, alongside clusters, diplococci, tetrads and octets.
questions.title: Introduction to Microbiology 2

questions.q: What distinguishes Gram-positive from Gram-negative bacteria according to the lecture?
options: Thickness of the peptidoglycan layer affecting crystal violet retention
Presence versus absence of a cell wall
Whether they are cocci or bacilli
Whether they possess flagella
Whether they form endospores
questions.explanation: Nearly all bacteria have a rigid peptidoglycan cell wall. Gram-positive bacteria have a thick PGN layer that retains crystal violet and stains purple, whereas Gram-negative bacteria have a thin PGN layer and do not retain the stain.
questions.title: Introduction to Microbiology 2

questions.q: Peptidoglycan is described as a target for which classes of agents?
options: β-lactams, glycopeptides and lysozyme
Macrolides and tetracyclines only
Quinolones and rifampicin
Antifungal azoles
Antiviral neuraminidase inhibitors
questions.explanation: Peptidoglycan is a lattice-like polymeric macromolecule built from NAG-NAM monomers and is targeted by β-lactams, glycopeptides and lysozyme.
