questions.title: Introduction to Microbiology 2

questions.q: How do β-lactam antibiotics relate to penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs)?
options: They resemble the natural PBP substrate D-Ala-D-Ala
They inhibit DNA gyrase directly
They block the outer membrane LPS
They prevent flagellin assembly
They dissolve the capsule
questions.explanation: PBPs catalyse final peptidoglycan synthesis steps. β-lactam antibiotics are structurally similar to the natural PBP substrate D-Ala-D-Ala and therefore inhibit PGN polymerisation and cross-linking.
questions.title: Introduction to Microbiology 2

questions.q: Which component of Gram-negative lipopolysaccharide (LPS) is responsible for toxicity?
options: Lipid A
O antigen only
Peptidoglycan monomers
Flagellin
Mycolic acids
questions.explanation: The outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria features LPS, synonymous with endotoxin. Lipid A is responsible for toxicity, while the O antigen outer polysaccharide is highly variable among species.
questions.title: Introduction to Microbiology 2

questions.q: Why are mycobacteria difficult to Gram-stain?
options: Their waxy cell wall contains mycolic acids in addition to peptidoglycan
They lack a cell wall entirely
They are too small to retain any dye
They are eukaryotic organisms
They possess only an outer membrane like Gram-negatives
questions.explanation: Mycobacteria cause diseases such as TB and leprosy. In addition to peptidoglycan, their cell wall contains long-chain mycolic acids, giving a waxy wall that makes standard Gram staining difficult and requires specialist stains.
questions.title: Introduction to Microbiology 2

questions.q: What is the function of bacterial flagella?
options: Motility via helical flagellin filaments with rotary motors
Conjugative DNA transfer
Adherence to host surfaces
Spore formation
Antibiotic resistance
questions.explanation: Flagella are helical protein (flagellin) filaments with a rotary motor at the base, used for motility in some bacilli and spiral-form bacteria, with arrangements such as monotrichous, amphitrichous and lophotrichous.
questions.title: Introduction to Microbiology 2

questions.q: What is the main role of fimbriae compared with pili?
options: Fimbriae adhere to surfaces; pili are mainly involved in conjugation and type IV movement
Fimbriae carry out conjugation; pili are used only for motility
Fimbriae form endospores; pili synthesise peptidoglycan
Fimbriae are found only on Gram-positive bacteria
Fimbriae and pili are identical structures with no functional difference
questions.explanation: Fimbriae and pili are fragile hair-like prokaryotic structures. Fimbriae are used to adhere to surfaces, whereas pili are mainly involved in conjugation (e.g. F pilus) and movement (type IV pili).
questions.title: Introduction to Microbiology 2

questions.q: Bacterial capsules are described as extracellular polymeric substances with which property?
options: Various protective functions, sometimes associated with increased disease severity
Essential for peptidoglycan synthesis
Required for Gram staining
The sole means of bacterial reproduction
Always preventing all antibiotic entry
questions.explanation: Many Gram-negative bacteria, some Gram-positive bacteria and most pathogenic mycobacteria produce EPS as capsules, slime layers or biofilms with various protective functions and sometimes increased disease severity.
questions.title: Introduction to Microbiology 2

questions.q: Which statement about bacterial endospores is correct?
options: They are resistant survival forms that are not a means of reproduction
They are the main method of bacterial reproduction
They are produced by all bacteria including E. coli
They are identical to fungal spores
They cannot germinate back into vegetative cells
questions.explanation: Endospores are resistant survival forms produced by some bacteria such as Bacillus and Clostridium spp. They resist heat, chemicals and UV, can germinate in favourable conditions, but are not a means of reproduction.
questions.title: Introduction to Microbiology 2

questions.q: According to the key points, why is peptidoglycan synthesis important in pharmacy?
options: It is a key target of antibiotic treatment
It determines fungal cell wall structure
It is absent in all pathogenic bacteria
It prevents all biofilm formation
It replaces the need for sterilisation
questions.explanation: Key points state that bacteria differ from eukaryotes in having a peptidoglycan cell wall and that peptidoglycan synthesis is a key target of antibiotic treatment, linking microbiology to manufacture, safety and infection control.
questions.title: Introduction to Microbiology 2

questions.q: Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease is caused by which type of microbial agent?
options: Prion
Bacterium
Fungus
Protozoan
Virus
questions.explanation: The lecture example MCQ states that Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease is caused by a prion, not a bacterium, fungus, protozoan or conventional virus.
questions.title: Introduction to Microbiology 2

questions.q: The normal microflora (microbiota) is best described as:
options: Organisms regularly found at anatomical sites, many beneficial to the host
Pathogens that always cause disease
Organisms found only in blood
Viruses that cannot colonise surface tissues
Fungi that replace all bacterial flora
questions.explanation: The normal microflora or microbiota comprises organisms regularly found at well-defined anatomical sites. Surface tissues are readily colonised from the environment and many members are beneficial to the host.
questions.title: Introduction to Microbiology 2

questions.q: In the chlamydial lifecycle, what is shown clustering at the edge of an immature inclusion body?
options: Reticulate bodies
Mature elementary bodies only
Bacterial endospores
Flagella
Peptidoglycan monomers
questions.explanation: The chlamydial lifecycle slide contrasts mature inclusions with immature inclusion bodies containing reticulate bodies clustering at the edge.
questions.title: Introduction to Microbiology 2

questions.q: Which textbook is recommended for independent reading on microbial pathogenicity?
options: Gilmore & Denyer, Hugo & Russell's Pharmaceutical Microbiology, 9th edition
Goodman & Gilman's Pharmacology
Rang & Dale's Pharmacology only
British National Formulary only
Martindale without microbiology content
questions.explanation: Independent reading directs students to Gilmore and Denyer (2023), Hugo & Russell's Pharmaceutical Microbiology, 9th edition, specifically Chapter 7 on principles of microbial pathogenicity and epidemiology.
questions.title: Introduction to Microbiology 2

questions.q: The Gram stain outcome relates to cell structure because:
options: Crystal violet retention depends on peptidoglycan layer thickness
All bacteria lack peptidoglycan
Mycobacteria stain strongly Gram-positive
Endospores always stain purple
Capsules determine the Gram reaction
questions.explanation: The example SAQ asks students to explain that the Gram stain depends on ability to retain crystal violet based on peptidoglycan thickness, linking purple Gram-positive and Gram-negative outcomes to cell wall structure.
questions.title: Introduction to Microbiology 2

questions.q: Why is the Gram stain unsuitable for mycobacteria?
options: Their waxy mycolic acid-rich wall prevents reliable Gram staining
They have no cell wall
They are too large to take up dye
They are eukaryotic
They lack peptidoglycan entirely
questions.explanation: Mycobacteria have a waxy cell wall with mycolic acids that makes standard Gram staining unsuitable; specialist stains are required instead.
questions.title: Introduction to Microbiology 2

questions.q: Why is DNA replication described as semi-conservative?
options: Because only half the genome is copied at each division
Because the replication process produces two DNA molecules, each with one original and one new strand
Because half the nucleotides are recycled from the parent strand
Because replication conserves energy by copying only the coding strand
Because both new molecules contain entirely new strands
questions.explanation: Because of base pairing, each DNA strand acts as a template for its complementary strand. The process results in two DNA molecules each with one original and one new strand, hence semi-conservative replication.
questions.title: Lectures 33 & 34 - DNA Replication, Transcription & Translation

questions.q: What happens at the origin of replication?
options: The replication complex forms, the double helix is opened and dsDNA is unwound by helicases, forming a replication fork or bubble
The mRNA transcript is spliced
Topoisomerases join the two daughter molecules
Ribosomes assemble on the DNA template
The DNA is permanently supercoiled
questions.explanation: The replication complex forms at the origin of replication. The double helix is opened at these sites and dsDNA unwound by helicases, forming a single stranded replication fork or replication bubble. Single-stranded DNA binding proteins prevent re-hybridisation to dsDNA.
questions.title: Lectures 33 & 34 - DNA Replication, Transcription & Translation

questions.q: What is the role of single-stranded DNA binding proteins?
options: They unwind the double helix
They prevent re-hybridisation of the separated strands back to dsDNA
They synthesise the RNA primer
They join Okazaki fragments together
They remove positive supercoils
questions.explanation: Single-stranded DNA binding proteins prevent re-hybridisation to double-stranded DNA at the replication fork, and prevent single-stranded DNA folding on itself.
questions.title: Lectures 33 & 34 - DNA Replication, Transcription & Translation

questions.q: Opening of coiled dsDNA by helicase introduces positive supercoils. How are these relaxed in bacteria?
options: By DNA gyrase, which introduces negative supercoils, with topoisomerase IV assisting in relaxing positive supercoiling
By helicase running in reverse
By single-stranded binding proteins
By RNA primase
By DNA polymerase proofreading activity
questions.explanation: In bacteria, type II topoisomerases relax the strain: DNA gyrase removes it by introducing negative supercoils, and topoisomerase IV assists in relaxing positive supercoiling.
questions.title: Lectures 33 & 34 - DNA Replication, Transcription & Translation

questions.q: DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV in bacteria are the targets of which antibiotic class?
options: Beta-lactams
Macrolides
Quinolones
Aminoglycosides
Glycopeptides
questions.explanation: DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV are both type II topoisomerases in bacteria and are the targets of quinolones such as ciprofloxacin.
questions.title: Lectures 33 & 34 - DNA Replication, Transcription & Translation

questions.q: Besides relaxing supercoils, what other role does topoisomerase IV have in bacterial DNA replication?
options: It separates the two newly replicated DNA strands, which become interlinked because of the double-helical, semiconservative mode of replication
It synthesises the RNA primer for the lagging strand
It proofreads newly synthesised DNA
It methylates the origin of replication
It ligates Okazaki fragments
questions.explanation: The double-helical nature of DNA and its semiconservative mode of replication cause the two newly replicated DNA strands to be interlinked, and topoisomerase IV resolves this in bacteria.
questions.title: Lectures 33 & 34 - DNA Replication, Transcription & Translation

questions.q: In which direction does DNA polymerase synthesise DNA?
options: Both directions simultaneously on the same strand
It depends on whether the strand is leading or lagging
From the centre outwards
questions.explanation: DNA polymerase synthesises DNA in a 5' to 3' direction, which is why the lagging strand must be made in short fragments.
questions.title: Lectures 33 & 34 - DNA Replication, Transcription & Translation

questions.q: What is the role of the RNA primer in DNA replication?
options: It provides the starting point for DNA synthesis, and is later replaced by DNA
It permanently forms part of the finished DNA strand
It unwinds the double helix ahead of the polymerase
It prevents supercoiling
It signals the end of replication
questions.explanation: RNA primers, synthesised by primase, provide the starting point for DNA synthesis. The primers are later replaced by DNA.
questions.title: Lectures 33 & 34 - DNA Replication, Transcription & Translation

questions.q: How does RNA differ structurally from DNA?
options: It has the same chemical linkages but some differences in chemical structure, and is single-stranded so can fold into a variety of shapes
It has completely different chemical linkages and is always double-stranded
It contains thymine instead of uracil
It has a deoxyribose sugar rather than ribose
It cannot form base pairs at all
questions.explanation: RNA has the same chemical linkages as DNA but some differences in chemical structure. It is a single-stranded molecule and can fold into a variety of shapes.
questions.title: Lectures 33 & 34 - DNA Replication, Transcription & Translation

questions.q: Which DNA strand is used as the template during transcription, and how does the mRNA sequence relate to the other strand?
options: The coding strand is the template, and mRNA matches the template strand
The template strand is copied, and the mRNA sequence directly corresponds to that of the coding strand
Both strands are copied simultaneously
The template strand is chosen at random for each gene
mRNA is copied from the coding strand and matches the template strand
questions.explanation: Genetic information is carried on the coding strand, but mRNA is made by copying the other, template, strand. The mRNA sequence therefore directly corresponds to that of the DNA coding strand, with U in place of T.
questions.title: Lectures 33 & 34 - DNA Replication, Transcription & Translation

questions.q: During transcription, in which directions does RNA polymerase move and synthesise the transcript?
options: It moves 3' to 5' along the template and synthesises mRNA 5' to 3'
It moves 5' to 3' along the template and synthesises mRNA 3' to 5'
Both movement and synthesis are 5' to 3'
Both movement and synthesis are 3' to 5'
Direction varies from gene to gene
questions.explanation: mRNA synthesis is initiated at a promoter sequence. RNA polymerase binds with accessory proteins and moves in a 3' to 5' direction along the template, while the complementary mRNA is synthesised 5' to 3'. The process stops at the transcription terminator sequence.
questions.title: Lectures 33 & 34 - DNA Replication, Transcription & Translation

questions.q: Why do prokaryotes require a sigma factor for transcription?
options: Because the core RNA polymerase is catalytically inactive without it
Because the core RNA polymerase is catalytically active but cannot recognise where transcription should start
Because it supplies the nucleotides for RNA synthesis
Because it splices the transcript after synthesis
Because it adds the 5' cap to the mRNA
questions.explanation: In prokaryotes the core RNA polymerase is catalytically active but cannot recognise where transcription should start. The sigma factor ensures RNA polymerase binds the correct promoter sequences and initiates at the proper site, facilitates DNA melting, stabilises the open complex and orientates the template strand.
questions.title: Lectures 33 & 34 - DNA Replication, Transcription & Translation

questions.q: What happens to the sigma factor after transcription begins?
options: It remains bound for the whole transcript
It usually dissociates after a short part of the RNA transcript has been synthesised
It is degraded immediately on binding
It becomes part of the finished mRNA
It converts into a general transcription factor
questions.explanation: The sigma factor usually dissociates after a short part of the RNA transcript has been synthesised.
questions.title: Lectures 33 & 34 - DNA Replication, Transcription & Translation

questions.q: How many RNA polymerases do eukaryotes have, and which transcribes protein-coding genes?
options: One; it transcribes all genes
Two; RNA pol I transcribes protein-coding genes
Three; RNA polymerase II transcribes all protein-coding genes
Three; RNA polymerase III transcribes all protein-coding genes
Five; each transcribes a different gene class
questions.explanation: Eukaryotes have three RNA polymerases: I, II and III. RNA polymerase II transcribes all protein-coding genes. Initiation begins when a complex of general transcription factors and RNA polymerase assembles at the promoter region.
questions.title: Lectures 33 & 34 - DNA Replication, Transcription & Translation

questions.q: How does the relationship between gene sequence and translated mRNA differ between prokaryotes and eukaryotes?
options: In prokaryotes the gene is colinear with the translated mRNA; in eukaryotes it usually is not, and the transcript must be spliced first
In eukaryotes the gene is colinear; in prokaryotes splicing is required
Both require splicing before translation
Neither requires any processing of the transcript
Prokaryotic transcripts require capping and polyadenylation
questions.explanation: The sequence of a prokaryotic protein-coding gene is colinear with the translated mRNA, so the transcript is the molecule translated. A eukaryotic gene is usually not colinear, and the transcript must be processed to remove extra sequences, that is spliced, before translation.
questions.title: Lectures 33 & 34 - DNA Replication, Transcription & Translation

questions.q: Which RNA type is correctly matched to its function?
options: tRNA makes up the ribosome with ribosomal proteins
rRNA brings amino acids to the ribosome
snRNA forms complexes with proteins used in RNA processing in eukaryotes
mRNA is a non-coding regulatory RNA
miRNA encodes the amino acid sequence of a polypeptide
questions.explanation: snRNA forms complexes with proteins used in RNA processing in eukaryotes and is not found in prokaryotes. tRNA brings amino acids to ribosomes, rRNA with ribosomal proteins makes up the ribosomes, mRNA encodes the polypeptide, and miRNA is a small regulatory RNA.
questions.title: Lectures 33 & 34 - DNA Replication, Transcription & Translation

questions.q: Which codon is the start codon and which amino acid does it encode?
options: AUG, encoding methionine
UAA, encoding methionine
AUG, encoding alanine
UGA, encoding tryptophan
GUA, encoding valine
questions.explanation: AUG is the start codon and encodes methionine. UAA, UAG and UGA are the stop codons.
questions.title: Lectures 33 & 34 - DNA Replication, Transcription & Translation

questions.q: What does it mean to say the genetic code is degenerate?
options: The code deteriorates over successive generations
In most cases there is more than one codon per amino acid, up to six
Some codons encode no amino acid at all
The same codon can encode different amino acids in different cells
The code differs completely between species
questions.explanation: The genetic code is degenerate, meaning in most cases there is more than one codon per amino acid, up to six for some amino acids.
questions.title: Lectures 33 & 34 - DNA Replication, Transcription & Translation

questions.q: How many reading frames does an mRNA sequence have?
options: One
Two
Three
Four
Six
questions.explanation: Because codons are read in triplets, the code has three possible reading frames for a given single strand of mRNA.
questions.title: Lectures 33 & 34 - DNA Replication, Transcription & Translation

questions.q: Why is the ribosome an important target for antibiotics?
options: Because bacteria have no other means of protein synthesis
Because many antibiotics specifically inhibit the prokaryotic ribosomal subunits, giving selective toxicity
Because ribosomes are absent from human cells
Because the ribosome is the site of DNA replication in bacteria
Because ribosomes carry the bacterial genome
questions.explanation: The ribosome is the molecular machine that interprets the genetic code. Many antibiotics specifically inhibit the prokaryotic ribosomal subunits, which are structurally different from human ones, giving selective toxicity.
questions.title: Lectures 33 & 34 - DNA Replication, Transcription & Translation

questions.q: What are the three stages of translation?
options: Initiation, elongation and termination
Transcription, splicing and capping
Priming, extension and ligation
Binding, folding and modification
Unwinding, copying and rewinding
questions.explanation: Translation is divided into three stages: initiation, elongation and termination.
questions.title: Lectures 33 & 34 - DNA Replication, Transcription & Translation

questions.q: How do eukaryotic and prokaryotic mRNAs differ in the number of genes they carry?
options: Eukaryotic mRNAs tend to be monocistronic while prokaryotic mRNAs are often polycistronic
Eukaryotic mRNAs are polycistronic while prokaryotic mRNAs are monocistronic
Both are always monocistronic
Both are always polycistronic
Prokaryotic mRNAs carry no genes and only regulate translation
questions.explanation: Eukaryotic mRNAs tend to be monocistronic, encoding one polypeptide, while prokaryotic mRNAs are often polycistronic. Eukaryotic mRNAs also carry a 5' cap and a polyA tail.
questions.title: Lectures 33 & 34 - DNA Replication, Transcription & Translation

questions.q: How is translation initiation signalled in prokaryotes compared with eukaryotes?
options: Prokaryotic mRNAs carry a Shine-Dalgarno sequence preceding the AUG codon that aligns with the 16S rRNA; eukaryotic mRNAs bind the 40S subunit via their 5' 7-methylguanosine cap with initiation factors
Prokaryotic mRNAs use a 5' cap; eukaryotic mRNAs use a Shine-Dalgarno sequence
Both use a 5' 7-methylguanosine cap
Both use the Shine-Dalgarno sequence aligned with 16S rRNA
Neither requires any initiation signal
questions.explanation: Eukaryotic mRNAs are bound to the 40S subunit via their 5' 7-methylguanosine cap with the help of initiation factors (eIFs). Prokaryotic mRNAs carry a Shine-Dalgarno sequence preceding the AUG codon which aligns with the 16S rRNA.
questions.title: Lectures 33 & 34 - DNA Replication, Transcription & Translation

questions.q: How many binding sites does a ribosome have, and for what?
options: One site for mRNA and three binding sites for tRNA
Three sites for mRNA and one for tRNA
One site each for mRNA and tRNA
Two sites for mRNA and two for tRNA
Four sites for tRNA and none for mRNA
questions.explanation: Each ribosome has a binding site for mRNA and three binding sites for tRNA, known as the A, P and E sites.
questions.title: Lectures 33 & 34 - DNA Replication, Transcription & Translation

questions.q: In elongation, what happens in step 2, after the incoming tRNA enters the A-site?
options: The ribosome dissociates from the mRNA
The carboxyl end of the polypeptide chain is uncoupled from the tRNA at the P-site and joined to the free amino group of the amino acid on the tRNA at the A-site
The small subunit moves three nucleotides along the mRNA
A release factor binds the A-site
The mRNA is spliced to remove introns
questions.explanation: In step 1 the tRNA carrying the next amino acid enters the A-site. In step 2, the carboxyl end of the polypeptide is uncoupled from the tRNA at the P-site and joined to the free amino group of the amino acid linked to the tRNA at the A-site.
questions.title: Lectures 33 & 34 - DNA Replication, Transcription & Translation

questions.q: How far does the small ribosomal subunit move along the mRNA in step 4 of elongation?
options: One nucleotide
Two nucleotides
Exactly three nucleotides
Six nucleotides
It does not move; the tRNAs move instead
questions.explanation: In step 3 a shift in the large subunit moves the two tRNAs to the E- and P-sites. In step 4 the small subunit moves exactly three nucleotides along the mRNA, resetting the ribosome so the A-site is empty for the next tRNA.
questions.title: Lectures 33 & 34 - DNA Replication, Transcription & Translation

questions.q: How is translation terminated?
options: A release factor binds the A-site showing a stop codon, the completed polypeptide is released and the ribosome dissociates
The ribosome runs off the end of the mRNA at random
The mRNA is degraded from the 5' end
A sigma factor binds and halts the ribosome
The tRNA supply is exhausted
questions.explanation: Binding of a release factor to the A-site when it displays a stop codon terminates translation. The completed polypeptide is released and the ribosome dissociates.
questions.title: Lectures 33 & 34 - DNA Replication, Transcription & Translation

questions.q: What are post-translational modifications, and roughly how many types have been identified?
options: Covalent modifications that change protein characteristics; approximately 650 types
Non-covalent interactions that fold the protein; about 20 types
Changes to the mRNA before translation; about 100 types
Mutations in the gene sequence; about 650 types
Additions of nucleotides to the transcript; about 3 types
questions.explanation: Post-translational modifications are covalent modifications that change characteristics such as conformation, activity, charge, stability and interactions with other biomolecules. Approximately 650 types have been identified.
questions.title: Lectures 33 & 34 - DNA Replication, Transcription & Translation

questions.q: Which residues are most commonly phosphorylated, and in what proportions?
options: Serine 86 per cent, threonine 12 per cent, tyrosine 2 per cent
Tyrosine 86 per cent, serine 12 per cent, threonine 2 per cent
Threonine 86 per cent, tyrosine 12 per cent, serine 2 per cent
Lysine 86 per cent, arginine 12 per cent, histidine 2 per cent
All three occur equally at 33 per cent each
questions.explanation: Phosphorylation is a reversible PTM occurring usually on serine (86 per cent), threonine (12 per cent) or tyrosine (2 per cent) residues, and it typically turns hydrophobic nonpolar proteins into hydrophilic polar proteins. 518 protein kinases had been identified as of 2023.
questions.title: Lectures 33 & 34 - DNA Replication, Transcription & Translation

questions.q: Which abnormal post-translational modification is linked to neurodegenerative disease?
options: Tau hyperphosphorylation
Acetylation of insulin receptors
Ubiquitination of tumour suppressors
Glycosylation of haemoglobin
Methylation of ribosomal RNA
questions.explanation: Tau hyperphosphorylation is linked to neurodegenerative disease. Reduced palmitoylation of mutant huntingtin may lead to Huntington's disease, acetylation regulates insulin sensitivity and metabolism, and cancers involve phosphorylation effects on signalling, ubiquitination of tumour suppressors and histone modifications.
questions.title: Lectures 33 & 34 - DNA Replication, Transcription & Translation

questions.q: How is epigenetics defined?
options: Changes in DNA that do not involve alterations to the underlying sequence, which can regulate gene expression
Mutations in the DNA sequence passed to offspring
The study of how proteins fold after translation
The removal of introns from a transcript
The rate at which DNA is replicated
questions.explanation: Epigenetics covers changes in DNA that do not involve alterations to the underlying sequence, chemical modifications that can regulate gene expression. These may be passed from parent cell to daughter cell during division or from one generation to the next.
questions.title: Lectures 33 & 34 - DNA Replication, Transcription & Translation

questions.q: Which key processes do antibiotics such as ciprofloxacin and azithromycin target?
options: Cell wall synthesis and membrane integrity only
DNA synthesis, transcription and translation, the key processes required for cell function and division
Only the bacterial cell membrane
Only the peptidoglycan cross-links
Only bacterial metabolism of glucose
questions.explanation: Antibiotics act on key processes required for cell function and division including DNA synthesis, transcription and translation. Ciprofloxacin targets the topoisomerases of DNA replication and azithromycin the ribosome in translation.
questions.title: Lectures 33 & 34 - DNA Replication, Transcription & Translation

questions.q: How is the DNA double helix held together?
options: By hydrogen bonds between paired bases on two strands
By peptide bonds between nucleotides
By disulfide bridges between sugar rings
By ionic bonds between phosphate groups only
By covalent bonds between complementary bases
questions.explanation: The DNA molecule is composed of two strands held together by hydrogen bonds between paired bases on each strand.
questions.title: Lectures 33 & 34 - DNA Replication, Transcription & Translation

questions.q: Which base pairs are held together by hydrogen bonding in DNA?
options: Adenine with thymine, and guanine with cytosine
Adenine with guanine, and thymine with cytosine
Cytosine with thymine, and adenine with guanine
All bases pair with any other base equally
Uracil pairs with adenine in DNA
questions.explanation: Hydrogen bonding occurs between complementary bases: adenine pairs with thymine (A-T) and guanine pairs with cytosine (G-C).
questions.title: Lectures 33 & 34 - DNA Replication, Transcription & Translation

questions.q: Once DNA replication is initiated at an origin, in which direction does it proceed?
options: In both directions from the replication fork
In one direction only from the 5 prime end
Only towards the telomeres in one direction
Only during G2 of the cell cycle
Only on the lagging strand
questions.explanation: After initiation of DNA replication, the process proceeds in both directions. DNA replication occurs at replication forks.
questions.title: Lectures 33 & 34 - DNA Replication, Transcription & Translation

questions.q: In the codon sequence 5'-CCA CAC GCA CGC AUG GCU UGC UAU-3', what does AUG code for?
options: Methionine, which also serves as the usual start codon
Phenylalanine only
A stop signal with no amino acid
Tryptophan
Leucine
questions.explanation: Triplet codons in mRNA code for different amino acids. In the PHARMACY example sequence, AUG codes for methionine and is also the usual start codon for translation.
questions.title: Lectures 33 & 34 - DNA Replication, Transcription & Translation

questions.q: During translation, which molecules interpret the mRNA codon sequence?
options: tRNAs that carry specific amino acids and match anticodons to codons
DNA polymerase
RNA polymerase
Topoisomerase
DNA ligase
questions.explanation: The mRNA code is interpreted by tRNAs, which carry specific amino acids and pair their anticodons with the complementary codons on the mRNA.
questions.title: Lectures 33 & 34 - DNA Replication, Transcription & Translation

questions.q: What must happen to a tRNA before it can participate in translation?
options: The appropriate amino acid must be joined to it
Its DNA template must be replicated
It must be shortened by removing introns
It must bind to the origin of replication
It must form a phosphodiester bond with the next tRNA
questions.explanation: Before translation, the appropriate amino acid is joined to the tRNA so that each tRNA can deliver the correct amino acid when its anticodon matches an mRNA codon.
questions.title: Lectures 33 & 34 - DNA Replication, Transcription & Translation

questions.q: Which processes are summarised in the lecture key points for central dogma?
options: Faithful DNA copying by base-pairing, transcription by RNA polymerase, and translation by ribosomes reading codons
Only DNA replication and mutation
Only protein degradation and folding
Only epigenetic silencing
Only cell membrane transport
questions.explanation: Key points state that specific base-pairing enables faithful DNA copying; transcription incorporates nucleotides into mRNA using a DNA template; and translation directs protein production as ribosomes read codons in mRNA.
questions.title: Lectures 33 & 34 - DNA Replication, Transcription & Translation

questions.q: What are molecular diagnostics?
options: Tests which analyse nucleic acids and/or proteins in a sample to detect genetic risk factors or identify infections
Tests which measure drug concentrations in plasma
Tests which culture organisms on selective media
Tests which measure the physical properties of a medicine
Tests which image internal organs at molecular resolution
questions.explanation: Molecular diagnostics are tests which analyse nucleic acids and/or proteins in a sample to detect genetic risk factors or identify infections, using techniques such as PCR and its modifications, microarray analysis, DNA sequencing and genotyping, and mass spectrometry.
questions.title: Molecular Biology

questions.q: Why does PCR require a primer?
options: Because DNA polymerase can only add nucleotides onto a pre-existing 3'-OH group
Because the template strand is otherwise too unstable
Because primers prevent the DNA from denaturing
Because primers supply the nucleotides for synthesis
Because polymerase cannot bind DNA without a primer
questions.explanation: PCR exploits the ability of DNA polymerase to synthesise DNA complementary to a template strand. The polymerase can only add nucleotides onto a pre-existing 3'-OH group, so a primer is required to which the first new nucleotide can be added.
questions.title: Molecular Biology

questions.q: Which six reagents are needed for PCR?
options: DNA template, a pair of primers flanking the region of interest, thermostable DNA polymerase, dNTPs, buffer and water
RNA template, one primer, RNA polymerase, ddNTPs, agarose and water
DNA template, restriction enzymes, ligase, dNTPs, buffer and ethanol
Protein template, primers, polymerase, amino acids, buffer and water
DNA template, a single primer, reverse transcriptase, dNTPs, gel and water
questions.explanation: PCR requires a DNA template, a pair of primers flanking the region of interest, a thermostable DNA polymerase, nucleotides (dNTPs), buffer and water.
questions.title: Molecular Biology

questions.q: At what temperature does the denaturation step of PCR occur?
options: 37 to 42 degrees C
50 to 60 degrees C
72 degrees C
94 to 96 degrees C
100 to 110 degrees C
questions.explanation: Denaturation is carried out at 94 to 96 degrees C to separate the strands. The annealing temperature that follows depends on the primer sequence.
questions.title: Molecular Biology

questions.q: Approximately how many copies of the target are produced after 30 cycles of PCR?
options: About 1,000
About 32,768
About 1 million
About 33 million
Over 1 billion
questions.explanation: PCR gives exponential amplification: 10 cycles give 1,024 copies, 20 give about 1 million, 25 give about 33.5 million and 30 cycles give 1,073,741,824, over a billion copies.
questions.title: Molecular Biology

questions.q: What is a negative control in PCR?
options: The same reagents and primers as the sample but with no template provided
The same reagents and primers as the sample but with a known template
A second genomic target co-amplified in the same tube
A sample from a healthy patient
A reaction run without any polymerase
questions.explanation: A negative control, also called a negative amplification control or no template control, uses the same reagents and primers as the experimental samples but with no template provided. A positive control uses a known template.
questions.title: Molecular Biology

questions.q: How does an internal control differ from a positive control in PCR?
options: It co-amplifies another genomic target in the same sample using the same conditions except for primers, and is typically a significantly larger target
It is run in a separate tube with a known template
It contains no template at all
It uses a different polymerase from the test reaction
It is the patient sample itself, re-tested
questions.explanation: An internal control co-amplifies another genomic target in the same sample as the test, using the same conditions except for the primers. It is significantly different in size, typically a larger target.
questions.title: Molecular Biology

questions.q: What does real-time or quantitative PCR (qPCR) allow?
options: The number of copies of template nucleic acid produced by PCR to be quantified
PCR to be run without primers
DNA to be sequenced directly during amplification
The reaction to be run at a single constant temperature
RNA to be amplified without conversion to DNA
questions.explanation: Real-time or quantitative PCR, introduced in the mid 1990s, allows the number of copies of template nucleic acid produced to be quantified. This is useful for estimating viral loads and monitoring the success of antimicrobial therapy.
questions.title: Molecular Biology

questions.q: How can RNA be used as a starting material for PCR?
options: Reverse transcription converts RNA into DNA that can be used as a template
RNA is amplified directly by DNA polymerase
RNA is chemically converted into protein first
RNA is denatured at 96 degrees C to become DNA
RNA cannot be used in any form of PCR
questions.explanation: Reverse transcription converts RNA into DNA that can then be used as a PCR template, which is how RNA viruses and gene expression can be assayed.
questions.title: Molecular Biology

questions.q: Why is PCR-based detection valuable for infectious disease?
options: Because traditional methods can lack sensitivity, some organisms are non-culturable or slow growers, and there are antimicrobial stewardship issues
Because it is cheaper than any culture method
Because it works without any laboratory equipment
Because it can treat the infection as well as detect it
Because it replaces the need for clinical examination
questions.explanation: Large numbers of cases go undiagnosed annually and are treated empirically, because traditional methods can lack sensitivity, some organisms are non-culturable or slow growers, and there are antimicrobial stewardship issues. PCR has excellent sensitivity and specificity.
questions.title: Molecular Biology

questions.q: Detection of the mecA gene by PCR identifies which organism?
options: Chlamydia trachomatis
MRSA (meticillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus)
Neisseria gonorrhoeae
Mycoplasma genitalium
Trichomonas vaginalis
questions.explanation: Antimicrobial resistance profiling by PCR includes detection of mecA, the gene identifying MRSA.
questions.title: Molecular Biology

questions.q: What are the three main categories of genetic disorder?
options: Single gene (monogenic) mutations, chromosomal disorders, and complex or multifactorial disorders
Inherited, acquired and infectious
Point mutations, insertions and deletions
Congenital, childhood and adult onset
Dominant, recessive and X-linked
questions.explanation: The three main categories are single gene or monogenic mutations such as cystic fibrosis and sickle cell disease, chromosomal disorders which may be numerical or structural such as Down syndrome (trisomy 21), and complex or multifactorial disorders such as Alzheimer disease and some cancers.
questions.title: Molecular Biology

questions.q: Cystic fibrosis and sickle cell disease are examples of which category of genetic disorder?
options: Chromosomal numerical disorders
Single gene (monogenic) mutations
Complex multifactorial disorders
Copy number variants
Tandem repeat disorders
questions.explanation: Cystic fibrosis, caused by CFTR gene mutation, and sickle cell disease, caused by beta-globin gene mutation, are single gene or monogenic disorders.
questions.title: Molecular Biology

questions.q: Which methods can PCR be used with to detect specific DNA mutations?
options: As an adjunct to DNA sequencing, restriction fragment length polymorphism analysis of PCR products, and short tandem repeat testing
Only by direct visual inspection of the gel
Only by mass spectrometry of the amplicon
Only by culture of the amplified organism
Only by microarray hybridisation
questions.explanation: PCR can detect specific DNA mutations as an adjunct to DNA sequencing, by restriction fragment length polymorphism analysis of PCR products (PCR-RFLP), and by short tandem repeat (STR) testing.
questions.title: Molecular Biology

questions.q: What is DNA sequencing?
options: The determination of the order of the four bases that make up a DNA molecule of interest
The amplification of a DNA region a billion-fold
The cutting of DNA at specific recognition sites
The measurement of the total quantity of DNA in a sample
The separation of DNA fragments by size
questions.explanation: DNA sequencing is the determination of the order of the four bases making up a DNA molecule of interest. Because the four bases always bond with the same partner, this underlies both DNA replication and most sequencing technologies.
questions.title: Molecular Biology

questions.q: How does Sanger sequencing work?
options: Target DNA is used as a template in PCR with normal dNTPs plus a low ratio of fluorescently labelled chain-terminating ddNTPs
DNA is cut by restriction enzymes and the fragments read directly
DNA is hybridised to a microarray and fluorescence measured
Single molecules are passed through a nanopore and current changes recorded
DNA is denatured and the bases counted by mass spectrometry
questions.explanation: Sanger, or chain termination or dideoxy sequencing (Sanger et al. 1977), uses target DNA as a template in PCR with a mix of normal bases (dNTPs) and a low ratio of fluorescently labelled chain-terminating bases (ddNTPs). Reads are typically 500 to 600 bp.
questions.title: Molecular Biology

questions.q: In Sanger sequencing, how is the sequence finally read out?
options: Fragments are separated by size using electrophoresis and the fluorescence of the terminating dideoxy base at each length is monitored to generate a chromatograph
The fragments are weighed and the mass converted to a base call
The DNA is cut with restriction enzymes and the bands counted
The reaction is monitored in real time as each base is added
The DNA is hybridised to a complementary reference sequence
questions.explanation: Random incorporation of a fluorescently labelled dideoxy base terminates the chain, generating fragments of different lengths. These are separated by size using electrophoresis, and the fluorescence of the terminating base for each length is recorded to produce a chromatograph showing the base at each position.
questions.title: Molecular Biology

questions.q: Which is a clinical application of DNA sequencing given in the lecture?
options: Diagnostic testing of the RB1 gene in hereditary retinoblastoma
Measuring plasma drug concentrations
Determining the melting point of a drug substance
Culturing slow-growing bacteria
Assessing tablet dissolution rate
questions.explanation: Applications include diagnostic testing of a specific gene such as RB1 in hereditary retinoblastoma, testing for familial sequence variants such as BRCA1 in at-risk relatives, determining carrier status for autosomal recessive conditions such as CF, prenatal testing, and gene expression studies using reverse transcription from mRNA.
questions.title: Molecular Biology

questions.q: What are restriction enzymes (restriction endonucleases)?
options: Enzymes which recognise and cut at specific double-stranded DNA sequences
Enzymes which join DNA fragments together
Enzymes which unwind the double helix
Enzymes which add fluorescent labels to DNA
Enzymes which synthesise DNA from an RNA template
questions.explanation: Restriction enzymes, or restriction endonucleases, recognise and cut at specific double-stranded DNA sequences, for example EcoRI and SalI. The fragments they produce are called restriction fragments.
questions.title: Molecular Biology

questions.q: What does PCR-RFLP detect, and what is its alternative name?
options: Differences in restriction fragment lengths caused by mutations such as SNPs and indels; also known as Cleaved Amplified Polymorphic Sequences (CAPS)
Differences in the number of tandem repeats; also known as STR testing
Differences in gene copy number; also known as aCGH
Differences in mRNA abundance; also known as qPCR
Differences in protein size; also known as electrophoresis
questions.explanation: RFLP analysis of PCR-amplified fragments, also known as Cleaved Amplified Polymorphic Sequences (CAPS), detects differences in restriction fragment lengths caused by mutation such as SNPs and indels. PCR with locus-specific primers generates the amplicons for analysis.
questions.title: Molecular Biology

questions.q: How do short tandem repeats and copy number variants differ?
options: STR mutational changes mainly affect the number of repeat units, whereas CNVs may consist of large repeats but frequently span entire genes or larger regions
STRs span entire genes while CNVs affect only single bases
STRs are found only in coding regions while CNVs are only in non-coding regions
STRs are inherited while CNVs are always acquired
They are two names for the same phenomenon
questions.explanation: Both are types of genetic variation driven by differences in the number of repeated DNA sequences but they differ in structure, scale and biological significance. STR changes mainly affect the number of repeat units, mutating at high rates and causing population polymorphism, while CNVs may consist of large repeats but frequently span entire genes or larger regions.
questions.title: Molecular Biology

questions.q: What are the typical characteristics of short tandem repeats in the human genome?
options: Repeat sequences typically 2 to 6 bp long, over 1 million loci known, comprising about 3 per cent of total DNA, mostly in non-coding regions
Repeat sequences typically 100 to 600 bp long, found only in coding regions
Repeat sequences of exactly 3 bp, comprising 30 per cent of the genome
Repeat sequences 2 to 6 bp long, found at only a few hundred loci
Repeat sequences of variable length making up half the genome
questions.explanation: STRs or microsatellites have repeat sequences typically 2 to 6 bp in length, with the number of repeats varying considerably between individuals. Over 1 million loci are known, comprising about 3 per cent of total DNA, mostly in non-coding regions though some lie within or near genes.
questions.title: Molecular Biology

questions.q: Huntington's disease is caused by expansion of which repeat, and at what repeat number does disease occur?
options: A CGG repeat in FMR1; disease above 200 repeats
A CAG repeat in the huntingtin (HTT) gene; normal 10 to 35 repeats, disease 36 to 120 or more
A CAG repeat in FMR1; disease above 55 repeats
A CGG repeat in HTT; normal 5 to 44 repeats
A GAA repeat in HTT; disease above 100 repeats
questions.explanation: Huntington's disease is caused by a CAG repeat expansion in the huntingtin (HTT) gene. The normal range is 10 to 35 repeats and disease occurs at 36 to 120 or more, with incomplete penetrance below 40 repeats.
questions.title: Molecular Biology

questions.q: Fragile X syndrome involves expansion of which repeat, in which gene?
options: A CAG repeat in HTT
A CGG trinucleotide repeat in the FMR1 gene on the X chromosome
A GAA repeat in the frataxin gene
A CTG repeat in the DMPK gene
A CGG repeat in the CFTR gene
questions.explanation: Fragile X syndrome, the most common inherited cause of intellectual and developmental disability, typically involves expansion of a CGG trinucleotide repeat in the FMR1 gene on the X chromosome. Normal is 5 to 44 repeats, a spectrum of conditions occurs above 55, and FXS itself is caused by 200 or more repeats.
questions.title: Molecular Biology

questions.q: What is genetic anticipation in the context of STR testing?
options: The number of repeats often correlates with age of disease onset and severity
The prediction of disease before any symptoms appear
The tendency for repeats to contract over generations
The screening of relatives before a diagnosis is made
The expectation that all carriers will develop disease
questions.explanation: In STR testing, the number of repeats is determined to diagnose disease, and the number of repeats often correlates with age of disease onset and severity, a phenomenon referred to as genetic anticipation.
questions.title: Molecular Biology

questions.q: In fluorescent PCR sizing for STR testing, how is the assay constructed?
options: A pair of locus-specific primers located either side of the repeat region, one of the pair labelled with fluorescent dye, with products separated by electrophoresis
A single primer within the repeat region, unlabelled
Restriction enzymes cut the repeat and fragments are weighed
The repeat is sequenced directly by the Sanger method only
The repeat is detected by hybridisation to a microarray
questions.explanation: In fluorescent PCR sizing, a pair of locus-specific primers is located either side of the repeat region, one of the pair labelled with a fluorescent dye, and the PCR products are separated by electrophoresis. Repeat-primed PCR is better for larger expansions.
questions.title: Molecular Biology

questions.q: How do copy number variants arise, and what is their consequence?
options: Via duplications, deletions and insertions, resulting in altered gene dosage affecting phenotype and disease risk
Via point mutations that change a single base
Via changes in the number of chromosomes only
Via epigenetic methylation without any sequence change
Via errors in mRNA splicing
questions.explanation: CNVs are variations in copy number of a specific DNA segment between individuals, resulting from structural changes via duplications, deletions and insertions. They can result in altered gene dosage, affecting phenotype and disease risk.
questions.title: Molecular Biology

questions.q: Rhesus negative blood group results from which type of copy number variation?
options: Complete deletion of the RHD gene
Duplication of the RHD gene
Multiple duplications of the AMY1 gene
Duplication of the CYP2D6 gene
Expansion of a trinucleotide repeat
questions.explanation: CNV examples given are presence or absence of a gene, with Rhesus negative resulting from complete deletion of the RHD gene; duplication of a genomic segment, for example the CYP2D6 cytochrome P450 gene; and multiple duplications, for example the AMY1 gene.
questions.title: Molecular Biology

questions.q: Which methods are currently used to detect copy number variants?
options: Microarray-based analysis such as array comparative genomic hybridisation, next generation sequencing, and digital PCR
Gel electrophoresis of restriction fragments only
Sanger sequencing alone
Culture and Gram staining
Mass spectrometry of the protein product
questions.explanation: CNVs are currently detected using microarray-based analysis such as array comparative genomic hybridisation (aCGH), next generation sequencing, and digital PCR.
questions.title: Molecular Biology

questions.q: How is amplified DNA typically analysed after PCR?
options: By electrophoresis in agarose or polyacrylamide gels
By centrifugation to separate the strands
By titration against a standard
By measuring the melting point of the amplicon
By culturing the product on agar plates
questions.explanation: Analysis of amplified DNA typically involves electrophoresis in agarose or polyacrylamide gels, which separates fragments by size.
questions.title: Molecular Biology

questions.q: Why do pharmacists need to know about genetic engineering?
options: Because many biologics, including all forms of insulin, are produced by genetic engineering, and biologics are the fastest growing sector of the pharmaceutical industry
Because all tablets are now manufactured using recombinant enzymes
Because genetic engineering determines how a drug is absorbed
Because pharmacists are required to perform PCR in practice
Because genetic engineering sets the price of medicines
questions.explanation: Many biologics, including all the various forms of insulin, are produced by genetic engineering. Biologics are the fastest growing sector of the pharmaceutical industry and biotechnology is a key area of modern biomedical and pharmaceutical science.
questions.title: Lecture 36 - Gene to Biologic

questions.q: What are the four steps of producing any biologic, in order?
options: Isolate the gene, clone it into a vector, express it in a host, then manufacture the recombinant product
Express the gene, isolate it, clone it, then purify the product
Clone the gene, isolate it, manufacture it, then express it
Manufacture the protein, sequence it, clone the gene, then express it
Purify the protein, isolate the gene, express it, then formulate
questions.explanation: The four steps are: isolate your gene from donor DNA, insert it into a suitable cloning vector such as a plasmid, introduce the vector into an expression host such as a bacterium or yeast, and use the recombinant host to scale up production, purify, formulate and QC test.
questions.title: Lecture 36 - Gene to Biologic

questions.q: In the context of this lecture, what does cloning mean?
options: The process of creating an exact copy of a biological unit, here specifically a defined sequence of DNA
The creation of a genetically identical organism only
The production of identical cells for transplantation only
The synthesis of a protein from an mRNA template
The copying of a whole genome by sequencing
questions.explanation: Cloning is the process of creating an exact copy of a biological unit. This can be a copy of a defined DNA sequence (gene cloning, molecular cloning, recombinant DNA technology), a genetically identical cell (cellular or therapeutic cloning), or an organism (reproductive cloning). This lecture covers gene cloning only.
questions.title: Lecture 36 - Gene to Biologic

questions.q: How is a gene best described?
options: A sequence of DNA that codes for a specific protein in a living organism, the basic genetic unit of heredity
Any stretch of DNA within a chromosome
A single molecule of messenger RNA
The complete set of DNA in an organism
A protein that has been copied from DNA
questions.explanation: A gene is best described as a sequence of DNA that codes for a specific protein in a living organism. It is the basic genetic unit of heredity, and it is imperative that the sequence does not change when copied.
questions.title: Lecture 36 - Gene to Biologic

questions.q: How many genes are in the human genome, compared with E. coli K-12 and HIV?
options: 19,000 to 20,000 in humans, 4,372 in E. coli K-12, and 9 in HIV
4,372 in humans, 19,000 in E. coli, and 90 in HIV
100,000 in humans, 10,000 in E. coli, and 900 in HIV
19,000 to 20,000 in humans, 437 in E. coli, and 90 in HIV
2,000 in humans, 4,372 in E. coli, and 9 in HIV
questions.explanation: The human genome contains 19,000 to 20,000 genes, a bacterial genome such as Escherichia coli K-12 contains 4,372 genes, and the HIV genome a mere 9 genes.
questions.title: Lecture 36 - Gene to Biologic

questions.q: Why is isolating mRNA and reverse-transcribing it to cDNA a useful route to obtaining a eukaryotic gene?
options: Because eukaryote genes are often very complex, so obtaining the DNA sequence that just encodes the protein can be problematic
Because mRNA is more stable than DNA
Because cDNA can be translated directly into protein
Because reverse transcription introduces useful mutations
Because bacteria cannot replicate genomic DNA
questions.explanation: Eukaryote genes such as insulin are often very complex, so obtaining the DNA sequence that just encodes the protein can be problematic. Isolating mRNA and reverse-transcribing it to cDNA is one way around the problem, and PCR can then isolate the gene from cDNA.
questions.title: Lecture 36 - Gene to Biologic

questions.q: Besides amplifying a gene, what two additional uses of PCR are highlighted in gene isolation?
options: Adding sequences that make cloning into a vector easier, and modifying the insulin gene to produce insulin analogues
Sequencing the gene directly and expressing the protein
Purifying the protein and testing its activity
Transforming bacteria and selecting colonies
Cutting the genome and ligating fragments
questions.explanation: PCR can also add sequences that make cloning your gene into a vector much easier, and it is a key method for modifying the insulin gene to produce the various insulin analogues.
questions.title: Lecture 36 - Gene to Biologic

questions.q: How is a cloning vector defined?
options: A small piece of DNA, taken from a virus, plasmid or the cell of a higher organism, that can be stably maintained in an organism and into which foreign DNA can be inserted for cloning
The host cell into which a gene is introduced
The enzyme that copies DNA during replication
The primer pair used to amplify a gene
The antibiotic used to select transformed cells
questions.explanation: A cloning vector is a small piece of DNA, taken from a virus, a plasmid, or the cell of a higher organism, that can be stably maintained in an organism, and into which a foreign DNA fragment can be inserted for cloning purposes.
questions.title: Lecture 36 - Gene to Biologic

questions.q: What are the three stages of cloning a gene into a plasmid vector?
options: Insert the gene into the vector to create a chimeric vector, transfect it into a prokaryotic cell so the cell becomes transformed, then screen transformed cells to confirm the correct gene and vector
Amplify the gene, sequence it, then express it
Transform the cell, express the protein, then purify it
Cut the genome, ligate the fragments, then sequence them
Select colonies, culture them, then extract the protein
questions.explanation: The three stages are: insert the gene into the cloning vector to create a chimeric or recombinant vector; transfect the chimeric vector into a prokaryotic cell, usually E. coli, with cells taking up the vector said to be transformed; and screen transformed cells to ensure the correct gene and vector are present, then scale up.
questions.title: Lecture 36 - Gene to Biologic

questions.q: Which description of a plasmid is correct?
options: A small (1 kb to 10 Mb) double-stranded, self-replicating circular DNA molecule, extrachromosomal, found in the cytoplasm of bacteria and some yeasts
A linear single-stranded DNA molecule found in the nucleus
A fragment of the bacterial chromosome that has broken off
An RNA molecule that carries antibiotic resistance
A protein complex that copies DNA
questions.explanation: Plasmids are small (1 kb to 10 Mb) double-stranded, self-replicating circular DNA molecules, distinct from the bacterial chromosome and therefore extrachromosomal. They are found in the cytoplasm of bacteria and some yeasts, and can be transmitted from one bacterium to another.
questions.title: Lecture 36 - Gene to Biologic

questions.q: In nature, what kind of genes do plasmids often carry?
options: Genes that may benefit the survival of the organism, for example antibiotic resistance
Only genes essential for basic metabolism
Genes for the bacterial chromosome's replication
Human genes acquired from the environment
No genes at all; they are non-coding
questions.explanation: In nature, plasmids often carry genes that may benefit the survival of the organism, for example antibiotic resistance. Most cloning plasmids used now are artificial constructs made from useful parts of naturally occurring plasmids.
questions.title: Lecture 36 - Gene to Biologic

questions.q: Which three features must a cloning plasmid have?
options: An origin of replication, a site to insert the gene, and a selectable marker usually conferring antibiotic resistance
A promoter, a ribosome and a polymerase
A signal peptide, a glycosylation site and a disulphide bond
Two primers and a thermostable polymerase
A chromosome, a nucleus and a cell wall
questions.explanation: Plasmids used for cloning have an origin of replication, a site to insert the gene, and a selectable marker, usually a gene conferring resistance to an antibiotic.
questions.title: Lecture 36 - Gene to Biologic

questions.q: What does it mean to make a bacterial cell competent?
options: To make it temporarily permeable so it takes up plasmid DNA, then stop the permeability so cell contents do not leak out
To give it the enzymes needed to replicate a plasmid
To make it resistant to the selective antibiotic
To increase its growth rate before transformation
To remove its own chromosome so the plasmid can function
questions.explanation: Transformation requires making the bacterial cell temporarily permeable, that is competent, so it takes up plasmid DNA, then stopping the permeability so cell contents do not leak out.
questions.title: Lecture 36 - Gene to Biologic

questions.q: Which method of transformation uses calcium chloride followed by a temperature shift?
options: Chemical transformation with heat shock: treat E. coli with CaCl2, add plasmid, raise to 42 degrees C then drop to 0 degrees C
Electroporation with a voltage spike of 200 to 2000 V
Lipofection using liposomes
Conjugation between two bacteria
Transduction by a bacteriophage
questions.explanation: Chemical transformation or heat shock treats E. coli with CaCl2 solution, adds the plasmid, then raises the temperature to 42 degrees C and drops it to 0 degrees C. Electrotransformation uses a voltage spike of 200 to 2000 V for a few milliseconds, and lipofection encases DNA in liposomes.
questions.title: Lecture 36 - Gene to Biologic

questions.q: Which transformation method is the method of choice for mammalian or insect cells?
options: Chemical transformation with heat shock
Electroporation
Lipofection, encasing DNA in liposomes that fuse with the cells
Conjugation
Natural uptake without treatment
questions.explanation: Lipofection encases DNA in liposomes which fuse with the cells. It is not normally used with E. coli but is the method of choice for mammalian and insect cells.
questions.title: Lecture 36 - Gene to Biologic

questions.q: How are bacterial colonies containing the chimeric plasmid selected?
options: Transformed E. coli are plated on agar containing the antibiotic to which the vector confers resistance, so only bacteria carrying the plasmid grow into colonies
Colonies are picked at random and sequenced individually
Colonies are stained and those that turn purple are selected
Colonies are grown at 42 degrees C so only transformed cells survive
All colonies are pooled and the protein extracted from the mixture
questions.explanation: After cloning the gene into a vector carrying an antibiotic resistance gene and transforming E. coli, the cells are plated on agar containing the appropriate antibiotic. Only bacteria carrying the plasmid grow into colonies, and a single colony (a clone) is picked and scaled up.
questions.title: Lecture 36 - Gene to Biologic

questions.q: What is an expression host, and why is it needed?
options: A cell providing the cellular machinery for DNA replication, transcription and translation, needed to copy the chimeric vector and produce recombinant protein
A laboratory device that synthesises protein chemically
The plasmid that carries the foreign gene
The antibiotic used to select transformed cells
The buffer in which the recombinant protein is stored
questions.explanation: To copy the chimeric vector and produce recombinant protein from the inserted foreign gene, the cellular machinery for DNA replication, transcription and translation is required. This is provided by the expression host.
questions.title: Lecture 36 - Gene to Biologic

questions.q: What are the three components of an expression system?
options: An expression host, an expression vector, and a transfection reagent or device to get the vector into the host
A primer pair, a polymerase and nucleotides
A gene, an mRNA and a protein
A plasmid, an antibiotic and an agar plate
A fermenter, a purification column and a QC laboratory
questions.explanation: All expression systems consist of three elements: an expression host such as E. coli cells, an expression vector such as a bacterial plasmid, and a transfection reagent or device to get the vector into the host.
questions.title: Lecture 36 - Gene to Biologic

questions.q: What determines the choice of expression system?
options: What the protein will be used for, since the system must perform all required post-translational modifications so the recombinant protein resembles the native protein as closely as possible
The cost of the culture medium alone
The size of the plasmid used
The country in which the product is manufactured
The colour of the final product
questions.explanation: The choice of expression system is determined by what the protein will be used for. A therapeutic antibody, for example, must have full biological functionality, so the system must perform all required post-translational modifications, though some extra modifications to improve stability or expression are permissible.
questions.title: Lecture 36 - Gene to Biologic

questions.q: How do E. coli, yeast and mammalian cells compare for post-translational modification?
options: E. coli cannot perform them, yeast is capable but often unlike human, mammalian cells produce modifications similar or identical to human
E. coli produces human-identical modifications, yeast cannot, mammalian cells are variable
All three produce identical human modifications
None of the three can perform post-translational modifications
Yeast is best, followed by E. coli, then mammalian cells
questions.explanation: E. coli is not capable of post-translational modifications. Yeast is capable but the modifications are often unlike human ones. Mammalian cells produce modifications similar or identical to human.
questions.title: Lecture 36 - Gene to Biologic

questions.q: How do the growth rates of the three main expression hosts compare?
options: E. coli 3.33 cycles/hour, yeast 0.25/hour, mammalian cells 0.02/hour
E. coli 0.02/hour, yeast 0.25/hour, mammalian cells 3.33/hour
All three grow at about 1 cycle per hour
E. coli 0.25/hour, yeast 3.33/hour, mammalian cells 0.02/hour
Mammalian cells are fastest, then E. coli, then yeast
questions.explanation: E. coli grows at 3.33 cycles per hour, yeast at 0.25 per hour and mammalian cells at 0.02 per hour. Cost also rises sharply, from cheap for E. coli through intermediate for yeast to over $1 million per kg for mammalian cells.
questions.title: Lecture 36 - Gene to Biologic

questions.q: Which is an advantage of the E. coli prokaryotic expression system?
options: Very fast growth kinetics, high cell densities good for scale-up beyond 20,000 L, cheap media, and cheap easy plasmid transformation
Full capacity for complex glycosylation
Products can be harvested without lysing the cells
Ability to express heterologous glycoproteins such as IgG
Guaranteed absence of inclusion bodies
questions.explanation: Advantages of E. coli include very fast growth kinetics, high cell densities allowing scale-up beyond 20,000 L, relatively cheap rich complex media, cheap and easy transformation with plasmids, many high copy number expression plasmids available, no genome integration, and high yields with bioactive product.
questions.title: Lecture 36 - Gene to Biologic

questions.q: What are inclusion bodies, and why are they a disadvantage of E. coli expression?
options: Solid lumps of aggregated recombinant protein that may form when yields are high
Vesicles that export the protein out of the cell
Plasmids that have integrated into the genome
Areas of the cell wall that resist lysis
Contaminating bacterial proteins in the final product
questions.explanation: Inclusion bodies are solid lumps of aggregated recombinant protein. Although E. coli gives high yields of product, the cells must be lysed to obtain it and inclusion bodies may be formed.
questions.title: Lecture 36 - Gene to Biologic

questions.q: Which recombinant biologics are produced in E. coli?
options: Short-acting insulin (Humulin), somatotropin (human growth hormone) and tissue plasminogen activator
Monoclonal IgG antibodies such as trastuzumab
Complex heterologous glycoproteins only
Live attenuated vaccines
Whole blood components
questions.explanation: Examples of recombinant protein biologics produced in E. coli include short-acting insulin (Humulin), somatotropin (human growth hormone) and tissue plasminogen activator. E. coli cannot be used for complex, disulphide-bonded heterologous glycoproteins like IgG.
questions.title: Lecture 36 - Gene to Biologic

questions.q: To express a recombinant protein with a simple structure that is not glycosylated, what is the preferred expression host?
options: A bacterium, such as Escherichia coli
A fungal mycelium, such as Aspergillus
A mammalian cell line, such as Chinese Hamster Ovary fibroblasts
A single-cell fungus, such as Saccharomyces cerevisiae
A viral vector, such as adenovirus
questions.explanation: For a simple, non-glycosylated protein, E. coli is preferred because it is fast growing, cheap, easy to transform and gives high yields. Its inability to perform post-translational modifications such as glycosylation does not matter for such a protein.
questions.title: Lecture 36 - Gene to Biologic

questions.q: Why must a recombinant protein that substitutes for a natural product be structurally identical to the parent molecule?
options: So that it possesses full biological functionality
So that it can be patented
So that it can be produced more cheaply
So that it grows faster in culture
So that it can be given orally
questions.explanation: Where a recombinant protein is a substitute for a natural product such as insulin, growth factors or antibodies, it must be as nearly as possible structurally identical to the parent molecule to possess full biological functionality, so the expression system chosen must provide that structural fidelity.
questions.title: Lecture 36 - Gene to Biologic

questions.q: Besides E. coli, yeast and mammalian cells, what else can express recombinant proteins?
options: Transgenic plants and animals
Cell-free chemical synthesis only
Viruses grown in isolation
Purified ribosomes in a test tube
Nothing else has been shown to work
questions.explanation: Hosts can be prokaryotic, such as E. coli, or eukaryotic, such as yeast cells and mammalian or insect cell lines, all of which are fast growing and can be scaled up. Transgenic plants and animals can also express recombinant proteins.
questions.title: Lecture 36 - Gene to Biologic

questions.q: In the biotechnology overview, from which cell is the human insulin gene originally isolated?
options: The beta pancreatic cell
The hepatocyte
The E. coli cell
A yeast cell
A Chinese Hamster Ovary cell
questions.explanation: Step one of the process is to isolate the gene from donor DNA, in the case of insulin from the beta pancreatic cell, before inserting it into a cloning vector and introducing that into an expression host.
questions.title: Lecture 36 - Gene to Biologic

questions.q: What is the overall topic of the 'From Gene to Biologic' lecture?
options: How drugs and medicinal products can be derived from the human genome using biotechnology
How to synthesise small molecule drugs by organic chemistry only
How antibiotics are discovered from soil fungi without DNA technology
How to perform Gram staining of clinical isolates
How to calculate MIC values from broth dilution
questions.explanation: Lecture 36 covers how biologics such as insulin are created from gene sequences through cloning, expression, and manufacturing steps using biotechnology.
questions.title: Lecture 36 - Gene to Biologic

questions.q: What topics are covered in section 1 'How to find your gene'?
options: Definitions of cloning, what a gene is, finding genes in cDNA, and PCR
Purification of recombinant protein by chromatography only
FDA approval of generic tablets
Sterility testing of non-sterile products
Enumeration by membrane filtration
questions.explanation: Section 1 covers cloning definitions, the nature of a gene, locating the desired gene in cDNA, and the polymerase chain reaction.
questions.title: Lecture 36 - Gene to Biologic

questions.q: How many PCR cycles are typically used to amplify cDNA for cloning?
options: 25–30 cycles of denature, anneal, and elongate in a thermal cycler
1–2 cycles only
Exactly 100 cycles always
PCR is not used for gene amplification
500 cycles without a thermal cycler
questions.explanation: PCR repeats denature–anneal–elongate 25–30 times in a thermal cycler to generate enough cDNA for cloning.
questions.title: Lecture 36 - Gene to Biologic

questions.q: What are the three steps of cloning a gene into a plasmid vector?
options: Insert gene into plasmid, transform into competent cells, verify the chimaeric plasmid
Lyse cells, stain with crystal violet, count on a haemocytometer
Ferment in bioreactor, lyophilise, and tablet compression
Perform Gram stain, catalase test, and coagulase test
Add antibiotic to broth and measure turbidity only
questions.explanation: Cloning into vectors involves inserting the gene into a plasmid, transforming the chimaeric plasmid into competent bacterial cells, and verifying the plasmid is present.
questions.title: Lecture 36 - Gene to Biologic

questions.q: After cloning a gene, what must be achieved in the expression stage?
options: The cloned gene must produce the protein it encodes by choosing an appropriate expression system
The gene must be sequenced only with no protein made
The plasmid must be destroyed before any protein forms
Expression occurs only in human patients, not in vitro
Only mRNA is required; protein is never made
questions.explanation: Gene expression means making the cloned gene produce its encoded protein. The correct expression host must be chosen based on the protein's characteristics.
questions.title: Lecture 36 - Gene to Biologic

questions.q: When is manufacturing of recombinant proteins covered in the pharmacy programme?
options: Year 3 in PY611/612, beyond the scope of this PY411 lecture
In the first week of PY411 only
It is not covered at any point in the degree
Only in the immunology module with no bioprocessing
Exclusively in the enumeration practical class
questions.explanation: Section 4 on manufacturing recombinant protein is deferred to Year 3 modules PY611/612.
questions.title: Lecture 36 - Gene to Biologic

questions.q: What general principle does the gene-to-biologic workflow illustrate?
options: The same cloning, expression, and manufacturing steps apply to any recombinant protein
Only insulin can ever be made by recombinant DNA technology
Each protein requires a completely unique process unrelated to others
Recombinant proteins cannot be manufactured at industrial scale
Gene cloning is theoretical and never used for medicines
questions.explanation: Although detailed, the workflow for insulin exemplifies steps that apply to cloning, expression, and manufacturing of any recombinant protein.
questions.title: Lecture 36 - Gene to Biologic

questions.q: Which reference is suggested for molecular biology techniques in the further reading?
options: Molecular Biology (3rd edn) by Craig et al., Chapter 19
British Pharmacopoeia Appendix XVI only
Hugo & Russell Chapter 2 on enumeration
Alberts Essential Cell Biology Chapter 1 only
No textbooks are recommended
questions.explanation: Further reading lists Molecular Biology (3rd edn) by N.L. Craig et al. (2021), with Chapter 19 recommended for techniques.
questions.title: Lecture 36 - Gene to Biologic

questions.q: Roughly how many microorganisms populate the human gut tract?
options: Up to 100 trillion, mainly bacteria, encoding far more genes than the human genome
About 1 million, mainly fungi
About 1 billion, mainly viruses
About 10 thousand, mainly protozoa
About 100 billion, mainly archaea
questions.explanation: The gut tract harbours a complex microbial ecosystem populated by up to 100 trillion microorganisms, mainly bacteria, which encode much more genes than the human genome.
questions.title: Lecture 37 - Microbiome in Health

questions.q: Which internal sites are usually free of microorganisms?
options: Brain, blood, cerebrospinal fluid and muscles
Skin and mucous membranes
Colon and ileum
Mouth and upper respiratory tract
Vagina and urethra
questions.explanation: Internal tissues are usually free of microorganisms, for example brain, blood, cerebrospinal fluid and muscles. Many other sites are colonised, inside the body by endosymbiosis and outside by ectosymbiosis, such as the skin and mucous membranes.
questions.title: Lecture 37 - Microbiome in Health

questions.q: How does the normal microbiota prevent colonisation by potential pathogens?
options: By producing fatty acids on skin, bacteriocins and colicins in the gut, maintaining an acid environment in the vagina, and competing for nutrients and space
By producing antibodies against invading organisms
By physically blocking all entry to the body
By raising body temperature to inhibit pathogens
By secreting antibiotics identical to prescription drugs
questions.explanation: Prevention of colonisation by potential pathogens involves production of fatty acids on the skin, bacteriocins and colicins in the gut, an acid environment in the vagina, and competition for nutrients and space by the intestinal flora.
questions.title: Lecture 37 - Microbiome in Health

questions.q: Which useful metabolic products does the normal microbiota provide?
options: Organic acids, vitamins B and K, and antigenic stimulation encouraging development of the immune system
Insulin and glucagon
Digestive enzymes such as amylase and lipase
Antibodies of the IgA class
Bile acids and pancreatic secretions
questions.explanation: The normal microbiota produces useful metabolic products including organic acids and vitamins B and K, and provides antigenic stimulation by the intestinal flora to encourage development of the immune system. It also metabolises certain food substrates including sterols and glucose.
questions.title: Lecture 37 - Microbiome in Health

questions.q: Which is an example of normal flora spreading to a normally sterile site?
options: Perianal Escherichia coli reaching the urethra in 'honeymoon' UTI, or streptococci entering the blood after tooth extraction causing endocarditis
Overgrowth of Candida after antibiotic treatment
Colonisation of the skin by Staphylococcus epidermidis
Lactobacillus maintaining vaginal acidity
Bifidobacterium predominating in breast-fed infants
questions.explanation: Problems caused by the microbiota include spread to other sterile sites: perforated intestine in appendicitis, gut flora entering tissues after surgery, streptococci entering the blood at tooth extraction causing endocarditis, and perianal E. coli reaching the urethra in 'honeymoon' UTI.
questions.title: Lecture 37 - Microbiome in Health

questions.q: Approximately how many bacteria does the skin surface support, and over what area?
options: About 10^12 bacteria over roughly 2 square metres
About 10^6 bacteria over roughly 2 square metres
About 10^14 bacteria over roughly 20 square metres
About 10^3 bacteria over roughly 1 square metre
About 10^9 bacteria over roughly 0.2 square metres
questions.explanation: The skin surface, approximately 2 square metres, supports approximately 10^12 bacteria. It is a mechanical barrier to microbial invasion and generally a hostile environment.
questions.title: Lecture 37 - Microbiome in Health

questions.q: Why do transient microorganisms normally die within a few hours on the skin?
options: Lack of moisture inhibits bacterial growth, the skin is slightly acidic and salty, and sweat glands excrete antibacterial compounds
The skin temperature is too high for bacterial survival
Ultraviolet light kills them immediately
The resident flora consume them
The skin surface has no available carbon source
