questions.explanation: Resident flora multiply on or in the skin but transient microorganisms normally die within a few hours, because lack of moisture inhibits bacterial growth, the skin is slightly acidic and salty, and sweat glands excrete antibacterial compounds.
questions.title: Lecture 37 - Microbiome in Health

questions.q: Overgrowth of which yeast causes pityriasis versicolor?
options: Candida albicans
Malassezia
Saccharomyces
Cryptococcus
Rhodotorula
questions.explanation: Pityriasis versicolor is caused by overgrowth of Malassezia, a yeast which may also be found on normal skin, particularly the scalp and skin.
questions.title: Lecture 37 - Microbiome in Health

questions.q: Which antibacterial substances are present in saliva?
options: Lysozyme and lactoperoxidase
Bacteriocins and colicins
Lactic acid and hydrogen peroxide
Bile salts and pancreatic enzymes
Immunoglobulin G and complement
questions.explanation: The mouth contains the antibacterial substances lysozyme and lactoperoxidase in saliva, but food particles and epithelial debris make the oral cavity a favourable site for microbes. Its normal microbiota includes streptococci, lactobacilli and actinomycetes.
questions.title: Lecture 37 - Microbiome in Health

questions.q: Which is the best-characterised biofilm in humans?
options: Dental plaque
The mucin layer of the colon
The vaginal epithelium
The skin surface film
Catheter-associated biofilm
questions.explanation: A well-characterised biofilm in humans is dental plaque, formed in the complex and heterogeneous habitat of the mouth.
questions.title: Lecture 37 - Microbiome in Health

questions.q: Which organism predominates in the vaginal flora, and how does it protect?
options: Lactobacillus acidophilus, which produces lactic acid and maintains an acidic environment
Escherichia coli, which competes for nutrients
Candida albicans, which occupies the mucosal surface
Staphylococcus epidermidis, which produces fatty acids
Proteus mirabilis, which raises the pH
questions.explanation: Vaginal flora changes with age, pH and hormone levels. Lactobacillus acidophilus predominates, producing lactic acid and maintaining an acidic environment. Candida species are transient organisms that frequently cause thrush, especially after oral antibiotics.
questions.title: Lecture 37 - Microbiome in Health

questions.q: Which organisms usually cause urinary tract infections?
options: A single species such as Escherichia coli or Proteus mirabilis
A mixture of at least four anaerobic species
Lactobacillus acidophilus and Candida together
Streptococcus pneumoniae and Neisseria meningitidis
Bacteroides and Clostridium species
questions.explanation: Urinary tract infections are usually caused by a single species such as Escherichia coli or Proteus mirabilis.
questions.title: Lecture 37 - Microbiome in Health

questions.q: Why is the small intestine a more challenging environment for microbes than the large intestine?
options: It has short transit times and high bile concentrations, whereas the large intestine has slow flow rates and neutral to mildly acidic pH
It has a much lower pH than the stomach
It contains no nutrients at all
It is fully aerobic while the large intestine is anaerobic
It has a thicker mucin layer preventing all colonisation
questions.explanation: The small intestine has short transit times and high bile concentrations, making it a more challenging environment. The large intestine is characterised by slow flow rates and neutral to mildly acidic pH and harbours the largest microbial community.
questions.title: Lecture 37 - Microbiome in Health

questions.q: Which two bacterial divisions make up the main gut species?
options: Firmicutes, mostly Gram-positive with low GC content, and Bacteroidetes, Gram-negative non-spore forming anaerobes
Proteobacteria and Actinobacteria
Verrucomicrobia and Proteobacteria
Actinobacteria and Firmicutes
Cyanobacteria and Bacteroidetes
questions.explanation: The main gut species belong to two major divisions: Firmicutes, mostly Gram-positive bacteria with low GC content such as Enterococcus, Lactobacillus, Clostridium and Eubacterium, and Bacteroidetes, Gram-negative non-spore forming anaerobic bacteria such as Bacteroides.
questions.title: Lecture 37 - Microbiome in Health

questions.q: Which minor gut groups are correctly described?
options: Proteobacteria are Gram-negative with an LPS outer membrane (Escherichia, Proteus), Actinobacteria are Gram-positive mostly with high GC content (Bifidobacterium), and Verrucomicrobia are Gram-negative
Proteobacteria are Gram-positive and Actinobacteria Gram-negative
Actinobacteria have low GC content and no cell wall
Verrucomicrobia are Gram-positive spore formers
All three groups are obligate aerobes
questions.explanation: Other groups constitute important but minor fractions: Proteobacteria, Gram-negative with an outer membrane mainly of lipopolysaccharides such as Escherichia and Proteus; Actinobacteria, Gram-positive mostly with high GC content such as Bifidobacterium; and Verrucomicrobia, Gram-negative.
questions.title: Lecture 37 - Microbiome in Health

questions.q: Why are bacterial numbers kept low in the stomach?
options: Most microorganisms are killed by the acidic conditions at pH 2 unless they pass through very quickly, keeping populations at 10^3 to 10^6 per gram
The stomach contains high concentrations of bile
The stomach is completely anaerobic
Gastric mucus is impermeable to all bacteria
The stomach lining secretes antibodies that kill bacteria
questions.explanation: Most microorganisms are killed by acidic conditions at pH 2 unless they pass through very quickly. Numbers rise immediately after a meal but decrease quickly, and organisms are usually transient with populations kept at 10^3 to 10^6 per gram of contents. Lactobacilli are the main flora.
questions.title: Lecture 37 - Microbiome in Health

questions.q: How does bacterial load change along the small intestine?
options: Low in the duodenum (0 to 10^3 per gram) because of stomach acidity, bile and pancreatic secretions, sparse in the jejunum, and moderately mixed in the ileum (10^6 to 10^8 per gram) resembling the colon
Highest in the duodenum and lowest in the ileum
Uniformly high throughout at 10^14 per gram
Uniformly sterile until the colon
Highest in the jejunum because of slow transit
questions.explanation: Gram-positive rods and cocci are found in the duodenum but in low numbers (0 to 10^3 per gram) because of stomach acidity and the inhibitory action of bile and pancreatic secretions. Jejunal flora is also sparse, while the ileum has a moderately mixed flora of 10^6 to 10^8 per gram resembling the colon.
questions.title: Lecture 37 - Microbiome in Health

questions.q: In which gut environment is the highest abundance and diversity of bacteria found?
options: Colon
Duodenum
Jejunum
Oral cavity
Stomach
questions.explanation: The colon has the largest microbial population of the body and the large intestine is one of the most densely populated microbial ecosystems on Earth. Over 300 different species have been isolated from human faeces, with many more non-cultivable taxa.
questions.title: Lecture 37 - Microbiome in Health

questions.q: What is the approximate anaerobe to facultative anaerobe ratio in the colon, and what proportion of faeces is bacteria by weight?
options: About 300:1, with bacteria making up about 30 per cent of faeces by weight
About 1:300, with bacteria making up about 3 per cent by weight
About 1:1, with bacteria making up about 50 per cent by weight
About 30:1, with bacteria making up about 3 per cent by weight
About 300:1, with bacteria making up about 90 per cent by weight
questions.explanation: Most colonisers are anaerobes such as Clostridium and Bacteroides, or facultative aerobes such as E. coli and Enterococcus faecalis growing anaerobically, with an anaerobe to facultative anaerobe ratio of about 300:1. Bacteria make up about 30 per cent by weight of faeces.
questions.title: Lecture 37 - Microbiome in Health

questions.q: How does colonic flora differ between breast-fed and bottle-fed neonates?
options: Bifidobacterium predominates in breast-fed infants, while mixed coliforms predominate in bottle-fed infants
Bacteroides predominates in breast-fed infants and Bifidobacterium in bottle-fed
Both have identical flora from birth
Coliforms predominate in breast-fed infants and Lactobacillus in bottle-fed
Neither group has any colonic flora until weaning
questions.explanation: Bifidobacterium predominates in breast-fed infants while mixed coliforms predominate in those bottle-fed. Diet also matters in adults: meat-eaters have more Bacteroides and fewer coliforms and lactic acid bacteria, while lactic acid bacteria and coliforms predominate in vegetarians.
questions.title: Lecture 37 - Microbiome in Health

questions.q: Which fungi predominate among cultivable gut mycobiota?
options: Candida species, for example Candida albicans
Aspergillus species
Cryptococcus species
Malassezia species
Agaricus species
questions.explanation: Fungi are present in the gastrointestinal tract in much lower quantities than bacteria, and among cultivable fungi Candida species predominate, for example Candida albicans. NGS approaches have shown gut fungi are more diverse and abundant than previously realised.
questions.title: Lecture 37 - Microbiome in Health

questions.q: How does mode of delivery affect the initial gut microbiota of the newborn?
options: Initial communities tend toward a skin-like community after caesarean section and a vaginal-like community after vaginal delivery
Both delivery modes give an identical adult-like community
Caesarean gives a vaginal-like community and vaginal delivery a skin-like community
Neither delivery mode results in colonisation for several months
The community depends only on feeding method, not delivery
questions.explanation: The gastrointestinal tract of the fetus is sterile until birth. Depending on delivery mode, initial communities tend toward a skin-like community after caesarean section or a vaginal-like community after vaginal delivery.
questions.title: Lecture 37 - Microbiome in Health

questions.q: What allows a stable gut community to establish during the first weeks of life?
options: Reduced activity of Toll-like receptors
Increased activity of Toll-like receptors
The absence of any immune system at birth
The introduction of solid foods immediately after birth
High gastric acid production from birth
questions.explanation: During the first weeks of life the reduced activity of Toll-like receptors allows the setting of a stable gut community. As the infant grows and solid foods are introduced, diversity increases toward an adult-like state and the immune system learns to differentiate commensal from pathogenic bacteria.
questions.title: Lecture 37 - Microbiome in Health

questions.q: Which factors influence the gut microbiota?
options: Diet, drugs such as antibiotics, age, genetics, stress, medical conditions, lifestyle and geography
Only diet and antibiotics
Only genetics
Only age and sex
Only geography and climate
questions.explanation: Factors influencing the gut microbiota include diet, use of drugs such as antibiotics, age, genetics, stress, medical conditions such as obesity, inflammatory bowel disease and type 2 diabetes, lifestyle factors such as physical activity, sleep and alcohol, and geography.
questions.title: Lecture 37 - Microbiome in Health

questions.q: Why is the gut microbiota described as an organ performing metabolic functions?
options: Because the diversity of metabolic and biotransforming reactions it carries out is thought to far exceed the capabilities of the liver
Because it has a defined anatomical structure and blood supply
Because it can be surgically removed and replaced
Because it produces hormones like the pancreas
Because it is made of human cells
questions.explanation: The gut microbiota can be thought of as an organ performing metabolic functions beneficial to us, because the diversity of metabolic and biotransforming reactions carried out is thought to far exceed the capabilities of the liver.
questions.title: Lecture 37 - Microbiome in Health

questions.q: Which is a potentially harmful activity of the gut microbiota?
options: Acting as a reservoir of antibiotic resistance genes and producing carcinogens or co-carcinogens implicated in colon cancer
Producing vitamins B and K
Stimulating development of the immune system
Competing with pathogens for nutrients
Maintaining an acidic environment
questions.explanation: Potentially harmful activities include spread to sterile sites, overgrowth by opportunistic normal flora pathogens, acting as a reservoir of antibiotic resistance genes, links to diseases such as diabetes and autism, a role in gut inflammatory diseases, and production of carcinogens or co-carcinogens with a role in colon cancer pathogenesis.
questions.title: Lecture 37 - Microbiome in Health

questions.q: How stable is the gut microbiota within and between individuals?
options: There is a high degree of temporal stability within individuals but wide variation between them, with twins sharing less than 50 per cent of their bacterial taxa
It is identical between all individuals but changes daily within a person
It is completely unstable both within and between individuals
Twins share more than 95 per cent of their bacterial taxa
It never changes once established in infancy
questions.explanation: There is a high degree of temporal stability in individuals, with the community structurally and functionally stable over time, but variation in diversity among different individuals, with twins sharing less than 50 per cent of their bacterial taxa.
questions.title: Lecture 37 - Microbiome in Health

questions.q: What is dysbiosis?
options: An imbalance in the composition of the microbiome, particularly the gut, with overgrowth of harmful bacteria and reduction in beneficial bacteria
The complete absence of gut bacteria
The spread of gut flora to sterile sites
The acquisition of antibiotic resistance genes
The formation of a biofilm on a medical device
questions.explanation: Dysbiosis is an imbalance in the composition of the microbiome, particularly the gut microbiome, occurring when there is an overgrowth of harmful bacteria and a reduction in beneficial bacteria.
questions.title: Lecture 37 - Microbiome in Health

questions.q: Which are recognised consequences of dysbiosis?
options: Digestive issues, immune system dysfunction, metabolic disorders and inflammatory bowel disease
Only diarrhoea and constipation
Only skin rashes
Only increased susceptibility to viral infection
Only weight loss
questions.explanation: Consequences of dysbiosis include digestive issues such as constipation, diarrhoea, bloating and abdominal pain; immune system dysfunction making the individual more susceptible to infections and allergies; metabolic disorders linked to obesity, type 2 diabetes and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease; and inflammatory bowel disease.
questions.title: Lecture 37 - Microbiome in Health

questions.q: How is a probiotic defined?
options: A viable non-pathogenic organism that confers health benefits to the host when administered in adequate doses
Any bacterium found in the normal gut flora
A dietary fibre that feeds beneficial bacteria
An antibiotic that selectively kills harmful bacteria
A dead bacterial preparation given to stimulate immunity
questions.explanation: Probiotic organisms are viable non-pathogenic organisms that confer health benefits to the host, human or animal, when administered in adequate doses.
questions.title: Lecture 37 - Microbiome in Health

questions.q: Which organism, isolated in 1917 from a soldier who resisted a shigellosis outbreak, is a recognised probiotic?
options: Escherichia coli Nissle 1917
Lactobacillus acidophilus
Bifidobacterium bifidum
Saccharomyces boulardii
Enterococcus faecalis
questions.explanation: In 1917 Alfred Nissle isolated an Escherichia coli strain from the faeces of a German soldier who did not develop enterocolitis during a severe shigellosis outbreak. That isolate, E. coli Nissle 1917, is today a recognised probiotic bacterium.
questions.title: Lecture 37 - Microbiome in Health

questions.q: Which organisms are generally used as probiotics?
options: Lactic acid bacteria such as lactobacilli and bifidobacteria, but also some Escherichia coli and yeasts
Only Bacteroides species
Only Clostridium species
Only Candida species
Only Staphylococcus epidermidis
questions.explanation: Probiotics are generally lactic acid bacteria, that is lactobacilli and bifidobacteria, but also include some Escherichia coli and yeasts. Proof of efficacy is complicated because different species and strains have different efficacies.
questions.title: Lecture 37 - Microbiome in Health

questions.q: Which characteristics should a probiotic organism have?
options: Human origin, gastric acid and bile salt stability, adherence to intestinal mucosa, colonisation of the intestinal tract, and production of antimicrobial compounds
Ability to grow only at room temperature
Resistance to all known antibiotics
Ability to produce endospores
Ability to survive only outside the body
questions.explanation: Desirable characteristics include human origin so it can survive the human GI tract, gastric acid and bile salt stability, adherence to intestinal mucosa for immune modulation and competitive inhibition of pathogens, colonisation of the intestinal tract, and production of antimicrobial compounds such as hydrogen peroxide, organic acids and bacteriocins.
questions.title: Lecture 37 - Microbiome in Health

questions.q: Why are probiotic characteristics described as strain-specific?
options: Because strains within the same species may vary in shelf stability, resistance to gastric acid and bile salts, adherence and colonisation capacity, antimicrobial production and clinical efficacy
Because each strain belongs to a different species
Because only one strain of each species exists
Because strains differ only in their name
Because efficacy depends solely on the dose given
questions.explanation: Probiotic characteristics are strain-specific. Strains within the same species may vary in shelf stability, resistance to gastric acid and bile salts, adherence capacity and method, colonisation capacity, ability to produce antimicrobial compounds, and clinical efficacy.
questions.title: Lecture 37 - Microbiome in Health

questions.q: From which three principal sources are live probiotic cells consumed?
options: Fermented milk products such as yogurt, supplemented foods and drinks, and pharmaceutical products such as tablets, capsules and granules
Only fresh fruit and vegetables
Only prescription medicines
Only raw meat and fish
Only intravenous preparations
questions.explanation: Live cells have been consumed from three principal sources: fermented milk products such as yogurt, supplemented foods and drinks, and pharmaceutical products including tablets, capsules and granules. Many commercial preparations have been found to contain mostly dead cells.
questions.title: Lecture 37 - Microbiome in Health

questions.q: What do the key points say about the scientific status of probiotic uses?
options: Most uses of probiotics still lack scientific validation
All probiotic uses are fully validated by clinical trials
Probiotics have been proven ineffective in all settings
Probiotics are validated only for use in animals
Probiotic efficacy is identical across all strains
questions.explanation: The key points note that probiotics may alter the intestinal microflora and exert their effects by a variety of mechanisms, that their characteristics are strain-specific, and that most uses of probiotics still lack scientific validation.
questions.title: Lecture 37 - Microbiome in Health

questions.q: What is the human normal microbiota?
options: Microorganisms on and inside the body that influence processes from digestion to behaviour and support homeostasis
Only pathogenic bacteria causing disease
Microorganisms found exclusively in blood and brain tissue
Viruses that infect plants but not humans
Laboratory contaminants with no physiological role
questions.explanation: Humans host diverse microbial communities comprising organisms on and inside the body. They influence digestion to behaviour and are a fundamental component of homeostasis.
questions.title: Lecture 37 - Microbiome in Health

questions.q: How are bacterial numbers on the body typically expressed?
options: Organisms per gram of tissue or fluid, or per cm2 of skin surface
Only as total genome copies in blood
As CFU per antibiotic disc
As percentage of body weight exclusively
As cells per mitochondrion
questions.explanation: Colonising bacteria are quantified as organisms per gram of tissue or fluid, or per cm2 of skin surface.
questions.title: Lecture 37 - Microbiome in Health

questions.q: Which statement about healthy human bacterial microbiota is correct?
options: It is relatively stable in healthy individuals with a shared core, acquired during and after birth
It changes completely every 24 hours in all healthy adults
It is identical in all humans regardless of geography
It is absent until puberty in every individual
It consists only of viruses with no bacteria
questions.explanation: Bacterial microbiota is stable in healthy individuals with a shared core of members, though populations may differ geographically. Microbiota is acquired during and after birth.
questions.title: Lecture 37 - Microbiome in Health

questions.q: Which organisms predominate in the higher respiratory tract microbiota?
options: Staphylococcus epidermidis and Staphylococcus aureus, with species such as Streptococcus pneumoniae that may cause infection
Only Escherichia coli and Klebsiella
Exclusively Candida albicans
No bacteria; the tract is sterile
Only anaerobic Clostridium species
questions.explanation: Staphylococcus epidermidis and S. aureus predominate in the higher respiratory tract, alongside species such as S. pneumoniae and Neisseria meningitidis that may cause infection.
questions.title: Lecture 37 - Microbiome in Health

questions.q: How is microbial colonisation distributed within the large intestine?
options: Minimal on the epithelial surface, specialist colonizers in the diffuse mucin layer, and a diverse community in the gut lumen
Uniform dense biofilm on the epithelium only
Absent in the lumen with all bacteria on skin
Confined to the stomach with pH 7 throughout
Only in the appendix with no luminal organisms
questions.explanation: The gut has minimal colonization on the epithelial surface, specialist colonizers in the diffuse mucin layer, diverse communities in the liquid-phase lumen, and specialists on substrate particles.
questions.title: Lecture 37 - Microbiome in Health

questions.q: How does microbial load in the gastrointestinal tract change from stomach to colon?
options: It increases along the tract as pH rises from acidic stomach to near-neutral colon
It is highest in the stomach at pH 2 and lowest in the colon
It is identical at every site from oesophagus to rectum
It is zero until the small intestine then drops in the colon
It depends only on dietary fat with no pH effect
questions.explanation: Microbial load increases along the GI tract; pH is low in the stomach (around 2), intermediate in the small intestine, and near neutral (pH 7) in the colon where bacterial numbers are highest.
questions.title: Lecture 37 - Microbiome in Health

questions.q: What is dysbiosis?
options: A disturbed microbial community associated with disease and altered cytokine production
The normal stable microbiota of healthy infants
Sterility of all internal tissues
Deliberate antibiotic eradication of all gut bacteria
Vertical transmission of gut bacteria at birth
questions.explanation: Dysbiosis refers to disturbance of the normal microbiota; different diseases are characterised by changes in microbiota and associated cytokine production.
questions.title: Lecture 37 - Microbiome in Health

questions.q: Why are probiotic characteristics described as strain-specific?
options: Strains within the same species may differ in acid resistance, adherence, colonisation, and clinical efficacy
All strains of Lactobacillus are identical in every property
Only the genus name determines probiotic effect
Strain differences apply only to shelf life, not biology
Probiotics work the same regardless of dose or strain
questions.explanation: Strains within one species can differ in shelf stability, gastric acid and bile resistance, adherence, colonisation, antimicrobial compound production, and clinical efficacy.
questions.title: Lecture 37 - Microbiome in Health

questions.q: Which key point about the human microbiome is correct?
options: The colon harbours the largest microbial populations; main gut species are Firmicutes and Bacteroidetes
The skin has more bacteria than the entire gut
Normal microbiota never act as opportunistic pathogens
Gut microbiota is identical between all individuals at all times
Probiotics are fully validated for all claimed uses
questions.explanation: Key points include the colon housing the largest populations, Firmicutes and Bacteroidetes as main gut divisions, temporal stability within individuals but diversity between them, and links between disturbed communities and disease.
questions.title: Lecture 37 - Microbiome in Health

questions.q: How does horizontal transmission differ from vertical transmission?
options: Horizontal is transmission of an infectious agent from an individual to a contemporary; vertical is passed from mother to baby during pregnancy, childbirth or breastfeeding
Horizontal is mother to baby; vertical is between contemporaries
Horizontal occurs only through the air; vertical only through contact
Horizontal involves vectors; vertical involves fomites
Horizontal occurs in hospitals; vertical in the community
questions.explanation: Horizontal transmission is transmission of an infectious agent from an individual to a contemporary. Vertical transmission is passed from mother to baby during pregnancy, childbirth or breastfeeding.
questions.title: Transmission of Infection

questions.q: Which portal of exit is correctly matched with its vehicle?
options: Intact skin with skin flakes, broken skin with blood, and anus with faeces
Intact skin with blood and broken skin with skin flakes
Mouth with urine and urethra with saliva
Eyes with sputum and nose with tears
Vagina with semen and seminal vesicle with secretions and blood
questions.explanation: Portals of exit include ears with ear wax, eyes with tears, nose with secretions, mouth with saliva and sputum, broken skin with blood, intact skin with skin flakes, mammary glands with milk and secretions, vagina with secretions and blood, seminal vesicle with semen, urethra with urine and anus with faeces.
questions.title: Transmission of Infection

questions.q: What is a fomite?
options: A non-living object that can harbour and transmit an infectious agent
A living organism that transmits disease to humans
A site at which microorganisms enter the body
An individual harbouring an agent without symptoms
A site in which organisms persist and maintain their ability to infect
questions.explanation: Fomites are non-living objects that can harbour and transmit an infectious agent. Examples include soiled handkerchiefs, eating utensils, doorknobs and handrails, bar soap, chopping boards, kitchen sponges, needles, stethoscopes, utility room sinks and hand-dryers.
questions.title: Transmission of Infection

questions.q: Which of these is listed as an example of a fomite?
options: Stethoscopes and hand-dryers
Mosquitoes and fleas
Contaminated drinking water
Airborne droplets from a cough
The placenta
questions.explanation: Examples of fomites given include soiled handkerchiefs, eating utensils, doorknobs and handrails, bar soap, chopping boards, kitchen sponges, needles, stethoscopes, utility room sinks and hand-dryers.
questions.title: Transmission of Infection

questions.q: Why are clinical handwashing sinks elbow, knee, foot or sensor operated rather than hand operated?
options: To avoid recontaminating clean hands by touching a tap that may act as a fomite
To save water during handwashing
To allow the sink to be used while carrying equipment only
Because hand-operated taps are more expensive
To increase the water temperature automatically
questions.explanation: Effective handwashing is an important barrier to the spread of infection. Elbow, knee, foot or sensor operated water supplies avoid the need to touch the tap with clean hands, since the tap could act as a fomite and recontaminate them, helping to reduce healthcare associated infections.
questions.title: Transmission of Infection

questions.q: What is a vehicle in the context of transmission?
options: A non-living carrier of an infectious agent from its reservoir to a susceptible host
A living organism that transmits disease to humans
A person who carries an agent without symptoms
A site at which microorganisms leave the body
The route by which an agent enters the body
questions.explanation: A vehicle is a non-living carrier of an infectious agent from its reservoir to a susceptible host. Transmission via vehicles includes foodborne, waterborne, airborne and body fluid routes.
questions.title: Transmission of Infection

questions.q: What is a vector?
options: A living organism that transmits disease to humans
A non-living object that harbours an agent
A non-living carrier such as food or water
A site at which organisms persist between infections
A person with no symptoms who spreads infection
questions.explanation: Vectors are living organisms that transmit disease to humans. Transmission by vectors may be biological or mechanical.
questions.title: Transmission of Infection

questions.q: Yersinia pestis, the causative agent of plague, completes part of its life cycle within the flea. The flea is acting as what?
options: A biological vector
A mechanical vector
A fomite
A portal of entry
A vehicle
questions.explanation: A biological vector is one in which the agent completes part of its life cycle, as Yersinia pestis does in the flea. A mechanical vector merely carries the organism on or in its body without the agent developing there.
questions.title: Transmission of Infection

questions.q: Which portals of entry are listed for infectious agents?
options: Ear, conjunctiva of the eye, nose, mouth, vagina or penis, urethra, anus, placenta and cross-cutaneous routes such as broken skin or insect bite
Only the mouth and nose
Only broken skin
Only the placenta in vertical transmission
Only the respiratory and gastrointestinal tracts
questions.explanation: Portals of entry include the ear, conjunctiva of the eye, nose, mouth, vagina or penis, urethra, anus, the placenta for mother-to-foetus vertical transmission, and cross-cutaneous routes such as broken skin or insect bite.
questions.title: Transmission of Infection

questions.q: Which diseases are transmitted by the respiratory route?
options: Pneumonia, diphtheria, tuberculosis, whooping cough, COVID-19 and chickenpox
Cholera, typhoid fever and shigellosis
Gonorrhoea, syphilis and chlamydia
Plague, malaria and yellow fever
Hepatitis B, HIV and genital warts
questions.explanation: Diseases spread by droplet or airborne transmission via the respiratory route include pneumonia, diphtheria, tuberculosis, whooping cough, COVID-19 and chickenpox.
questions.title: Transmission of Infection

questions.q: Which diseases are transmitted by the faecal-oral route?
options: Cholera, typhoid fever, shigellosis, travellers' diarrhoea and viral enteritis
Tuberculosis, whooping cough and diphtheria
Syphilis, chancroid and HIV
Plague and Rocky Mountain spotted fever
Chickenpox and COVID-19
questions.explanation: Diseases transmitted by the faecal-oral route, either directly or indirectly, include cholera, typhoid fever, shigellosis, travellers' diarrhoea and viral enteritis.
questions.title: Transmission of Infection

questions.q: Which diseases are transmitted by the sexual route?
options: Gonorrhoea, syphilis, chlamydia, chancroid, HIV/AIDS, hepatitis B and genital warts
Cholera, shigellosis and typhoid
Tuberculosis, pneumonia and diphtheria
Plague, typhus and Q-fever
Viral enteritis and travellers' diarrhoea
questions.explanation: Diseases transmitted by the sexual route, directly or indirectly, include gonorrhoea, syphilis, chlamydia, chancroid, HIV/AIDS, hepatitis B and genital warts.
questions.title: Transmission of Infection

questions.q: Can sexually transmitted diseases be caught from toilet seats?
options: Highly unlikely, because most organisms responsible for STDs require close contact as they are susceptible to drying
Yes, this is a common route of transmission
Yes, but only for viral STDs
Only if the seat is visibly contaminated
Only in hospital settings
questions.explanation: Catching STDs from toilet seats is highly unlikely. Most organisms responsible for STDs require close contact because they are susceptible to drying.
questions.title: Transmission of Infection

questions.q: What is a carrier?
options: An individual who harbours an infectious agent without having observable clinical signs or symptoms
A non-living object that transmits infection
A living organism that transmits disease to humans
A site in which organisms persist between infections
A person who has recovered from an infection
questions.explanation: A carrier is an individual who harbours an infectious agent without having observable clinical signs or symptoms.
questions.title: Transmission of Infection

questions.q: How do an epidemic and a pandemic differ?
options: An epidemic is the occurrence of a disease in unusually high numbers in a localised population; a pandemic is a worldwide epidemic
An epidemic is worldwide; a pandemic is localised
An epidemic affects animals; a pandemic affects humans
An epidemic is caused by bacteria; a pandemic by viruses
They mean the same thing
questions.explanation: An epidemic is the occurrence of a disease in unusually high numbers in a localised population, while a pandemic is a worldwide epidemic.
questions.title: Transmission of Infection

questions.q: What is a hospital acquired infection?
options: An infection acquired during the process of receiving health care that was not present at the time of admission
Any infection treated in a hospital
An infection present on admission but diagnosed later
An infection transmitted from a patient to a healthcare worker only
An infection resistant to all antibiotics
questions.explanation: A hospital acquired infection is an infection acquired during the process of receiving health care that was not present at the time of admission.
questions.title: Transmission of Infection

questions.q: What is a reservoir of infection, and why does it matter?
options: A site in which organisms can persist and maintain their ability to infect, essential for new infections to occur
The organ in which an infection first establishes in a patient
A container of contaminated water
The bloodstream of an infected individual only
A laboratory store of pathogenic organisms
questions.explanation: A reservoir of infection is a site in which organisms can persist and maintain their ability to infect. Reservoirs are essential for new infections to occur, which is why the infection cycle requires the organism to maintain one.
questions.title: Transmission of Infection

questions.q: What are zoonoses?
options: Diseases which can be transmitted under natural conditions to humans from other vertebrates
Diseases transmitted only between humans
Diseases transmitted only by insect vectors
Diseases caused exclusively by viruses
Diseases transmitted from mother to baby
questions.explanation: Zoonoses are diseases which can be transmitted under natural conditions to humans from other vertebrates.
questions.title: Transmission of Infection

questions.q: Which broad routes of transmission are described?
options: Contact transmission (direct and indirect, including droplets), transmission via vehicles (foodborne, airborne, waterborne, body fluids), and transmission by vectors (biological and mechanical)
Only direct contact and airborne routes
Only vector-borne and waterborne routes
Only horizontal transmission between adults
Only faecal-oral and respiratory routes
questions.explanation: Routes of transmission fall into contact transmission, which may be direct or indirect and includes droplets; transmission via vehicles such as foodborne, airborne, waterborne and body fluids; and transmission by vectors, which may be biological or mechanical.
questions.title: Transmission of Infection

questions.q: Why is understanding routes of transmission relevant to pharmacy?
options: It underpins infection control measures, awareness of how our own actions affect transmission, advising patients on protecting themselves and others, and prevention of healthcare associated infections
It determines which antibiotics are stocked
It sets the price of infection control products
It is required only for hospital pharmacists
It affects only the manufacture of sterile products
questions.explanation: Understanding transmission underpins infection control measures, for example in hospital, awareness of how our actions impact transmission, the ability to advise patients how to protect themselves and others, and the prevention of healthcare associated infections.
questions.title: Transmission of Infection

questions.q: According to the key points, why must transmission routes be understood?
options: In order to prevent or limit the spread of disease through applied measures and awareness
In order to identify the causative organism in the laboratory
In order to calculate the correct antibiotic dose
In order to develop new vaccines only
In order to classify diseases taxonomically
questions.explanation: Infectious agents may use different modes of transmission to reach the necessary portal of entry, whether by direct contact or indirectly through fomites, vectors and vehicles. Understanding these routes is necessary to prevent or limit the spread of disease through applied measures and awareness.
questions.title: Transmission of Infection

questions.q: A faecal microbiota transplant transfers faecal bacteria from a healthy donor to a recipient for what purpose?
options: To restore the balance of the colonic microflora
To immunise the recipient against enteric pathogens
To treat a vitamin deficiency
To deliver antibiotics directly to the colon
To diagnose inflammatory bowel disease
questions.explanation: Faecal microbiota transplants have been used to transfer faecal bacteria from a healthy person to a recipient in order to restore the balance of the colonic microflora.
questions.title: Transmission of Infection

questions.q: Which types of agent can cause infection?
options: Bacteria, viruses, fungi and protozoa
Only bacteria and viruses
Only bacteria
Only viruses and prions
Only organisms visible by light microscopy
questions.explanation: Infections can be caused by a range of agents including bacteria, viruses, fungi and protozoa, each of which may use different modes of transmission.
questions.title: Transmission of Infection

questions.q: Which learning outcomes are set for the transmission of infection lecture?
options: Only how to culture bacteria on agar plates
Describe the infectious cycle and chain of infection; understand person-to-person transmission routes; know why transmission routes matter; apply this knowledge to infection control
Only the pharmacology of antiviral drugs
Only the structure of bacterial ribosomes
Only how to prepare sterile injections
questions.explanation: Learning outcomes include describing the infectious cycle and chain of infection, understanding routes of person-to-person transmission with examples, appreciating why transmission routes matter, and applying this knowledge to their control.
questions.title: Transmission of Infection

questions.q: The Mr. and Mrs. Malady scenario is used to prompt consideration of:
options: Only vertical transmission from mother to child
The various ways infectious diseases could be passed between individuals, linking to routes and the chain of infection
Only airborne transmission in open fields
Only food spoilage in the refrigerator
Only laboratory biosafety level 4 procedures
questions.explanation: The Mr. and Mrs. Malady case asks students to consider the ways in which they could pass infectious diseases to each other, connecting to direct contact, droplets, fomites, body fluids and other transmission routes covered in the lecture.
questions.title: Transmission of Infection

questions.q: Why are elbow or foot operated handwashing taps important in clinical areas?
options: They heat water to sterilising temperature automatically
They allow handwashing without recontaminating clean hands by touching a hand-operated tap, helping reduce healthcare acquired infections
They dispense antiseptic instead of water
They eliminate the need for any soap
They replace all other infection control measures
questions.explanation: The example SAQ explains that elbow or foot operated supplies avoid touching taps with clean hands, since taps can act as fomites. Effective handwashing is a key barrier to spread of infection and helps reduce healthcare acquired infections.
questions.title: Transmission of Infection

questions.q: Piret and Boivin (2021) in Frontiers in Microbiology is recommended as further reading on:
options: Bacterial ribosome structure only
Pandemics throughout history
Sterilisation of surgical instruments only
Antibiotic MIC testing methods
Vaccine cold-chain logistics only
questions.explanation: The articles for interest list includes Piret and Boivin (2021) 'Pandemics Throughout History' in Frontiers in Microbiology, complementing the lecture's discussion of major pandemics and global transmission.
questions.title: Transmission of Infection

questions.q: What determines the clinical presentation of an infectious disease?
options: The dynamic interaction between the host immune system and the invading organism
The size of the pathogen alone
The patient's age at first exposure only
The route of antibiotic administration
The number of commensal species in the gut
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of an infectious disease is a result of the dynamic interaction between the host's immune system and the invading organism.
questions.title: Lectures 39 & 40 - Infection and Immunity

questions.q: According to the lecture, how many requirements must an organism meet to set up an infection?
options: Five
Six
Seven
Eight
Ten
questions.explanation: For an organism to set up an infection it has seven requirements: reservoir host, transmission, invasion, adherence, infection/multiplication, interference with host function, and exit/transmission.
questions.title: Lectures 39 & 40 - Infection and Immunity

questions.q: Which pair correctly lists examples of persistent infections given in the lecture?
options: HHV, TB, Candida albicans thrush, and Schistosoma spp.
Influenza A, measles, and smallpox only
E. coli, Lactobacilli, and normal skin flora
Prions and rabies virus exclusively
COVID-19 and Ebola as lifelong infections in all survivors
questions.explanation: Persistent infections can last years; examples include HHV (virus), TB (bacteria), thrush (Candida albicans), and Schistosoma spp.
questions.title: Lectures 39 & 40 - Infection and Immunity

questions.q: What is the incubation period?
options: The time to reach the threshold of microbial numbers before disease symptoms appear
The period after recovery when immunity is lifelong
The time antibiotics must be taken before culture
The interval between two antigenic shift events
The duration of innate immunity only
questions.explanation: A specific threshold of microbial numbers must be reached before disease symptoms are apparent; the time to reach that threshold is the incubation period.
questions.title: Lectures 39 & 40 - Infection and Immunity

questions.q: If pathogen numbers never reach the disease threshold, the infection is described as:
options: Asymptomatic
Chronic
Fatal
Superantigen-mediated
Opportunistic only
questions.explanation: If numbers never reach the threshold, infection is asymptomatic. Chronic infection applies when infection is not eliminated.
questions.title: Lectures 39 & 40 - Infection and Immunity

questions.q: How does pathogenesis differ from the behaviour of normal microbiota?
options: Pathogens have the capacity to interfere with normal host activities
Pathogens never colonise mucosal surfaces
Normal microbiota always produce exotoxins
Pathogens cannot be transmitted between hosts
Normal microbiota always cause fever
questions.explanation: Normal microbiota do many of the same things as pathogens but do not cause disease because pathogens can interfere with normal host activities; this capacity is pathogenesis.
questions.title: Lectures 39 & 40 - Infection and Immunity

questions.q: Which virulence factor is associated with Gram-negative bacteria causing septic shock?
options: Endotoxins
Exotoxins causing muscle rigidity
Viral oncogenes
Superantigens from Staphylococcus aureus only
Cytopathic effects in lung inclusion bodies
questions.explanation: Gram-negative bacterial endotoxins cause septic shock. Exotoxins include tetanus (muscle rigidity), cholera (diarrhoea), and diphtheria (cell death).
questions.title: Lectures 39 & 40 - Infection and Immunity

questions.q: What is a key consequence of superantigen binding to MHC II and TCR?
options: Massive non-specific T-cell proliferation and cytokine storm
Highly epitope-specific antibody production only
Permanent elimination of all CD8+ CTLs
Complete shutdown of innate immunity
Prevention of all phagocytosis
questions.explanation: Superantigens massively overstimulate T-cell proliferation non-specifically, generating a cytokine storm (e.g. IFN-γ) and immunopathology, undermining antigen-specific adaptive immunity.
questions.title: Lectures 39 & 40 - Infection and Immunity

questions.q: Which example illustrates immunopathology caused by innate responses rather than direct pathogen damage?
options: Pus discharge in gonorrhoea from dead neutrophils and tissue debris
HPV oncogene-driven cervical cancer
Cholera exotoxin fluid loss
Tetanus exotoxin muscle rigidity
HIV integration into the host genome
questions.explanation: Innate responses can cause pathology: pus in gonorrhoea (dead neutrophils and debris), fever from IL-1, TB tubercules, and schistosome egg granulomas.
questions.title: Lectures 39 & 40 - Infection and Immunity

questions.q: When are microbes most likely to cause opportunistic infections?
options: In hosts with compromised immunity or physical defence deficits such as wounds
Only in patients who have never been exposed to the organism
Exclusively during the incubation period
Only when superantigens are absent
When adaptive immunity is at its peak
questions.explanation: Microbes generally establish infections in humans with deficits in physical defences (e.g. wounds) or compromised immune systems; these are opportunistic pathogens.
questions.title: Lectures 39 & 40 - Infection and Immunity

questions.q: Which CD4+ Th subset is associated with IFN-γ and macrophage activation against intracellular pathogens?
options: Th1
Th2
Th17
Treg only
None; only B cells respond
questions.explanation: CD4+ Th1 cells produce IFN-γ and activate macrophages against intracellular pathogens (viruses, some bacteria, some protozoa).
questions.title: Lectures 39 & 40 - Infection and Immunity

questions.q: Plan A of human immune defence involves:
options: Blocking infection using barriers such as skin, tears, stomach acid and mucus
Immediate activation of memory B cells only
Antibiotic production by host cells
Destruction of all commensal bacteria
Vaccination before any exposure
questions.explanation: Plan A blocks infection using barriers to entry (skin, tears, stomach acids, mucus). Plan B destroys invaders via innate immunity and, if needed, adaptive immunity.
questions.title: Lectures 39 & 40 - Infection and Immunity

questions.q: According to the lecture, what is a key test of how well our adaptive immune system deals with a pathogen?
options: Whether we can easily make an effective vaccine against it
Whether the pathogen is Gram-positive
Whether it replicates only in the gut
Whether it produces a capsule
Whether it is larger than a red blood cell
questions.explanation: Ease of making an effective vaccine is a key test: immutable immunodominant epitopes make vaccines easier; mutable epitopes (e.g. HIV envelope) or complex organisms make it harder.
questions.title: Lectures 39 & 40 - Infection and Immunity

questions.q: Which list correctly names the 'deadly six' groups of human pathogens?
options: Prions, viruses, bacteria, protozoa, helminths, fungi
Viruses, bacteria, fungi, archaea, plants, prions
Bacteria, viruses, helminths, algae, protozoa, prions
Protozoa, bacteria, viruses, fungi, insects, prions
Viruses, bacteria, rickettsia, protozoa, helminths, algae
questions.explanation: Human infections are caused by six groups: prions, viruses, bacteria, protozoa, helminths (worms), and fungi.
questions.title: Lectures 39 & 40 - Infection and Immunity

questions.q: Which statement about adaptive immunity to viruses is correct according to the lecture?
options: Infection often leads to lifelong protection if the host survives, but some viruses mutate (HIV, influenza, COVID-19)
No vaccines exist for any viral disease
Immunity is always antibody-only with no cellular component
All viruses are equally easy to vaccinate against
Viruses never cause cytopathic effects
questions.explanation: Viral immunity is usually good with lifelong protection if the host survives, but mutation in HIV, influenza and COVID-19 complicates control. Many vaccines exist.
questions.title: Lectures 39 & 40 - Infection and Immunity

questions.q: Which pathogen group has NO vaccines according to the lecture summary?
options: Fungi
Bacteria
Viruses
Protozoa with malaria vaccine noted as exception
Helminths and ectoparasites also lack vaccines
questions.explanation: The lecture states NO VACCINES for fungi. Bacteria and viruses have many vaccines; protozoa have one (malaria); helminths and ectoparasites have none.
questions.title: Lectures 39 & 40 - Infection and Immunity

questions.q: Helminth immunity in the lecture is characterised by:
options: Strong Th2 responses with IgE and mast cells, but minimal response to adult worms
Predominantly intracellular CTL control of adult worms
No allergic-type responses
Effective lifelong vaccines
Immunity that is never predominantly allergic
questions.explanation: Helminth immunity involves Th2/IgE/mast cell responses (like allergy) but adults have few surface antigens; adaptive responses to adults are minimal or very slow.
questions.title: Lectures 39 & 40 - Infection and Immunity

questions.q: Antigenic variation enables a pathogen to:
options: Alter surface proteins to avoid immune response and allow re-infection of previously infected hosts
Increase its generation time in culture media
Produce only endotoxin instead of exotoxin
Eliminate the need for a reservoir host
Prevent all innate immune responses permanently
questions.explanation: Antigenic variation alters surface proteins/carbohydrates so the pathogen evades immunity in the current host and can re-infect previously infected hosts whose memory cells no longer recognise the altered antigen.
questions.title: Lectures 39 & 40 - Infection and Immunity

questions.q: Which pair correctly matches antigenic variation type with mechanism?
options: Genetic: mutation/recombination; Epigenetic: different phenotypes of the same antigen
Genetic: phase variation in Neisseria; Epigenetic: only point mutations in DNA viruses
Genetic: VSG switching; Epigenetic: influenza shift only
Genetic: always slow; Epigenetic: always due to horizontal gene transfer
Genetic: host antibody production; Epigenetic: complement activation
questions.explanation: Two basic types: genetic (gene mutation/recombination) and epigenetic (genes encode different phenotypes of the same antigen, e.g. Neisseria phase variation, trypanosome VSG).
questions.title: Lectures 39 & 40 - Infection and Immunity

questions.q: Why are antibodies to influenza H and N types not fully cross-reactive?
options: Antibodies to each H and N type are specific (e.g. to H1, N2), not to all H or N types
Influenza has no surface antigens
Only internal capsid proteins induce antibodies
H and N are not immunodominant
Influenza B never mutates
questions.explanation: H and N are immunodominant; antibodies to each type are specific. Exposure to H1N1 does not produce cross-reactive antibodies to H2N2, though partial protection to H2N1 may occur.
questions.title: Lectures 39 & 40 - Infection and Immunity

questions.q: How does antigenic DRIFT differ from antigenic SHIFT in influenza?
options: Drift is accumulation of small mutations in H and N genes; shift is sudden complete change often causing pandemics
Drift requires co-infection of human and animal viruses; shift is slow mutation only
Drift occurs only in influenza B; shift only in HIV
Drift is epigenetic; shift is always due to antibiotics
Drift causes pandemics; shift is continuous and minor
questions.explanation: Antigenic drift results from accumulation of small mutations in H and N (genetic AV, ongoing). Shift is sudden complete change in H or N, often from RNA segment swapping, causing pandemics.
questions.title: Lectures 39 & 40 - Infection and Immunity

questions.q: Why does HIV envelope mutation make vaccine development difficult?
options: Constant env gene mutation from low-fidelity reverse transcriptase undermines humoral control
HIV has no envelope protein
Envelope binds only to B cells, not CD4
Reverse transcriptase corrects all errors
HIV never integrates into the host genome
questions.explanation: HIV-1 envelope interacts with CD4 defining tropism; constant env mutation from low-fidelity reverse transcriptase makes humoral responses and effective vaccines very hard to achieve.
questions.title: Lectures 39 & 40 - Infection and Immunity

questions.q: Phase variation in Neisseria involves:
options: Varying pili (pilin subunits), the principal antigen, between two or more phenotypes
Switching between DNA and RNA genomes
Complete loss of all MHC expression
Production of beta-lactamase only
Elimination of all CD4+ T cells within hours
questions.explanation: Neisseria spp. vary their pili (pilin subunits critical for adhesion and principal antigen) between phenotypes in phase variation, forcing the immune system to respond to each phenotype.
questions.title: Lectures 39 & 40 - Infection and Immunity

questions.q: Trypanosoma brucei evades immunity primarily by:
options: Expressing variant surface glycoprotein (VSG) coat with over 1000 genes activated one at a time by gene conversion
Hiding exclusively inside red blood cells only
Producing superantigens like Staphylococcus aureus
Coating itself with host fibronectin like Treponema pallidum
Blocking all type 1 interferons via VP24
questions.explanation: T. brucei decorates itself with a dense VSG coat; over 1000 VSG genes are activated hierarchically one at a time by gene conversion, so immunity chases many variants.
questions.title: Lectures 39 & 40 - Infection and Immunity

questions.q: How does hepatitis C virus evade type 1 interferons?
options: It produces a peptide that downregulates IFN-stimulated genes
It blocks CD4 binding exclusively
It coats itself with host MHC class II
It prevents all T-cell proliferation via superantigen
It destroys all neutrophils at the portal of entry
questions.explanation: HCV produces a peptide downregulating IFN-stimulated genes. Ebola VP24 blocks the interferon channel; EBV produces IL-10-like molecules; HSV-1 binds C3b; CMV/HSV/HIV down-regulate MHC.
questions.title: Lectures 39 & 40 - Infection and Immunity

questions.q: Which bacterial group in the lecture is described as the microbiome?
options: Non-pathogenic bacteria such as Lactobacilli that rarely cause human disease
Primary pathogens such as C. difficile
Opportunistic pathogens such as Salmonella spp. in immunosuppressed patients
All Gram-negative bacteria
Only Streptococcus pyogenes
questions.explanation: Bacteria are clinically divided into primary pathogens, opportunistic pathogens in immunosuppressed patients, and non-pathogenic microbiome organisms such as Lactobacilli.
questions.title: Lectures 39 & 40 - Infection and Immunity

questions.q: Which bacterial structure confers protection from phagocytosis and is associated with 'NHS pathogens'?
options: Sugary capsules (Neisseria, Haemophilus, Streptococci)
Flagella used only for motility in blood
Ribosomes identical to mammalian ribosomes
Endotoxin in Gram-positive bacteria only
Plasmids encoding only antibiotic resistance
questions.explanation: Sugary capsules protect from phagocytosis and are characteristic of NHS pathogens (Neisseria, Haemophilus, Streptococci). Pili, toxins and superantigens are also important virulence factors.
questions.title: Lectures 39 & 40 - Infection and Immunity

questions.q: Treponema pallidum evades phagocytosis partly by:
options: Binding fibronectin to its surface to camouflage as 'self'
Producing beta-lactamase
Living only in the urinary bladder lumen
Expressing VSG coats like trypanosomes
Down-regulating all host MHC class I permanently
questions.explanation: Pathogens can camouflage with host-like surface components; T. pallidum binds fibronectin, hiding antigenic surfaces and minimising opsonisation and phagocyte recognition.
questions.title: Lectures 39 & 40 - Infection and Immunity

questions.q: Which parasites use a 'safe house' evasion strategy?
options: Leishmania amastigotes in macrophages and Plasmodium trophozoites in RBCs
Only extracellular Giardia in the gut lumen
Adult schistosomes with no host antigen coating
Fungi that only infect intact skin
Viruses that never enter cells
questions.explanation: Safe house examples include Leishmania amastigotes in macrophages, Plasmodium trophozoites in RBCs, and Trichinella larvae in muscle cells.
questions.title: Lectures 39 & 40 - Infection and Immunity

questions.q: Schistosomes are described as masters of which evasion strategy?
options: Camouflage — coating themselves with host antigens and immunosilent membranocalyx
Producing only exotoxins like tetanus
Antigenic shift like influenza
Living only as free planktonic bacteria
Eliminating all host IgE production
questions.explanation: Schistosomes camouflage with host antigens (MHC I, IgG, serum glycoproteins), host-like macroglobulins, and immunosilent membranocalyx on cercariae; they also shed/replace outer surfaces.
questions.title: Lectures 39 & 40 - Infection and Immunity

questions.q: Gut and tissue helminth infections are characterised by elevated levels of:
options: IgA antibodies
IgE antibodies
IgG antibodies only
IL-2 cytokines exclusively
IL-10 as the sole mediator
questions.explanation: Formative MCQ: characteristic of gut and tissue helminth infections is elevated IgE, accompanying Th2 responses and mast cell involvement.
questions.title: Lectures 39 & 40 - Infection and Immunity

questions.q: A microbe's capacity to interfere with normal host functions is termed pathogenesis. One example is:
options: Destruction of macrophages as the only mechanism
Elevated bloodstream antibodies as pathogenesis itself
Elevated bloodstream cytotoxic T-cells defining pathogenesis
Joint pain as the definition of pathogenesis
Production of virulence factors such as exo- and endotoxins
questions.explanation: Formative MCQ: pathogenesis is interference with host function; virulence factors including exo- and endotoxins are examples.
questions.title: Lectures 39 & 40 - Infection and Immunity

questions.q: Why are host responses against adult helminths often ineffective?
options: Helminths are large, mobile, shed outer surfaces frequently and have complex multiantigenic life cycles
Adult helminths are always intracellular in hepatocytes
Helminths produce no antigens at any life stage
Th1 responses are always fully protective against worms
IgE is never produced in helminth infection
questions.explanation: Helminths are large, mobile, frequently shed surfaces, and have complex life cycles with few immunodominant adult surface antigens; responses are stronger to larvae, eggs and E/S antigens.
questions.title: Lectures 39 & 40 - Infection and Immunity

questions.q: Intracellular protozoa such as Plasmodium in RBCs are controlled predominantly by:
options: Cellular Th1 responses, with humoral Th2 also important
Th2 antibody responses only with no cellular component
IgE and mast cells exclusively
Complement alone without phagocytosis
No immune response of any kind
questions.explanation: Intracellular protozoa (Plasmodium in RBC, Leishmania, Toxoplasma in WBC) are controlled predominantly by cellular Th1 responses; humoral Th2 also contributes.
questions.title: Lectures 39 & 40 - Infection and Immunity

questions.q: Which fungal infection is noted as especially dangerous in HIV with 20–50% mortality?
options: Candida auris
Athlete's foot only
Ringworm in immunocompetent skin
Lactobacillus overgrowth
Normal oral commensal Candida in healthy hosts only
questions.explanation: C. auris is a new highly pathogenic fungus with 20–50% mortality. C. albicans can go rogue in immunosuppression; cryptococcal meningitis is fatal in HIV.
questions.title: Lectures 39 & 40 - Infection and Immunity

questions.q: RNA viruses are generally more mutation-prone than DNA viruses because:
options: RNA polymerases cause errors that are not corrected, unlike DNA polymerase error correction
RNA viruses never use polymerases
DNA viruses always have larger genomes with no mutations
RNA viruses replicate only in the nucleus with proofreading
DNA viruses cannot cause pandemics
questions.explanation: RNA/DNA polymerases during viral replication are prone to errors; DNA polymerases correct errors more than RNA polymerases, so RNA viruses mutate more readily.
questions.title: Lectures 39 & 40 - Infection and Immunity

questions.q: Which six categories summarise parasitic immune evasion strategies in the lecture?
options: Safe house; stay quiet; camouflage; keep changing disguise; false information; neutralise threats
Shift; drift; conjugation; transformation; transduction; mutation
Exotoxin; endotoxin; superantigen; capsule; pili; biofilm
Th1; Th2; Th17; Treg; CTL; NK only
Innate; adaptive; humoral; cellular; complement; fever
questions.explanation: Six parasite evasion categories: live in a safe house; stay quiet (encyst); camouflage; keep changing disguise; put out false information; neutralise threats.
questions.title: Lectures 39 & 40 - Infection and Immunity

questions.q: SARS-CoV-2 ('COVID-19') spillover is described as originating from:
options: Bats, spreading via an unknown mammal to humans, with aerosol transmission
Soil bacteria only with no animal reservoir
Vertical transmission from mother to baby exclusively
Fomites as the only route with no respiratory spread
Influenza antigenic shift in pigs only
questions.explanation: SARS-CoV-2 originally came from bats, spread via an unknown mammal to humans, can mutate like RNA viruses, and is highly infectious via aerosol.
questions.title: Lectures 39 & 40 - Infection and Immunity

questions.q: In the influenza A example, how does the virus initially enter human cells?
options: Viral haemagglutinin binds to lung cell receptors after spillover from avian or pig reservoirs
It crosses intact skin without binding any receptor
It is ingested and absorbed unchanged from the gut lumen
It enters only through blood transfusion
It binds erythrocytes and never reaches lung tissue
questions.explanation: Influenza A can spill over from birds or pigs. Viral haemagglutinin binds lung cell receptors, the virus enters, multiplies, and can evade intracellular defences.
questions.title: Lectures 39 & 40 - Infection and Immunity

questions.q: Which pathogens are given as examples of antigenic variation?
options: Influenza and HIV (viral), Neisseria (bacterial), Trypanosoma brucei (protozoa), Pneumocystis (fungal)
Only E. coli and Staphylococcus aureus
Exclusively helminths with no viral examples
Only antibiotic-resistant bacteria
Malaria and tuberculosis only
questions.explanation: Examples span viruses (Influenza, HIV), bacteria (Neisseria spp.), protozoa (Trypanosoma brucei), and fungi (Pneumocystis).
questions.title: Lectures 39 & 40 - Infection and Immunity

questions.q: Why is influenza particularly dangerous from an immune evasion perspective?
options: It has two potent genetic antigen-variation-based immune evasion mechanisms
It lacks any surface antigens for the immune system to recognise
It cannot mutate because it has a DNA genome
It is eliminated before any innate response begins
It infects only bacteria, not human cells
questions.explanation: Influenza is dangerous partly because it possesses two potent genetic antigen-variation-based immune evasion mechanisms (antigenic shift and drift).
questions.title: Lectures 39 & 40 - Infection and Immunity

questions.q: Why has HIV been difficult to target with conventional vaccines?
options: Multiple immune evasion mechanisms including genome integration, CD4+ T cell destruction, and relentless mutation
It has no antigens on its surface
It infects only plants
It is cleared within hours by innate immunity alone
It cannot be cultured in any laboratory system
questions.explanation: HIV integrates its genome, destroys CD4+ T helper cells, mutates to form quasispecies, and dampens immunity—failing the 'vaccine test' for proven modalities.
questions.title: Lectures 39 & 40 - Infection and Immunity

questions.q: How do some bacteria inhibit phagocytic engulfment?
options: Surface substances such as polysaccharide capsules or M protein reduce adsorption or engulfment
They secrete antibodies that coat phagocytes
They increase phagocyte metabolism to speed killing
They dissolve all complement proteins irreversibly in seconds
They convert phagocytes into erythrocytes
questions.explanation: Some bacteria have surface components—capsules of S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, K. pneumoniae, or M protein and fimbriae of group A streptococci—that inhibit phagocytic adsorption or engulfment.
questions.title: Lectures 39 & 40 - Infection and Immunity

questions.q: How are parasite immune evasion strategies broadly categorised?
options: Either the host fails to generate an immune response, or the response generated is not protective
Only antibody-mediated killing with no cellular component
Exclusively by antibiotic resistance genes on plasmids
Only through fever and interferon release
Parasites cannot evade immunity because they are too large
questions.explanation: Parasites have numerous evasion strategies falling into two categories: the host does not mount an effective immune response, or the response is not protective.
questions.title: Lectures 39 & 40 - Infection and Immunity

questions.q: What is the role of IgE in helminth infections and type I hypersensitivity?
options: IgE binds parasite allergens and mast cells, triggering release of inflammatory mediators
IgE directly lyses bacteria by complement activation
IgE is absent during allergic responses
IgE only opsonises helminths for phagocytosis with no mast cell involvement
IgE blocks T cell activation permanently
questions.explanation: IgE binds allergens and mast cells, triggering mediator release. In helminth defence and allergy (type I hypersensitivity), repeated allergen exposure drives T cells to activate B cells producing more IgE.
questions.title: Lectures 39 & 40 - Infection and Immunity

questions.q: What happens when helminth allergen-bound IgE activates mast cells?
options: Inflammatory mediators are released that can damage parasites but may also cause allergic responses
Mast cells immediately phagocytose the entire worm
No mediators are released; only antibody levels rise
Mast cells produce only IgG with no inflammation
The response is always fully effective against large worm burdens
questions.explanation: Mast cells release inflammatory mediators when helminth allergen-bound IgE binds them. These can punch holes in worms but are often ineffective against large parasites, and the same pathway underlies allergic responses.
questions.title: Lectures 39 & 40 - Infection and Immunity

questions.q: What is a culture medium?
options: A preparation containing nutrients and conditions required for microbial growth
A stain used to identify Gram-positive bacteria
A method for counting dead cells only
An antibiotic sensitivity test plate
A vaccine preparation for laboratory staff
questions.explanation: Culture medium is a preparation containing/possessing the nutrients and conditions required for growth.
questions.title: Microbial Cultures, Culture Media and Growth

questions.q: When cells are added to a growth medium to start a culture, the cells added are called the:
options: Inoculum
Colony
Agar
Peptone
Diluent
questions.explanation: Adding cells to medium is inoculation; the cells added are the inoculum (plural inocula).
questions.title: Microbial Cultures, Culture Media and Growth

questions.q: How is bacterial growth defined in this lecture?
options: Increase in cell mass followed by increase in cell numbers
Increase in cell size only with no division
Formation of spores exclusively
Production of endotoxin only
Attachment to host tissue without replication
questions.explanation: Bacterial growth is an increase in cell mass followed by an increase in cell numbers, primarily via transverse binary fission.
questions.title: Microbial Cultures, Culture Media and Growth

questions.q: Transverse binary fission is described as:
options: An asexual process leading to rapid increase in cell numbers
Sexual recombination between two bacterial species
Division that produces four spores per cell
Growth only on solid media
A process unique to fungi
questions.explanation: After doubling in size, bacteria divide by transverse binary fission — an asexual process causing rapid population growth.
questions.title: Microbial Cultures, Culture Media and Growth

questions.q: Which is a criterion for culture media listed in the lecture?
options: Sterile — complete absence of viable microorganisms
Must contain blood in all cases
Must be kept at 4°C during incubation
Must always be anaerobic
Must contain antibiotics by default
questions.explanation: Culture media criteria include appropriate nutrients, moisture, correct pH, suitable oxygen level, and sterility (no viable microorganisms).
questions.title: Microbial Cultures, Culture Media and Growth

questions.q: An organism that requires oxygen for growth is termed:
options: Obligate aerobe
Obligate anaerobe
Facultative anaerobe
Microaerophile
Aerotolerant anaerobe
questions.explanation: Obligate aerobes require oxygen. Facultative anaerobes grow better with oxygen but do not require it; obligate anaerobes do not tolerate oxygen.
questions.title: Microbial Cultures, Culture Media and Growth

questions.q: Facultative anaerobes are organisms that:
options: Do not require oxygen but grow better if it is present
Require oxygen and die without it
Cannot survive in the presence of any oxygen
Require lower than atmospheric oxygen levels only
Use oxygen but cannot grow in its presence
questions.explanation: Facultative anaerobes do not require oxygen but grow better if present, unlike obligate aerobes or anaerobes.
questions.title: Microbial Cultures, Culture Media and Growth

questions.q: In broth culture, organisms grow in:
options: Suspension (planktonic phase)
Isolated colonies on a surface only
Spore form exclusively
A vacuum-sealed membrane
Pairs attached to glass slides only
questions.explanation: Broth is a fluid medium; in broth culture organisms grow in suspension (planktonic phase). Solid media produce colony growth.
questions.title: Microbial Cultures, Culture Media and Growth

questions.q: A batch culture is:
options: A closed system with nothing added or removed during incubation
A continuous flow system with constant nutrient input
A culture grown only on membrane filters
A mixed culture that cannot be purified
A culture that never enters log phase
questions.explanation: Batch culture is a closed system; nothing is added or taken away during incubation.
questions.title: Microbial Cultures, Culture Media and Growth

questions.q: Which growth phases are observed in batch culture?
options: Lag, log, stationary, death
Only exponential growth indefinitely
Lag and death only
Stationary phase before lag phase
Log phase only with no lag
questions.explanation: Batch culture shows lag, log (exponential), stationary, and death phases.
questions.title: Microbial Cultures, Culture Media and Growth

questions.q: During exponential growth, cell number increases as 2^n where n is:
options: The number of generations
The dilution factor of the sample
The incubation temperature in °C
The number of antibiotics added
The pH of the medium
questions.explanation: During exponential growth the increase is 2^n where n is the number of generations; t is the generation (doubling) time.
questions.title: Microbial Cultures, Culture Media and Growth

questions.q: Which bacterium has the shortest generation time listed in the lecture table at 37°C?
options: Escherichia coli (21 minutes at 40°C in table; fastest listed)
Mycobacterium tuberculosis (12 h)
Treponema pallidum (33 h)
Staphylococcus aureus (28.2 min — slower than E. coli at 40°C)
Pseudomonas aeruginosa (34.8 min)
questions.explanation: E. coli has a generation time of 21 min at 40°C in the table — the shortest listed. M. tuberculosis and T. pallidum are much slower.
questions.title: Microbial Cultures, Culture Media and Growth

questions.q: What is the most commonly used solidifying agent for bacterial culture media?
options: Agar
Gelatin only
Paraffin wax
Silica gel
Starch exclusively
questions.explanation: A solid medium contains a setting agent; agar is the most commonly used solidifying agent.
questions.title: Microbial Cultures, Culture Media and Growth

questions.q: Why is agar suitable as a solidifying agent?
options: It is solid at incubation temperatures, not utilised by microbes, non-inhibitory, and withstands sterilisation
It is a rich carbon source rapidly hydrolysed by all bacteria
It contains inhibitory substances for Gram-negative bacteria
It precipitates all peptones during autoclaving
It melts at 37°C allowing only liquid culture
questions.explanation: Agar must be solid at incubation temperature, not utilised or inhibitory, not interact adversely with media components, and withstand sterilisation.
questions.title: Microbial Cultures, Culture Media and Growth

questions.q: The streak plate method is used to:
options: Obtain isolated colonies (pure cultures) on agar
Measure turbidity of a broth
Filter viruses from water samples
Count total cells microscopically without growth
Determine antibiotic MIC by broth dilution only
questions.explanation: Streak plating dilutes cells across agar to yield isolated colonies — pure cultures — a revolution in microbiology.
questions.title: Microbial Cultures, Culture Media and Growth

questions.q: Most pathogenic organisms discussed are:
options: Chemoorganoheterotrophs
Photoautotrophs only
Obligate intracellular viruses
Organisms that use CO2 as their sole carbon source
Organisms requiring no trace elements
questions.explanation: Most pathogenic organisms are chemoorganoheterotrophs — they obtain energy from oxidation of organic compounds and carbon from substrates other than CO2.
questions.title: Microbial Cultures, Culture Media and Growth

questions.q: Defined media differ from complex media because defined media:
options: Contain precise amounts of known highly purified substances
Always contain blood and yeast extract
Have unknown variable composition from batch to batch
Cannot support any fastidious organisms
Are only used for fungal cultures
questions.explanation: Defined media contain precise known purified components. Complex (non-defined) media such as those with peptone, blood or yeast extract vary between batches.
questions.title: Microbial Cultures, Culture Media and Growth

questions.q: In the example complex medium recipe, peptone serves as:
options: Partially hydrolysed protein; carbon and/or nitrogen source
Solidifying agent replacing agar
A pH indicator only
An antibiotic selective agent
A source of oxygen for obligate aerobes
questions.explanation: In the example medium, glucose is carbon/energy, yeast extract provides B vitamins, and peptone is partially hydrolysed protein as carbon/nitrogen source.
questions.title: Microbial Cultures, Culture Media and Growth

questions.q: Selective media are designed to:
options: Encourage growth of some organisms while suppressing others
Kill all bacteria equally
Measure turbidity without incubation
Replace the need for any incubation step
Identify viruses by PCR only
questions.explanation: Selective media encourage growth of some organisms while suppressing others; differential media show observable changes when specific reactions occur.
questions.title: Microbial Cultures, Culture Media and Growth

questions.q: Growth factors in microbiology are:
options: Compounds that must be added because the organism cannot synthesise them
Antibiotics that stimulate faster division
Enzymes that hydrolyse agar
Indicators that turn red in acid
Only required by viruses, never bacteria
questions.explanation: Growth factors are compounds that must be added to media for selected organisms because they cannot synthesise them.
questions.title: Microbial Cultures, Culture Media and Growth

questions.q: Treponema pallidum and Mycobacterium leprae are examples of organisms that:
options: Cannot be grown artificially in standard laboratory media (require host cells)
Grow fastest on nutrient agar at room temperature
Are obligate aerobes with 20-minute generation times
Are routinely cultured on MacConkey agar
Produce visible pigmented colonies on blood agar
questions.explanation: Some organisms cannot be grown artificially; others grow only in living host cells — examples include M. leprae and T. pallidum.
questions.title: Microbial Cultures, Culture Media and Growth

questions.q: Colonies on agar plates typically contain:
options: Hundreds of thousands to millions of cells
Exactly one cell always
Only dead cells from stationary phase
Viruses without any bacteria
Fewer than ten cells per colony
questions.explanation: Colonies on agar plates contain hundreds of thousands to millions of cells arising from colony-forming units.
questions.title: Microbial Cultures, Culture Media and Growth

questions.q: Why does the microbial cultures handout contain intentional gaps?
options: Because the lecture content was accidentally deleted
To allow discussion during the session; full lecture slides are provided afterwards
Because cultures cannot be grown in the laboratory
Because all culture media are identical
Because bacteria do not require nutrients to grow
questions.explanation: The handout states that gaps are intentional to allow discussion in the session and that the full lecture slides will be uploaded after the lecture.
questions.title: Microbial Cultures, Culture Media and Growth

questions.q: If an E. coli cell divides every 20 minutes for 24 hours, what does the lecture illustrate?
options: Bacterial populations remain constant in size
