Exponential growth can produce trillions of cells weighing the equivalent of tens of thousands of people
E. coli cannot survive beyond one hour
Division always stops after 100 cells
Growth rate is independent of nutrient supply
questions.explanation: The population explosion example shows that after 24 hours of division every 20 minutes there would be about 4.7 x 10^21 cells, weighing roughly 4.7 x 10^12 g, equivalent to about 65,010 people, illustrating dramatic exponential growth.
questions.title: Microbial Cultures, Culture Media and Growth

questions.q: When growing bacteria in the laboratory, what are the two main options described?
options: Only anaerobic versus aerobic incubation
Liquid growth media giving planktonic growth, or solid growth media giving colony growth after inoculation and incubation
Only microscopy without any culture
Only viral culture in host cells
Only storage at room temperature without inoculation
questions.explanation: Laboratory growth uses liquid growth media for planktonic growth in suspension, or solid growth media where inoculated organisms are incubated to form visible colonies.
questions.title: Microbial Cultures, Culture Media and Growth

questions.q: Why might we need to enumerate microorganisms? One reason given is:
options: Measuring microbial contamination in a raw material or manufactured medicine
Determining the Gram stain reaction only
Identifying viral oncogenes
Measuring host IgE levels
Counting white blood cells in blood films
questions.explanation: Reasons include measuring contamination in materials/medicines, evaluating antimicrobials/decontamination, manufacturing therapeutics, assessing media, and experimental work.
questions.title: Enumeration of Microorganisms

questions.q: Viable counts differ from total counts because viable counts:
options: Estimate the number of living cells capable of forming colonies or growth
Include all dead and living cells without distinction
Measure only viral particles
Require no incubation step
Count only spores that cannot grow
questions.explanation: Viable counts estimate living cells (plate counts, membrane filtration, MPN). Total counts include living and dead cells (turbidity, counting chambers, gravimetric methods).
questions.title: Enumeration of Microorganisms

questions.q: Plate count techniques are based on:
options: Colony counts from colony-forming units (CFUs)
Turbidity without any growth
Weighing dried cell mass only
ATP measurement as the direct colony method
Gram staining of individual cells in suspension
questions.explanation: Plate count techniques (spread and pour plates) are viable count methods based on counting colonies arising from CFUs.
questions.title: Enumeration of Microorganisms

questions.q: In a standard serial dilution, 1 mL added to 9 mL diluent gives:
options: A 1 in 10 dilution with dilution factor 10
A 1 in 100 dilution with dilution factor 100
No change in concentration
A 1 in 1000 dilution
Complete sterilisation of the sample
questions.explanation: 1 mL into 9 mL gives 1/10 (1×10⁻¹) dilution; the dilution factor (how much more dilute) is the inverse: 10.
questions.title: Enumeration of Microorganisms

questions.q: For spread plates, the ideal colony count per plate is:
options: No more than 250 colonies (same for pour plates; fewer for membrane filtration)
Exactly 1000 colonies for best accuracy
Fewer than 10 always
Only plates with confluent growth
Zero colonies on every plate
questions.explanation: Ideally count plates from dilutions with no more than 250 colonies per plate for spread and pour plates (fewer for membrane filtration).
questions.title: Enumeration of Microorganisms

questions.q: The equation for CFU per mL original sample is:
options: Average colony count × (1/volume used in mL) × dilution factor
Average colony count ÷ dilution factor only
Colony count × volume used × 10
Total turbidity × dilution factor
Colony count minus dilution factor
questions.explanation: CFU per mL = average colony count × (1/volume used in mL) × dilution factor. This applies to spread and pour plates (volume differs).
questions.title: Enumeration of Microorganisms

questions.q: In the worked example, dilution B (two 1:10 steps) and 0.1 mL spread giving average 57 colonies gives:
options: 5.7 × 10⁴ CFU mL⁻¹
57 CFU mL⁻¹
5.7 × 10² CFU mL⁻¹
5.7 × 10⁶ CFU mL⁻¹
570 CFU mL⁻¹
questions.explanation: Dilution factor = 10 × 10 = 100. CFU/mL = 57 × (1/0.1) × 100 = 5.7 × 10⁴ CFU mL⁻¹.
questions.title: Enumeration of Microorganisms

questions.q: Pour plate technique differs from spread plates because in pour plates:
options: Diluted sample is mixed with molten agar and colonies develop IN and ON the agar
Sample is never diluted before plating
Colonies grow only on the agar surface
No incubation is required
Only fungi can be counted
questions.explanation: Pour plates mix diluted sample (usually 1 mL) with 20–25 mL warm molten agar (~45°C); after solidification colonies form within and on the agar (lenticular colonies).
questions.title: Enumeration of Microorganisms

questions.q: Serial dilutions A, B and C (three 1:10 steps) give dilution C a dilution factor of:
options: 100 only for B
1 × 10⁻³ as the dilution factor
questions.explanation: Each 1 mL into 9 mL is a 10-fold dilution. Three steps: 10 × 10 × 10 = 1000 (10³) dilution factor for C.
questions.title: Enumeration of Microorganisms

questions.q: Membrane filtration enumeration involves:
options: Filtering sample through a membrane, transferring it to agar, and counting colonies that grow on the membrane
Pouring molten agar directly onto a spectrophotometer
Counting cells only by turbidity without growth
Spreading 10 mL undiluted sample on one plate always
Using only total counts with no viable colonies
questions.explanation: Membrane filtration traps cells on a filter, which is transferred to agar; colonies grow on the membrane after incubation — a viable count method.
questions.title: Enumeration of Microorganisms

questions.q: Filtering 100 mL purified water in triplicate giving 190, 200 and 210 colonies yields:
options: 2 CFU mL⁻¹
200 CFU mL⁻¹
6 CFU mL⁻¹
0 CFU mL⁻¹
20 CFU mL⁻¹
questions.explanation: Average = 200 CFU. CFU/mL = 200 × (1/100) × 1 = 2 CFU mL⁻¹. Membrane filtration suits low-contamination samples like purified water.
questions.title: Enumeration of Microorganisms

questions.q: Turbidity measurements are classified as:
options: Total counts based on light scattering by particles in suspension
Viable counts based on colony formation
Methods that always distinguish live from dead cells
Techniques requiring no calibration curve
Methods that count only bacterial spores
questions.explanation: Turbidity methods measure total counts — particles in suspension scatter light. Increased turbidity reflects more particles but includes all particulate matter.
questions.title: Enumeration of Microorganisms

questions.q: A limitation of turbidity for cell counting is that:
options: A calibration plot is required for each organism and all particulate matter is measured
It can only count viable colonies
It never requires a homogeneous suspension
It distinguishes live and dead cells automatically
It replaces the need for any dilution in all samples
questions.explanation: Turbidity requires calibration per organism, homogeneous suspension, and measures all particulate matter — not selectively viable cells.
questions.title: Enumeration of Microorganisms

questions.q: A colony-forming unit (CFU) may arise from:
options: A single cell or a group of cells
Only exactly one bacterial cell always
Only fungal spores never bacteria
Dead cells that cannot grow
Viruses exclusively
questions.explanation: Colonies form from CFUs which may be single cells or groups of cells; both are referred to as colony-forming units.
questions.title: Enumeration of Microorganisms

questions.q: Membrane filtration is particularly well suited for:
options: Samples expected to have low levels of contamination such as purified water
Samples with extremely high counts requiring no dilution ever
Measuring only turbidity without incubation
Identifying Gram stain reactions
Culturing obligate anaerobes without any special equipment
questions.explanation: Membrane filtration is well suited to low-contamination samples (e.g. purified water BP) where large volumes can be filtered to concentrate organisms.
questions.title: Enumeration of Microorganisms

questions.q: TAMC and TYMC refer to:
options: Total aerobic microbial count and total yeasts/moulds combined count
Total anaerobic microbial count only
Turbidity-adjusted minimum concentration
Therapeutic antimicrobial minimum concentration
Total antibody-mediated clearance
questions.explanation: Important terminology includes TAMC (total aerobic microbial count) and TYMC (total yeasts/moulds combined count).
questions.title: Enumeration of Microorganisms

questions.q: When results are needed immediately without incubation, which method may estimate cell number?
options: Turbidity measurements
Pour plate colony counts after 48 h
Membrane filtration with overnight incubation
Spread plate with 72 h incubation
Most probable number with 5-day incubation
questions.explanation: When incubation is inappropriate, turbidity can provide immediate estimation of cell number, though it is a total count requiring calibration.
questions.title: Enumeration of Microorganisms

questions.q: Example MCQ: What volume of sample is typically applied to a spread plate?
options: 0.1 μL
10 μL
100 μL
questions.explanation: The example MCQ lists 1000 μL (0.1 mL) as the typical spread plate volume — consistent with the worked calculations using 0.1 mL.
questions.title: Enumeration of Microorganisms

questions.q: Any growth-based enumeration method will:
options: Select for a specific population able to grow on that medium
Count all microorganisms in a sample equally
Distinguish all species without incubation
Eliminate the need for serial dilution in all cases
Measure only dead cells
questions.explanation: Plate counts rely on growth on a medium, which always selects for organisms capable of growing under those conditions.
questions.title: Enumeration of Microorganisms

questions.q: Exam answers for CFU calculations should:
options: Show the equation, all working including average, scientific notation, units, and 2 significant figures
Give only the final number with no working
Round to the nearest whole number without units
Omit the dilution factor if under 100
Use words instead of scientific notation always
questions.explanation: Answers should present the equation, full working (including average), scientific notation with units, and report to 2 significant figures.
questions.title: Enumeration of Microorganisms

questions.q: Plate count examples of viable count methods include:
options: Spread plates and pour plates
Gravimetric methods and turbidity only
Counting chambers as the primary viable method
ATP determination as a direct plate method
Gram staining of colonies without growth
questions.explanation: Viable count examples include plate counts (spread and pour), membrane filter count, MPN, ATP (indirect), and some staining microscopic methods.
questions.title: Enumeration of Microorganisms

questions.q: Why must original samples often be diluted before plating?
options: So colony numbers fall in a countable range on the plate
To kill all viable organisms before counting
Because agar cannot solidify without diluent
To convert viable counts to total counts
Because spread plates require at least 10 mL per plate
questions.explanation: Undiluted samples may yield too many colonies (too many to count); serial dilution brings counts into the suitable range (e.g. up to 250 per plate).
questions.title: Enumeration of Microorganisms

questions.q: Total count methods listed include:
options: Microscopic counting chambers, turbidity, gravimetric methods, and analysis of cell components
Spread plates and pour plates only
Membrane filtration with colony counts only
Coagulase testing and API strips
Selective enrichment in MacConkey broth only
questions.explanation: Total counts use microscopic methods, turbidity, gravimetric approaches, and cell component analysis. Viable counts use growth-based techniques.
questions.title: Enumeration of Microorganisms

questions.q: In pour plate side view, colonies growing within the agar are described as:
options: Lenticular colonies
Punctiform colonies only on the surface
Filamentous rhizoid colonies exclusively
Membrane-bound colonies
Turbid colonies without defined edges
questions.explanation: Pour plates produce colonies within and on the agar; those within appear lenticular in side view.
questions.title: Enumeration of Microorganisms

questions.q: Viable counts estimate living cells whereas total counts:
options: Estimate living plus dead cells
Count only spores that will never germinate
Measure antibiotic MIC values
Replace all pharmacopoeial tests
Require no calibration or incubation ever
questions.explanation: Key point: viable counts estimate living cells; total counts estimate living and dead cells together.
questions.title: Enumeration of Microorganisms

questions.q: What are the main steps of plate count (viable count) techniques?
options: Serially dilute sample, plate known volumes on agar, incubate, and count colonies
Filter sample then measure turbidity without incubation
Stain cells and count under oil immersion only
Add antibiotic and measure zone diameter
Centrifuge and weigh the pellet without dilution
questions.explanation: Plate count techniques serially dilute the sample, place a known amount of each dilution on or in agar (spread or pour plates), incubate, and count resulting colonies.
questions.title: Enumeration of Microorganisms

questions.q: When counting colonies on spread plates, which dilution plates should ideally be counted?
options: Plates with no more than about 250 colonies, typically from dilutions giving countable numbers
Only plates with more than 1000 colonies
Plates with zero colonies from the most concentrated dilution
Any plate regardless of colony number
Only the undiluted original sample plate
questions.explanation: Count plates arising from dilutions that give no more than about 250 colonies; very dense plates are too numerous to count accurately.
questions.title: Enumeration of Microorganisms

questions.q: In the spread plate method, what is the ideal colony count range per plate?
options: 25 to 250 colonies per plate
1 to 5 colonies only
500 to 5000 colonies
Exactly 10 colonies always
Any number above zero is equally valid
questions.explanation: Ideally count plates from dilutions generating 25–250 colonies per plate after spreading a known volume on dried agar and incubating.
questions.title: Enumeration of Microorganisms

questions.q: In the example calculation, 0.1 mL of dilution B (1:100) gave average 57 colonies. What is the CFU mL-1 of the original suspension?
options: 57 CFU mL-1
0.57 CFU mL-1
questions.explanation: CFU mL-1 = average count × (1/volume mL) × dilution factor = 57 × (1/0.1) × 100 = 5.7 × 10^4 CFU mL-1.
questions.title: Enumeration of Microorganisms

questions.q: How does calculating CFU mL-1 from pour plates differ from spread plates?
options: The same equation is used but the volume of sample added to molten agar is typically larger
Pour plates use a completely different equation with no dilution factor
Pour plates never require incubation
Spread plates use volume in litres while pour plates use grams
Only pour plates count dead cells
questions.explanation: The CFU mL-1 equation is the same for pour plates, but the volume of sample incorporated into the agar is different (usually larger) than the small volume spread on the surface.
questions.title: Enumeration of Microorganisms

questions.q: A membrane filtration count gives average 200 CFU with 100 mL filtered and dilution factor 1. What is the CFU mL-1?
options: 2 CFU mL-1
0 CFU mL-1
6 CFU mL-1
200 CFU mL-1
questions.explanation: CFU mL-1 = 200 × (1/100) × 1 = 2 CFU mL-1, matching the worked solution on the following slide.
questions.title: Enumeration of Microorganisms

questions.q: What does turbidity mean in the context of microbial enumeration?
options: Cloudiness of a suspension due to cells or particles scattering light
Complete clarity indicating no cells present
Colour change after Gram staining
Formation of a pellicle on broth surface
Antibiotic zone of inhibition around a disc
questions.explanation: A turbid sample is not clear because cells in suspension scatter light; a clear sample lacks this cloudiness.
questions.title: Enumeration of Microorganisms

questions.q: How does a spectrophotometer measure turbidity?
options: Particles in suspension scatter incident light, reducing transmitted light detected by a photocell
It counts individual cells by autofluorescence only
It measures colony diameter on agar
It detects antibiotic resistance genes by PCR
It weighs the dry mass of filtered cells
questions.explanation: Particles cause light scattering so less light reaches the photocell; the spectrophotometer readout reflects transmitted light after passing through the suspension.
questions.title: Enumeration of Microorganisms

questions.q: Membrane filtration for enumeration is particularly useful for which samples?
options: Samples expected to have low levels of contamination, where concentrating cells on a filter improves detection
Only samples with very high bacterial loads above 10^9 CFU mL-1
Samples that must never be incubated under any circumstances
Exclusively fungal cultures on Sabouraud agar
Only sterile water with guaranteed zero organisms
questions.explanation: Membrane filtration traps organisms from a known volume on a filter transferred to agar; it suits dilute samples where low contamination must still be detected.
questions.title: Enumeration of Microorganisms

questions.q: What is the principle of membrane filtration enumeration?
options: A known volume is filtered to trap microorganisms on a membrane, which is incubated on agar so colonies can be counted
Organisms are lysed and DNA quantified by PCR only
Turbidity is measured without any filtration step
Antibiotics are added to the filter to test MIC
Cells are stained and counted directly in the original sample without growth
questions.explanation: Membrane filtration passes sample through a filter that retains cells; the membrane is placed on growth medium, incubated, and colonies growing on the filter are counted.
questions.title: Enumeration of Microorganisms

questions.q: Tools for bacterial detection and identification listed in the lecture include:
options: Morphology, cultural reactions, staining, biochemical reactions, and PCR
Only Gram staining with no other tests
Host antibody levels exclusively
Vaccination status of personnel only
Turbidity measurement without any culture
questions.explanation: Identification uses morphology, cultural reactions/physiology, staining, biochemical/nutritional reactions, and PCR.
questions.title: Identification of Microorganisms

questions.q: Colony morphology features used for identification include:
options: Form, elevation, margin, surface and pigment production
Only the incubation temperature
The price of the culture medium
Host CD4+ T-cell count
Antibiotic MIC values only
questions.explanation: Colony morphology includes form (circular, irregular etc.), elevation (flat, convex etc.), margin (entire, lobate etc.), surface (smooth, rugose etc.) and pigment.
questions.title: Identification of Microorganisms

questions.q: The environmental monitoring contaminant is described as having colonies that are:
options: Smooth, circular, convex with entire margin and yellow pigment
Filamentous, flat, with erose margin and no pigment
Gram-negative rods in chains
Large fungal hyphae with no pigment
Pink nonfermenting colonies on MacConkey only
questions.explanation: The contaminant produces yellow pigmented, circular, smooth, convex colonies with entire margins.
questions.title: Identification of Microorganisms

questions.q: Microscopic examination of the contaminant shows:
options: Gram-positive clusters of cocci
Gram-negative bacilli in pairs
Acid-fast branching filaments
Yeast buds with pseudohyphae only
Spirochaetes with no Gram reaction
questions.explanation: The contaminant cells are Gram-positive clusters of cocci — consistent with staphylococcal morphology.
questions.title: Identification of Microorganisms

questions.q: For aqueous oral products, pharmacopoeial limits include max TAMC of:
options: 10² CFU/g or mL with absence of E. coli in 1 g or 1 mL
10³ CFU/g with no specified organism tests
10¹ CFU/g with absence of Salmonella only
Zero TAMC with no yeast limits
10⁴ CFU/g for all routes equally
questions.explanation: Aqueous oral products: max TAMC 10², max TYMC 10¹, and absence of E. coli in 1 g or 1 mL.
questions.title: Identification of Microorganisms

questions.q: Specified microorganisms tested pharmacopoeially (USP, EP, BP) include:
options: E. coli, Salmonella, P. aeruginosa, S. aureus, C. perfringens (EP/BP), C. albicans, bile-tolerant Gram-negatives
Only HIV and influenza virus
Mycobacterium leprae exclusively
All Lactobacillus species
Prions and helminths only
questions.explanation: Pharmacopoeial tests detect E. coli, salmonellae, P. aeruginosa, S. aureus, C. perfringens (EP & BP), C. albicans, and bile-tolerant Gram-negative bacteria.
questions.title: Identification of Microorganisms

questions.q: The general pharmacopoeial detection procedure involves:
options: Enrichment, then selective/differential solid media, then confirmatory tests
PCR only with no culture steps
Single Gram stain with no further testing
Turbidity reading without incubation
Immediate antibiotic prescribing without isolation
questions.explanation: Procedure: enrichment in liquid media to increase numbers, selective/differential solid media for indicative colonies, then confirmatory biochemical/immunological tests.
questions.title: Identification of Microorganisms

questions.q: Selective media are defined as media that:
options: Favour growth of one group while inhibiting others by added substances
Contain no nutrients and prevent all growth
Change colour only without affecting growth
Are always non-defined complex media only
Require no incubation after inoculation
questions.explanation: Selective media contain substances favouring one group and inhibiting others. Differential media show diagnostically useful changes after incubation.
questions.title: Identification of Microorganisms

questions.q: Mannitol salt agar is useful in the contaminant work-up because:
options: It supports staphylococci; mannitol fermentation turns the agar yellow
It selects only for E. coli lactose fermenters
It inhibits all Gram-positive bacteria
It detects only fungal contamination
It replaces the need for any Gram stain
questions.explanation: Mannitol salt agar is selective for staphylococci; yellow colonies with yellow surrounding agar indicate mannitol fermentation — presumptive S. aureus.
questions.title: Identification of Microorganisms

questions.q: MacConkey agar is selective due to:
options: Bile salts and crystal violet
7.5% NaCl only
Mannitol as the sole carbon source
Blood and heated red cells exclusively
Phenyl red without any inhibitors
questions.explanation: MacConkey is selective (bile salts and crystal violet) and differential (neutral red pH indicator for lactose fermentation) — recommended for E. coli detection.
questions.title: Identification of Microorganisms

questions.q: On MacConkey agar, E. coli is described as:
options: A lactose fermenter
A nonfermenter like Serratia marcescens
A weak fermenter only like Enterobacter aerogenes
Unable to grow on the medium
Always producing a yellow pigment
questions.explanation: MacConkey distinguishes lactose fermenters (E. coli, Enterobacter, Klebsiella) from nonfermenters (e.g. Serratia marcescens). E. coli is a fermenter.
questions.title: Identification of Microorganisms

questions.q: For oral mucosal and cutaneous products, specified absent organisms include:
options: Staph. aureus and Ps. aeruginosa
E. coli only
Candida albicans only
Salmonella and C. perfringens exclusively
No specified organisms for any topical product
questions.explanation: Oral mucosal, gingival, cutaneous, nasal and ear products: max TAMC 10², TYMC 10¹, absence of S. aureus and P. aeruginosa in 1 g or 1 mL.
questions.title: Identification of Microorganisms

questions.q: The coagulase test is used to:
options: Confirm Staphylococcus aureus by detecting coagulase that clots plasma
Identify E. coli by lactose fermentation
Detect beta-lactamase in Gram-negative rods
Measure turbidity of broth cultures
Enumerate CFU on spread plates
questions.explanation: Coagulase test is a confirmatory test for S. aureus — coagulase causes plasma to clot (latex bead agglutination commercial test); differentiates S. aureus (+) from S. epidermidis (−).
questions.title: Identification of Microorganisms

questions.q: After coagulase-positive confirmation, the contaminant most likely originated from:
options: Personnel
Raw water supply only
Air filtration systems exclusively
The mannitol in the culture medium
A fungal spore from soil only
questions.explanation: Confirmed S. aureus in pharmaceutical environmental monitoring most likely arose from personnel — a common skin commensal and contaminant.
questions.title: Identification of Microorganisms

questions.q: API test strips work by:
options: Miniaturised dehydrated biochemical tests inoculated and incubated, giving a profile number matched to a database
Measuring only colony pigment on blood agar
PCR amplification of 16S rRNA without culture
Counting CFU by membrane filtration only
Gram staining without any biochemical reactions
questions.explanation: API (Analytical Profile Index) uses dehydrated miniaturised biochemical/nutritional tests; colour chart interpretation yields a 7-figure profile cross-referenced to a database.
questions.title: Identification of Microorganisms

questions.q: Example MCQ: What component of Mannitol Salt agar inhibits most bacteria other than staphylococci and micrococci?
options: 7.5% NaCl
Bile salts
Crystal violet
Mannitol
Phenyl red
questions.explanation: Example MCQ answer: 7.5% NaCl in mannitol salt agar inhibits most bacteria except staphylococci and micrococci.
questions.title: Identification of Microorganisms

questions.q: Enrichment media in pharmacopoeial testing are used to:
options: Increase numbers of the organism of interest to improve detection chances
Kill all organisms except fungi
Replace confirmatory biochemical tests
Measure turbidity without growth
Prevent any selective growth
questions.explanation: Enrichment media contain nutrients encouraging growth of a particular organism so it increases in number and can be detected and identified.
questions.title: Identification of Microorganisms

questions.q: Differential media are defined as media that:
options: Incorporate chemicals causing diagnostically useful growth or visible medium change after incubation
Contain no carbon source
Always inhibit Gram-positive bacteria
Are used only for viral identification
Never change colour during incubation
questions.explanation: Differential media incorporate chemicals producing diagnostically useful growth or visible changes (e.g. pH indicator colour change on lactose fermentation in MacConkey).
questions.title: Identification of Microorganisms

questions.q: Vaginal products must be free of which specified organisms in 1 g or 1 mL?
options: Staph. aureus, Ps. aeruginosa and Candida albicans
E. coli only
Salmonella and C. perfringens only
No specified organisms
HIV and hepatitis B virus
questions.explanation: Vaginal products: max TAMC 10², TYMC 10¹, absence of S. aureus, P. aeruginosa and C. albicans in 1 g or 1 mL.
questions.title: Identification of Microorganisms

questions.q: Pigment-producing bacteria mentioned as identification examples include:
options: Serratia marcescens, Staphylococcus aureus, Pseudomonas aeruginosa
E. coli only with no pigment
Lactobacillus rhamnosus exclusively
Treponema pallidum with yellow colonies
Mycobacterium tuberculosis on mannitol salt agar
questions.explanation: Examples of pigment production include Serratia marcescens, Staphylococcus aureus, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa — useful macroscopic identification features.
questions.title: Identification of Microorganisms

questions.q: Colony elevation terms include:
options: Flat, raised, effuse, convex, umbonate
Only punctiform and filamentous
Lag, log, stationary and death
Gram-positive and Gram-negative only
Susceptible, intermediate and resistant
questions.explanation: Colony elevation categories include flat, raised, effuse, convex, and umbonate alongside form (circular, irregular etc.) and margin types.
questions.title: Identification of Microorganisms

questions.q: Inhalation products (excluding nebulised liquids) must be free of:
options: Staph. aureus, Ps. aeruginosa and bile-tolerant Gram-negative bacteria
E. coli only
Candida albicans only
All bacteria regardless of type
No specified microorganisms
questions.explanation: Inhalation products (excl. nebulised liquids): max TAMC 10², TYMC 10¹, absence of S. aureus, P. aeruginosa and bile-tolerant Gram-negative bacteria.
questions.title: Identification of Microorganisms

questions.q: Further identification tests are chosen based on:
options: Initial observations and presumptive identifications
Random selection without prior morphology
Patient age alone
Antibiotic cost only
Turbidity of enrichment broth only
questions.explanation: Key point: confirmatory enzyme and growth tests depend on initial observations and presumptive IDs from colony and cell morphology, staining, etc.
questions.title: Identification of Microorganisms

questions.q: On mannitol salt agar, Staphylococcus epidermidis compared to S. aureus typically:
options: Does not ferment mannitol (shown as example B vs fermenting S. aureus A)
Ferments mannitol turning the whole plate yellow like S. aureus always
Is a Gram-negative rod
Grows only on MacConkey agar
Produces coagulase strongly positive
questions.explanation: Mannitol salt agar example: S. aureus (A) ferments mannitol; S. epidermidis (B) does not; E. coli (C) is inhibited.
questions.title: Identification of Microorganisms

questions.q: Information gained from simple observations for bacterial ID includes:
options: Colony size, pigmentation, appearance, cell shape, motility, spores and staining
Only PCR results without any culture
Host IgE levels exclusively
Antibiotic therapeutic index only
Generation time in hours only
questions.explanation: Much information comes from colony size, pigmentation, appearance, cell size/shape, motility, spore production and staining reactions before biochemical confirmation.
questions.title: Identification of Microorganisms

questions.q: Which skills should students gain from the identification of microorganisms lecture?
options: Describing morphological and staining features, pharmacopoeial tests, and selective/differential media including API kits
Calculating drug half-lives from dose-response curves
Designing PCR primers for human insulin cloning
Measuring resting membrane potential in neurons
Synthesising beta-lactam antibiotics in the lab
questions.explanation: Learning outcomes include morphological and staining characteristics, pharmacopoeial detection tests, selective and differential media, and miniaturised biochemical kits such as API.
questions.title: Identification of Microorganisms

questions.q: In the pharmaceutical contamination scenario, what is the initial task?
options: Identify an environmental contaminant isolated during monitoring of manufacturing premises
Calculate the MIC of vancomycin for the isolate only
Determine the patient's white cell count
Perform a pregnancy test on the manufacturing line
Measure the pH of paracetamol syrup only
questions.explanation: The scenario places students in environmental monitoring of pharmaceutical premises where a contaminant has arisen and must be identified.
questions.title: Identification of Microorganisms

questions.q: Which bacterial structures are listed in the revision slide on cell anatomy?
options: Plasma membrane, capsule, flagellum, plasmid, ribosomes, chromosome, fimbriae, cell wall, and pilus
Nuclear envelope, nucleolus, and spindle fibres only
Mitochondrial cristae and chloroplast thylakoids in all bacteria
Endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi in prokaryotes
Actin filaments and microtubules as the cell wall
questions.explanation: The revision slide lists plasma membrane, capsule, flagellum, plasmid, ribosomes, storage granule, chromosome (nucleoid), fimbriae, cytoplasm, cell wall, and pilus.
questions.title: Identification of Microorganisms

questions.q: What macroscopic observation helps identify an organism on solid media?
options: Colony appearance on media such as MacConkey agar
Only the colour of the broth without plating
Zone of inhibition around an antibiotic disc exclusively
Turbidity reading without any culture
Gram stain of colonies before they have grown
questions.explanation: Macroscopic observations include growth appearance on solid media such as MacConkey agar plates—what the organism looks like when cultured.
questions.title: Identification of Microorganisms

questions.q: During identification of the pharmaceutical contaminant, what should students consider mid-investigation?
options: Potential identity of the organism and its likely source of origin
Only the molecular weight of penicillin
The patient's blood glucose level
The half-life of ibuprofen in plasma
The structure of the ribosome in eukaryotes only
questions.explanation: The lecture prompts students to consider the potential identity of the contaminant and where it might have originated from based on evidence gathered so far.
questions.title: Identification of Microorganisms

questions.q: What is known about the pharmaceutical contaminant at this stage of the case?
options: Yellow pigmented, circular, smooth, convex colonies with entire margins; Gram-positive cocci in clusters
Pink flat colonies; Gram-negative rods in chains
No growth on any medium; cells are acid-fast bacilli
Large mould colonies; cells are spiral-shaped and motile
Colourless pinpoint colonies; Gram-variable diplococci only
questions.explanation: The contaminant produces yellow pigmented, circular, smooth, convex colonies with entire margins, and the cells are Gram-positive cocci in clusters—suggesting staphylococci.
questions.title: Identification of Microorganisms

questions.q: Which microorganisms are tested for in pharmacopoeial detection procedures (USP, EP & BP)?
options: E. coli, salmonellae, P. aeruginosa, S. aureus, C. perfringens (EP/BP), C. albicans, and bile-tolerant Gram negatives
Only HIV and influenza A
Exclusively Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium
Only Mycobacterium tuberculosis
No specified organisms are listed in pharmacopoeias
questions.explanation: Pharmacopoeial tests target specified organisms including E. coli, salmonellae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Staphylococcus aureus, Clostridium perfringens (EP & BP), Candida albicans, and Gram-negative bile-tolerant bacteria.
questions.title: Identification of Microorganisms

questions.q: What are the three general stages of pharmacopoeial detection of specified microorganisms?
options: Enrichment in liquid medium, growth on selective/differential solid media, then confirmatory biochemical or immunological tests
Gram stain only, then immediate release of product
PCR only with no culture steps
Antibiotic disc diffusion then MIC broth dilution
Membrane filtration with no confirmatory testing
questions.explanation: The general procedure is enrichment to increase numbers, selective/differential solid media to identify suspect colonies, then confirmatory biochemical or immunological tests.
questions.title: Identification of Microorganisms

questions.q: How do enrichment, selective, and differential media differ?
options: Enrichment boosts target organisms; selective favours one group; differential gives visible diagnostic changes after incubation
All three terms mean identical media with no additives
Selective media contain no nutrients; enrichment is always solid
Differential media kill all organisms except fungi
Enrichment replaces confirmatory biochemical testing
questions.explanation: Enrichment encourages growth of a particular organism; selective media inhibit unwanted groups; differential media incorporate indicators producing diagnostically useful changes.
questions.title: Identification of Microorganisms

questions.q: On mannitol salt agar, which organism ferments mannitol and turns the medium yellow?
options: Staphylococcus aureus
Staphylococcus epidermidis
Escherichia coli
Pseudomonas aeruginosa
Salmonella enterica
questions.explanation: Mannitol salt agar is selective for staphylococci. S. aureus ferments mannitol producing acid that changes the indicator, while S. epidermidis does not and E. coli is inhibited.
questions.title: Identification of Microorganisms

questions.q: What makes MacConkey agar both selective and differential?
options: Bile salts and crystal violet inhibit Gram positives; neutral red indicates lactose fermentation
It contains only mannitol and salt with no pH indicator
It supports only fungi because of cycloheximide
It differentiates cells by Gram stain colour in the plate
It is selective for staphylococci only
questions.explanation: MacConkey agar uses bile salts and crystal violet (selective against Gram positives) and neutral red pH indicator to distinguish lactose fermenters such as E. coli from non-fermenters.
questions.title: Identification of Microorganisms

questions.q: Given Gram-positive cocci in clusters with yellow colonies, which medium is appropriate for further testing?
options: Mannitol salt agar to distinguish Staphylococcus aureus from other staphylococci
MacConkey agar to detect E. coli
Sabouraud dextrose agar for dermatophytes
Lowenstein-Jensen medium for M. tuberculosis
Thiosulfate citrate bile salts for salmonellae only
questions.explanation: The contaminant resembles staphylococci (Gram-positive cocci in clusters). Mannitol salt agar is the selective/differential medium used to differentiate S. aureus.
questions.title: Identification of Microorganisms

questions.q: Using MacConkey agar as an example, what is a selective medium?
options: A medium with additives that favour growth of one group while inhibiting others, such as bile salts and crystal violet
A medium that changes colour only after confirmatory coagulase testing
A medium with no carbon source
A medium used only for enrichment in liquid form
A medium that identifies organisms by API profile alone
questions.explanation: The example SAQ asks students to explain selective and differential media using MacConkey agar; selective components such as bile salts and crystal violet inhibit unwanted organisms.
questions.title: Identification of Microorganisms

questions.q: Bacteriostatic action means the agent:
options: Stops bacteria reproducing without necessarily killing them
Always lyses the cell wall immediately
Works only against fungi
Must be applied to inanimate surfaces only
Prevents all host immune responses
questions.explanation: Bacteriostatic agents stop bacterial reproduction; bactericides kill bacterial cells. Both 'cidal and 'static terms apply across antiseptics, disinfectants, preservatives and antibiotics.
questions.title: Lecture 44 - Introduction to Antimicrobial Drugs I

questions.q: Antiseptics are applied to:
options: Skin or living tissues and must not be toxic or irritating to skin/mucous membranes
Non-living objects only at high concentration
Food exclusively as preservatives
Bloodstream as the only route
Soil samples for antibiotic discovery only
questions.explanation: Antiseptics are applied to skin or living tissues (e.g. before needles/catheters) and must not be toxic or irritating. Examples include chlorhexidine, cetrimide, alcohols, peroxigens.
questions.title: Lecture 44 - Introduction to Antimicrobial Drugs I

questions.q: Disinfectants differ from antiseptics mainly in that disinfectants:
options: Are applied to non-living objects and are more likely to harm humans if misused
Are always safe to drink at any concentration
Cannot kill any bacterial spores under any circumstances
Are only used inside the bloodstream
Never share chemical classes with antiseptics
questions.explanation: Disinfectants target inanimate objects; antiseptics target tissues. Disinfectants usually have wider activity and higher human toxicity risk. Many chemicals serve both at different concentrations.
questions.title: Lecture 44 - Introduction to Antimicrobial Drugs I

questions.q: High-level disinfectants:
options: Kill most microbes unless extreme challenge of resistant bacterial spores
Kill only enveloped viruses and no bacteria
Cannot kill mycobacteria or fungi
Are identical to low-level antiseptics
Work only at room temperature without contact time
questions.explanation: High-level disinfectants kill most microbes except extreme spore challenges. Intermediate level kills most vegetative bacteria, mycobacteria, most viruses/fungi. Low level excludes spores and mycobacteria.
questions.title: Lecture 44 - Introduction to Antimicrobial Drugs I

questions.q: Preservatives in medicines are used to:
options: Protect against microbial spoilage in non-sterile products and multi-dose sterile containers
Replace all antibiotics in systemic infection
Sterilise surgical instruments exclusively
Kill all commensal gut flora permanently
Increase bacterial generation time in culture
questions.explanation: Preservatives protect non-sterile products from spoilage and multi-dose sterile products from microbes introduced when doses are repeatedly withdrawn.
questions.title: Lecture 44 - Introduction to Antimicrobial Drugs I

questions.q: Which is listed as a preservative example?
options: Benzalkonium chloride (a QAC)
Benzylpenicillin for systemic sepsis
Bleach for floor disinfection only
Metronidazole for anaerobic gut infection only
Rifampicin for tuberculosis
questions.explanation: Preservative examples include parabens, phenylethanol, bronopol, chlorhexidine, thiomersal, phenol, and QACs such as benzalkonium chloride.
questions.title: Lecture 44 - Introduction to Antimicrobial Drugs I

questions.q: According to the original 1940s definition, is metronidazole an antibiotic?
options: No — it is a chemically synthesised agent, not produced by a microorganism
Yes — it is secreted by Streptomyces species
Yes — all antiseptics are antibiotics by that definition
No — it has no antimicrobial activity
Yes — it only works topically
questions.explanation: Original definition: substance produced by one microorganism inhibiting others in low concentration. Metronidazole is synthetic, so not an antibiotic by that narrow definition.
questions.title: Lecture 44 - Introduction to Antimicrobial Drugs I

questions.q: By the current widespread definition, antibiotics include:
options: All agents with systemic antimicrobial activity including synthetic analogues
Only naturally fermented products with no synthetic drugs
Antiseptics and disinfectants at any concentration
Food preservatives never used in humans
Vaccines and monoclonal antibodies only
questions.explanation: Current definition covers all systemic antimicrobial agents including synthetic derivatives and mimics with potency, low toxicity and systemic action. Antiseptics/disinfectants are not antibiotics.
questions.title: Lecture 44 - Introduction to Antimicrobial Drugs I

questions.q: Penicillin development for WWII involved:
options: Fleming's 1929 discovery, Oxford development over 10 years, then US industrial scale-up
Immediate mass production in 1929 without further work
Discovery by Streptomyces fermentation only
Development solely for agricultural use in cattle
Synthesis entirely in the laboratory without fermentation
questions.explanation: Fleming discovered penicillin in 1929; Oxford developed it over the next decade; US pharmaceutical industry scaled manufacturing for WWII battlefield infections and gonorrhoea.
questions.title: Lecture 44 - Introduction to Antimicrobial Drugs I

questions.q: Most antibiotics have historically been produced from:
options: Streptomyces species
Escherichia coli exclusively
Human cell cultures only
Synthetic chemistry with no microbial source ever
Plant alkaloids exclusively
questions.explanation: Streptomycin, tetracyclines and most antibiotics come from Streptomyces. Other sources include Bacillus, Micromonospora, fungi (Penicillium), and Pseudomonas/Gluconobacter for monobactams.
questions.title: Lecture 44 - Introduction to Antimicrobial Drugs I

questions.q: Selective toxicity in antimicrobial chemotherapy is achieved by:
options: Exploiting structural and metabolic differences between pathogens and host cells
Using the highest possible dose in all patients
Treating all human cells identically to bacteria
Avoiding any target in the pathogen
Relying only on host fever responses
questions.explanation: Selective toxicity is the essence of antimicrobial chemotherapy — exploiting differences such as bacterial cell walls, ribosomes, and enzymes not found in mammalian cells.
questions.title: Lecture 44 - Introduction to Antimicrobial Drugs I

questions.q: The main component of the bacterial cell wall discussed is:
options: Peptidoglycan with alternating NAM and NAG units cross-linked by peptides
Cholesterol identical to mammalian membranes
Lipopolysaccharide in all bacteria including Gram-positive
Cellulose like plant cell walls
Phospholipid bilayer with no macromolecular mesh
questions.explanation: Peptidoglycan is vital — glycan chains (NAM and NAG) cross-linked by short peptides. It determines shape, acts as diffusion barrier, and protects against osmotic lysis.
questions.title: Lecture 44 - Introduction to Antimicrobial Drugs I

questions.q: If peptidoglycan synthesis is inhibited, bacterial cells:
options: Become distorted and lyse due to high internal osmotic pressure
Grow larger without any shape change
Are unaffected because mammalian cells also have peptidoglycan
Immediately form spores
Switch to viral replication
questions.explanation: Damaged or inhibited peptidoglycan leads to distorted cells that burst from osmotic pressure. Mammalian cells lack peptidoglycan — excellent selective toxicity target.
questions.title: Lecture 44 - Introduction to Antimicrobial Drugs I

questions.q: Beta-lactam antibiotics inhibit transpeptidases by:
options: Mimicking D-alanyl-D-alanine residues and reacting covalently with penicillin-binding proteins
Blocking DNA gyrase directly
Binding mammalian 80S ribosomes
Preventing folic acid uptake in human cells
Activating host complement only
questions.explanation: β-lactams inhibit transpeptidases (PBPs) by mimicking D-alanyl-D-alanine in peptidoglycan precursors, covalently binding PBPs, weakening the wall until osmotic lysis.
questions.title: Lecture 44 - Introduction to Antimicrobial Drugs I

questions.q: Fluoroquinolones such as ciprofloxacin are bactericidal by inhibiting:
options: DNA gyrase (not present in human cells)
Peptidoglycan transpeptidase only
Human dihydrofolate reductase
Host mitochondrial ribosomes
Viral reverse transcriptase
questions.explanation: DNA gyrase catalyses ATP-dependent negative supercoiling of bacterial closed-circular DNA and is absent in human cells. Fluoroquinolones inhibit it bactericidally.
questions.title: Lecture 44 - Introduction to Antimicrobial Drugs I

questions.q: Antibiotics targeting bacterial ribosomes exploit the fact that:
options: Bacterial ribosomes have different structural proteins from mammalian ribosomes
Bacterial and human ribosomes are identical
Only human cells have ribosomes
Ribosomes exist only in Gram-negative bacteria
All antibiotics bind both ribosome types equally
questions.explanation: Bacteria have 70S ribosomes with different proteins; tetracyclines, chloramphenicol, macrolides and aminoglycosides bind bacterial ribosomes selectively.
questions.title: Lecture 44 - Introduction to Antimicrobial Drugs I

questions.q: Trimethoprim shows selective toxicity because it:
options: Binds bacterial dihydrofolate reductase ~50,000 times more strongly than the human enzyme
Cannot enter any bacterial cell
Works only at pH 2 in the stomach
Inhibits human DNA gyrase preferentially
Is inactive until host liver metabolises it
questions.explanation: Folic acid activation by dihydrofolate reductase differs between species; trimethoprim binds the bacterial enzyme far more strongly (pyrimethamine targets the malaria parasite enzyme).
questions.title: Lecture 44 - Introduction to Antimicrobial Drugs I

questions.q: Aminoglycosides enter bacterial cells preferentially because:
options: Bacterial active transport enzymes uptake them; human cells lack these transporters
They are highly lipophilic and cross all membranes equally
They bind only to human ribosomes
They are too large to enter any cell
They require viral co-infection for activity
questions.explanation: Aminoglycosides are polar and poorly penetrate by diffusion, but bacterial uptake transporters exist — not in human cells — providing selective entry.
questions.title: Lecture 44 - Introduction to Antimicrobial Drugs I

questions.q: Metronidazole becomes active by:
options: Reduction within microbial cells with low redox potential (e.g. obligate anaerobes), causing DNA breakage
Binding peptidoglycan in aerobic bacteria only
Inhibition of mammalian folate synthesis exclusively
Blocking influenza neuraminidase
Hydrolysis by beta-lactamase enzymes
questions.explanation: Metronidazole is inactive until reduced in cells with sufficiently low redox potential (obligate anaerobes); reduced metronidazole causes DNA breakage — used e.g. in diabetic foot ulcers.
questions.title: Lecture 44 - Introduction to Antimicrobial Drugs I

questions.q: Antibiotics interfering with peptidoglycan include:
options: Beta-lactams, glycopeptides (vancomycin, teicoplanin), bacitracin and cycloserine
Fluoroquinolones and rifampicin only
Trimethoprim and pyrimethamine only
Chlorhexidine and bleach
Acyclovir and oseltamivir
questions.explanation: Cell wall agents include β-lactams (penicillins, cephalosporins), glycopeptides, bacitracin and cycloserine targeting peptidoglycan synthesis or integrity.
questions.title: Lecture 44 - Introduction to Antimicrobial Drugs I

questions.q: Gentamicin is obtained from:
options: Micromonospora purpurea
Penicillium chrysogenum
Streptomyces griseus only for all aminoglycosides
Escherichia coli fermentation
Synthetic chemistry with no microbial source
questions.explanation: Gentamicin comes from Micromonospora purpurea. Bacitracin/polymyxin from Bacillus; many drugs from Streptomyces; penicillins/cephalosporins from fungi such as Penicillium.
questions.title: Lecture 44 - Introduction to Antimicrobial Drugs I

questions.q: Scientists traditionally find new antibiotics by:
options: Screening environmental samples such as soil for antibiotic-producing microbes
Synthesising random polymers without any screening
Using only host immune sera
Culturing viruses on blood agar exclusively
Measuring turbidity without isolation
questions.explanation: Nature (especially soil) is the best source; traditional discovery screens environmental samples for microbes producing inhibitory substances.
questions.title: Lecture 44 - Introduction to Antimicrobial Drugs I

questions.q: Formative MCQ: Which term refers to harming the pathogen without harming the host?
options: Mechanism of resistance
Mode of action
Selective toxicity
Spectrum of activity
Therapeutic level
questions.explanation: Formative MCQ answer: selective toxicity is the ability to harm the target microorganism without harming the host.
questions.title: Lecture 44 - Introduction to Antimicrobial Drugs I

questions.q: Bacterial spores are most resistant to disinfectants, but some sporicidal agents include:
options: Certain aldehydes, halogens and peroxygen products
Low-level quaternary ammonium compounds alone
Distilled water at room temperature
All beta-lactam antibiotics at low concentration
Food-grade sorbic acid preservatives only
questions.explanation: Bacterial spores resist most disinfectants; some aldehydes, halogens and peroxygen products are sporicidal. High-level disinfectants kill most microbes except extreme spore challenges.
questions.title: Lecture 44 - Introduction to Antimicrobial Drugs I

questions.q: Key functions of the bacterial cell wall include:
options: Determining cell shape, acting as a diffusion barrier, and protecting against osmotic lysis
Producing endotoxin in all Gram-positive species
Hosting human-style 80S ribosomes
Synthesising folic acid for human cells
Replacing the need for a cell membrane
questions.explanation: The cell wall determines shape, is a diffusion barrier, and protects against osmotic lysis — making it an excellent antibiotic target with no mammalian counterpart.
questions.title: Lecture 44 - Introduction to Antimicrobial Drugs I

questions.q: Which categories of antimicrobial agents are introduced at the start of the lecture?
options: Only systemic antibiotics administered orally
Antiseptics, disinfectants, preservatives and antibiotics, which may be described as -cidal or -static
Only vaccines and immunoglobulins
Only antifungal tablets
Only antiviral nucleoside analogues
questions.explanation: The lecture introduces antiseptics, disinfectants, preservatives and antibiotics. All of these may be described as cidal (e.g. bactericidal, fungicidal) or static (e.g. bacteriostatic).
questions.title: Lecture 44 - Introduction to Antimicrobial Drugs I

questions.q: Which antibiotics are noted as being obtained from certain fungal genera such as Penicillium and Acremonium?
options: Streptomycin and tetracyclines only
Griseofulvin and some penicillins and cephalosporins
Trimethoprim and sulfonamides only
Aminoglycosides such as gentamicin only
Quinolones such as ciprofloxacin only
questions.explanation: Griseofulvin and some penicillins and cephalosporins are obtained from certain fungal genera such as Penicillium and Acremonium, whereas many other antibiotics come from Streptomyces species.
questions.title: Lecture 44 - Introduction to Antimicrobial Drugs I

questions.q: Which differences between bacterial and mammalian cells underpin selective antibiotic toxicity?
options: Bacteria lack DNA and RNA
Bacteria possess a cell wall, have different ribosomes and different enzymes
Mammalian cells always have peptidoglycan walls
Bacteria and humans have identical 80S ribosomes
Only mammalian cells require folic acid
questions.explanation: Key differences include the bacterial cell wall, different ribosomes and different enzymes. These distinctions allow antibiotics to target pathogens while minimising harm to host cells.
questions.title: Lecture 44 - Introduction to Antimicrobial Drugs I

questions.q: Why can some antibiotics selectively inhibit bacterial protein synthesis?
options: Bacterial and human ribosomes are identical in structure
Bacteria have different ribosomes with different structural proteins; some antibiotics bind only to bacterial ribosomes
Ribosomes are absent in bacteria
Antibiotics block all protein synthesis in every cell type equally
Only human ribosomes contain RNA
questions.explanation: Bacteria have different ribosomes with different structural proteins. Some antibiotics such as tetracyclines, chloramphenicol, macrolides and aminoglycosides bind only to bacterial ribosomes, providing selective toxicity.
questions.title: Lecture 44 - Introduction to Antimicrobial Drugs I

questions.q: Which summary correctly distinguishes antiseptics, disinfectants, preservatives and antibiotics?
options: All four are applied only to inanimate surfaces
Antiseptics are for living tissues; disinfectants for inanimate surfaces; preservatives protect medicines from spoilage; antibiotics are administered to animals and exploit pathogen-host differences
Preservatives are always bactericidal systemic drugs
Antibiotics are only synthetic with no natural sources
Disinfectants must be non-toxic to skin at all concentrations
questions.explanation: Key points state antiseptics are applied on living tissues, disinfectants on inanimate surfaces, preservatives protect medicines against microbial spoilage, and antibiotics are naturally produced, semi-synthetic or synthetic agents administered to animals, with selective toxicity from exploiting cell differences.
questions.title: Lecture 44 - Introduction to Antimicrobial Drugs I

questions.q: The therapeutic index of an antibiotic is defined as:
options: TD₅₀ / ED₅₀ — toxic dose for 50% divided by effective dose for 50%
ED₅₀ / TD₅₀ only
MIC divided by MBC always
Half-life multiplied by dose frequency
Cost per tablet divided by spectrum width
questions.explanation: Therapeutic index = TD₅₀/ED₅₀ where TD₅₀ causes toxicity in 50% and ED₅₀ is effective in 50%. Safer drugs have wider (higher) therapeutic indexes.
questions.title: Lecture 45 - Introduction to Antimicrobial Drugs II

questions.q: Which antibiotics typically have a narrow therapeutic index requiring monitoring?
options: Aminoglycosides and vancomycin
Penicillins and macrolides
All beta-lactams without exception
Fluoroquinolones exclusively with no exceptions
Topical antiseptics only
questions.explanation: Most antibiotics have wide therapeutic indexes (β-lactams, macrolides, quinolones). Aminoglycosides and vancomycin have narrow indexes — TDM may be appropriate.
questions.title: Lecture 45 - Introduction to Antimicrobial Drugs II

questions.q: Vancomycin is an example of:
options: A narrow-spectrum antibiotic active only against Gram-positive bacteria
A broad-spectrum drug active against all fungi and viruses
An antiseptic for skin cleansing only
A preservative in oral liquids exclusively
A bacteriostatic sulphonamide only
questions.explanation: Vancomycin (glycopeptide) is narrow spectrum — only Gram-positive. Broad spectrum examples include tetracyclines and fluoroquinolones (Gram+ and Gram−).
questions.title: Lecture 45 - Introduction to Antimicrobial Drugs II

questions.q: Polymyxins are usually effective against:
options: Gram-negative bacteria only
Gram-positive bacteria only
Fungi and protozoa exclusively
Viruses and prions
All organisms equally
questions.explanation: Narrow spectrum examples: glycopeptides against Gram-positive; polymyxins usually only against Gram-negative bacteria.
questions.title: Lecture 45 - Introduction to Antimicrobial Drugs II

questions.q: Whether an antibiotic is bactericidal or bacteriostatic may depend on:
options: Concentration, infection site, and microbial growth rate
Patient eye colour only
The colour of the capsule only
Whether the drug is a preservative
Incubation temperature of the pharmacy
questions.explanation: Cidal vs static can depend on concentration (e.g. penicillins, tetracyclines), site tissue levels, and growth rate — cidal drugs work poorly against non-growing bacteria.
questions.title: Lecture 45 - Introduction to Antimicrobial Drugs II

questions.q: According to the lecture table, which pairing is correct?
options: Beta-lactams bactericidal; tetracyclines bacteriostatic
Gentamicin bacteriostatic; chloramphenicol bactericidal only
Trimethoprim bactericidal; rifampicin bacteriostatic
Vancomycin bacteriostatic; fluoroquinolones bacteriostatic only
Erythromycin bactericidal; sulphonamides bactericidal
questions.explanation: Table: bactericidal include β-lactams, aminoglycosides, rifampicin, fluoroquinolones, glycopeptides; bacteriostatic include tetracyclines, macrolides, chloramphenicol, sulphonamides, trimethoprim.
questions.title: Lecture 45 - Introduction to Antimicrobial Drugs II

questions.q: Parenteral antibiotic therapy is preferred when:
options: Patient cannot take oral medication or prompt high serum levels are needed for severe infection
The infection is always mild and superficial
Only topical fungi are present
The drug has a half-life of weeks
No microbiology sampling is possible ever
questions.explanation: Parenteral route used when oral intake is difficult or greater/prompt antimicrobial activity is needed; oral when tolerated and adequate.
questions.title: Lecture 45 - Introduction to Antimicrobial Drugs II

questions.q: Which antibiotics are listed as oral-only (not parenteral in the table)?
options: Erythromycin/macrolides, tetracyclines, sulphonamides/trimethoprim, first-line TB drugs
All aminoglycosides and all glycopeptides
Ceftazidime and all IV cephalosporins only
Vancomycin IV and gentamicin tablets
Linezolid exclusively topical
questions.explanation: Oral examples: some β-lactams (amoxicillin), all fluoroquinolones, macrolides, tetracyclines, sulphonamides/trimethoprim, first-line TB antibiotics. Aminoglycosides and glycopeptides are injectable.
questions.title: Lecture 45 - Introduction to Antimicrobial Drugs II

questions.q: Beta-lactam antibiotics typically have:
options: Short half-life values requiring frequent administration
Half-lives of several weeks like benzathine penicillin for all penicillins
No renal excretion
Half-lives longer than hydroxychloroquine always
Zero metabolism in the liver
questions.explanation: β-lactams usually have short half-lives (e.g. benzylpenicillin 30 min) demanding frequent dosing; exceptions like benzathine penicillin (14 days) exist.
questions.title: Lecture 45 - Introduction to Antimicrobial Drugs II

questions.q: Tetracycline binding to calcium ions can cause:
options: Permanent staining of teeth if given during development
Enhanced Gram-positive coverage only
Irreversible ototoxicity like gentamicin
Spontaneous resistance to vancomycin
Increased uptake into anaerobic cells
questions.explanation: Tetracyclines bind calcium and may permanently stain teeth. β-lactams may be broken down by stomach acid or bacterial β-lactamases.
questions.title: Lecture 45 - Introduction to Antimicrobial Drugs II

questions.q: The UK price comparison illustrates that modern antibiotics:
options: Are very expensive — e.g. >400-fold cost difference between trimethoprim (1960s) and linezolid (2000)
Are always cheaper than antiseptics
Have unlimited patent life
Never develop resistance
Are only used for 1-day courses always
questions.explanation: Modern antibiotics are expensive due to short therapy, stewardship, short patents, and resistance likelihood — illustrated by trimethoprim vs linezolid price differential.
questions.title: Lecture 45 - Introduction to Antimicrobial Drugs II

questions.q: Broad-spectrum antibiotics can harm patients by:
options: Killing normal flora allowing resistant pathogens and superinfections such as C. difficile colitis
Always causing immediate anaphylaxis
Preventing all allergic responses
Eliminating the need for narrow-spectrum drugs permanently
Increasing vitamin K production only
questions.explanation: Broad spectrum kills many normal microbiota species, allowing resistant/pathogenic organisms to colonise — superinfections, oral/vaginal thrush, and C. difficile pseudomembranous colitis.
questions.title: Lecture 45 - Introduction to Antimicrobial Drugs II

questions.q: Penicillin hypersensitivity: patients sensitive to one penicillin:
options: Will be sensitive to all penicillins; ~10% also sensitive to cephalosporins
Can safely take any beta-lactam without testing
Are never allergic via non-IV routes
Always develop resistance not allergy
Only react to topical antiseptics
questions.explanation: Basic penicillin structure drives hypersensitivity; sensitivity to one penicillin means all penicillins. ~10% penicillin-allergic patients cross-react with cephalosporins. Anaphylaxis 0.005–0.05%.
questions.title: Lecture 45 - Introduction to Antimicrobial Drugs II

questions.q: Serious aminoglycoside adverse effects include:
options: Ototoxicity, nephrotoxicity, and neuromuscular blockade at high local doses
Only mild skin rash without any organ toxicity
Permanent tooth staining exclusively
Pseudomembranous colitis as the main effect
Therapeutic widening of the therapeutic index
questions.explanation: Aminoglycosides (e.g. gentamicin): ototoxicity (irreversible hearing/vestibular), nephrotoxicity (often reversible), neuromuscular blockade with large intrapleural/peritoneal doses.
questions.title: Lecture 45 - Introduction to Antimicrobial Drugs II

questions.q: Organisms are clinically resistant when:
options: Not killed or inhibited by concentrations safely achievable at the infection site
They appear pink on MacConkey agar
They ferment mannitol on MSA
They are Gram-positive cocci in clusters
They grow in batch culture log phase
questions.explanation: Susceptible organisms are inhibited/killed by safely achievable concentrations at the site. Resistant organisms withstand the highest safe concentrations.
questions.title: Lecture 45 - Introduction to Antimicrobial Drugs II

questions.q: EUCAST category 'I' (Susceptible, Increased exposure) means:
options: Success likely if exposure is increased by dosing adjustment or site concentration
Therapeutic failure likely even with increased exposure
Standard dosing always succeeds
The organism is a yeast not a bacterium
The drug must never be used
questions.explanation: S = susceptible with standard dosing; I = susceptible with increased exposure; R = resistant — high likelihood of failure even with increased exposure.
questions.title: Lecture 45 - Introduction to Antimicrobial Drugs II

questions.q: Antibiotic resistance is described as:
options: The rule not the exception — often appearing during clinical trials and increasing over an antibiotic's lifetime
A new phenomenon starting only in the 21st century
Impossible for beta-lactams
Only caused by patient non-compliance never by genetics
Always reversible within hours without selection pressure
questions.explanation: Resistance is not new (penicillinase before widespread penicillin use). First reports often arise in trials; resistance increases during an antibiotic's lifetime.
questions.title: Lecture 45 - Introduction to Antimicrobial Drugs II

questions.q: Which factor promoting resistance involves 70–80% of antibiotics produced?
options: Excessive use in agriculture/animal husbandry as growth promoters
Urban vaccination programmes only
Increased use of sterile surgical technique
Shorter hospital stays exclusively
Reduced global travel
questions.explanation: Factors include overcrowding, pollution, travel, ageing population, immunocompromise, inappropriate prescribing (~50%), and agricultural use (70–80% of antibiotics produced).
questions.title: Lecture 45 - Introduction to Antimicrobial Drugs II

questions.q: Innate (intrinsic) resistance mechanisms include:
options: Prevention of uptake, lack/alteration of targets, and proteins that modify/inactivate or export antibiotics
Only horizontal gene transfer from plasmids
Always transient adaptation without genes
Host IgE production
Vaccination-induced immunity
questions.explanation: Innate resistance: prevent uptake, lack/alter targets, produce modifying/inactivating proteins or efflux pumps. Adaptive resistance is transient physiological change; genetic change is permanent.
questions.title: Lecture 45 - Introduction to Antimicrobial Drugs II

questions.q: Rifampicin resistance in M. tuberculosis involves mutations in:
options: rpoB encoding the β-subunit of RNA polymerase
Peptidoglycan transpeptidase genes only
Host dihydrofolate reductase
Porin channels exclusively in Gram-negatives
The HIV env gene
questions.explanation: Rifampicin inhibits mycobacterial RNA polymerase; resistance arises from rpoB mutations encoding the β-subunit — a major cause of TB treatment failure.
questions.title: Lecture 45 - Introduction to Antimicrobial Drugs II

questions.q: Horizontal gene transfer mechanisms include:
options: Transformation, transduction, and conjugation
Binary fission only
Antigenic drift and shift only
Host complement activation
Spore formation exclusively
questions.explanation: Acquisition of new genetic information: transformation (naked DNA), transduction (phage vector), conjugation (plasmids/transposons via pilus).
questions.title: Lecture 45 - Introduction to Antimicrobial Drugs II

questions.q: Conjugative plasmids:
options: Are self-transmissible and encode replication and cell-to-cell transfer
Cannot carry antibiotic resistance genes
Require no cell contact
Are essential chromosomes for survival
Only exist in viruses
questions.explanation: Plasmids are mini-chromosomes encoding accessory functions (toxins, resistance). Conjugative plasmids are self-transmissible; mobilisable plasmids need another plasmid's conjugation apparatus.
questions.title: Lecture 45 - Introduction to Antimicrobial Drugs II

questions.q: The most important example of antibiotic-inactivating enzymes in Gram-negative bacteria is:
options: Beta-lactamase destroying beta-lactam antibiotics
Coagulase clotting plasma
Catalase neutralising host peroxide only
Reverse transcriptase in bacteria
DNA gyrase supercoiling DNA
questions.explanation: Antibiotic inactivation by enzymes — best characterised is β-lactamase inactivating β-lactams, especially important in Gram-negative bacteria.
questions.title: Lecture 45 - Introduction to Antimicrobial Drugs II

questions.q: Reduced permeability resistance may involve:
options: Denser lipopolysaccharide and fewer/smaller porin channels
Thicker peptidoglycan in Gram-positive bacteria only
Loss of all ribosomes
Increased host antibody production
Complete absence of a cell membrane
questions.explanation: Permeability reduction: denser LPS layer and porin modification/mutation giving fewer or smaller channels, decreasing antibiotic entry.
questions.title: Lecture 45 - Introduction to Antimicrobial Drugs II

questions.q: Efflux pumps contribute to resistance by:
options: Actively expelling antibiotics and other toxic compounds from the cell
Increasing peptidoglycan cross-linking
Binding antibiotics irreversibly in the periplasm
Preventing all binary fission
Synthesising new ribosomes
questions.explanation: Efflux pumps extrude antibiotics, heavy metals and toxins; innate in many species, acquirable or derepressible — common resistance mechanism.
questions.title: Lecture 45 - Introduction to Antimicrobial Drugs II

questions.q: Target modification resistance means:
options: Small structural changes prevent antibiotic binding to ribosomes, enzymes or transporters
The host cell wall is destroyed
Antibiotics are converted to preservatives
Only vaccines can restore susceptibility
Porins are always enlarged
questions.explanation: Target modification: altered ribosomes, DNA gyrase, PBPs, folate enzymes etc. so antibiotics no longer bind; mutations may also alter drug uptake receptors.
questions.title: Lecture 45 - Introduction to Antimicrobial Drugs II

questions.q: Oral thrush after antibiotics is caused by:
options: Overgrowth of Candida (especially C. albicans) after disruption of normal microbiota
Direct antibiotic activation of HIV
Permanent loss of all T cells
Resistance to vancomycin in saliva only
Excessive coagulase production
questions.explanation: Antibiotics killing normal flora allow Candida overgrowth — oral thrush; vaginal thrush similarly after elimination of vaginal microbiota.
questions.title: Lecture 45 - Introduction to Antimicrobial Drugs II

questions.q: Clostridioides difficile pseudomembranous colitis is associated with antibiotics such as:
options: Ampicillin, clindamycin, fluoroquinolones and cephalosporins
Topical chlorhexidine skin wash only
Single-dose surgical prophylaxis always
Metronidazole prophylaxis never causing imbalance
Preservative levels of parabens only
questions.explanation: Gut microbiota imbalance after incompletely absorbed oral antibiotics; ampicillin, clindamycin, fluoroquinolones, cephalosporins are problematic — C. difficile overgrowth may be life-threatening.
questions.title: Lecture 45 - Introduction to Antimicrobial Drugs II

questions.q: Adaptive (physiological) resistance:
options: Is usually transient and reverts when the inducing condition is removed
Is always permanent and conjugative
Requires only horizontal gene transfer
Occurs only in mammalian cells
Cannot affect gene expression
questions.explanation: Adaptive resistance at infection sites from altered gene/protein expression — transient, usually reverting when inducing conditions (e.g. antibiotic presence) end.
questions.title: Lecture 45 - Introduction to Antimicrobial Drugs II

questions.q: Formative MCQ: Increased penicillin resistance in Gram-negative bacteria is most associated with:
options: Acquisition of genes for new penicillin-binding proteins
Change in size of outer membrane porin channels
Decreased permeability of the cytoplasmic membrane
Expression of beta-lactamase enzymes
Increased expression of multi-drug efflux pumps
questions.explanation: Formative MCQ answer: expression of β-lactamase enzymes is the mechanism most associated with increased penicillin resistance in Gram-negative bacteria.
questions.title: Lecture 45 - Introduction to Antimicrobial Drugs II

questions.q: Transformation in bacteria involves transfer of:
options: Naked DNA without attached RNA or protein under specific conditions
Whole plasmids only via a pilus
Phage particles exclusively
Host mRNA into bacterial ribosomes
Antibiotics from soil into spores
questions.explanation: Transformation transfers naked DNA under specific environmental/nutritional conditions; competent organisms (e.g. some Streptococcus) can take it up.
questions.title: Lecture 45 - Introduction to Antimicrobial Drugs II

questions.q: Reversible protein binding of antibiotics in body fluids may:
options: Act as a reservoir increasing duration of effect
Always eliminate all antibacterial activity
Prevent any renal excretion
Cause immediate anaphylaxis in all patients
Convert bactericidal drugs to antiseptics
questions.explanation: Antibiotics may bind plasma proteins reducing free drug, but reversible binding can also serve as a reservoir prolonging effect. Tissue penetration varies by drug.
questions.title: Lecture 45 - Introduction to Antimicrobial Drugs II

questions.q: Which characteristics describe an ideal antibiotic according to the lecture?
options: Selective toxicity, useful spectrum, good absorption, tissue penetration, stability, and few side effects
Toxic to host cells, narrow spectrum only, and unstable in all formulations
Must kill all human cells and commensals equally
Oral inactivity and very short half-life are required
High cost and many drug interactions are desirable
questions.explanation: Ideal antibiotics are non-toxic (selectively toxic), have appropriate spectrum, can be oral with good absorption and tissue penetration, are stable, inexpensive, and have few side effects without killing friendly bacteria.
questions.title: Lecture 45 - Introduction to Antimicrobial Drugs II

questions.q: What do ED50 and TD50 represent on antibiotic dose-response curves?
options: ED50 is the dose effective in 50% of the population; TD50 causes toxicity in 50%
ED50 is the toxic dose; TD50 is the effective dose
Both measure only bacterial MIC values
ED50 is maximum serum concentration; TD50 is urine output
They are identical for all antibiotics
questions.explanation: ED50 and TD50 are derived from dose-response curves: ED50 is therapeutically effective in 50% of individuals, TD50 produces toxicity in 50%. Safer drugs have wider therapeutic indexes.
questions.title: Lecture 45 - Introduction to Antimicrobial Drugs II

questions.q: What is the difference between bacteriostatic and bactericidal antibiotics?
options: Bacteriostatic agents stop bacterial reproduction; bactericides kill bacterial cells
Bacteriostatic agents always kill faster than bactericides
Bactericides only work on fungi
Bacteriostatic means the drug is excreted unchanged in urine
There is no practical difference between the terms
questions.explanation: A bacteriostatic agent stops bacteria reproducing without necessarily killing them; a bactericide kills bacterial cells.
questions.title: Lecture 45 - Introduction to Antimicrobial Drugs II

questions.q: Which harm can antibiotics cause beyond treating infection?
options: Allergies, disruption of normal flora leading to diarrhoea or C. difficile infection, and serious toxicities such as gentamicin-induced deafness
Only improved vitamin synthesis in the gut
Permanent strengthening of all commensal bacteria
No side effects because of selective toxicity
Exclusive benefit to fungal microbiota
questions.explanation: Antibiotics can cause allergies (including anaphylaxis with penicillins), kill beneficial flora causing diarrhoea or C. difficile infection, and rarely cause serious harm such as gentamicin-related deafness.
questions.title: Lecture 45 - Introduction to Antimicrobial Drugs II

questions.q: When is a microorganism considered susceptible to an antibiotic?
options: When it is killed or inhibited by a concentration safely achievable at the infection site
When it grows in the presence of any antibiotic concentration
When it produces beta-lactamase only
When it is always resistant in vitro but sensitive in vivo
When the MIC exceeds the toxic dose
questions.explanation: Susceptible organisms are killed or growth-inhibited by concentrations that can safely be achieved at the site of infection; otherwise they are resistant.
questions.title: Lecture 45 - Introduction to Antimicrobial Drugs II

questions.q: For staphylococci and vancomycin, which MIC range indicates susceptible (S) category?
options: Less than 4 micrograms/mL
8 to 16 micrograms/mL
Greater than 32 micrograms/mL
Exactly 32 micrograms/mL only
Any detectable MIC is always resistant
questions.explanation: Staphylococci requiring <4 microg/mL vancomycin for growth inhibition are susceptible (S); 8–16 is susceptible with increased exposure (I); >32 is resistant (R).
questions.title: Lecture 45 - Introduction to Antimicrobial Drugs II

questions.q: What does the timeline of antibiotic introduction and resistance demonstrate?
options: Resistance has appeared soon after introduction of many antibiotics; it is not a new phenomenon
No resistance developed until the year 2000
Resistance occurs only in viruses, never bacteria
New antibiotics never select for resistant organisms
Resistance always takes centuries to emerge
questions.explanation: The slide pairs antibiotic introductions with dates resistance was identified—for example penicillin resistance in Staphylococcus by 1940, shortly after penicillin's introduction.
questions.title: Lecture 45 - Introduction to Antimicrobial Drugs II

questions.q: What is innate (intrinsic) antibiotic resistance?
options: Natural resistance because the organism lacks targets, prevents uptake, or produces inactivating/export proteins
Resistance acquired only by conjugation in the laboratory
Temporary resistance that always reverts within minutes
Sensitivity to all antibiotics at all concentrations
Resistance caused exclusively by patient non-adherence
questions.explanation: Innate resistance means the organism is naturally resistant through factors such as prevented uptake, absent or altered targets, or proteins that modify, inactivate, or export the antibiotic.
questions.title: Lecture 45 - Introduction to Antimicrobial Drugs II

questions.q: Which examples illustrate resistance arising from mutations?
options: Streptomycin and rifampicin resistance in M. tuberculosis; methicillin resistance in S. aureus; glycopeptide resistance in enterococci
Only plasmid-mediated beta-lactamase in one strain
Transformation of naked DNA in all gut commensals daily
Phase variation of Neisseria pili only
