Adaptive resistance that always reverses immediately
questions.explanation: Mutation-based examples include streptomycin and rifampicin resistance in M. tuberculosis, methicillin resistance in S. aureus, and glycopeptide and aminoglycoside resistance in enterococci.
questions.title: Lecture 45 - Introduction to Antimicrobial Drugs II

questions.q: What is bacterial transformation in the context of antibiotic resistance?
options: Uptake of naked DNA without attached RNA or protein, occurring when cells are competent
Transfer of DNA by bacteriophage particles
Cell-to-cell plasmid transfer via a pilus
Spontaneous deletion of all chromosomal genes
Active efflux of antibiotic without any genetic change
questions.explanation: Transformation is transfer of naked DNA under specific conditions; competent organisms such as some streptococci can acquire resistance genes this way.
questions.title: Lecture 45 - Introduction to Antimicrobial Drugs II

questions.q: How does transduction transfer antibiotic resistance genes?
options: A bacteriophage packages host DNA and transfers it between infected cells
Two bacteria join by a pilus and exchange plasmids directly
Naked DNA is taken up from the environment without a vector
The antibiotic induces mutations in RNA polymerase only
Resistant cells fuse with host erythrocytes
questions.explanation: Transduction moves genetic information via a bacteriophage that can acquire host DNA, package it, and deliver it to other cells. It is relatively rare and strain-specific.
questions.title: Lecture 45 - Introduction to Antimicrobial Drugs II

questions.q: Which cellular changes mediate antibiotic resistance at the biochemical level?
options: Enzymatic inactivation, reduced permeability, efflux pumps, and target modification
Increased susceptibility of all porins only
Permanent loss of all cell wall material
Switch from prokaryotic to eukaryotic metabolism
Exclusive use of passive diffusion for all drugs
questions.explanation: Microbial cells resist antibiotics by inactivating or modifying the drug, reducing permeability, actively effluxing the antibiotic, or modifying the target so the drug cannot bind.
questions.title: Lecture 45 - Introduction to Antimicrobial Drugs II

questions.q: How can target modification confer antibiotic resistance?
options: Small structural changes prevent antibiotic binding or alter drug transport receptors
The target is always completely deleted with no replacement
Modification only affects human receptors, not bacterial ones
It increases binding affinity for all antibiotics
It converts bacteriostatic drugs into vitamins
questions.explanation: Small changes in enzyme structure can dramatically reduce antibiotic binding. Mutations may also alter receptors involved in transporting drugs into the cell.
questions.title: Lecture 45 - Introduction to Antimicrobial Drugs II

questions.q: Which key point about antibiotic spectrum is correct?
options: Broad-spectrum agents act against a larger group of bacteria than narrow-spectrum agents
All antibiotics are equally active against viruses and fungi
Narrow-spectrum drugs always harm commensals more than broad-spectrum drugs
Spectrum is unrelated to clinical choice
Vancomycin is a broad-spectrum Gram-negative drug
questions.explanation: Key points note that broad-spectrum antibiotics act against a larger bacterial group than narrow-spectrum agents, with clinical implications for commensal disruption.
questions.title: Lecture 45 - Introduction to Antimicrobial Drugs II

questions.q: What is the most common serious side effect associated with antibiotics?
options: Hypersensitivity reactions such as allergies
Permanent bone marrow aplasia in all patients
Universal kidney failure after one dose
Immediate resistance in every commensal within seconds
Complete loss of immunity to all pathogens
questions.explanation: Key points state that hypersensitivity reactions, particularly allergies, are the most common serious side effects of antibiotics such as beta-lactams.
questions.title: Lecture 45 - Introduction to Antimicrobial Drugs II

questions.q: Important considerations when prescribing antimicrobial therapy include:
options: Accurate diagnosis, empiric vs definitive therapy, pharmacodynamics at infection site, and host factors
Selecting the most expensive broad-spectrum drug always
Avoiding all microbiology tests in serious infections
Using only topical antiseptics for meningitis
Prescribing until cultures return in all critical cases without exception
questions.explanation: Considerations include accurate diagnosis, empiric vs definitive therapy, narrowing spectrum when possible, pharmacodynamics at site, host factors, and adverse effects.
questions.title: Lecture 47 - Principles of Antimicrobial Drug Therapy

questions.q: In life-threatening infections such as endocarditis or meningitis, microbiology testing is critical because:
options: Pathogen isolation is needed for prolonged therapy decisions
Antibiotics are never required
Only total counts by turbidity are used
Empiric therapy is always contraindicated
Host IgE levels determine the drug choice exclusively
questions.explanation: Serious life-threatening infections likely need prolonged therapy; isolating the pathogen is critical when possible.
questions.title: Lecture 47 - Principles of Antimicrobial Drug Therapy

questions.q: Empiric antimicrobial therapy in septic shock should be:
options: Initiated immediately — inadequate therapy in critical illness worsens outcomes
Delayed until all culture results return (24–72 h)
Avoided in favour of antiseptics only
Limited to narrow-spectrum oral agents only
Withheld until radiology confirms abscess
questions.explanation: Critically ill patients (septic shock, bacterial meningitis) need immediate empiric therapy; delay is associated with greater morbidity, mortality and length of stay.
questions.title: Lecture 47 - Principles of Antimicrobial Drug Therapy

questions.q: Empiric therapy for suspected bacterial meningitis in healthy young adults commonly includes:
options: Third-generation cephalosporin (ceftriaxone) plus vancomycin
Topical fusidic acid cream only
Oral metronidazole monotherapy
Chlorhexidine mouthwash
Antifungal azoles without any antibacterial
questions.explanation: Likely pathogens are S. pneumoniae and N. meningitidis; empiric recommendation is third-generation cephalosporin (ceftriaxone) plus vancomycin.
questions.title: Lecture 47 - Principles of Antimicrobial Drug Therapy

questions.q: Once microbiology identifies the pathogen, therapy should be narrowed to:
options: Reduce cost and toxicity and prevent emergence of resistance
Always switch to the broadest possible spectrum
Stop all antibiotics immediately in every case
Add three more broad-spectrum drugs
Use only antiseptics for the remainder of treatment
questions.explanation: After identification/susceptibility data, narrow spectrum where possible to reduce cost, toxicity, and resistance emergence.
questions.title: Lecture 47 - Principles of Antimicrobial Drug Therapy

questions.q: Combination antibiotic therapy for enterococcal endocarditis (penicillin + gentamicin) exploits:
options: Synergy — penicillin facilitates aminoglycoside uptake into enterococci
Identical mechanisms targeting folate only
Prevention of all host renal elimination
Reduced cost compared to either drug alone always
Avoidance of any bactericidal effect
questions.explanation: Enterococci are relatively penicillin-resistant; penicillin (cell wall) plus gentamicin (ribosome) is synergistic — penicillin facilitates intracellular aminoglycoside uptake.
questions.title: Lecture 47 - Principles of Antimicrobial Drug Therapy

questions.q: Combination therapy for suspected Pseudomonas in septic shock might use:
options: Antipseudomonal beta-lactam plus aminoglycoside or fluoroquinolone
Oral trimethoprim alone for all Gram-negatives
Topical chlorhexidine IV infusion
Vancomycin monotherapy only
Metronidazole for aerobic Pseudomonas
questions.explanation: Empiric combinations for resistant Gram-negative bacilli like P. aeruginosa: antipseudomonal β-lactam with aminoglycoside or fluoroquinolone when blood cultures show Gram-negative bacilli in septic shock.
questions.title: Lecture 47 - Principles of Antimicrobial Drug Therapy

questions.q: Intra-abdominal polymicrobial infections may be treated with:
options: Third-generation cephalosporin or fluoroquinolone plus metronidazole for anaerobes
Vancomycin monotherapy only
Topical eye ointment
Antiviral acyclovir exclusively
Single narrow-spectrum penicillin for aerobes only
questions.explanation: Polymicrobial intra-abdominal infections involve Gram+ cocci, Gram− bacilli and anaerobes — combinations such as cephalosporin or fluoroquinolone plus metronidazole extend spectrum.
questions.title: Lecture 47 - Principles of Antimicrobial Drug Therapy

questions.q: Tuberculosis treatment uses drug combinations mainly to:
options: Prevent rapid emergence of resistance — monotherapy not recommended as rifampicin resistance develops quickly
Reduce treatment duration to 3 days always
Avoid any hepatotoxicity entirely
Eliminate the need for directly observed therapy
Target only dormant non-replicating bacilli with one drug
questions.explanation: TB needs prolonged combination therapy; monotherapy is not recommended because rifampicin resistance emerges quickly if used alone.
questions.title: Lecture 47 - Principles of Antimicrobial Drug Therapy

questions.q: In patients with reduced renal function, antibiotic dosing should often be:
options: Reduced to prevent accumulation and toxicity
Doubled to maintain peak levels
Unchanged regardless of creatinine clearance
Stopped only after ototoxicity develops
Given as a single lifetime depot dose
questions.explanation: Kidney and liver eliminate most antibiotics; impaired renal/hepatic function may require dose reduction to prevent toxicity, while young healthy patients may need increases if elimination is rapid.
questions.title: Lecture 47 - Principles of Antimicrobial Drug Therapy

questions.q: Tetracyclines should generally be avoided in children under 12 because:
options: They deposit in growing bones and teeth causing staining
They are ineffective against all paediatric infections
They cause immediate anaphylaxis in 100% of children
They are only available IV
They selectively kill only Gram-negative bacteria in children
questions.explanation: Children at extremes of age handle drugs differently; tetracyclines not used <12 years due to bone/teeth deposition and staining; nitrofurantoin avoided <3 months (haemolysis risk).
questions.title: Lecture 47 - Principles of Antimicrobial Drug Therapy

questions.q: G6PD deficiency increases risk of haemolysis with:
options: Dapsone, primaquine and nitrofurantoin
Penicillin and cephalosporins only
Topical chlorhexidine
All aminoglycosides in every patient
Vaccines against influenza
questions.explanation: G6PD deficiency can cause haemolysis with dapsone, primaquine, nitrofurantoin — testing advisable in at-risk populations (e.g. African Americans).
questions.title: Lecture 47 - Principles of Antimicrobial Drug Therapy

questions.q: In pregnancy, which antibiotic class is usually considered safe?
options: Penicillins, cephalosporins and macrolides
Tetracyclines and chloramphenicol
All fluoroquinolones as first choice
Aminoglycosides without any monitoring
Topical bleach preparations systemically
questions.explanation: Penicillins, cephalosporins and macrolides usually safe in pregnancy. Tetracyclines and chloramphenicol have well-described fetal/neonatal adverse effects.
questions.title: Lecture 47 - Principles of Antimicrobial Drug Therapy

questions.q: Recent antibiotic exposure is relevant because:
options: Pathogens emerging under that selective pressure are likely resistant to the same drug
It always guarantees susceptibility to the same agent
It eliminates the need for culture
It contraindicates all future oral therapy
It prevents C. difficile infection
questions.explanation: If the current pathogen emerged under selective pressure of a recently used antibiotic, it is likely resistant to that drug — history guides empiric choices.
questions.title: Lecture 47 - Principles of Antimicrobial Drug Therapy

questions.q: IV antibiotics are indicated when:
options: High serum levels needed for severe/deep infection, patient cannot take oral drugs, or no effective oral form exists
The infection is always mild community-acquired pneumonia treated at home
Only for prophylactic dental procedures in all patients
Topical conjunctivitis is present
The drug has a 14-day half-life and oral absorption is complete
questions.explanation: IV use: ensure high concentrations for severe/deep infections (sepsis, endocarditis), enteral intolerance, absorption concerns, no oral preparation, or intravascular line infections.
questions.title: Lecture 47 - Principles of Antimicrobial Drug Therapy

questions.q: Topical antibiotics are appropriate for:
options: Bacterial conjunctivitis and small areas of impetigo where systemic drugs do not reach adequate surface concentrations
All cases of bacterial meningitis
Septic shock with Gram-negative bacteraemia
Endocarditis requiring weeks of IV therapy
TB pulmonary infection as monotherapy
questions.explanation: Topical therapy suits indications like bacterial conjunctivitis (eye ointment) and small impetigo areas (fusidic acid) where systemic antibiotics lack adequate surface levels.
questions.title: Lecture 47 - Principles of Antimicrobial Drug Therapy

questions.q: Time-dependent killing antibiotics (e.g. beta-lactams, vancomycin) require:
options: Serum concentration above MIC throughout the dosing interval — frequent dosing or infusion
Only a high peak concentration with long intervals
No consideration of MIC values
Single weekly doses always
Concentration far below MIC for most of the interval
questions.explanation: Time-dependent agents need drug levels above MIC for the dosing interval — achieved by continuous infusion or frequent dosing (β-lactams, vancomycin).
questions.title: Lecture 47 - Principles of Antimicrobial Drug Therapy

questions.q: Concentration-dependent killing antibiotics (e.g. aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones) have efficacy most linked to:
options: Peak serum concentration rather than dosing frequency alone
Time below MIC exclusively
Binding to host ribosomes
Preservative concentration in the bottle
Number of colony colours on agar
questions.explanation: Concentration-dependent killers (aminoglycosides, daptomycin, fluoroquinolones, metronidazole) show better activity as peak concentration increases.
questions.title: Lecture 47 - Principles of Antimicrobial Drug Therapy

questions.q: Evidence supports limiting uncomplicated UTI in women to:
options: 3 days of therapy
12 weeks minimum always
A single dose of vancomycin IV
Topical antiseptic only without antibiotics
Lifetime prophylactic fluoroquinolone
questions.explanation: Studies support shorter courses where evidence exists: uncomplicated UTI in women 3 days; community-acquired pneumonia 5 days. Endocarditis needs 4–6 weeks; invasive mycosis weeks–months.
questions.title: Lecture 47 - Principles of Antimicrobial Drug Therapy

questions.q: Clinical parameters to assess treatment response include:
options: Fever resolution, falling leukocyte count, and improving radiology (e.g. abscess size)
Colony colour on mannitol salt agar only
Therapeutic index calculation in vitro only
Patient height and weight exclusively
Gram stain colour without symptoms
questions.explanation: Response assessed clinically (symptoms, fever, lab values like WBC, radiology) and microbiologically (e.g. clearing bacteraemia on repeat cultures).
questions.title: Lecture 47 - Principles of Antimicrobial Drug Therapy

questions.q: Pre-surgical antimicrobial prophylaxis typically uses:
options: A single cephalosporin dose about 1 hour before incision targeting skin flora organisms
Weeks of oral tetracycline after surgery
IV vancomycin only for all procedures without timing
Topical antifungals for all abdominal surgery
No antibiotics even for dirty wounds
questions.explanation: Prophylaxis reduces surgical site infections — e.g. single cephalosporin dose 1 h before incision covering likely skin flora for most procedures.
questions.title: Lecture 47 - Principles of Antimicrobial Drug Therapy

questions.q: Antimicrobial prophylaxis for meningococcal contacts may use:
options: Ciprofloxacin for close contacts of N. meningitidis meningitis
Oral chlorhexidine for all hospital visitors
Lifetime penicillin for the index case only
Metronidazole for aerobic cocci
No prophylaxis is ever indicated
questions.explanation: Prophylaxis prevents transmission — e.g. ciprofloxacin for N. meningitidis contacts; macrolides for Bordetella pertussis; dental prophylaxis in selected endocarditis-risk patients.
questions.title: Lecture 47 - Principles of Antimicrobial Drug Therapy

questions.q: A common misuse of antibiotics is:
options: Prolonged empiric therapy without evidence of infection
Narrowing therapy once the organism is identified
Using single-dose surgical prophylaxis appropriately
Switching IV to oral when clinically stable
Taking an allergy history before prescribing penicillin
questions.explanation: Misuses include prolonged empiric therapy without infection, treating positive cultures without disease, failure to narrow therapy, prolonged prophylaxis, and excessive use of certain agents.
questions.title: Lecture 47 - Principles of Antimicrobial Drug Therapy

questions.q: Formative MCQ: Enterococcal endocarditis is treated with cell-wall agent plus aminoglycoside mainly to:
options: Ensure at least one drug is active against the organism
Prevent emergence of resistance only
Prevent polymicrobial superinfection only
Prevent toxicity in hepatic impairment
Take advantage of synergy between the two antibiotics
questions.explanation: Formative MCQ answer: the combination exploits synergy — penicillin facilitates gentamicin uptake into relatively penicillin-resistant enterococci.
questions.title: Lecture 47 - Principles of Antimicrobial Drug Therapy

questions.q: For serious infection with unknown pathogen, broad-spectrum therapy is preferred because:
options: It covers both Gram-positive and Gram-negative possibilities until identification allows narrowing
Narrow spectrum always covers unknown organisms better
Broad spectrum eliminates all resistance permanently
It is always the cheapest option
Microbiology results are available immediately within minutes
questions.explanation: Formative SAQ logic: if the agent is unknown (could be Gram+ or Gram−), broad-spectrum therapy maximises chance of controlling infection until definitive identification.
questions.title: Lecture 47 - Principles of Antimicrobial Drug Therapy

questions.q: Why is penicillin combined with gentamicin in enterococcal endocarditis?
options: To prevent toxicity in hepatic impairment
Because penicillin facilitates intracellular uptake of the aminoglycoside into relatively penicillin-resistant enterococci, producing synergistic bactericidal activity
Because gentamicin alone penetrates all Gram-positive cell walls equally
To ensure both drugs are always static
Because enterococci are always sensitive to penicillin alone
questions.explanation: Enterococci are relatively resistant to penicillin. In combination with gentamicin, penicillin facilitates intracellular uptake of the aminoglycoside, which would otherwise have little uptake, producing synergistic bactericidal activity against enterococci.
questions.title: Lecture 47 - Principles of Antimicrobial Drug Therapy

questions.q: What must be established for effective antibiotic therapy according to the lecture key points?
options: Only the cheapest available generic brand
Accurate diagnosis of infection and understanding of how the drug works and interacts with the host; antibiotics must reach infection sites at sufficient concentration for long enough
Immediate narrowing to the narrowest spectrum before any cultures
Treatment based solely on patient age without microbiology
Use of only one antibiotic class for all infections
questions.explanation: Key points emphasise accurate diagnosis, understanding drug action and host interactions, and ensuring antibiotics access infection sites for sufficient time and concentration to kill or inhibit infecting agents.
questions.title: Lecture 47 - Principles of Antimicrobial Drug Therapy

questions.q: How is interfacial (surface) tension best described?
options: The force acting parallel to the surface plane, in units of joules
The force acting perpendicular to the surface plane, in units of dyne/cm or mN/m
The pressure exerted by a liquid on its container, in pascals
The energy stored in hydrogen bonds within the bulk liquid
The rate at which a liquid spreads across a solid, in mm/s
questions.explanation: Interfacial tension is manifested as a toughening of the surface and is the force acting perpendicular to the surface plane, with units of dyne/cm or mN/m. It is given the symbol gamma and is influenced by the composition of the interface.
questions.title: Colloids & Surfactants

questions.q: What is surface free energy?
options: The work required to increase the surface area by 1 square metre at standard temperature and pressure
The energy released when a surfactant adsorbs at an interface
The total kinetic energy of molecules within the bulk liquid
The energy needed to raise a liquid by one degree in temperature
The energy stored in a micelle above the CMC
questions.explanation: Surface free energy is the work required to increase the area by 1 square metre under standard temperature and pressure, with units mJ/m2. Interfacial tension represents the minimisation of surface free energy.
questions.title: Colloids & Surfactants

questions.q: Which three factors are listed as affecting surface tension?
options: Pressure, volume and density
Type of liquid, temperature and solute
pH, ionic strength and viscosity
Particle size, shape and charge
Molecular weight, polarity and pKa
questions.explanation: The three factors given are the type of liquid, the temperature and the solute present, with vapour pressure and time for the solute to equilibrate at the surface also mentioned.
questions.title: Colloids & Surfactants

questions.q: What is the surface tension of pure water at 20 degrees C?
questions.explanation: Water has a surface tension of 72.8 mN/m at 20 degrees C, high because of strong cohesive forces between molecules. Mercury is far higher at 485.0, while n-hexane is only 18.4.
questions.title: Colloids & Surfactants

questions.q: Why does surface tension decrease as temperature rises?
options: The liquid evaporates and reduces the surface area
Kinetic energy increases, disrupting and reducing intermolecular forces
The density of the liquid increases with temperature
Solute molecules become less soluble and leave the surface
Hydrogen bonds become stronger at higher temperatures
questions.explanation: Surface tension falls as temperature rises because kinetic energy increases with temperature, disrupting and reducing intermolecular forces. The relationship is linear over a wide temperature range.
questions.title: Colloids & Surfactants

questions.q: Why do surface-active molecules adsorb at the water surface at low concentrations?
options: They are too large to dissolve in the bulk water
They are attracted electrostatically to the air
It is the only way both their polar and non-polar regions can sit in the environment each prefers
They are denser than water and float
The surface is the site of lowest temperature
questions.explanation: Surfactants contain both polar hydrophilic and non-polar hydrophobic regions. At low concentration the only way both regions are satisfied is by adsorbing at the surface, with the polar head in the water and the hydrophobic part in the air.
questions.title: Colloids & Surfactants

questions.q: What does Traube's rule state?
options: The longer the hydrocarbon chain in a wetting agent, the greater the reduction in surface tension
Surface tension falls linearly with temperature
Micelles form only above the critical micelle concentration
Larger particles scatter light in proportion to the sixth power of diameter
The HLB value equals the ratio of hydrophilic to hydrophobic parts
questions.explanation: Traube's rule states that the longer the hydrocarbon chain in wetting agents, the greater the reduction in surface tension.
questions.title: Colloids & Surfactants

questions.q: What is the critical micelle concentration (CMC)?
options: The concentration at which the surfactant precipitates from solution
The concentration at which surface tension is at its maximum
The concentration at which micelles start to form
The concentration at which the surfactant becomes toxic
The concentration at which the solution becomes opaque
questions.explanation: As surfactant concentration rises, monomers adsorb at the surface and lower surface tension until no more can fit. Beyond that they can only shield their hydrophobic groups by aggregating, and the concentration at which micelles start to form is the CMC.
questions.title: Colloids & Surfactants

questions.q: What happens to surface tension as surfactant concentration is increased beyond the CMC?
options: It continues to fall steeply
It levels off and does not fall further
It rises back towards the value for pure water
It oscillates around the value at the CMC
It falls to zero
questions.explanation: Above the CMC no more monomers can fit at the surface, so surface tension levels off with increasing surfactant concentration without any further lowering.
questions.title: Colloids & Surfactants

questions.q: Which thermodynamic driver explains micellisation, through the hydrophobic effect?
options: A large negative enthalpy change on aggregation
A favourable increase in entropy as ordered water around the hydrophobic chains is released
An increase in the free energy of the system
A decrease in temperature within the micelle core
A reduction in the surface area of the water
questions.explanation: Micelles form to minimise free energy (delta G = delta H - T delta S). The ordered water structure around the hydrophobic part of the surfactant lowers entropy, so micellisation produces a favourable increase in entropy, the most influential contribution.
questions.title: Colloids & Surfactants

questions.q: For a liquid B spreading on substrate A, the spreading coefficient is S = gammaA - (gammaB + gammaA/B). What values allow spreading?
options: Only strongly negative values
Zero or positive values
Values between -1 and 0
Any value provided the temperature is above 20 degrees C
Only values greater than 72.8
questions.explanation: Zero or positive values of the spreading coefficient allow spreading. This governs, for example, whether eye drops spread on the eye surface or a liquid spreads on a drug particle.
questions.title: Colloids & Surfactants

questions.q: Which factor is NOT listed as influencing the spreading of a solvent droplet on a surface?
options: Surface roughness
The surface energy or hydrophobicity of the surface
The presence of surfactants
Temperature, through its influence on viscosity
The molecular weight of the dissolved drug
questions.explanation: The factors given are surface roughness, the surface energy or hydrophobicity of the surface, the presence of surfactants, and temperature through its effect on viscosity.
questions.title: Colloids & Surfactants

questions.q: Sodium dodecyl sulphate (SDS) belongs to which class of surfactant?
options: Anionic
Cationic
Non-ionic
Ampholytic
Lyophobic solid
questions.explanation: SDS is the example of an anionic surfactant. Cationic examples include cetrimide and benzalkonium chloride, non-ionic examples polysorbates and pluronics, and ampholytic examples lecithin and proteins.
questions.title: Colloids & Surfactants

questions.q: What does the HLB value of a surfactant indicate?
options: The concentration at which it forms micelles
Its ratio of hydrophilic to hydrophobic parts, and hence its overall affinity for water
Its toxicity relative to benzalkonium chloride
The surface tension it produces at 20 degrees C
The number of monomers in each micelle it forms
questions.explanation: HLB is the ratio of hydrophilic to hydrophobic parts and indicates the overall affinity for water. Low values relate to anti-foaming oils; higher values indicate solubilisers and detergents.
questions.title: Colloids & Surfactants

questions.q: A surfactant has an HLB of 4.3 at 20 degrees C. What does this tell you?
options: It is an extreme hydrophile suitable as a solubiliser
It is an extreme lipophile, poorly water dispersible
It is a good wetting agent but a poor solubiliser
It is ampholytic and pH dependent
It will form liposomes rather than micelles
questions.explanation: Span 80 has HLB 4.3 and is an extreme lipophile, poorly water dispersible. An HLB of 15 or more indicates a solubiliser and 9 or above a wetting agent; SDS is 40 and Tween 20 is 16.7.
questions.title: Colloids & Surfactants

questions.q: Over what size range do colloidal dispersions fall?
options: 1 pm to 1 nm
1 nm to 1 micron
1 to 100 microns
0.1 to 100 mm
Greater than 100 microns
questions.explanation: Disperse systems have one component dispersed through another; those in the size range 1 nm to 1 micron are termed colloids. Coarse dispersions are micrometre sized or bigger.
questions.title: Colloids & Surfactants

questions.q: How do colloids and coarse dispersions differ thermodynamically?
options: Colloids are thermodynamically unstable; coarse dispersions are stable
Colloids are thermodynamically stable; coarse dispersions are unstable with high surface free energy and cannot be reconstituted
Both are thermodynamically stable but differ only in particle size
Both are unstable, but colloids settle faster
Neither has any defined thermodynamic behaviour
questions.explanation: Colloids are thermodynamically stable. Coarse dispersions such as emulsions, crude suspensions, sols, gels and aerosols are thermodynamically unstable, have high surface free energy and cannot be reconstituted.
questions.title: Colloids & Surfactants

questions.q: What distinguishes a lyophilic from a lyophobic emulsifier?
options: Lyophilic emulsifiers have affinity for the continuous phase; lyophobic ones have poor affinity for it
Lyophilic emulsifiers are always ionic; lyophobic ones are always non-ionic
Lyophilic emulsifiers are solids; lyophobic ones are liquids
Lyophilic emulsifiers form liposomes; lyophobic ones form micelles
Lyophilic emulsifiers work only above the CMC
questions.explanation: A lyophilic emulsifier has affinity for the continuous phase or solvent, for example celluloses, gums and polysorbates. A lyophobic emulsifier has poor affinity for it, for example solid nanoparticles such as silica and latex.
questions.title: Colloids & Surfactants

questions.q: What is Brownian motion, and how does particle size affect it?
options: Movement caused by gravity; increased with larger particles
Random collisions with dispersion medium molecules; increased with small particles
Movement caused by applied shear; independent of particle size
Electrophoretic movement in an applied field; increased with charged particles
Spontaneous movement down a concentration gradient; increased with large particles
questions.explanation: Brownian motion arises from random collisions with dispersion medium molecules and is increased with small particles. It produces a zig-zag random walk described by the Einstein equation, average displacement equal to the square root of 2Dt.
questions.title: Colloids & Surfactants

questions.q: In photon correlation spectroscopy, how does scattering intensity depend on particle diameter?
options: Intensity is proportional to diameter
Intensity is proportional to the square of the diameter
Intensity is proportional to the sixth power of the diameter
Intensity is inversely proportional to diameter
Intensity is independent of diameter
questions.explanation: Large particles scatter light much more than small ones, with intensity proportional to d to the power 6. PCS is used in the sub-micron range and measures Brownian motion.
questions.title: Colloids & Surfactants

questions.q: In the Stokes-Einstein relation used in PCS, why must temperature be measured accurately?
options: Because it determines the wavelength of the scattered light
Because it influences the viscosity of the solvent, which affects the diffusion coefficient
Because particles change shape with temperature
Because it sets the critical micelle concentration
Because the Boltzmann constant varies with temperature
questions.explanation: Temperature must be measured accurately because it influences viscosity. In d(h) = kT/(3 pi eta DT), the hydrodynamic diameter depends on the Boltzmann constant, temperature, solvent viscosity and translational diffusion coefficient.
questions.title: Colloids & Surfactants

questions.q: Which of these describes depletion flocculation?
options: Cross-linking of particles by a bifunctional agent such as Ca2+ or a polymer
Particles forced to join because of a shortage of surface-active polymer, arising from differential osmotic pressure
Aggregation caused by raising the temperature above the cloud point
Precipitation caused by very high ionic strength
Fusion of liposomes into larger vesicles over time
questions.explanation: Two steric mechanisms are described. Bridging flocculation is cross-linking of particles by a bifunctional agent; depletion flocculation forces particles together because of a surface-active polymer shortage, arising from differential solution osmotic pressure.
questions.title: Colloids & Surfactants

questions.q: How many surfactant molecules typically make up a micelle, and what size are they?
options: 5 to 10 molecules, about 0.5 nm
50 to 100 molecules, about 2 to 10 nm
500 to 1000 molecules, about 50 nm
50 to 100 molecules, about 100 to 500 nm
Several thousand molecules, about 1 micron
questions.explanation: Micelles are colloidal spherical or near spherical nanoparticles composed of 50 to 100 surfactant molecules, about 2 to 10 nm in size. Ionic micelles are around 2 to 5 nm and non-ionic micelles around 10 nm.
questions.title: Colloids & Surfactants

questions.q: Why do micelle solutions appear as clear liquids?
options: Because the surfactant absorbs visible light
Because the micelles are small enough not to scatter light appreciably
Because micelles sediment rapidly out of the light path
Because the refractive index of the micelle matches that of water
Because micelles form only in non-aqueous solvents
questions.explanation: Micelles form clear liquids due to their small size. Solubilising a high log P drug such as miconazole in the micelle core gives an optically transparent suspension that looks like a solution.
questions.title: Colloids & Surfactants

questions.q: Where in a micelle would a non-polar solute such as octane be located?
options: In the core of the micelle
In the mantle or palisade region
Adsorbed on the outer surface
In the aqueous compartment inside the micelle
Between two adjacent bilayers
questions.explanation: Non-polar solutes sit in the core of the micelle. Semi-polar solutes orientate with the polar group buried deep or nearer the surface, and polar solutes sit in the mantle or palisade region of non-ionic micelles or adsorbed on the surface of ionic micelles.
questions.title: Colloids & Surfactants

questions.q: Solubilisation of a poorly water-soluble drug by micelles occurs under what condition?
options: Only below the CMC
Only above the CMC
Only at the isoelectric point of the surfactant
Only when the HLB is below 9
Only in the presence of a co-surfactant
questions.explanation: Solubilisation only occurs above the CMC, since micelles must be present. It increases the apparent solubility of a water-insoluble material and allows insoluble drugs to be given to the eye, intravenously and by other routes.
questions.title: Colloids & Surfactants

questions.q: According to the critical packing parameter (CPP), which structure forms when CPP is approximately 1?
options: Micelles
Liposomes or lamellar systems
Reverse micelles
A bicontinuous sponge phase
A molecular solution
questions.explanation: CPP = V/(lc.a). When CPP is less than or equal to one third, micelles form; when CPP is around 1, liposomes and lamellar systems form; and when CPP is greater than 1, reverse micelles form.
questions.title: Colloids & Surfactants

questions.q: Microemulsions are best described as which of the following?
options: Coarse emulsions with droplets of 1 to 100 microns
Swollen micelles of 5 to 50 nm, transparent, monodispersed and of low viscosity
Multilamellar vesicles greater than 500 nm
Solid nanoparticle sols dispersed in water
Gels formed by water dispersed in a solid
questions.explanation: Microemulsions are best referred to as swollen micelles, 5 to 50 nm, and can be water-in-oil or oil-in-water. They are transparent, monodispersed and of low viscosity, and are classified using the Winsor system.
questions.title: Colloids & Surfactants

questions.q: Why does a microemulsion require an emulsifying adjunct or co-surfactant?
options: To raise the interfacial tension so droplets stay separate
To drive the interfacial tension towards zero, allowing spontaneous emulsification
To increase the viscosity of the continuous phase
To provide a charge that prevents flocculation
To reduce the amount of primary surfactant needed to about 1 per cent
questions.explanation: A co-surfactant such as dodecanol alongside a primary surfactant such as SDS drives interfacial tension towards zero or less, giving spontaneous emulsification. Microemulsions need more surfactant than conventional emulsions, around 25 per cent.
questions.title: Colloids & Surfactants

questions.q: Why do bilayer-forming lipids produce liposomes rather than micelles?
options: They carry a net positive charge
They are cylindrical in shape because they have two hydrocarbon chains, rather than cone-shaped with one chain
They have a much higher HLB than surfactants
They are insoluble in water at all concentrations
They have no hydrophilic head group
questions.explanation: Liposomes form from bilayers of lipid amphiphiles that are cylindrical rather than cone-shaped. Lipids are cylindrical because they have two hydrocarbon chains attached to the head group, whereas surfactants have one.
questions.title: Colloids & Surfactants

questions.q: Which is a key difference between micelles and liposomes?
options: Micelles encapsulate an aqueous compartment while liposomes have only an oily core
Liposomes encapsulate an aqueous compartment, useful for hydrophilic drugs, while micelles have only an oily core
Micelles are much larger than liposomes
Liposome formation is spontaneous while micelles need energy input
Liposomes are more stable than micelles over time
questions.explanation: Liposomes encapsulate an aqueous compartment, useful for hydrophilic drugs, whereas micelles have only an oily core. Micelles (2-10 nm) are much smaller, form spontaneously, and liposomes need special formulation methods and energy input and are not very stable.
questions.title: Colloids & Surfactants

questions.q: In the classification of vesicles, what does MLV stand for and what size are they?
options: Small unilamellar vesicles, up to 100 nm
Large unilamellar vesicles, greater than 100 nm
Multilamellar vesicles, greater than 500 nm, with an onion-like structure
Multivesicular vesicles, always greater than 1 micron
Giant unilamellar vesicles, greater than 1 micron
questions.explanation: Liposomes are classified by size and lamellarity: SUV up to 100 nm, LUV over 100 nm, MLV over 500 nm with an onion-like structure of multiple bilayers, MVV of variable size, and GUV over 1 micron.
questions.title: Colloids & Surfactants

questions.q: Which is a stated advantage of liposomal drug formulations?
options: They eliminate the need for any excipients
They protect the body from the drug and the drug from the body, increase circulation time and allow controlled release
They convert insoluble drugs into water-soluble salts
They guarantee oral bioavailability of cytotoxic drugs
They are more chemically stable than the free drug in all conditions
questions.explanation: Liposomes encapsulate water-soluble drugs, deliver large charged or cytotoxic molecules, protect the body from the drug and the drug from degradation, increase circulation time and bioavailability, give controlled release, and can be surface-decorated with targeting ligands.
questions.title: Colloids & Surfactants

questions.q: Where would a polar, water-soluble solute be carried in a liposome?
options: In the hydrophobic core of the bilayer
At the boundary between the hydrophobic and hydrophilic regions
In the aqueous core, and between bilayers if more than one is present
Adsorbed on the outer surface only
Covalently attached to the head groups
questions.explanation: Polar water-soluble solutes sit in the aqueous core and between bilayers if more than one is present. Non-polar solutes go into the hydrophobic core of the bilayer and semi-polar solutes at the boundary between the two regions.
questions.title: Colloids & Surfactants

questions.q: Who invented or discovered the liposome?
options: Marie Curie
Frederick Sanger
Linus Pauling
Alec Bangham
Richard Feynman
questions.explanation: Alec Bangham described the liposome in 1961. Related association structures include ethosomes, invasomes and niosomes.
questions.title: Colloids & Surfactants

questions.q: The van der Waals type forces behind inter-particle attraction, based on electronic polarisation, are known as which dispersion forces?
options: Hamaker
Traube
Laplace
London
Boltzmann
questions.explanation: These are London dispersion forces. Hamaker gives his name to the constant used in DLVO calculations of van der Waals attraction, but the forces themselves are London dispersion forces.
questions.title: Colloids & Surfactants

questions.q: A niosome differs from a conventional liposome in which way?
options: It is made with a synthetic surfactant rather than a phospholipid
It contains no aqueous compartment
It is always multilamellar
It is smaller than 5 nm
It carries a permanent positive charge
questions.explanation: A niosome is a vesicle made with a synthetic surfactant rather than a phospholipid, invented by L'Oreal. EstroGel, an oestradiol niosome for transdermal hormone therapy, is the example given.
questions.title: Colloids & Surfactants

questions.q: Why is the Marangoni effect described as weak but quick to repair?
options: It relies on covalent cross-links that reform rapidly
It is a small-molecule surfactant mechanism, unlike interactive polymers which are strong and elastic but very slow to repair
It depends on temperature gradients that dissipate instantly
It only operates above the critical micelle concentration
It requires solid nanoparticles that resettle quickly
questions.explanation: Three adsorbed layer behaviours are contrasted: Marangoni (weak but quick to repair), interactive polymer (very strong and elastic but very slow to repair), and interactive small emulsifier plus polymer (strong and quick to repair), the last being widely used in pharmacy.
questions.title: Colloids & Surfactants

questions.q: Which surfactant examples are listed under surfactants with adsorption, charge and steric effects?
options: Polysorbates (Tweens), benzalkonium chloride, SDS/SLS and poloxamers
Only sodium chloride and glucose
Only phospholipids from cell membranes
Only mineral oil and paraffin wax
Only cross-linked polyethylene
questions.explanation: The slide lists polysorbates (20-85) aka Tweens, benzalkonium chloride, SDS/SLS, and polymer surfactants poloxamers as wetting agents.
questions.title: Colloids & Surfactants

questions.q: What phenomena illustrate the power of surface tension in the lecture images?
options: Surface elasticity and beading
Only gravitational sedimentation
Electrophoretic mobility only
Micelle core solubilisation
Glass transition temperature
questions.explanation: The power of surface tension slide is illustrated with images showing surface elasticity and beading behaviour.
questions.title: Colloids & Surfactants

questions.q: Why do molecules at an air-water interface experience a net pull into the liquid body?
options: They are subject to fewer attraction forces at the surface
They have higher kinetic energy than bulk molecules
They are always ionised surfactants
They repel all neighbouring water molecules
They are bound only by covalent bonds
questions.explanation: Molecules at the surface are subject to fewer attraction forces, with a net pull into the body of the liquid, measured as gamma or surface free energy.
questions.title: Colloids & Surfactants

questions.q: In the spreading monolayer demonstration, what is the surface tension of very pure water?
options: 72 mN/m
20 mN/m
10 mN/m
485 mN/m
0 mN/m
questions.explanation: Micron-sized carbon beads float on very pure water with gamma = 72 mN/m until a spreading monolayer of surfactant is added.
questions.title: Colloids & Surfactants

questions.q: How many interface environments are used when measuring surface or interfacial tension (excluding S/S and G/G)?
options: Four environments
Two environments only
Six environments
One environment
Eight environments
questions.explanation: Surface or interfacial tension is measured at four environments, excluding solid-solid and gas-gas combinations.
questions.title: Colloids & Surfactants

questions.q: How does solute concentration affect surface tension of aqueous solutions according to the solute slide?
options: Three types of behaviour are observed depending on nature and concentration
All solutes always increase surface tension
Surface tension is independent of solute
Only ionic strength matters, not solute type
Only temperature changes surface tension
questions.explanation: Surface tension of a solution in water varies with the nature and concentration of the solute, with three types of behaviour shown.
questions.title: Colloids & Surfactants

questions.q: How do wetting agent molecules on the surface reduce interfacial tension?
options: They disrupt binding between water molecules at the surface
They increase hydrogen bonding in the bulk only
They remove all surfactant from solution
They increase the density of water
They polymerise into cross-linked gels
questions.explanation: Presence of wetting agent molecules on the surface disrupts binding between water molecules, resulting in a reduction in surface tension.
questions.title: Colloids & Surfactants

questions.q: What defines surfactants as distinct from simple co-surfactant amphiphiles?
options: An ionised charged head or a large polar polymeric head group
Absence of any hydrocarbon chain
Being insoluble in all solvents
Having only non-polar regions with no polar head
Being identical to simple salts
questions.explanation: Surfactants have an ionised charged head group or a large polar non-charged polymeric head, plus a hydrocarbon chain, unlike simple IWAs.
questions.title: Colloids & Surfactants

questions.q: What surface tension values are given for pure water and simple surfactants at 20 degrees C (G/L and L/water)?
options: Pure water 72.8; simple surfactants 20 and 10 mN/m
Pure water 20; simple surfactants 72.8 mN/m
Both are 72.8 mN/m
Pure water 485; simple surfactants 18.4 mN/m
Pure water 10; polymer surfactants 72.8 mN/m
questions.explanation: At 20 C, pure water is 72.8 mN/m and simple surfactants give about 20 (G/L) and 10 (L/water). Polymer surfactants are about 55.
questions.title: Colloids & Surfactants

questions.q: Which compounds are named as common wetting agents?
options: Tyloxapol, polysorbate 20/80 (Tween) and hyaluronate/hyaluronic acid
Only sodium dodecyl sulfate
Only cholesterol and ergosterol
Only calcium carbonate
Only polystyrene beads
questions.explanation: Common wetting agents listed are tyloxapol, polysorbate 20/80 (Tween), and hyaluronate/hyaluronic acid at approximately percent concentrations.
questions.title: Colloids & Surfactants

questions.q: For an acid drug at pH above pKa, what happens when an anionic surfactant wets the particle?
options: The particle gains a negative surface charge
The particle becomes permanently cationic
The drug cannot disperse in water
Surfactant prevents all adsorption
The particle dissolves instantly as atomic ions
questions.explanation: At pH above pKa an acid drug has net negative surface charge, and when an anionic surfactant wets the macromolecule it gives the particle a negative surface charge.
questions.title: Colloids & Surfactants

questions.q: Where do colloidal particles sit in the scheme of dispersion complexity?
options: Between molecular solutions and coarse dispersions
Below simple molecular solutions only
Above coarse dispersions only
Outside any classification by particle size
Only in the gas phase
questions.explanation: Colloids occupy a place between solution (molecular dispersion) and dispersion/coarse dispersion based on complexity and extent of particle solvation.
questions.title: Colloids & Surfactants

questions.q: What is a suspension of nanoparticles called according to the colloidal suspensions slide?
options: A colloidal or fine suspension
A true molecular solution
A gas aerosol only
A bulk precipitate with no continuous phase
An emulsion of two immiscible gases
questions.explanation: A suspension of nanoparticles is called a colloidal or fine suspension, with examples including vaccines, protein suspensions and colloidal metals.
questions.title: Colloids & Surfactants

questions.q: Which topics are listed in the first colloids lecture key takeaways?
options: Surface tension, wetting agents, association structures, energetics and stability
Only DNA sequencing
Only tablet compression force
Only Young's modulus of steel
Only Fischer projections of sugars
questions.explanation: Key points include surface (interfacial) tension, wetting agents and surfactancy, association structures (colloids), energetics and stability, and stability diagrams.
questions.title: Colloids & Surfactants

questions.q: What does the example SAQ ask students to explain about amphiphiles?
options: Mechanism of surface coverage by small-molecule and polymer amphiphiles and effects when mixed
Synthesis of polyethylene from ethylene
Calculation of pKa from titration data
Assignment of R and S configuration
Mechanism of beta-lactamase inhibition
questions.explanation: The SAQ asks students to explain the mechanism behind coverage of a surface with the two main classes of amphiphile and what happens when they are mixed.
questions.title: Colloids & Surfactants

questions.q: How many metres is one nanometre according to the refresh slide?
questions.explanation: The refresh slide states that a nanometre (nm) is 1 x 10^-9 m and a micrometre is 1 x 10^-6 m.
questions.title: Colloids & Surfactants

questions.q: How is metastability described for coarse drug dispersions and suspensions?
options: Meta-stability like most coarse drug dispersions and suspensions
True thermodynamic stability at all times
Instantaneous phase separation with no recovery
Only applicable to molecular solutions
Identical to crystalline solid equilibrium
questions.explanation: The slide states that metastability applies like most coarse drug dispersions and suspensions in suspension and emulsion contexts.
questions.title: Colloids & Surfactants

questions.q: What are lyophilic colloid hydrocolloids described as doing with water?
options: Loving and binding copious amounts of water with solvation and a hydration sheath
Repelling all water and remaining completely dry
Forming only gas-phase aerosols
Precipitating instantly in all buffers
Existing only as crystalline metals
questions.explanation: Lyophilic colloids or hydrocolloids love and bind copious amounts of water through solvation and a hydration sheath, with examples including acacia gum and gelatin.
questions.title: Colloids & Surfactants

questions.q: What approximate size range is given for a simple micelle in nano-suspensions?
options: 2-5 nm
1-100 micrometres
1-2 mm
Greater than 1 cm
questions.explanation: Nano-suspensions include simple micelles at 2-5 nm, polymeric micelles, microemulsions at 5-50 nm, and vesicles or liposomes at 25-1000 nm.
questions.title: Colloids & Surfactants

questions.q: Which physical methods are listed for determining molecular weight, size and shape of colloids?
options: Light scattering, microscopy, ultracentrifuge and Coulter counter
Only pH electrode measurement
Only refractive index of bulk solvent
Only Karl Fischer water content
Only flame photometry of sodium
questions.explanation: Physical methods listed include light scattering, microscopy (SEM, AFM), ultracentrifuge, Coulter counter, and colligative properties to follow kinetics.
questions.title: Colloids & Surfactants

questions.q: What causes Tyndall scattering of light in colloidal systems?
options: Inhomogeneity in the medium
Complete homogeneity at molecular level
Absence of any particles
Only UV absorption by water
Gravitational settling alone
questions.explanation: Scattering of light is due to inhomogeneity (Tyndall). Photon correlation spectroscopy covers roughly 1 nm to 1 mm using Mie, Rayleigh and Fraunhofer theory.
questions.title: Colloids & Surfactants

questions.q: Compared with a pure liquid, how does a colloid scatter light in Raman spectroscopy context?
options: Colloid gives strong scatter versus weak scatter from pure liquid
Both scatter equally with no difference
Pure liquid scatters more strongly
Colloids do not interact with light
Only dust in air scatters, not colloids
questions.explanation: The Raman spectroscopy slide contrasts pure liquid (weak scatter) with colloid (strong scatter) and dust particles in air under a light beam.
questions.title: Colloids & Surfactants

questions.q: Which moiety has the higher diffusion coefficient D on the comparison slide?
options: Sorbitol molecule at 130 x 10^-11 m2 s^-1
Paracetamol solid nanoparticle at 0.3 x 10^-11 m2 s^-1
Both have identical D values
Large flocculated clusters move fastest
Diffusion coefficient is independent of size
questions.explanation: Big particles move slowly. Sorbitol molecule has D about 130 x 10^-11 m2 s^-1 versus paracetamol solid nanoparticle at about 0.3 x 10^-11 m2 s^-1.
questions.title: Colloids & Surfactants

questions.q: In Fick's First Law, what does a large surface area promote for drug dissolution?
options: Better drug dissolution
Complete insolubility of all drugs
Elimination of diffusion
Zero concentration gradient
Only endothermic melting
questions.explanation: Fick's First Law relates material flux to the diffusion coefficient, area and concentration gradient. Large surface areas promote better drug dissolution.
questions.title: Colloids & Surfactants

questions.q: Why can mixing with a suitable solvent give a negative delta G for dissolution despite positive delta H?
options: Positive delta S from increased disorder can make delta G negative
Entropy always decreases on mixing
Delta H is always negative for dissolution
Temperature has no role in delta G
Adsorption is always exothermic with no entropy term
questions.explanation: Dissolution is often endothermic (positive delta H), but mixing increases disorder giving positive delta S, which can produce negative delta G promoting dissolution.
questions.title: Colloids & Surfactants

questions.q: What is shown for a sol of solid silica nanoparticles?
options: Fine dispersion with possible flocculated clusters and strands
Only a true molecular solution
A gas-phase aerosol
A bulk metal ingot
A dry powder with no continuous phase
questions.explanation: The slide shows a sol (fine dispersion) of solid silica nanoparticles and flocculated clusters and strands of silica nanoparticles.
questions.title: Colloids & Surfactants

questions.q: What size comparison is used to convey how small a colloid is?
options: A nano-unit to a football is what a football is to the Earth
A colloid is larger than a football
Colloids are visible to the naked eye as grains
Micelles are always larger than liposomes
Colloids are bigger than coarse dispersions
questions.explanation: The slide states a nano-unit to a football (0.25 m) is what a football is to the Earth (1.3 x 10^6 m). Colloids are small enough to stay permanently suspended.
questions.title: Colloids & Surfactants

questions.q: In micelle formation above the CMC, where is the hydrophobic part located?
options: In the centre of the aggregate with hydrophilic part outside
On the exterior facing the bulk water only
Uniformly mixed with no internal structure
Only in the aqueous continuous phase as monomers
Bonded covalently into a cross-linked network
questions.explanation: Above the critical micelle concentration, molecules aggregate with the hydrophobic non-polar part in the centre and the hydrophilic part on the outside.
questions.title: Colloids & Surfactants

questions.q: What soft matter phases are shown in the lyotropic liquid crystal assembly diagram?
options: Temperature-water-surfactant concentration phases including bicontinuous or sponge phase
Only crystalline metal lattices
Only ideal gas behaviour
Only Newtonian oil flow curves
Only covalent polymer cross-linking
questions.explanation: The soft matter assembly slide shows lyotropic liquid crystal and soft matter phases varying with temperature and surfactant concentration, including a bicontinuous or sponge phase.
questions.title: Colloids & Surfactants

questions.q: A microemulsion is also described as which structure?
options: A swollen micelle with oil, primary emulsifier and adjunct co-surfactant
A dry powder blend only
A bulk precipitate of salt
A crystalline tablet core
A gas at standard temperature
questions.explanation: The micro-emulsion slide labels the structure as a swollen micelle with oil, primary emulsifier and adjunct emulsifier (co-surfactant), referencing Schulman (1959).
questions.title: Colloids & Surfactants

questions.q: Which lipid is given as an example of a zwitterionic cell membrane bilayer-forming lipid?
options: 1-palmitoyl-2-oleoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine (POPC)
Sodium dodecyl sulfate only
Cetyltrimethylammonium bromide
Polystyrene
Polyethylene glycol only
questions.explanation: POPC is the example zwitterionic cell membrane lipid. DOTMA is cationic and DOPG is anionic among the bilayer-forming lipids listed.
questions.title: Colloids & Surfactants

questions.q: Which therapeutic areas are named on the historical liposomal drug formulations slide?
options: Fungal infection, cancer, macular degeneration, PDT, meningitis, pain relief and myopia
Only veterinary vaccines
Only industrial lubricants
Only household detergents
Only semiconductor fabrication
questions.explanation: Historical celebrated liposomal formulations are grouped under indications including fungal infection, cancer, macular degeneration, PDT, cancer and meningitis, pain relief, myopia and cancer.
questions.title: Colloids & Surfactants

questions.q: Which topics are in the second colloids lecture key takeaways?
options: Micelles, microemulsions, liposomes, encapsulation and measurement of colloids
Only Henderson-Hasselbalch equation
Only cis and trans nomenclature
Only tablet friability testing
Only polymer tacticity
questions.explanation: Part 2 key points include micelles (normal and reverse), microemulsions, liposomes, encapsulation approaches, and measurement of colloids.
questions.title: Colloids & Surfactants

questions.q: The word polymer derives from the Greek polys and meros. What do these mean?
options: Many parts
Long chains
Strong bonds
Repeated shapes
Large molecules
questions.explanation: Polymer comes from the Greek polys meaning many and meros meaning parts. A polymer is many of the same monomer covalently joined together, as glucose units form starch.
questions.title: Polymers

questions.q: Why can polymers never exist in the gas state?
options: They decompose below their boiling point in all cases
They have huge molecular weights, for example around 100 kDa, so exist only as solids and liquids
They are always cross-linked
Their intermolecular forces are too weak to be overcome
They are always dissolved in a solvent
questions.explanation: Small molecules exist as liquid, solid and gas, but polymers have huge molecular weights, for example 100 kDa, and only exist as solids and liquids. Oligomers may reach the gas state.
questions.title: Polymers

questions.q: What is the first stage of polymer dissolution?
options: Disintegration into primary particles
Ionisation of the end groups
Swelling
Melting of the crystalline regions
Cross-linking of adjacent chains
questions.explanation: The first stage of polymer dissolution is swelling. It is a two-stage process: diffusion of solvent molecules into the polymer to give a swollen gel, then dissolution or dispersal of the polymer.
questions.title: Polymers

questions.q: How does the viscosity of a polymer suspension compare with a low molecular weight solution at the same concentration?
options: The polymer suspension has a higher viscosity
The polymer suspension has a lower viscosity
They have identical viscosities
The polymer suspension has zero viscosity until the gel point
The comparison depends only on temperature
questions.explanation: Polymer suspensions have higher viscosity than solutions of low molecular weight substances at the same concentration, because the coils are mobile and become entangled even at low concentration.
questions.title: Polymers

questions.q: A polymer composed of two or more different monomer types is called what?
options: A homopolymer
A copolymer or heteropolymer
An oligomer
A dendrimer
A monomer blend
questions.explanation: A homopolymer is composed of only one monomer type. Heteropolymers or copolymers contain two or more monomer types and may be random, alternating or block.
questions.title: Polymers

questions.q: How do cross-linked polymers differ from linear and branched ones?
options: Cross-linked polymers soften when heated and dissolve readily
Linear and branched polymers have high melting points and are insoluble
Cross-linked polymers have high melting points and are often insoluble, unlike thermoplastic linear and branched polymers
Cross-linked polymers cannot swell in any solvent
Cross-linked polymers always have lower molecular weights
questions.explanation: Linear and branched polymers are thermoplastic: they soften when heated and are usually soluble in solvents. Cross-linked polymers have high melting points and are often insoluble.
questions.title: Polymers

questions.q: Which of the following is a recognised shape of a polymer molecule?
options: Box
Car
Star
Staircase
Trench
questions.explanation: Polymer molecule shapes include linear, branched, ladder, cross-linked, star and dendrimer.
questions.title: Polymers

questions.q: Why is the dissolution profile of a drug embedded in a polymer more complex than for a small molecule?
options: The polymer chemically binds the drug irreversibly
Swollen and gel layers form next to the polymer, and the drug must diffuse through these as well as the diffusion layer
The polymer raises the saturation solubility of the drug
Polymers dissolve instantaneously, releasing all the drug at once
The polymer prevents any contact between drug and solvent
questions.explanation: A swollen layer and gel layer form next to the dissolving polymer. An embedded drug must diffuse through those layers as well as the diffusion layer to reach solution, which is the basis of controlled release.
questions.title: Polymers

questions.q: Rather than true solutions, what do polymers form when dispersed in a solvent?
options: Coarse suspensions
Emulsions
Colloidal dispersions
Saturated solutions
Eutectic mixtures
questions.explanation: Polymers do not form solutions but rather colloidal dispersions. Dispersibility depends on polymer-solvent interactions, cross-links or strong intramolecular interactions, molecular weight and temperature.
questions.title: Polymers

questions.q: What is the gel point?
options: The temperature at which a gel melts
The critical concentration below which gelling does not occur
The pH at which a polymer precipitates
The point at which all cross-links have formed
The shear stress needed to make a gel flow
questions.explanation: There is a critical concentration below which gelling does not occur, called the gel point. It is determined by HLB, polymer-solvent interactions, molecular weight and chain flexibility.
questions.title: Polymers

questions.q: How does a gel trap its solvent?
options: By chemical reaction between polymer and solvent
By three-dimensional interactions of the polymer chains that trap the solvent within them
By encapsulating solvent inside closed vesicles
By adsorbing solvent onto the polymer surface only
By reducing the vapour pressure of the solvent to zero
questions.explanation: Gels are highly concentrated polymer suspensions of very high viscosity, caused by three-dimensional interactions of the polymer chains which trap the solvent within them. A gel is a liquid-in-solid dispersion or network.
questions.title: Polymers

questions.q: What distinguishes a Type I (chemical) gel?
options: It is held together by irreversible covalent cross-links, swelling in solvent but not dissolving
It is held together by calcium ion junctions in an egg-box arrangement
It is formed by cooling below 30 degrees C and melts on warming
It forms only above the critical micelle concentration
It is stabilised solely by hydrogen bonding and is fully reversible
questions.explanation: Type I chemical gels are chemically cross-linked by irreversible covalent bonds. The polymer swells in solvent but does not dissolve and holds a firm shape; swelling decreases as the degree of cross-linking increases.
questions.title: Polymers

questions.q: Gelatin forms a gel below 30 degrees C and methylcellulose gels above 50 degrees C. What type of gelation is this?
options: Type I chemical gelation, irreversible
Type II physical gelation, usually reversible
Eutectic crystallisation
Covalent cross-linking
Depletion flocculation
questions.explanation: These are Type II physical gels, cross-linked by chain entanglements and intermolecular bonding such as electrostatic attraction, hydrogen bonding or hydrophobic interactions. They form on changing temperature, pH or adding salts and are usually reversible.
questions.title: Polymers

questions.q: Gelatin is derived from which natural material, and what structural change accompanies gelation on cooling?
options: Cellulose; random coil converts to a crystalline lattice
Collagen; random coil converts to a triple helix
Chitin; helix converts to a random coil
Starch; amylose converts to amylopectin
Alginate; egg-box junctions form with calcium
questions.explanation: Gelatin is a natural protein polymer derived from collagen. On cooling below 30 degrees C the water-soluble random coil structure converts to a triple helix, forming a colourless transparent gel.
questions.title: Polymers

questions.q: Sodium alginate gels in calcium chloride solution but not in sodium chloride solution. Why?
options: Calcium raises the pH sufficiently to precipitate the polymer
Divalent calcium ions form egg-box junction zones between chains
Sodium chloride dissolves the alginate chemically
Calcium chloride lowers the temperature of the solution
Calcium reacts covalently with the carboxyl groups
questions.explanation: Type II physical gels can be formed by adding salts. Divalent Ca2+ ions form ionic junction zones between alginate chains in the egg-box arrangement, precipitating the polymer while the solvent remains trapped.
questions.title: Polymers

questions.q: Poly(hydroxyethyl)methacrylate (HEMA) forms a gel that is insoluble in water but swells. Which application follows from this?
options: Use as an enteric coating that dissolves in the intestine
Use as an effervescent disintegrant
Use in soft contact lenses and in implants giving prolonged antibiotic release
Use as a tonicity adjuster in infusions
Use as an anti-foaming agent
questions.explanation: HEMA, an acrylic acid derivative, forms a gel that is insoluble in water but swells as water binds to the OH groups. Loaded with antibiotic it gives prolonged release, and it is also used to make contact lenses.
questions.title: Polymers

questions.q: Cellulose itself is insoluble. How is it made soluble?
options: By amidation, methylation or carboxymethylation
By raising the temperature above 100 degrees C
By cross-linking with calcium ions
By reducing its molecular weight below 1 kDa
By dissolving it in ethanol
questions.explanation: Cellulose is insoluble but can be made soluble by amidation, methylation or carboxymethylation, giving derivatives such as methylcellulose and hydroxypropylmethylcellulose.
questions.title: Polymers

questions.q: Hypromellose (HPMC) is used in eye drops for which purpose?
options: To sterilise the preparation
To adjust the tonicity of the drops
To prolong the action of medicated drops, or to act alone as an artificial tear fluid
To lower the pH to match the tear film
To act as a preservative
questions.explanation: HPMC or hypromellose is a highly viscous mixture of cellulose derivatives used in eye drops to prolong the action of medicated drops, or alone as an artificial tear fluid.
questions.title: Polymers

questions.q: Which natural gum contains amine groups and can become positively charged, and is used to make granules or microparticles?
options: Acacia (gum arabic)
Tragacanth
Xanthan
Chitosan
Pectin
questions.explanation: Chitosan is a polysaccharide with amine groups that can become positively charged, used in making granules or microparticles. Acacia contains COOH groups and is used as an emulsifier; tragacanth is a suspending or thickening agent.
questions.title: Polymers

questions.q: Which polymer is often sold as Carbomer or Carbopol and forms highly viscous suspensions?
options: Polyvinylpyrrolidone
Polyethylene glycol
Acrylic acid polymer
Methylcellulose
Gelatin
questions.explanation: Acrylic acid polymers are often called Carbomer or Carbopol. They form highly viscous suspensions and are used as eye lubricants, tablet binders, in slow-release tablets, as suspending agents and, as derivatives, in enteric coating.
questions.title: Polymers

questions.q: Which polymer, when attached to hydrophobic chains, forms non-ionic surfactants such as cetomacrogol and the Tweens?
options: Polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP)
Polyethylene glycol (PEG or macrogol)
Chitosan
Poly(acrylic acid)
Hydroxypropylmethylcellulose
questions.explanation: PEGs or macrogols are hydrophilic polymers that can be attached to hydrophobic chains to form non-ionic surfactants such as cetomacrogol and the Tweens, used as emulsifying and wetting agents, and also in tablet binding, film coatings and lubricants.
questions.title: Polymers

questions.q: Which hydrophilic polymer is used as a thickening agent for spreadable pharmaceutical gels?
options: Poly(butylene terephthalate) (PBT)
Poly(epsilon-caprolactone) (PCL)
Poly(dimethylsiloxane) (PDS)
Poly(methyl methacrylate) (PMMA)
Poly(tetrafluoroethylene) (PTFE)
questions.explanation: Of these, poly(methyl methacrylate) is the acrylic polymer related to the Carbomer and methacrylate family used in pharmaceutical gels and coatings; the others are hydrophobic engineering or device polymers.
questions.title: Polymers

questions.q: How is viscosity defined?
options: The frictional resistance of the medium to flow, arising from internal friction of its particles
The force required to break a solid material
The energy needed to increase surface area by one square metre
The ratio of stress to strain in an elastic solid
The rate at which a liquid evaporates
questions.explanation: Viscosity is the frictional resistance of the medium to flow, a result of the internal friction of the material's particles. Rheology of a colloidal preparation depends on medium viscosity, particle concentration, size and shape, and particle interactions.
questions.title: Polymers

questions.q: What are the units of dynamic viscosity, and how is kinematic viscosity obtained from it?
options: Pa.s; kinematic viscosity = dynamic viscosity x density
Pa.s; kinematic viscosity = dynamic viscosity / density
N/m2; kinematic viscosity = dynamic viscosity x area
m2/s; kinematic viscosity = dynamic viscosity / temperature
J/s; kinematic viscosity = dynamic viscosity x volume
questions.explanation: Dynamic (absolute) viscosity has units Pa.s, equivalent to kg/m.s or Ns/m2, with 1 cP = 1 mPa.s. Kinematic viscosity, in m2/s, is dynamic viscosity divided by density.
questions.title: Polymers

questions.q: Glycerol viscosity falls from 12,070 mPas at 0 degrees C to 102 mPas at 60 degrees C. What explains this?
options: The glycerol becomes non-Newtonian at higher temperature
Higher temperatures weaken intermolecular forces, reducing viscosity
Glycerol evaporates progressively as temperature rises
The density of glycerol increases with temperature
Shear thinning occurs as the sample is heated
questions.explanation: Higher temperatures reduce viscosity by weakening intermolecular forces. Glycerol shows Newtonian behaviour throughout, so the change is purely a temperature effect.
questions.title: Polymers

questions.q: Why are polymer solutions pseudoplastic (shear thinning)?
options: Because the polymer degrades under shear
Because increasing shear stress makes coils uncoil and become streamlined, stopping rotation and releasing trapped solvent
Because shear raises the temperature of the sample
Because shear breaks the covalent cross-links permanently
Because the polymer precipitates out of solution under shear
questions.explanation: A polymer coil drags a solvation sheath with it and rotates as it crosses a velocity gradient, giving high flow resistance. Increasing shear stress makes the coils uncoil, become more streamlined and stop rotating, releasing trapped solvent and reducing viscosity.
questions.title: Polymers

questions.q: Which flow type shows an increase in viscosity as shear rate increases, and is typical of pastes?
options: Newtonian
Pseudoplastic
Plastic (Bingham)
Dilatant (shear thickening)
Thixotropic
questions.explanation: Shear thickening or dilatant behaviour is typical in pastes, showing an increase in viscosity on mixing. Shear thinning, in which viscosity falls with increasing shear, is the more common behaviour in pharmaceutical products.
questions.title: Polymers

questions.q: What characterises plastic, also called Bingham or Casson, flow?
options: Flow begins only when shear stress exceeds the yield point of the network
Viscosity is constant at all shear rates
Viscosity increases with time at constant shear
The material recovers its structure instantly after shearing
Flow occurs only above 50 degrees C
questions.explanation: Plastic (Bingham or Casson) systems have yielding structures and flow only when the shear stress exceeds the break or yield point of the network. Most pharmaceutical materials follow plastic flow.
questions.title: Polymers

questions.q: Which behaviour describes a sample that thins with time at constant shear as its structure breaks down?
options: Rheopexy
Dilatancy
Thixotropy
Newtonian flow
Rheodestruction
questions.explanation: Thixotropy is time-dependent thinning as the structure is broken down, typified by chain entanglements and showing rheological hysteresis. Rheopexy is thickening with time; rheodestruction means linkages are permanently broken.
questions.title: Polymers

questions.q: Why are oscillatory (creep) measurements preferred for viscoelastic semi-solids?
options: They are faster than continuous shear measurements
Continuous shear is destructive whereas oscillatory measurements are non-destructive and more revealing
They require no temperature control
They work only for Newtonian liquids
They avoid the need for a viscometer
questions.explanation: Continuous shear is destructive, whereas oscillatory or creep measurements are non-destructive and can be much more revealing, which matters because many samples such as creams, emulsifiers and gelling agents show both viscous and elastic properties.
questions.title: Polymers

questions.q: In oscillatory rheometry, what do G' and G'' represent?
options: G' is the storage modulus measuring elasticity; G'' is the loss modulus measuring viscosity
G' is the loss modulus measuring viscosity; G'' is the storage modulus measuring elasticity
G' is the yield stress; G'' is the shear rate
G' is Young's modulus; G'' is the tensile strength
Both measure elasticity, at different frequencies
questions.explanation: G' is the storage modulus, a measure of elasticity, seen when input and output are in phase. G'' is the loss modulus, a measure of viscosity, seen when they are out of phase.
questions.title: Polymers

questions.q: Solid polymers characteristically show which thermal transition?
options: A sharp melting point peak (Tm) with a well-defined enthalpy
A glass transition temperature (Tg) relating to chain movement
A boiling point that can be measured directly
A eutectic point with the solvent
No thermal transition of any kind
questions.explanation: Polymers frequently do not form crystals but do form solids. Instead of a clearly defined enthalpy and melting point peak they show a glass transition temperature, Tg, which relates to chain movement. Tm is usually higher than Tg.
questions.title: Polymers

questions.q: How does tacticity affect the melting point of a polymer?
options: Atactic gives the lowest Tm, isotactic the higher
Atactic gives the highest Tm, isotactic the lowest
Tacticity has no effect on Tm
Syndiotactic always gives the highest Tm
Tacticity affects only the glass transition, not Tm
questions.explanation: Tacticity, the pattern of substitution along the chain, affects melting point: atactic gives the lowest Tm, syndiotactic a low Tm and isotactic a higher Tm.
questions.title: Polymers

questions.q: Why does amorphous or glassy polymer such as garden furniture become brittle with age?
options: The polymer chains break by hydrolysis
Crystallites form, making the material increasingly less plastic and more brittle
The glass transition temperature falls below room temperature
The material absorbs water and swells
Cross-links are progressively broken by sunlight
questions.explanation: Amorphous or glassy polymer materials tend to age. As crystallites such as spherulites form, the material becomes increasingly less plastic and more brittle.
questions.title: Polymers

questions.q: Young's modulus of elasticity is defined as which ratio?
options: Shear stress divided by shear rate
Stress (force/area) divided by strain (change in length/length)
Strain divided by stress
Force divided by length
Storage modulus divided by loss modulus
questions.explanation: Young's modulus of elasticity E is stress divided by strain, where stress is force per unit area and strain is the change in length divided by the original length. It is the gradient of the stress-strain plot.
questions.title: Polymers

questions.q: Comparing Young's moduli, which ranking is correct?
options: Rubber 0.1 GPa, polyethylene 0.5 GPa, aluminium 70 GPa, steel 210 GPa
Steel 0.1 GPa, rubber 70 GPa, glass 210 GPa, graphene 0.5 GPa
Polyethylene 210 GPa, aluminium 0.5 GPa, rubber 90 GPa, steel 70 GPa
Rubber 70 GPa, aluminium 0.1 GPa, steel 4 GPa, graphene 0.5 GPa
All polymers exceed 100 GPa while metals are below 10 GPa
