questions.explanation: Young's modulus rises from hydrogels (a few kPa) through rubber at 0.1 GPa, polyethylene 0.5, polypropylene 1.5, cardboard 4, aluminium 70, soda glass about 90, steel 210 and graphene above 1000 GPa.
questions.title: Polymers

questions.q: Human cornea has a Young's modulus of about 0.0012 GPa and adult skin about 0.095 GPa. What does this tell you about a PVP/HPMC transdermal patch at 0.009 to 0.028 GPa?
options: It is far more rigid than skin and would not conform to it
It is more compliant than adult skin, sitting between cornea and skin in stiffness
It has the same rigidity as polyproline surgical suture
It is stiffer than human cartilage
Its modulus is too high to be measured by this method
questions.explanation: The patch modulus of 0.009 to 0.028 GPa sits between the cornea at 0.0012 and adult skin at 0.095 GPa, so it is more compliant than skin. Cartilage is 0.95 GPa and steel 210 GPa for comparison.
questions.title: Polymers

questions.q: Which mechanical parameters are listed as the main ones for polymers used in medicine?
options: Young's modulus of elasticity, tensile strength, break or yield force, and elongation
Viscosity, density, refractive index and melting point
Storage modulus, loss modulus, gel point and CMC
Hardness, colour, opacity and porosity
Molecular weight, tacticity, polydispersity and crystallinity
questions.explanation: The main mechanical parameters are Young's modulus of elasticity (rigidity), tensile strength, break or yield force, and elongation.
questions.title: Polymers

questions.q: Which use of polymers in pharmacy is correctly matched?
options: Rubbers are used for bottles and devices, but are brittle
Glass, a silicate polymer, is used for tubing and textiles and is highly deformable
Polyolefins such as polythene are used for tubing, bottles, bags and textiles, are flexible, but are not recycled
Polyolefins are used for septa and catheters and are poorly recycled
Rubbers are used for blister packs and are tough but brittle
questions.explanation: Polyolefins such as polythene are used for tubing, bottles, bags and textiles, are flexible, and their drawback is that they are not recycled. Rubbers are used for septa, catheters and dressings and are poorly recycled; glass is tough but brittle.
questions.title: Polymers

questions.q: Which is listed as a use of polymers in pharmacy?
options: Reducing the molecular weight of the drug
Sterilising the finished dosage form
Adhering to bio-surfaces as mucoadhesives and controlling release kinetics
Increasing the crystal lattice energy of the drug
Removing the need for a diffusion layer during dissolution
questions.explanation: Polymers solubilise and protect drugs, increase suspension viscosity, adhere to bio-surfaces as mucoadhesives, improve physicochemical stability, form films, patches and depots, control release kinetics, target specific sites, and can be drugs themselves such as insulin.
questions.title: Polymers

questions.q: Which pharmacy uses are listed for polymers in drug delivery and formulation?
options: Tablets, coatings, capsules, gels, suspensions, creams, wound dressings and skin patches
Only gas-phase aerosols
Only metal surgical instruments
Only glass primary packaging
Only volatile anaesthetic gases
questions.explanation: Polymers in pharmacy include tablets, coatings, capsules, gels, suspensions, creams/ointments, wound dressings and skin patches, plus devices and packaging.

questions.q: How is polymer nomenclature defined in the lecture?

Polymer name = monomer name minus 'ene'
Polymers are always named by molecular weight only
Only trade names such as Teflon may be used
Polymers have no systematic names
questions.explanation: Nomenclature is polymer name = poly(monomer name), with examples methylmethacrylate to poly(methylmethacrylate) and ethylene to polyethylene.

The density of the solvent only
The glass transition temperature

The critical micelle concentration
questions.explanation: Ethylene glycol monomer gives polyethylene glycol polymer, with degree of polymerisation defined as the number of repeat units between end-groups.

questions.q: How do solid polymers differ mechanically from small molecules according to the lecture?
options: Solid polymers show elasticity and reversible deformation
Polymers cannot deform under any stress
Small molecules always show necking in tension
Polymers are always brittle ceramics
Only metals exhibit elasticity
questions.explanation: Mechanical properties differ because solid polymers show elasticity and reversible deformation, as covered further in rheology of solids.

Only the study of gases at high pressure
Only crystal lattice energy
Only enzyme kinetics
Only microbial growth curves
questions.explanation: Rheology is the science of deformation, spanning viscosity of liquids and semi-solids, plasticity/elasticity of solids, and compressibility, rigidity and hardness.

questions.q: In Newton's viscosity theory, what is stress tau equal to?
options: F/A, which equals viscosity times velocity gradient
Mass times acceleration only
Pressure times volume
Density divided by temperature
pH plus pKa
questions.explanation: Stress tau = F/A = eta times velocity gradient, where velocity gradient or rate of shear is du/dy. Alternatively stress/strain = eta.

questions.q: When is Newtonian viscosity most likely according to the lecture?

Highly asymmetric flocculated suspensions only
All commercial pharmaceutical creams
Cross-linked polymer gels only
Thixotropic synovial fluid only
questions.explanation: Newtonian viscosity is the simplest system, relatively rare in complex commercial samples, occurring where particles are sparse, spheroidal or highly regular.
